Initially created: 2025-12-06T12:09:34.461+09:00 by chris Translate the following text from Classical Chinese into English.
Requirements: 1. The text contains page numbers in square brackets, such as [01], [02], etc. - These must be passed through unchanged. - Each page number must appear in exactly the same position in the translation as in the source. - The number of page markers in the output must match the input exactly.
2. Personal names, place names, titles, and other proper nouns should be rendered in Hànyǔ Pīnyīn with tone marks.
3. Do NOT transcribe the full Classical Chinese text into Pinyin.
4. Do NOT include explanatory notes, annotations, or commentary — output only the English translation.
5. The target language is English.

p.seg: Sīmǎ Guāng
compiled by imperial decree.
Later Study Heaven Platform
Song Jì yī
Beginning in shàngzhāng tūntān (gēngshēn),
ending in zhāoyáng dàyuānxiàn (guǐhài),
a total of four years.
The Liú clan resided in Péngchéng for generations.
Péngchéng, during the Spring and Autumn period, was Sòng territory.
Therefore, when the emperor first established his state, he named it Sòng.
Gāozǔ Wǔhuángdì
whose taboo name was Yù,
courtesy name Déyú,
and childhood name Jìnú,
was of the Liú clan,
a native of Suídé Lǐ, Péngchéng County.
He was the twenty-first generation descendant of Hàn Chǔyuánwáng Jiāo.
Péngchéng,
the capital of Chǔ,
was where his descendants made their home.
When the Jìn clan moved east,
the Liú clan relocated to Jīngkǒu Lǐ, Dāntú, Jìnlíng.
Yǒngchū Yuánnián (gēngshēn, 420 CE)
In the sixth month of this year, the era name was changed.
1 Spring,
First month,
jǐhài,
The Wèi ruler returned to his palace.
When Jìn held the empire,
the Zīzhì Tōngjiàn always referred to the Wèi ruler by combining his title and name;
this year,
Sòng received the abdication,
and from then on, the practice of writing according to the example of various states began.
2 Qín Wáng Chìpán established his son Qífú
Mùmò as Crown Prince,
who concurrently held the titles of Fǔjūn Dàjiàngjūn and Dūdū Zhōngwài Zhūjūnshì.
A general amnesty was declared,
and the era name was changed to Jiànhóng.
3 The Sòng King wished to receive the abdication but found it difficult to speak.
So he gathered his court officials for a banquet.
These were officials of the Sòng court.
Cháo (朝),
read as zhí yáo.
“Huán Xuán usurped the throne,
and the imperial mandate had already shifted.
I first proclaimed the great cause,
restored the imperial house,
campaigned in the south and fought in the north,
and brought peace to the four seas.
Having achieved success and established my enterprise,
I was granted the Nine Bestowals.
This year I am nearing old age;
having reached such an extreme of honor,
things are averse to being full and prosperous,
and it cannot last long in peace.
I now wish to return my爵位 (rank and position),
and retire to the capital.”
The officials only highly praised his achievements and virtues,
not understanding his intention.
Late in the day,
the gathering dispersed.
Zhōngshū Lìng Fù Liàng returned outside,
then realized,
but the palace gates were already closed.
Liàng knocked on the door and requested an audience.
The King immediately opened the door and met him.
Liàng entered,
and merely said,
“Your servant should temporarily return to the capital.”
The King understood his meaning,
and said nothing further,
only stating,
“How many people do you need to send you off?”
Liàng replied,
“A few dozen will suffice.”
He then took his leave immediately.
When Liàng emerged,
it was already night.
Seeing a long star spanning the sky,
he slapped his thigh and sighed,
“I never believed in astronomy,
but now it is proven.”
A long star removes the old and brings forth the new,
hence he said so.
Summer,
Fourth month,
the King was summoned to assist.
The King left his son Yìkāng as Dūdū Yù, Sī, Yōng, Bìng Sì Zhōu Zhūjūnshì and Yùzhōu Cìshǐ,
stationed at Shòuyáng.
Yùzhōu,
was governed at Qiáo during the Later Hàn;
at Rǔnán Ānchéng during Wèi;
after Jìn pacified Wú, it was governed at Chénguó;
south of the Yangtze, it was governed at Shòuyáng, Wúhú, Zhūchéng, Niúzhǔ, Lìyáng, Mǎtóu, Shòuchūn, Gūshú,
not always staying in one place.
At the end of Āndì’s reign,
the Emperor wished to expand into Hénán
and pacify the territory of Yù.
He carved out the area west of the Great River and north of Dàléi from Yángzhōu
and assigned it all to Yùzhōu.
The foundation of Yùzhōu
was thus established.
After the Emperor pacified Guān and Luò,
he appointed Sīzhōu Cìshǐ,
governed at Hǔláo,
and administered the three actual commanderies of Hénán, Xíngyáng, and Hóngnóng,
and the two relocated commanderies of Hénèi and Dōngjīngzhào.
Yōngzhōu remained temporarily governed at Xiāngyáng.
The Qín and Bìngzhōu Cìshǐ were stationed at Púbǎn.
Since Máo Dézǔ had retreated from Púbǎn to Hǔláo,
Bìngzhōu must have been temporarily governed at Hǔláo.
Yōng (雍),
read as yú yòng.
He appointed Nányáng Liú Zhàn, who was an advisor to the Prime Minister, as Chángshǐ,
to decide matters of the fǔ and zhōu.
The fǔ and zhōu
refer to the Dūdū Fǔ and Yùzhōu.
He often compared himself to Guǎn Zhòng and Zhūgě Liàng,
meaning Guǎn Zhòng and Zhūgě Liàng.
He did not write essays
and did not enjoy discussions.
The King greatly esteemed him.
4 Fifth month,
yǐyǒu,
Wèi posthumously re-titled Xuānwǔdì as Dàowǔdì.
In the second year of Yǒngxīng, the Wèi ruler
posthumously named his father Guī as Xuānwǔ Huángdì.
Gēng (更),
read as gǔ héng.
5 Wèi Huáinán Gōng Sīmǎ Guófán and Chíyáng Zǐ Sīmǎ Dàocì conspired to rebel externally.
Sīmǎ Wénsī reported them.
gēngxū,
The Wèi ruler executed Guófán and Dàocì,
and bestowed upon Wénsī the title of Yùlín Gōng.
Guófán and others surrendered to Wèi, as mentioned in the previous volume, Jìn Āndì Yìxī Shísān Nián.
Fán (璠),
read as fú yuán.
Dozens of people of their clan were implicated and executed.
Fēng Xuánzhī, son of Zhāng’ān Hóu Fēng Yì, was supposed to be implicated.
The Wèi ruler, considering Xuánzhī to be from an old family of the Yān court—
Mùróng Kuì rose from Chānglí,
and the Fēng clan depended on him,
thus serving Yān for generations,
and becoming noble and prominent—
said,
“My younger brother Mónú was orphaned early;
I beg for his life to be spared.”
So, Xuánzhī’s four sons were executed, but Mónú was pardoned.
6 Sixth month,
rénxū,
The King arrived in Jiànkāng.
Fù Liàng hinted to Jìn Gōngdì to abdicate the throne to Sòng,
presented the draft of the imperial edict to the Emperor,
and bade him write it.
The Emperor joyfully picked up the brush,
and said to his attendants,
“During Huán Xuán’s time,
the Jìn clan had already lost the empire.
It was extended again by Lord Liú
for nearly twenty years.
Jìn Āndì Yuánxīng Sān Nián Yù campaigned against Huán Xuán,
up to this point, it was seventeen years in total.
Cāo (操),
read as qiān gāo.
Chóng (重),
read as zhí lóng.
Zài (載),
read as zǐ hài.
This was what I was willing to do all along.”
He then wrote the edict on red paper.
jiǎzǐ,
The Emperor ceded his throne at Lángyá Dì.
All officials bowed to bid farewell.
Mìshū Jiān Xú Guǎng wept profusely in sorrow.
Jìn Wǔdì received the abdication in Tàishǐ Yuánnián,
which was the year yǐyǒu;
in Jiànxīng Sì Nián,
Cháng’ān fell,
which was the year bǐngzǐ.
A total of fifty-two years.
The next year,
Yuándì established his reign east of the river,
changing the era name to Jiànwǔ.
Up to this year, gēngshēn,
it was a total of one hundred and three years.
The Western and Eastern Jìn together enjoyed the country for one hundred and fifty-seven years before their demise.
On the *dīngmǎo* day,
the King made a sacrifice at the southern suburb
and ascended the imperial throne.
After the ceremony,
he returned from Shítou to Jiànkāng Palace in the imperial carriage.
Xú Guǎng wept with sorrow and emotion.
The Attendant-in-ordinary Xiè Huì said to him,
"Is Master Xú perhaps a little out of line?"
Guǎng replied,
"You are a meritorious minister of the Sòng Dynasty,
while I am an old remnant of the Jìn house.
Our joys and sorrows
are naturally not to be shared."
Guǎng
was the younger brother of Miǎo.
Xú Miǎo was deeply cherished and esteemed by Emperor Xiàowǔ of Jìn.
The Emperor ascended the Tàijí Hall,
issued a general amnesty,
and changed the reign title.
Those who had incurred the criticism of local public opinion and pure discourse
were all cleared
and given a new start.
"Incurred the criticism of local public opinion and pure discourse"
means having offended against the teachings of the eminent.
*Gēng* (更),
pronounced *gōnghéng fān*.
Péi Zǐyě commented: In the past, when Chónghuá received the mandate,
the Four Fiends were banished.
The *Shū* says: Yáo made Shùn succeed to the throne.
On the first day of the first month,
he received the mandate in the Ancestral Temple.
Gònggōng was banished to Yōuzhōu,
Huāndōu was exiled to Chóngshān,
Sānmíáo was driven out to Sānwēi,
and Gǔn was executed at Yǔshān.
The four criminals were punished, and the world submitted.
*Chóng* (重),
pronounced *zhílóng fān*.
The stubborn people were moved to Luò.
When King Wǔ conquered Yīn,
he moved the stubborn people to Luòyì.
To abolish local public opinion and pure discourse
is
a mistake!
Emperor Gōng of Jìn was honored as the King of Línglíng;
the rites of preferential treatment
all imitated the precedents from the early Jìn,
and a palace was established in the former Mòlíng County.
Shěn Yuē said: Mòlíng County's original seat was sixty *lǐ* from the capital.
The present-day former village is it.
In the ninth year of Yìxī of Emperor Ān of Jìn,
its seat was moved to the capital,
to Dòuchǎng.
In the first year of Yuánxī of Emperor Gōng,
the security officer of Yángzhōu was abolished,
and the county seat was moved to that location.
Empress Chǔ was demoted to Queen.
His deceased father was posthumously honored as Emperor Xiàomù,
and his deceased mother, Lady Zhào, as Empress Xiàomù;
his mother, the Queen Dowager Xiāo, was honored as Empress Dowager.
The Emperor's father, Qiáo, married Lady Zhào,
who died after giving birth to the Emperor.
He then married Lady Xiāo as his second wife.
When the Emperor ascended the throne,
he was already advanced in years.
Every morning, he paid court to the Empress Dowager,
never missing the appointed time.
An edict declared that the Jìn clan's enfeoffments and ranks
should be altered with the change of dynasty,
but only the five dukes of Shǐxīng, Lúlíng, Shǐ'ān, Chángshā, and Kānglè were retained,
their ranks being demoted to County Duke or County Marquis.
Shǐxīng, Lúlíng, Shǐ'ān, and Chángshā were all Commandery Dukes,
while only Kānglè
was a County Duke.
According to the *Nán Shǐ*,
the Duke of Shǐxīng Commandery was demoted to Duke of Huáróng County,
the Duke of Lúlíng to Duke of Cháisāng County,
the Duke of Shǐ'ān to Marquis of Lìpǔ County,
and the Duke of Chángshā to Marquis of Lǐlíng County.
pronounced *luò*.
Those who had exerted their efforts in Yìxī and shared in the difficulties
all retained their original ranks.
On the *gēngwǔ* day,
Sīkōng Dàolián was appointed Grand Commandant
and enfeoffed as the King of Chángshā.
The deceased Sītú Dàoguī was posthumously enfeoffed as the King of Línchuān,
and Dàolián's son Yìqìng inherited his title.
The remaining meritorious officials, such as Xú Xiànzhī,
were all promoted in rank and title in varying degrees.
Liú Mùzhī was posthumously enfeoffed as Duke of Nánkāng Commandery,
and Wáng Zhèn'è as Marquis of Lóngyáng County.
The Emperor often sighed and thought of Mùzhī,
saying,
"If Mùzhī had not died,
he would have helped me govern the world.
It can be said, 'When a man of worth perishes,
the state is ruined and afflicted!'"
This is a phrase from the *Shī* (Poetry) "Zhān Áng" (瞻卬).
*Cuì* (瘁),
pronounced *qínzuì fān*.
"With Mùzhī's death,
people take me lightly."
His imperial son, Duke of Guìyáng Yìzhēn, was established as King of Lúlíng;
Duke of Péngchéng Yìlóng as King of Yídū;
and Yìkāng as King of Péngchéng.
On the *jǐmǎo* day,
the Tàishǐ calendar was changed to the Yǒngchū calendar.
The calendar was changed with the new reign.
8 The Wèi ruler went to Yìdú Mountain,
and then to Fēnglǔ Lake.
According to the *Běi Shǐ*,
Yìdú Mountain is west of Píngchéng
and east of Wǔyuán.
Fēnglǔ Lake is the salt lake of Wǔyuán,
which belonged to Yánzhōu in the Táng Dynasty.
pronounced *lóngwǔ fān*.
He summoned Cuī Hào by express courier and told him,
"Your words from last year have proven true."
Hào's words can be found in the previous volume, under the fourteenth year of Yìxī of Emperor Ān of Jìn.
9 In autumn,
the seventh month,
on the *dīngyǒu* day,
the Wèi ruler went to Wǔyuán.
10 On the *jiǎchén* day,
an edict appointed Liánggōng Xīn as the Grand Administrator of military affairs of Gāochāng and other seven commanderies, Grand General of the Expedition to the West, and Duke of Jiǔquán;
and King Chìpán of Qín as Grand General Pacifying the West.
11 The Governor of Jiāozhōu, Dù Huìdù, attacked Línyì,
and severely defeated them.
Línyì had repeatedly made incursions,
which is why Huìdù attacked them.
Línyì pleaded for surrender,
and all those who had been plundered in previous raids were sent back.
Huìdù governed Jiāozhōu with meticulous attention,
just like managing a household.
Officials and common people feared and loved him;
city gates were open at night,
and things were not picked up from the roads.
12 On the *jǐ*
*wèi* day,
the Wèi ruler went to Yúnzhōng.
13 The King of Héxī, Méngxùn, intended to attack Liáng,
and first led his troops to attack Qínhàowěi;
upon arrival, he secretly withdrew his troops and encamped at Chuānyán.
Liánggōng Xīn wanted to take advantage of the emptiness
to raid Zhāngyè;
Sòng Yáo and Zhāng Tǐshùn earnestly remonstrated,
but he would not listen.
The Empress Dowager Yǐn said to Xīn,
"Your newly established state
has a small territory and sparse population.
Even defending yourself, you fear it's not enough,
so how can you have time to attack others?
Your late father, before his death,
(Lǐ Gǎo's death is found in the previous volume, under the thirteenth year of Yìxī of Emperor Ān of Jìn.)
was very cautious about using troops,
protecting the borders and pacifying the people,
to await the opportune moment.
His words are still in your ears,
how can you abandon them?
Méngxùn is skilled in warfare,
not your equal.
For several years now,
he has always had ambitions of annexation.
Though your state is small,
it is capable of good governance.
Cultivate virtue, nurture the people,
and wait quietly for him.
If he becomes tyrannical,
the people will turn to you;
if he is excellent and enlightened—
*xiū* (休)
means beautiful—
how can you lightly undertake actions
and hope for what is beyond your grasp?
In my opinion,
not only will you lose your army,
but you will likely destroy your state!"
He also did not listen.
Sòng Yáo sighed,
"This time,
the great enterprise is lost!"
Xīn (歆) led 30,000 cavalry and infantry eastward.
Méngxùn (蒙遜) heard of this and said:
"Xīn (歆) has already fallen into my trap;
however, hearing that I am turning back my army,
he will surely not dare to advance."
Thereupon, he openly announced in the western borders
that he had already captured Hàomín (浩亹)
and would advance to attack Huánggǔ (黃谷).
This open announcement was not necessarily posted on a lacquered pole,
as was the custom for announcing victories in Wèi (魏) and Jìn (晉);
it merely meant openly publishing the dispatch to state the matter.
Xīn (歆) was pleased,
and advanced into Dūdújiàn (都瀆澗).
Méngxùn (蒙遜) led his troops to attack him,
fighting at Huáichéng (懷城),
where Xīn (歆) suffered a great defeat.
Some advised Xīn (歆) to return and defend Jiǔquán (酒泉).
Xīn (歆) said:
"I disobeyed my old mother's words and suffered defeat;
if I do not kill this barbarian,
how can I face my mother again!"
So he rallied his troops and fought at Liáoquán (蓼泉),
where he was killed by Méngxùn (蒙遜).

Xīn's (歆) younger brothers Fān (翻), the Grand Administrator of Jiǔquán (酒泉); Yù (預), the Grand Administrator of Xīnchéng (新城); Mì (密), the Right Supervisor of the Yǔlín (羽林); Tiào (眺), the Left General; and Liàng (亮), the Right General, fled west to Dūnhuáng (敦煌).
Méngxùn (蒙遜) entered Jiǔquán (酒泉).
In the 4th year of Lóng'ān (隆安) of Emperor Ān (安),
Lǐ Gǎo (李暠) had held Dūnhuáng (敦煌).
In all, two rulers
for twenty-one years before it was destroyed.
The gentry and common people settled down in peace.
Sòng Yáo (宋繇) was appointed Lìbù Lángzhōng (吏部郎中),
and entrusted with selecting officials;
those former officials of Liáng (涼) who had talent and reputation
were all respectfully employed.
His son Mùjiān (牧犍) was made Grand Administrator of Jiǔquán (酒泉).
Lǐ Xún (李恂), the Grand Administrator of Dūnhuáng (敦煌),
was Fān's (翻) younger brother.
He, along with Fān (翻) and others, abandoned Dūnhuáng (敦煌) and fled to Běishān (北山).
Méngxùn (蒙遜) appointed Yuánxù (元緒), the son of Suǒ Sì (索嗣), to act as Grand Administrator of Dūnhuáng (敦煌).
The account of Suǒ Sì's (索嗣) death is found in Volume 111, in the 4th year of Lóng'ān (隆安) of Emperor Ān (安) of Jìn (晉).
Suǒ (索),
formerly pronounced gè (各) fān (翻).
Méngxùn (蒙遜) returned to Gūzāng (姑臧)
and visited the Empress Dowager Yǐn (尹) of Liáng (涼), offering her condolences.
Empress Dowager Yǐn (尹) said:
"The Lǐ (李) family has been destroyed by barbarians,
what more can one say!"
Méngxùn (蒙遜) was a Lúshuǐ Hú (盧水胡) from Zhāngyè (張掖).
Láo (勞),
pronounced lì dào (力到) fān (翻).
Fù (復),
pronounced fú yòu (扶又) fān (翻);
below, it can be similarly pronounced.
"Now that the lives of mother and son are in the hands of others,
why are you so arrogant!
Moreover, your state is destroyed and your son is dead,
yet you show no sign of sorrow,
why is this?"
Empress Dowager Yǐn (尹) said:
"Survival, destruction, death, and life
are all determined by Heaven's will.
Why should I behave like common people,
grieving like women and children!
I am an old woman,
my state is destroyed and my family broken.
How can I cling to my remaining life
and become someone's concubine!
My only wish is a swift death."
Méngxùn (蒙遜) admired her and pardoned her,
and married her daughter to Mùjiān (牧犍).
14. In the eighth month,
on the day of Xīnwèi (辛未),
Zāng (臧) was posthumously honored as Empress Jìng (敬皇后).
On the day of Guǐyǒu (癸酉),
Yìfú (義符), the royal heir apparent, was established as Crown Prince.
15. In the intercalary month,
on the day of Rénwǔ (壬午),
an imperial edict mandated that all imperial tombs of the Jìn (晉) dynasty be guarded.
16. In the ninth month,
Wáng Jī (王基) and others, generals of Zhènwǔ (振武) of Qín (秦), raided Méngxùn's (蒙遜) Húyuán (胡園) outpost in Héxī (河西),
capturing over two thousand people before returning.
17. Lǐ Xún (李恂) had governed Dūnhuáng (敦煌) with benevolence;
Suǒ Yuánxù (索元緒) was crude, harsh, and fond of killing,
greatly losing the hearts of the people.
Sòng Chéng (宋承) and Zhāng Hóng (張弘), residents of the commandery, secretly invited Xún (恂).
In winter,
Xún (恂) led several tens of cavalry into Dūnhuáng (敦煌),
and Yuánxù (元緒) fled east to Liángxìng (涼興).
Liángxìng (涼興) Commandery was within the boundaries of Chánglè (常樂) County, Guāzhōu (瓜州), of the Táng (唐) dynasty.
Shuài (帥),
read as lǜ (率).
The era name was changed to Yǒngjiàn (永建).
Méngxùn (蒙遜), the King of Héxī (河西), sent his heir apparent Zhèngdé (政德) to attack Dūnhuáng (敦煌),
but Xún (恂) closed the city gates and did not fight.
18. In the twelfth month,
on the day of Dīnghài (丁亥),
Dí Wēnzǐ (狄溫子), the Qiāng (羌) chieftain of Xìngchéng (杏城), led over three thousand households to surrender to Wèi (魏).
They deserted Xià (夏) and surrendered to Wèi (魏).
Qiú (酋),
pronounced cí yóu (慈由) fān (翻).
Shuài (帥),
read as lǜ (率).
Jiàng (降),
pronounced hù jiāng (戶江) fān (翻).
19. In this year,
Lady Yáo (姚), consort of Wèi (魏), passed away.
She was posthumously honored as Empress Zhāo'āi (昭哀皇后).
The account of Lady Yáo's (姚) return to Wèi (魏) is found in Volume 117, in the 11th year of Yìxī (義熙) of Emperor Ān (安) of Jìn (晉).
2nd Year (Xīnyǒu (辛酉), 421 CE)
1. In spring,
the first month,
on the day of Xīnyǒu (辛酉),
the Emperor performed sacrifices in the southern suburbs,
and proclaimed a general amnesty.
Péi Zǐyě (裴子野) commented: "Sacrificing to Heaven and Earth is a performance of annual rites;
but granting amnesty to those who have committed crimes,
for what purpose is that!"
2. Yìzhēn (義真), the Prince of Lúlíng (廬陵) and Inspector of Yángzhōu (揚州), was appointed Sītú (司徒);
Xú Xiànzhī (徐羨之), the Shàngshū Púyè (尚書僕射), was appointed Shàngshū Lìng (尚書令) and Inspector of Yángzhōu (揚zhōu);
Fù Liàng (傅亮), the Zhōngshū Lìng (中書令), was appointed Shàngshū Púyè (尚書僕射).
3. On the day of Xīnwèi (辛未),
the ruler of Wèi (魏) departed on a journey to Gōngyáng (公陽).
4. Méngxùn (蒙遜), the King of Héxī (河西), led an army of 20,000 to attack Lǐ Xún (李恂) at Dūnhuáng (敦煌).
5. Chìpán (熾磐), the King of Qín (秦), sent Mù Yìgān (木弈干), General of Conquering the North, and Yuán Jī (元基), General of Aiding the State, to attack Shàngguī (上邽),
but they encountered continuous rain and returned.
6. In the third month,
on the day of Jiǎzǐ (甲子),
Xī (熙), the Prince of Yángpíng (陽平) of Wèi (魏), passed away.
7. The ruler of Wèi (魏) dispatched six thousand men from the capital, Dài (代), to construct an imperial park,
encompassing Báidēng (白登) to the east,
with a circumference of over thirty *lǐ*.
8. Méngxùn (蒙遜), the King of Héxī (河西), built a dike to block the water and flood Dūnhuáng (敦煌);
Lǐ Xún (李恂) begged to surrender,
but was refused.
Xún's (恂) generals, Sòng Chéng (宋承) and others, surrendered the city,
and Xún (恂) committed suicide.
Méngxùn (蒙遜) massacred the city,
captured Xún's (恂) younger brother Bǎo (寶),
and imprisoned him in Gūzāng (姑臧).
The Lǐ (李) family was thus destroyed.
Lǐ Bǎo (李寶) eventually laid the foundation for the Táng (唐) dynasty.
Who can overturn what Heaven initiates?
(They) presented themselves as subjects and offered tribute.
9. In summer,
the fourth month,
on the first day of Jǐmǎo (己卯),
an imperial edict stated:
"All illicit shrines from Jiǎng Zǐwén (蔣子文) downwards are to be abolished;
however, shrines established for former worthies and those with meritorious virtue
are not subject to this rule."
10. Āchái (阿柴), the King of Tǔyùhún (吐谷渾), sent an envoy to surrender to Qín (秦).
Chìpán (熾磐), the King of Qín (秦), appointed Āchái (阿柴) as Grand General of Conquering the West,
Kāifǔ Yítóng Sānsī (開府儀同三司), Governor of Ānzhōu (安州), and King of Báilán (白蘭).
Qín (秦) indeed established Ānzhōu (安州) in the territory of Tǔyùhún (吐谷渾).
11. In the sixth month,
on the day of Yǐyǒu (乙酉),
the ruler of Wèi (魏) journeyed north to Pányángshān (蟠羊山);
Pányángshān (蟠羊山) is east of Cānhépō (參合陂).
In the seventh month,
he journeyed west to the river.
12. Méngxùn (蒙遜), the King of Héxī (河西), sent Jǔqú Shànshàn (沮渠鄯善), Right Guard General, and Jǔqú Gǒushēng (沮渠苟生), Jiànjié General, to lead an army of seven thousand to attack Qín (秦).
Chìpán (熾磐), the King of Qín (秦), sent Mù Yìgān (木弈干), General of Conquering the North, and others, to lead five thousand cavalry and infantry to resist them.
They defeated Shànshàn (鄯善) and others at Wǔjiàn (五澗).
Wǔjiàn (五澗) is north of Hóngchílǐng (洪池嶺).
The Shuǐjīngzhù (水經註) states: Wǔjiànshǔi (五澗水) flows out from east of Gūzāng (姑臧) city and goes west,
flowing north into Mǎchénghé (馬城河).
Bài (敗),
pronounced bǔ mài (補邁) fān (翻).
They beheaded two thousand and returned.
13 Earlier,
the Emperor gave a jar of poisoned wine
to Zhāng Wěi (張偉), the former Administrator of Lángyá (琅邪),
and ordered him to poison the Prince of Línglíng (零陵).
Wěi (偉) sighed and said,
"To poison a lord in order to preserve one's own life
is worse than dying!"
So he drank it himself on the road and died.
Wěi (偉)
was the elder brother of Shào (卲).
Earlier,
when the Emperor governed Yángzhōu (揚州),
he invited Shào (卲) to be a subordinate official.
All of them were the Prince's elder brothers.
Whenever the Prince had a son,
the Emperor would immediately order Xiù (秀) and his brothers to conveniently kill him.
"Conveniently" means
to dispose of them as appropriate,
without making the matter public.
Deeply worried about disaster striking,
he shared a room with Chǔ (褚),
cooking his own food in front of the bed.
All the provisions for his food and drink
came from Chǔ (褚),
so the Sòng (宋) people could not find any vulnerability.
In the ninth month,
the Emperor ordered Dànzhī (淡之) to go with his elder brother, the General of the Right Guard, Shúdù (叔度), to see him.
He came out to meet them in a separate room.
Soldiers climbed over the wall and entered,
offering medicine to the Prince.
The Prince refused to drink it,
saying,
"Buddhism teaches
that those who commit suicide will not regain human form."
The soldiers covered him with a quilt and killed him.
The Emperor led his hundred officials to mourn at the imperial court for three days.
From this time onward,
few rulers who abdicated
managed to survive.
帥 (shuài)
is read as 率 (lǜ).
臨 (lín),
pronunciation lì zhèn fān (力鴆翻).
朝 (cháo),
pronunciation zhí yáo fān (直遙翻).
14 On *gēngxū* (庚戌),
the Wèi (魏) ruler returned to his palace.
15 In winter,
in the tenth month,
on *jǐhài* (己亥),
an imperial edict appointed Héxī Wáng (河西王) Méngxùn (蒙遜) as Grand General Guarding the Army, *Kāifǔ Yítóng Sānsī* (開府儀同三司), and Governor of Liángzhōu (涼州).
16 On *jǐhài* (己亥),
the Wèi (魏) ruler went to Dài (代).
17 In the eleventh month,
on *xīnhài* (辛亥),
Emperor Gōng (恭) of Jìn (晉) was buried at Chōngpínglíng (沖平陵).
The Emperor led his hundred officials to observe the farewell.
18 In the twelfth month,
on *bǐngshēn* (丙申),
the Wèi (魏) ruler made a western tour
and reached Yúnzhōng (雲中).
19 Qín Wáng (秦王) Chìpán (熾磐) dispatched the General Conquering the West, Kǒngzǐ (孔子), and others, leading twenty thousand cavalry to attack Qìhàn Tūzhēn (契汗禿真) at Luóchuān (羅川).
20 Táng Qì (唐契), the Administrator of Jìnchāng (晉昌) appointed by Héxī Wáng (河西王) Méngxùn (蒙遜), rebelled with his commandery.
Méngxùn (蒙遜) sent his heir apparent, Zhèngdé (政德), to suppress him.
Qì (契)
was the son of Yáo (瑤).
Táng Yáo (唐瑤) is mentioned in Volume 111, fourth year of Lóng'ān (隆安) during the reign of Emperor Ān (安) of Jìn (晉).
21 When the Emperor was Dà Sònggōng (大宋公),
Xiè Zhān (謝瞻) was *Zhōngshū Shìláng* (中書侍郎) of Sòng Tái (宋臺),
and his younger brother Huì (晦) was General of the Right Guard.
At that time, Huì (晦)'s power and influence were already considerable.
He returned to the capital from Péngchéng (彭城) to bring his family.
The Emperor, as Sònggōng (宋公),
established Sòng Tái (宋臺) in Péngchéng (彭chéng).
The gates and alleys were crowded.
Zhān (瞻) was alarmed at home and said to Huì (晦),
"Your rank and position are not yet high,
but people gather around you to such an extent!
Our family has always made tranquility and retirement its business,
not wishing to interfere in current affairs,
and our acquaintances are merely relatives and friends.
Yet you have shaken the court and the common people.
How can this be a blessing for our household!"
He then put up a fence to separate his courtyard, saying,
"I cannot bear to see this."
When he returned to Péngchéng (彭chéng),
he said to Sònggōng (宋公),
"Your servant was originally a humble scholar;
my father and grandfather's highest positions were no more than two thousand *shí* (石).
Zhān (瞻) and Huì (晦) were great-grandsons of Xiè Póu (謝裒), the Grand Minister of the Court of Jin,
and cousin-grandsons of Xiè Ān (謝安).
This means their great-grandparents and Xiè Ān (謝安) shared the same ancestor,
but their positions and fame were not as great.
My ambition and abilities are ordinary,
yet I wear the coronet of the Bureau,
and hold prominent and confidential positions.
When fortune exceeds its bounds, disaster will arise;
its manifestation will not be distant.
I especially beg for a demotion
to preserve my declining family."
He repeatedly made this plea.
Sometimes Huì (晦) would tell Zhān (瞻) secrets of the court,
but Zhān (瞻) would intentionally relate them to relatives and old friends,
treating them as jokes,
to cut off his words.
When the Emperor ascended the throne,
Huì (晦), due to his contributions to the founding of the dynasty,
held even greater positions and responsibilities.
Zhān (瞻) became increasingly worried and fearful.
That year,
Zhān (瞻) became Administrator of Yùzhāng (豫章),
fell ill, and did not seek treatment.
Before his death,
he left a letter to Huì (晦) saying,
"I am fortunate to have my body whole;
what regret can I have?
Brother, think of striving to encourage yourself,
for the country and for the family."
To contemplate danger while enjoying favor,
Xiè Zhān (謝瞻) possessed this quality.
This foreshadowed the destruction of Xiè Huì (謝晦)'s life and family.
為 (wèi),
pronunciation yú wěi fān (于偽翻).
Third year (壬戌, 422 CE)
1 In spring,
in the first month,
on *jiǎchén shuò* (甲辰朔),
the Wèi (魏) ruler traveled west from Yúnzhōng (雲中)
to Wūdòu Chéng (屋竇城).
According to the *Běi Shǐ* (北史),
Wūdòu Chéng (屋竇城) was east of Xuělín Shān (薛林山).
2 On *guǐchǒu* (癸丑),
Xú Xiànzhī (徐羨之) was appointed *Sīkōng* (司空) and *Lù Shàngshūshì* (錄尚書事),
retaining his previous governorship.
Wáng Hóng (王弘), Governor of Jiāngzhōu (江州), was appointed *Wèi Jiāngjūn* (衞將軍) and *Kāifǔ Yítóng Sānsī* (開府儀同三司);
Xiè Huì (謝晦), Central Commander of the Guards, was appointed *Lǐngjūn Jiāngjūn* (領軍將軍) concurrently *Sànqí Chángshì* (散騎常侍),
entering the palace to guard the inner halls,
and generally commanding the imperial guard.
散 (sàn),
pronunciation xī dàn fān (悉亶翻).
騎 (qí),
pronunciation qí jì fān (奇寄翻).
Xú Xiànzhī (徐羨之) was a staff officer in the army of Huán Xiū (桓脩).
He was in the same bureau as the Emperor and they were deeply close;
and when the righteous army was raised,
he was even more trusted and relied upon.
He was straightforward in his will and ability,
and when he suddenly occupied a high position in the court,
the court and the people admired and submitted to him,
all saying he had the potential of a prime minister.
He was reticent and spoke little,
not showing joy or worry on his face;
he was quite skilled at playing *yìqí* (弈棋) and watching plays,
often appearing as if he didn't understand,
which made people of the time respect him even more.
Fù Liàng (傅亮) and Cài Kuò (蔡廓) often said:
"Master Xú (徐公) understands all matters
and reconciles differences."
He once feasted with Fù Liàng (傅亮) and Xiè Huì (謝晦).
Liàng (亮) and Huì (晦) were talented, learned, and eloquent,
while Xiànzhī (羨之) had a dignified and composed demeanor,
speaking only when the time was right.
Zhèng Xiānzhī (鄭鮮之) sighed and said:
"Observing Xú (徐) and Fù (傅)'s discussions,
one no longer considers learning to be their greatest strength."
3 Qín (秦)'s General Conquering the West, Kǒngzǐ (孔子), and others thoroughly defeated Qìhàn Tūzhēn (契汗禿真),
capturing twenty thousand men and women
and over five hundred thousand cattle and sheep.
Tūzhēn (禿真) led several thousand cavalry and fled west.
His separate tribe, the Shùxī (樹奚) tribe, with five thousand households, surrendered to Qín (秦).
4 In the second month,
on *dīngchǒu* (丁丑),
an imperial edict divided Yùzhōu (豫州) east of the Huái (淮) into Nányùzhōu (南豫州),
with its seat at Lìyáng (歷陽),
and appointed Péngchéng Wáng (彭城王) Yìkāng (義康) as its governor.
At the beginning of Yìxī (義熙),
the Emperor wanted to expand Hénán (河南)
and pacify the lands of Yù (豫).
By the ninth year,
the area west of the Great River and north of Dàléi (大雷) in Yángzhōu (揚州) was entirely assigned to Yùzhōu (豫州).
At this time,
the land west of the Huái (淮) was made Běiyùzhōu (北豫州),
with its seat at Rǔnán (汝南).
According to Shěn Yuē (沈約)'s record,

Nányùzhōu (南豫州) governed nineteen commanderies: Lìyáng (歷陽), Nánqiáo (南譙), Lújiāng (廬江), Nánrǔyīn (南汝陰), Nánliáng (南梁), Jìnxī (晉熙), Yìyáng (弋陽), Ānfēng (安豐), Nánrǔnán (南汝南), Xīncài (新蔡), Dōngjùn (東郡), Nányǐng (南潁), Yǐngchuān (潁川), Xīrǔyīn (西汝陰), Rǔyáng (汝陽), Chénliú (陳留), Nánchén Zuǒjùn (南陳左郡), Biānchéng Zuǒjùn (邊城左郡), and Guāngchéng Zuǒjùn (光城左郡).
According to Xú Zhì (徐志) and the *Yǒngchū Jùnguó Zhì* (永初郡國志), it only governed thirteen commanderies.
This is probably because Shěn Zhì (沈志) includes commanderies established later, after Jǐngpíng (景平).
Its seat was Línxiāng (臨湘).
In the thirteenth year of Yìxī (義熙) of Emperor Ān (安) of Jìn (晉), Xiāngzhōu (湘州) was abolished;
now it is re-established.
Línxiāng (臨湘)
was an old county from the Hàn (漢) dynasty; in the Táng (唐) dynasty, it was Chángshā Xiàn (長沙縣) of Tánzhōu (潭州).
5 On *bǐngxū* (丙戌),
the Wèi (魏) ruler returned to his palace.
6 In the third month,
the Emperor was unwell.

Grand Commandant Chángshā Wáng Dáolián (長沙王道憐), Minister of Works Xú Xiànzhī (徐羨之), Minister of the Imperial Secretariat Fù Liàng (傅亮), General of the Left Army Xiè Huì (謝晦), and General of the Guards Tán Dàojì (檀道濟) all attended him with medicines.
His retainers requested prayers to the gods,
but the Emperor refused,
only allowing Palace Attendant Xiè Fāngmíng (謝方明) to report his illness to the ancestral temples.
The Emperor was by nature not superstitious.
When he was humble, there were many auspicious signs,
but when he became noble,
when the historians inquired carefully about what they had heard,
the Emperor refused to answer.
Tán Dàojì (檀道濟) was appointed General Who Guards the North and Governor of Southern Yánzhōu (南兗州),
garrisoned at Guǎnglíng (廣陵),
overseeing all armies south of the Huái River.
Emperor Chéng (成帝) of Jìn (晉) established Southern Yánzhōu (南兗州),
with its seat at Jīngkǒu (京口).
From this point, its seat was at Guǎnglíng (廣陵),
governing Guǎnglíng (廣陵), Hǎilíng (海陵), Shānyáng (山陽),
Xūyí (盱眙), Qínjùn (秦郡), and Southern Pèi (南沛) commanderies.
Jiān (監),
read gōng xián fān.
The Crown Prince was often close to inferiors.
Xiè Huì (謝晦) spoke to the Emperor, saying:
"Your Majesty's years are already advanced.
You should consider the myriad generations.
The divine vessel is extremely important
and cannot be entrusted to one who is not talented."
When Huì (晦) spoke these words,
he already had the intention of deposing the inept and establishing the sagacious.
Hè (荷),
read xià kě fān,
also pronounced as written.
"How is Lúlín (廬陵)?"
Huì (晦) replied:
"I request to observe him."
He went out to visit Lúlín Wáng Yìzhēn (廬陵王義真).
Yìzhēn (義真) greatly wished to converse with him,
but Huì (晦) did not answer much.
Upon his return, he said:
"His virtue is lighter than his talent;
he is not fit to be a ruler."
On the *dīngwèi* day,

Yìzhēn (義真) was appointed Area Commander of the armies of the six provinces of Southern Yù (南豫), Yù (豫), Yōng (雍), Sī (司), Qín (秦), and Bīng (幷), General of Chariots and Cavalry, Open-Palace Administrator with the Honors of the Three Ducal Ministers, and Governor of Southern Yùzhōu (南豫州).
This laid the groundwork for Huì (晦) and others to kill Yìzhēn (義真).
Yōng (雍),
read yú yòng fān.
Qí (騎),
read qí jì fān.
Large provinces were generally given Area Commanders,
with many sometimes reaching fifty provinces,
which cannot be detailed here.
By the end of Sòng (宋),
there were only twenty-two provinces within the territory.
By the time of Emperor Wǔ (武帝) of Liáng (梁),
various provinces were established along the borders,
beginning with fifty provinces.
Fù (復),
read fú yòu fān.
7 When the Emperor recovered from his illness,
on the *jǐwèi* day,
a general amnesty was declared.
8 Refugees from Qín (秦) and Yōng (雍) moved south into Liángzhōu (梁州).
On the *gēngshēn* day,
an envoy was sent to deliver ten thousand bolts of silk,
and to transport grain from Jīng (荊) and Yōng (雍) to relieve them.
The Yōng (雍) of Qín (秦) and Yōng (雍) was the ancient Yōngzhōu (雍州),
the land within Guānzhōng (關中).
The Yōng (雍) of Jīng (荊) and Yōng (雍) was the Southern Yōngzhōu (南雍州) established at the end of Jìn (晉),
with its seat at Xiāngyáng (襄陽).
Shǐ (使),
read shū lì fān.
Zhèn (賑),
read zhī rěn fān.
9 When Diāo Kuí (刁逵) was executed,
the event is recorded in volume 113 under Jìn (晉) Emperor Ān's (安帝) Yuánxīng (元興) third year.
On the *xīnyǒu* day,
Mí Shuài (彌帥) and several tens of men entered Jīngkǒu (京口).
Lù Zhòngyuán (陸仲元), the Staff Officer of the Grand Commandant's Resident Office, attacked and slew them.
At that time, Chángshā Wáng Dáolián (長沙王道憐) was garrisoned at Jīngkǒu (京口) as Grand Commandant,
but had entered to attend to the Emperor's medicine,
hence there was a resident office.
10On the *yǐchǒu* day,
Yáo (曜), Prince of Hénán (河南) of Wèi (魏), died.
11In summer,
in the fourth month,
on the *jiǎxū* day,
Wèi (魏) established Imperial Prince Táo (燾) as Tàipíng Wáng (太平王)
and appointed him Prime Minister,
with the additional title of Grand General.
Pī (丕) was made Lèpíng Wáng (樂平王),
Mí (彌) as Āndìng Wáng (安定王),
Fàn (範) as Lè'ān Wáng (樂安王),
Jiàn (健) as Yǒngchāng Wáng (永昌王),
Chóng (崇) as Jiànníng Wáng (建寧王),
Jùn (俊) as Xīnxīng Wáng (新興王).
12On the *yǐhài* day,
an imperial edict enfeoffed the Duke of Qiúchí (仇池), Yáng Shèng (楊盛), as Wǔdū Wáng (武都王).
13Qín Wáng (秦王) Chìpán (熾磐) appointed General of the Flank Qífú Shìchén (乞伏是辰) as Western Hú (胡) Commander,
and built Lièhún (列渾) city at Zhíluó (汁羅) to garrison it.
Zhíluó (汁羅) is probably the land of Luóchuān (羅川).
14In the fifth month,
the Emperor's illness worsened.
He summoned the Crown Prince and admonished him, saying:
"Tán Dàojì (檀道濟), though capable and strategic,
lacks far-reaching ambition,
unlike his brother Sháo (韶) who has a difficult-to-control demeanor.
Xú Xiànzhī (徐羨之) and Fù Liàng (傅亮)
will not harbor different intentions.
Xiè Huì (謝晦) has frequently participated in campaigns
and is quite familiar with schemes and changes.
If there is any disloyalty,
it will surely be this man."
The Emperor already had suspicions about Huì (晦).
Shù (數),
read suǒ jiǎo fān.
"If in future generations there is a young ruler,
all court affairs should be entrusted to the chief minister,
and the Empress Dowager need not attend court."

Minister of Works Xú Xiànzhī (徐羨之), Central Secretariat Director Fù Liàng (傅亮), General of the Left Army Xiè Huì (謝晦), and General Who Guards the North Tán Dàojì (檀道濟) were all appointed to receive the dying command.
On the *guǐhài* day,
the Emperor passed away in the Western Palace.
He was sixty years old.
From this time onward,
the demise of rulers of the Northern and Southern Dynasties was all referred to as *cú* (殂).
Bèi (被),
read pí yì fān.
Gù (顧),
pronounced *gǔ*.
He was strict and adhered to rules.
In his clothing and abode,
he was frugal with plain cloth.
He rarely held feasts,
and his concubines and attendants were few.
He once obtained a niece of Emperor Gāozǔ (高祖) of Later Qín (後秦).
Emperor Xìng (興) of Later Qín (後秦)
had the temple name Gāozǔ (高祖).
Cóng (從),
read cái yòng fān.
He somewhat neglected affairs because of her;
Xiè Huì (謝晦) subtly remonstrated,
and she was immediately sent away.
All his wealth and silk were kept in the outer treasury,
with no private hoarding within.
Língnán (嶺南) once presented a bolt of fine cloth in a tube, eight *zhàng* long.
The Emperor disliked its exquisite beauty and the labor it caused people.
Yáng Xióng's (揚雄) *Shǔ Dū Fù* (蜀都賦) says: "The cloth is like spider silk,
invisible to the wind;
yellow and moist within a tube,
one bolt is worth several gold."
Referring to its fineness.
È (惡),
read wū lù fān.
He returned the cloth,
and also decreed that Língnán (嶺南) was forbidden from making such cloth.
When a princess was married,
the gifts sent did not exceed two hundred thousand (coins),
and there were no embroidered or brocade items.
Both within and outside the court, prohibitions were observed,
and no one dared to be extravagant.
The Crown Prince immediately ascended the imperial throne,
at the age of seventeen.
A general amnesty was declared.
The Empress Dowager was honored as Grand Empress Dowager,
and Lady Sīmǎ (司馬氏) was established as Empress.
The Empress
was Princess Hǎiyán (海鹽公主), daughter of Emperor Gōng (恭帝) of Jìn (晉).
The Wèi zhǔ (ruler of Wèi) took the Cold Food Powder,
and for several years, when the medicine took effect,
frequent ominous signs appeared.
He was quite worried about himself.
He secretly sent a palace envoy to ask Bái Mǎ Gōng (Duke of Bái Mǎ), Cuī Hào, saying:
"Recently, there was a solar eclipse in the region of Zhào and Dài.
'Shǔ zhě' (屬者)
means 'bǐ zhě' (比者) or 'jìn zhě' (近者), i.e., 'recently.'
Shǔ (屬)
reads as 'zhī yù' (之欲) fan.
Fēn (分)
reads as 'fú wèn' (扶問) fan.
I fear that if I were to suddenly pass away,
with my sons all being young,
what should be done?
Please consider a plan for me after my death!"
Hào replied:
"Your Majesty is in the prime of your life,
and will soon recover fully.
But if it is absolutely necessary,
please allow me to offer my humble opinion.
Since our sacred dynasty arose,
the crown prince position has not been established early,
which is why at the beginning of Yǒngxīng,
the state was almost in danger.
This incident is recorded in volume 115, in the fifth year of Yìxī of Jìn Āndì.
Jī (幾)
reads as 'jū xī' (居希) fan,
also pronounced 'qí' (祁).
Select worthy high officials to be his teachers,
and trusted ministers to be his companions;
let him manage all affairs of state internally,
and oversee military and government matters externally.
If this is done,
Your Majesty can enjoy leisure and tranquility,
nourishing your spirit and prolonging your life.
After ten thousand years (Your Majesty's death),
the country will have an established ruler,
the people will have someone to rely on,
wicked elements will cease their ambitions,
and disaster will have no way to arise."
"The imperial prince Táo is nearing his 'zhōu xīng' (周星, a full cycle of Jupiter, i.e., 12 years).
A 'suì xīng' (歲星) completes a cycle in twelve years.
Establishing the eldest son is
a great principle of ritual.
If we must wait until he comes of age before choosing,
that would invert the natural order of family,
and thus is a path to inviting chaos."
"Dào cuò" (倒錯)
means setting aside the eldest and establishing the youngest.
"Zhǎng" (長)
reads as 'zhī liǎng' (知兩) fan;
same below.
The Emperor replied:
"Establishing the eldest is in accord with custom,
while appointing the worthy commands respect;
Táo is both eldest and worthy, which is Heaven's command."
The Emperor followed his advice,
and established Tàipíng Wáng (Prince of Tàipíng) Táo as the Crown Prince,
making him reside in the main hall to oversee court,
as the deputy ruler of the country.
He appointed Zhǎngsūn Sōng, Shānyáng Gōng (Duke of Shānyáng) Xī Jīn,
(Wèi Shōu's Guānshì Zhì states: Wèi Xiàndì's (Wei Emperor Xiàn) younger brother's clan was Dáxī,
which Xiàowén changed to Xī).
to sit in the east wing,
facing west;
Cuī Hào, along with Tàiwèi (Grand Commandant) Mù Guān, Sànqí Chángshì (Palace Attendant) Dàirén Qiū Duī, were appointed as the Right Support,
(Wèi Xiàowén (Emperor Xiàowén of Wèi) changed Xiàndì's (Emperor Xiàn) fifth elder brother, Dūnqiū's clan, to Qiū).
facing east;
all officials generally reported to him.
Those sitting in the east wing faced west,
those sitting in the west wing faced east,
all bowing to the Crown Prince.
At that time, he (the Emperor) secretly watched them,
(meaning he concealed himself and watched them).
He was greatly pleased,
and said to his attendants:
"Sōng is an old official of long-standing virtue,
having served four reigns,
and contributed greatly to the state.
(Sōng served Emperor Zhāochéng, Emperor Dàowǔ, Emperor Míngyuán, and Crown Prince Táo, making four reigns).
His fame is widespread;
Tóng is astute in understanding popular sentiment,
and adept in practical matters;
Guān is insightful in governance,
and understands my intentions;
Hào is extensively learned and has a strong memory,
discerning in both heavenly and human affairs;
although Duī has no great use,
he is diligent and careful in public service.
With these six men assisting the Crown Prince,
I and you all can tour the four borders,
attacking the rebellious and pacifying the submissive,
and will surely achieve our ambitions throughout the world."
In fact, Sōng's surname was Bábá,
Jīn's surname was Dáxī,
Guān's surname was Qiūmùlíng,
and Duī's surname was Qiūdūn.
At this time,
many of the powerful ministers of Wèi who came from Dài Běi
had repeated surnames.
When Gāozǔ (Emperor Gāozǔ) moved to Luòyáng,
they all began to change them.
Old histories disliked
their complexity and difficulty to know,
so they all followed the later surnames for simplicity.
We follow that here.
The Wèi zhǔ also ordered Liú Jié, who managed the eastern and western departments, Gǔ Bì, a Dàirén (person from Dài) who reported on matters in the palace gate,
and Zhíláng (Palace Attendant) Túhé Lú Lǔyuán
(Tuòbá, along with Mùróng and Duàn clans, came from the Xiānbēi,
and later became powerful,
calling the eastern branch Túhé.
Guānshì Zhì states: Among the surnames that entered the interior, Tǔfúlú changed to Lú).
to attend to the Eastern Palace (Crown Prince's residence),
manage key confidential matters,
and transmit decrees.
The Crown Prince was intelligent
and had a grand demeanor.
When powerful ministers occasionally presented him with doubts,
the Emperor would say:
"This is not something I should know;
it should be decided by your lord, the ruler of the state."
16 In the sixth month,
on the day Rénshēn,
Fù Liàng, Shàngshū Púyè (Director of the Imperial Secretariat), was appointed Zhōngshū Jiān (Palace Secretary) and Shàngshū Lìng (President of the Imperial Secretariat).
Xiè Huì, Língjūn Jiāngjūn (General of the Imperial Guards), was appointed to oversee the Zhōngshū Lìng.
Shìzhōng (Palace Attendant) Xiè Fāngmíng was made Dānyáng Yǐn (Administrator of Dānyáng).
Fāngmíng was skilled in governing commanderies,
and wherever he went, he earned a reputation for competence.
Succeeding previous administrators,
he did not alter their policies;
if changes were necessary,
he gradually shifted them
so that no trace could be found.
17 On the day Wùzǐ,
Chángshā Jǐng Wáng (Prince Jǐng of Chángshā) Dào Lián passed away.
18 Diāo Yōng, Wèi Jiànyì Jiāngjūn (General who Establishes Righteousness of Wèi), attacked Qīngzhōu (Qīng Prefecture).
The provincial troops defeated him.
Yōng gathered his scattered soldiers
and fled to secure Dàxiāng Shān (Mount Dàxiāng).
(Wèi Shōu's Dìxíng Zhì states: In Chéngshì Xiàn (Chéngshì County) of Jìyīn Jùn (Jìyīn Commandery), there is Dàxiāng Chéng (Dàxiāng City).
Yōng (雍) reads as 'yú róng' (於容) fan).
19 In autumn,
in the seventh month, on the day Jǐyǒu,
Emperor Wǔ was buried in Chūníng Líng (Chūníng Mausoleum).
(The mausoleum is on Jiǎng Shān (Mount Jiǎng) in Jiànkāng Xiàn (Jiànkāng County) of Dānyáng).
20 Héxī Wáng (Prince of Héxī) Méngxùn sent Qián Jiāngjūn (General of the Vanguard) Jūqú Chéngdū to lead an army of ten thousand,
to display their military strength south of the ridge (Lǐngnán),
and then encamp at Wǔjiàn.
(This means they displayed their military strength south of Hóngchí Lǐng, and then returned to encamp at Wǔjiàn.
Jū (沮) reads as 'zǐ yú' (子余) fan.
Shuài (帥)
reads as 'lǜ' (率);
same below).
Qín Wáng (Prince of Qín) Chìpán sent Zhēng Běi Jiāngjūn (General who Attacks the North) Chūlián Qián and others to lead six thousand cavalry to attack him.
21 Initially,
the Lord of Wèi heard that Gāo Zǔ had conquered Cháng'ān.
This is found in volume 116, Jin An Dì Yìxī 13th year.
He sent an envoy to request peace.
From then on, annual exchanges of envoys were uninterrupted.
When Gāo Zǔ passed away,
the Palace General Shěn Fàn and others were serving as envoys in Wèi.
The Jìn established two guards,
and still maintained the position of Palace General.
"Envoy" (使)
is read "shū lì fān";
similarly below.
When they reached the Hé [Yellow River],
the Lord of Wèi sent men to pursue and seize them,
and debated dispatching troops to capture Luòyáng, Hǔláo, and Huátái.
Cuī Hào remonstrated, saying:
"Your Majesty did not consider Liú Yù's sudden rise,
but accepted his envoys and tributes.
Yù also respectfully served Your Majesty.
Unfortunately, he has died now.
To immediately take advantage of the mourning to attack him,
even if successful, would not be honorable.
Furthermore, the state today is not yet able to conquer Jiāngnán in one go,
and would only gain the name of attacking during mourning.
It is not ritual to attack during mourning.
Your servant suggests that we should send someone to offer condolences,
preserve his orphaned and weak,
and sympathize with his misfortune,
so that a righteous reputation spreads throughout the world.
Then Jiāngnán will submit without being attacked.
Moreover, Yù has just died,
and his partisans have not yet dispersed.
If troops approach their border,
they will surely unite to resist and fight,
and success cannot be guaranteed.
It is better to delay,
wait for his powerful ministers to contend for power,
and for chaos and difficulties to certainly arise.
Then, when generals are ordered to lead armies,
it will be possible to avoid tiring the troops
and simply gain Huáinán."
The Lord of Wèi said:
"Liú Yù took advantage of Yáo Xīng's death to destroy him.
This event is found in volume 117, Jin An Dì Yìxī 12th year, and volume 116, Yìxī 13th year.
Why should it not be permissible?"
Hào said:
"Not so.
When Yáo Xīng died,
his sons contended with each other,
so Yù took advantage of the rift to attack him.
Now there is no rift in Jiāngnán,
so they cannot be compared."
The Lord of Wèi did not heed him.
He granted Xī Jīn, Acting Sīkōng, a staff of authority,
promoted him to General-in-chief of Jin Soldiers and Acting Governor of Yángzhōu,
and made him supervise Zhōu Jǐ, General of Song Soldiers and Governor of Jiāozhōu,
The Later Wèi Emperor Xiàowén established the Zhōu clan as descendants of Pǔshì, the second elder brother of Emperor Xiàndì.
and the generals of Jin Soldiers, Song Soldiers, Wú Soldiers, Zhèng Soldiers, Chǔ Soldiers, etc.
All were established by Wèi.
22 On the day Yǐsì,
the Lord of Wèi went to the Nángōng palace in Luǐ.
Then he went to Guǎngníng.
In the first year of Jìn Mǐn Dì's Jiànxīng era,
Yī Lú built Xīnpíngchéng north of Luǐ,
and later built a palace south of Luǐ.
Lì Dàoyuán said: Guǎngníng is fifty *lǐ* from Píngchéng.
Guǎngníng County
belonged to Shànggǔ Commandery during the Hàn,
and was established as a commandery during the Tàikāng era of Jìn.
Luǐ (灅)
is read "lì shuǐ fān".
23 On the day Xīnhài,
the Wèi people built an outer wall for Píngchéng,
thirty-two *lǐ* in circumference.
24 The Lord of Wèi went to Qiáo Shān.
The *History of the Five Dynasties* states: Qiáo Shān is in Huáiróng County, Zhuō Commandery.
Liú Xù said: Táng Guīzhōu's Huáiróng County
was Pān County of Shànggǔ during the Later Hàn.
In winter,
the tenth month,
on the day Jiǎxū,
he returned to the palace.
25 When the Wèi army was about to depart,
the high officials and ministers gathered for a discussion before the Regent,
debating whether to attack cities first or to plunder territory first.
Xī Jīn wanted to attack cities first.
Cuī Hào said:
"Southerners are skilled at defending cities.
In the past, Fú Shì attacked Xiāngyáng
and could not capture it for a year.
This event is found in volume 104, Jin Xiàowǔ Dì Tàiyuán 3rd and 4th years.
If it cannot be captured in time,
the army's morale will be damaged,
the enemy will arrive slowly and sternly,
and we will be weary while they are sharp;
this is a dangerous path.
It is better to divide the army to plunder territory,
with the Huái River as the boundary,
set up governors and magistrates,
and collect rents and grain.
Then Luòyáng, Huátái, and Hǔláo will be to the north of the army,
completely cut off from southern aid,
and will surely flee east along the river;
otherwise, they will be like animals in a preserve.
Why worry that they will not be captured!"
Gōngsūn Biǎo insisted on attacking cities,
and the Lord of Wèi followed his advice.
Thereupon, Xī Jīn and others led two tens of thousands of infantry and cavalry,
crossed the Hé,
and encamped east of Huátái.
At that time, Máo Dézǔ, Governor of Sīzhōu, garrisoned Hǔláo.
Wáng Jǐngdù, Administrator of Dōngjùn, reported the emergency to Dézǔ.
Wáng Jǐngdù, as Administrator of Dōngjùn, garrisoned Huátái.
Earlier,
Sīmǎ Chǔzhī had gathered a multitude in the area of Chénliú.
Hearing that the Wèi troops had crossed the Hé,
he sent an envoy to surrender.
Wèi appointed Chǔzhī as General Who Conquers the South and Governor of Jīngzhōu,
and ordered him to harass the northern border.
This refers to the northern border of Sòng.
Shàolíng County
belonged to Rǔnán Commandery during the Hàn,
and to Yǐngchuān Commandery after the Jìn.
Dù Yòu said: Yǎnlíng County of Cáizhōu has the old city of Zhàolíng.
Chǔzhī led troops to attack Lán,
but failed to capture it.
At that time, the court sent military supplies,
and Lán went out to receive them.
Wáng Yù, a commoner from Suānzǎo, rode to inform Wèi.
Suānzǎo County belonged to Chénliú Commandery from the Hàn to the Táng,
and to Huázhōu during the Táng.
On the day Dīngyǒu,
the Wèi Minister Huá Jī led troops to attack Cāngyuán.
Kāng said: Huá (滑),
read "hù bā qiē",
is a surname.
It originated from the State of Huá Bó,
of the Jī surname,
whose descendants adopted the state name as their clan name.
During the Hàn, there was the Grand Master of Ceremonies Huá Diǎn.
Yán Líng from Fēngyì, Administrator of Chénliú, went to Jīn and surrendered.
Wèi appointed Wáng Yù as Administrator of Chénliú,
and gave him troops to guard Cāngyuán.
Wèi Shōu's *Topographical Treatise* states: Chénliú Commandery's seat was Jùnyí County,
which had Cāngyuán City.
Xī Jīn and others attacked Huátái,
but could not capture it,
and requested more troops.
The Lord of Wèi was angry
and severely reproached him.
On the day Rénchén,
he personally led fifty thousand and more troops from various states south out of Tiānguān,
and crossed the Hénglíng.
This was the route by which Yàn Lord Chuí attacked Wèi's Píngchéng in the 21st year of Jin Xiàowǔ Dì's Tàiyuán era.
After Wèi Lord Guī pacified Zhōngshān,
he dug through the Hénglíng from Wàngdū Tiěguān to Dài, a distance of over five hundred *lǐ*.
Jiāng (將)
is read "jí liàng fān";
similarly below.
26 Qín Chūlián Qián fought against Jǔqú Chéngdū from Hexi [the region west of the Yellow River]
and captured him.
Jǔqú Chéngdū was garrisoned at Wǔjiàn at that time.
27 In the eleventh month,
Wèi Crown Prince Tào led troops to garrison on Sàishàng.
The Lord of Wèi went south to reinforce the troops attacking Hénán,
so the Crown Prince garrisoned on Sàishàng to guard against the Rouran.
On the day Gēngxū,
Xī Jīn and others fiercely attacked Huátái
and captured it.
Wáng Jǐngdù fled;
Jǐngdù's Military Advisor Yáng Zàn was captured by Wèi
and died without surrendering.
The Lord of Wèi appointed Gǒu Ér, Marquis of Chénggāo, as Governor of Yǎnzhōu,
to guard Huátái.
The *Treatise on Officials and Clans in the Book of Wèi* states: Among the internally assimilated surnames, Ruògān Shì became Gǒu Shì.
Jīn and others advanced to attack Zhái Guǎng and others at Tǔlóu,
and defeated them.
Tǔlóu was east of Hǔláo.
The *Jiǔyù Zhì* states: Chánzhōu's Línhé County has Tǔlóu Town.
Máo Dézǔ fought against them
and defeated them repeatedly.
The Lord of Wèi separately sent General of Black Spears Yú Lìtí to lead three thousand men to garrison Háyáng,
planning to capture Jīnyǒng.
Dézǔ sent General of Inspiring Awe Dòu Huàng and others to resist them along the river.
In the twelfth month,
on the day Bǐngxū,
the Lord of Wèi arrived at Jìzhōu,
and sent General of Chǔ Soldiers and Governor of Xúzhōu, Shūsūn Jiàn, to lead troops to cross the Hé from Píngyuán
and campaign in Qīng and Yǎn.
Liú Cuì, Governor of Yùzhōu, sent his Adjutant Gāo Dàojǐn to lead five hundred infantry and cavalry to hold Xiàngchéng.
Sòng Yùzhōu governed Rǔnán, Xīncài, Qiáo, Liáng, Chén, Nándùn, Yǐngchuān, Rǔyáng, Rǔyīn, Chénliú and other commanderies.
Xúzhōu governed Péngchéng, Pèi, Xiàpī, Lánlíng, Dōnghǎi, Dōngguǎn, Dōng'ān, Lángyá, Huáiyáng, Yángpíng, Jìyīn, Běijìyīn, Zhōnglí, Mǎtóu and other commanderies.
He joined forces with Xī Jīn and others to attack Dòu Huàng and others
and defeated them.

The Lord of Wèi dispatched É Qīng of Dàirén, the Central Army Commander, and Ròurán Lǘ Dàféi, the Marquis of Qīsī, leading seven thousand soldiers to join Zhōu Jǐ and Shúsūn Jiàn in crossing the Hé southwards.
They encamped at Quègǎo.
Quègǎo city overlooked a ford on the Hé.
Later, Wèi established it as the seat of Jìzhōu.
The Shuǐ Jīng Zhù states: The city is the former Chípíng county.
On the kuǐwèi day,
Xú Yǎn, the Inspector of Yǎnzhōu, abandoned Yǐnmǎo and fled south.
The Shuǐ Jīng says: The Jǐ River flows northwest from Xūchāng county, past the east of Yúshān,
and then north, passing west of Gǔchéng county.
The commentary says: On the bank of the Jǐ River there is Yǐnmǎo rampart,
over forty lǐ south of Yúshān.
This is the former Xiǎogǔchéng of the Spring and Autumn period, within Gǔchéng county.
Jīnxiāng county
belonged to Shānyáng in the Hàn dynasty,
and to Gāopíng in the Jìn dynasty.
It was probably established as a separate commandery at the end of the Jìn dynasty.
Sīmǎ Àizhī and Jìzhī had previously gathered a multitude east of the Jǐ River,
and both surrendered to Wèi.
The area east of the Jǐ River was within Qīngzhōu.
Jǐ,
pronounced zǐ lǐ.
On the wùzǐ day,
Wèi forces pressed towards Hǔláo.
Zhú Kuí of Dōngguǎn, the Inspector of Qīngzhōu, garrisoned Dōngyáng chéng.
Since Cáo Yì, Qīngzhōu had been governed from Guǎnggù.
When Emperor Wǔ conquered Mùróng Chāo,
he razed its city.
Qīngzhōu’s seat was moved to Dōngyáng chéng,
southwest of Guǎng county.
Sòng Bái says: The current seat of Qīngzhōu is Yìdū county,
and the eastern part of the prefectural city is Dōngyáng chéng.
In the early Táikāng reign of Emperor Wǔ of Jìn,
Dōngguǎn Commandery was established by partitioning Lángxié.
Qīngzhōu administered the commanderies of Qí, Jǐnán, Gāomì, Lè'ān, Píngchāng, Běihǎi, Dōnglái, Tàiyuán, and Chángguǎng.
Guǎn,
pronounced guān.
On the jǐchǒu day,
an imperial edict appointed Tán Dàojì, the Inspector of Nányǎnzhōu, to oversee all military operations,
and to jointly relieve the siege with Wáng Zhòngdé.
Yìzhēn, Prince of Lúlíng, dispatched Shěn Shūlí, the General of Longxiáng, with three thousand men to join Liú Cuì,
to assess the situation and provide reinforcements.
Yìzhēn was then stationed at Shòuyáng,
and Liú Cuì at Xuánhù.
Xiáng,
pronounced sī jiāng.
Liáng is pronounced liáng.
Yíngyáng Wáng
was named Yìfú,
with the courtesy name Chēbīng.
He was the eldest son of Emperor Wǔ.
The Kǎoyì states: The annals of Sòng,
and Gāo Shì Xiǎo Shǐ all write
"Xíngyáng";
The biographies of Zāng Hòu, Xiè Huì, and Cài Kuò write
"Yíngyáng."
Yíngyáng is
a southern commandery name.
We follow this now.
First year of Jǐngpíng (guǐhài, 423)
1. Spring,
First month.
On the jǐhài day, the first day of the month,
a great amnesty was proclaimed,
and the reign title was changed.
2. On the xīnchǒu day,
the emperor performed sacrifices at the Southern Suburb.
3. Yú Lìtí of Wèi attacked Jīnyǒng.
On the guǐmǎo day,
Wáng Juānzhī, the Administrator of Hénán, abandoned the city and fled.
The Lord of Wèi appointed Yú Lìtí as the Inspector of Yùzhōu,
garrisoning Luòyáng.
4. The Lord of Wèi made a southern tour to Héngyuè.
On the bǐngchén day,
he arrived at Yè.
Last year, in the twelfth month, it was recorded that the Lord of Wèi reached Jìzhōu.
Now it is again recorded that he made a southern tour to Héngyuè.
One of these must be an error.
5. On the jǐwèi day,
an imperial edict summoned Cài Kuò, the Administrator of Yùzhāng, to be Minister of Personnel.
Since the Jìn dynasty,
the Minister of Personnel has been called "Great Minister,"
because he ranked above all other departments,
and his authority was crucial and heavy.
"If the selection process is entirely entrusted to me,
there will be no discussion."
"No discussion" means
not to deliberate further on accepting or declining the post.
"I cannot accept the appointment."
Liàng spoke this to Xú Xiànzhī, the Minister Overseeing Affairs.
Xiànzhī said:
"All officials from Huángmén and Sànjì downwards will be entrusted to Cài;
we will no longer need to worry about them."
Huángmén and Sànjì
refer to the Palace Gentlemen and the Palace Attendants and Palace Gentlemen-in-waiting.
Fù,
pronounced fú yòu.
"Therefore, we should jointly consult on what is different or similar."
Kuò said:
"I cannot sign the end of the paper for Xú Gānmù!"
Thus, he did not accept the appointment.
Gānmù was
Xiànzhī's courtesy name.
Selection documents were on yellow paper,
with the Minister Overseeing Affairs and the Minister of Personnel signing jointly.
Xuǎn'àn refers to the official documents of the Personnel Department.
Hóng Mài says: Yè Shílín claimed that the use of yellow paper for imperial edicts began during Emperor Gāozōng's reign,
which is incorrect.
During the reign of Emperor Gōng of Jìn,
Wáng Sháozhī was promoted to Palace Gentleman;
all imperial edicts on yellow paper
were written by him.
Thus, yellow paper was already used for imperial edicts during the Eastern Jìn dynasty.
Furthermore,
during the reign of Emperor Míng of Sòng,
Chǔ Yuān, the Minister of Personnel, conducted selections at Zhěqí.
In this campaign,
all ranks were awarded after battles;
official documents were insufficient,
hence the use of yellow paper tallies.
Thus, in the Sòng dynasty, when officials were appointed and rewarded for merit on military campaigns,
yellow paper was also frequently used.
Moreover,
when Xú Xiànzhī summoned Cài Kuò to be Minister of Personnel,
Kuò said:
"I cannot sign the end of the paper for Xú Gānmù,"
indicating that yellow paper was used for official documents in the Sòng dynasty.
In the Qí dynasty,
a system of Left and Right Chancellors' official documents was established: called "white documents,"
where the Right Chancellor's name was written first,
followed by the Left Chancellor's;
"yellow documents,"
where the Left Chancellor wrote first,
followed by the Right Chancellor.
Although the era is distant and it is unknown which were "yellow documents" and which were "white documents,"
what is certain is
that the paper was already divided into two colors, yellow and white.
During the time of Dōnghūn,
eunuchs wrapped fish and meat in paper to take home,
and these were all yellow documents from the five departments.
Thus, the use of yellow paper for official documents
has a long history.
During Emperor Gāozōng's reign,
it was merely that all copies of imperial edicts distributed to prefectures and counties below [the capital] began to use yellow paper;
to generally say that imperial edicts began to use yellow paper during Gāozōng's reign
is not accurate.
Xuǎn, pronounced xū juàn.
Shěn Yuē's commentary states: Cài Kuò firmly declined the position of personnel selection,
ashamed to yield his ambition.
How could he not know that selection and oversight are of one body,
and there is no principle of partial judgment?
The Minister of Personnel presides over selection;
the Minister Overseeing Affairs concurrently oversees the affairs of all departmental ministers.
Duàn,
pronounced dīng luàn.
He did not wish to hold a position that determined success or failure.
In the role of personnel selection,
if the right person is found, the path for the worthy is open;
if not, the path for the worthy is blocked.
Sè,
pronounced xī zé.
6. On the gēngshēn day,
Tán Dàojì's army encamped at Péngchéng.
Shúsūn Jiàn of Wèi entered Línzī,
and all cities and towns in his path collapsed.
The Kǎoyì states: The Suǒ Lǔ Zhuàn says:
"The barbarians also dispatched Shè Guīfān Néngjiàn, General of Chǔ soldiers, Inspector of Xúzhōu, and Duke of Ānpíng;
Xuē Dàoqiān, General of Yuè soldiers, Inspector of Qīngzhōu, and Marquis of Línzī;
and Zhāng Mó, General of Chén soldiers, Inspector of Huáizhōu, and Viscount of Shòuzhāng, to attack Qīngzhōu in the east.
All cities and towns in their path fled."
The Běnjì also says
"Duke of Ānpíng, Shè Guī, attacked Qīngzhōu."
According to the Hòu Wèi Shū, there are no names like Shè Guī;
these are probably old Hú names,
referring to Shúsūn Jiàn and others.
Those who did not enter the cities were ordered to occupy mountain strongholds,
and to cut down and destroy crops.
When the Wèi army arrived,
they found nothing to eat.
Yuán Miáo, the Administrator of Jǐnán, led his troops to rely on Kuí.
Yuán Miáo abandoned Lìchéng and relied on Kuí.
Jǐ,
pronounced zǐ lǐ.
Shuài,
read as lǜ;
same below.
Diāo Yōng (刁雍) saw the Wèi (魏) ruler at Yè (鄴).
The Wèi (魏) ruler said:
"Shūsūn Jiàn (叔孫建) and others entered Qīngzhōu (青州),
the people all hid,
and the siege of the city was unsuccessful.
They have always respected your authority and trustworthiness,
and Yōng (雍) previously gathered troops between the Hé (河) and Jì (濟)."
Yōng (雍),
from the fanqie pronunciation 'yú róng' (於容).
So Yōng (雍) was made Inspector of Qīngzhōu (青州),
given cavalry,
and sent to recruit soldiers to take Qīngzhōu (青州).
The Wèi (魏) troops who crossed the Hé (河) towards Qīngzhōu (青州) totaled sixty thousand cavalry.
Diāo Yōng (刁雍) recruited five thousand soldiers,
pacified and comforted the officers and people,
who all sent rent to supply the army.
7 Ròurán (柔然) raided the Wèi (魏) border.
In the second month,
on the day Wùchén (戊辰),
Wèi (魏) built a Great Wall,
from Chìchéng (赤城) west to Wǔyuán (五原),
extending over two thousand *lǐ* (里),
with garrisons stationed
to guard against the Ròurán (柔然).
8 On the day Dīngchǒu (丁丑),
Grand Empress Dowager Xiāo (蕭) passed away.
9 The King of Héxī (河西), Méngxùn (蒙遜), and the King of Tǔyùhún (吐谷渾), Āchái (阿柴), both sent envoys to pay tribute.
On the day Gēngchén (庚辰),

an imperial edict appointed Méngxùn (蒙遜) as Grand Administrator of Military Affairs of the four prefectures of Liáng (涼), Qín (秦), Hé (河), and Shā (沙), General of Swift Cavalry, Administrator of Liángzhōu (涼州), and King of Héxī (河西);
Āchái (阿柴) was appointed Grand Administrator of Military Affairs beyond the frontier, General Quelling the West, Inspector of Shāzhōu (沙州), and Duke of Jiāohé (澆河).
As Tǔyùhún (吐谷渾) occupied the desert-Qiāng (沙漒) land beyond the frontier,
he was thus ordered to oversee military affairs beyond the frontier.
Jiāo (澆),
from the fanqie pronunciation 'jiān yáo' (堅堯).
10 In the third month,
on the day Rénzǐ (壬子),
Empress Xiàoyì (孝懿) was buried at Xīngnínglíng (興寧陵).
Xīngnínglíng (興寧陵) is in Yúshān (雩山), Jiànbì (諫壁) *lǐ* (里), Dāntú (丹徒) county, Jìnlíng (晉陵).
11 Xī Jīn (奚斤) and Gōngsūn Biǎo (公孫表) of Wèi (魏) jointly attacked Hǔláo (虎牢).
The Wèi (魏) ruler dispatched troops from Yè (鄴) to assist them.
Máo Dézǔ (毛德祖) dug a tunnel seven *zhàng* (丈) deep inside the city,
dividing it into six paths,
emerging outside the Wèi (魏) encirclement.
He recruited four hundred dare-to-die soldiers
and had Staff Officer Fàn Dàojī (范道基) and others lead them
out from the tunnels,
to launch a surprise attack on their rear.
The Wèi (魏) army was startled and thrown into disarray,
several hundred heads were severed,
and their siege equipment was burned before they returned.
Although the Wèi (魏) troops retreated and dispersed,
they soon reassembled,
attacking with increasing urgency.
Xī Jīn (奚斤) led three thousand infantry and cavalry from Hǔláo (虎牢) to attack Lǐ Yuándé (李元德), Administrator of Yǐngchuān (潁川), and others at Xǔchāng (許昌).
Yuándé (元德) and others were defeated and fled.
Wèi (魏) appointed Yǔ Lóng (庾龍) from Yǐngchuān (潁川) as Administrator of Yǐngchuān (潁chuān),
garrisoning Xǔchāng (許昌).
Máo Dézǔ (毛德祖) led out his troops and fought a great battle with Gōngsūn Biǎo (公孫表),
from morning until evening,
killing several hundred Wèi (魏) soldiers.
It happened that Xī Jīn (奚斤) returned from Xǔchāng (許昌),
and they jointly attacked Dézǔ (德祖),
heavily defeating him,
losing over a thousand armored soldiers,
and he again defended himself by entrenching within the city.
The Wèi (魏) ruler again sent over ten thousand men to cross the Hé (河) from Báishā (白沙),
camping south of Púyáng (濮陽).
Opposite Púyáng (濮陽) is the territory of Dùnqiū (頓丘),
Báishā (白沙) should be within the present-day bounds of Chányáng (澶陽).
The court deliberated that Xiàngchéng (項城) was not far from Wèi (魏),
and could not be resisted by a small force,
so Liú Cuì (劉粹) was ordered to recall Gāo Dàojǐn (高道瑾) to Shòuyáng (壽陽);
if Shěn Shūlí (沈叔貍) had already advanced,
he should also be recalled for the time being.
Cuì (粹) reported:
"The barbarians are attacking Hǔláo (虎牢) and have not yet turned south.
If the army is suddenly withdrawn, abandoning Xiàngchéng (項城),
then the various commanderies west of the Huái (淮) will have nothing to rely on.
Shěn Shūlí (沈叔貍) has already encamped at Féikǒu (肥口)."
Féikǒu (肥口),
the mouth where the Féi (肥) River enters the Huái (淮).
At that time, Lǐ Yuándé (李元德) led two hundred scattered soldiers to Xiàng (項),
and Liú Cuì (劉粹) sent them to assist Gāo Dàojǐn (高道瑾) in garrisoning and defending,
requesting pardon for his crime of defeat and flight,
which the court deliberated and granted.
On the day Yǐsì (乙巳),
the Wèi (魏) ruler hunted at Hánlíngshān (韓陵山).
Hánlíngshān (韓陵山) is in Yè (鄴) county, Wèijùn (魏郡).
He reached Fāngtóu (枋頭).
Earlier,
when Máo Dézǔ (毛德祖) was in the north,
Máo Dézǔ (毛德祖) was originally from Xíngyáng (滎陽).
Before Emperor Wǔ (武) took Guān (關) and Luò (洛),
Dézǔ (德祖) came from the north to surrender.
Biǎo (表) was known for his stratagems,
and Dézǔ (德祖) was concerned by this,
so he exchanged letters and messages with him;
he secretly sent someone to persuade Xī Jīn (奚斤),
saying that Biǎo (表) was conspiring with him.
Each time he replied to Biǎo's (表) letters,
he would make many revisions and corrections.
This was the wisdom of Cáo Cāo (曹操) in sowing discord between Hán (韓) and Mǎ (馬).
Shuì (說),
from the fanqie pronunciation 'shū ruì' (輸芮).
Zhì (治),
from the fanqie pronunciation 'zhí zhī' (直之).
Jīn (斤) suspected this and
reported it to the Wèi (魏) ruler.
Previously,
Biǎo (表) and Grand Astrologer Wáng Liàng (王亮) had served in the same camp in their youth,
and Biǎo (表) was fond of slighting Liàng (亮).
Liàng (亮) memorialized,
"Biǎo (表) stationed his army east of Hǔláo (虎牢),
failing to secure a favorable position,
which is why the rebels are not eradicated in time."
The Wèi (魏) ruler had always been fond of numerology,
believed this to be true,
and, accumulating his previous resentments,
sent someone to strangle him in his tent that night.
On the day
Yǐmǎo (乙卯), the Wèi (魏) ruler crossed from Língchāngjīn (靈昌津).
Língchāngjīn (靈昌津)
was formerly Yánjīn (延津);
Shí Lè (石勒) attacked Liú Yào (劉曜),
his route passed through here,
and he considered the frozen river a divine aid,
so he renamed it Língchāngjīn (靈昌津).
Shūsūn Jiàn (叔孫建) led thirty thousand cavalry to approach Dōngyángchéng (東陽城).
The city's civil and military personnel numbered only fifteen hundred.
Zhú Kuí (竺夔) and Yuán Miáo (垣苗) exerted all their strength to defend it,
occasionally sending out surprise troops to attack Wèi (魏),
defeating them.
The Wèi (魏) infantry and cavalry arrayed themselves around the city for over ten *lǐ* (里),
constructing many siege engines.
Kuí (夔) dug four layers of moats.
The Wèi (魏) people filled three of them
and made battering rams to attack the city.
Kuí (夔) sent people out from underground tunnels
to pull them down with large hemp ropes, causing them to break.
The Wèi (魏) people then constructed a long siege wall,
pressing the attack more urgently.
As time went on,
the city walls gradually collapsed,
many warriors died or were wounded,
and the remaining troops were exhausted,
on the verge of falling at any moment.
Tán Dàojì (檀道濟) reached Péngchéng (彭城).
Since both Sī (司) and Qīng (青) prefectures were in dire straits,
and his commanded troops were few,
insufficient to divide and send to both;
Qīngzhōu (青州) was closer,
and Zhú Kuí's (竺夔) forces were weaker,
so he and Wáng Zhòngdé (王仲德) proceeded rapidly to relieve it first.
On the day Jiǎzǐ (甲子),
Liú Cuì (劉粹) sent Lǐ Yuándé (李元德) to attack Xǔchāng (許昌),
beheading Yǔ Lóng (庾龍).
Yuándé (元德) then stayed to pacify and comfort the people,
and also submitted rent and provisions.
The Wèi (魏) ruler arrived at Méngjīn (盟津).
Yú Lìtí (于栗磾) built a pontoon bridge at Yěbǎnjīn (冶阪津).
Guō Yuánshēng's (郭緣生) *Shù Zhēng Jì* (述征記) says: Jiàntǔ (踐土)
is today's Yěbǎnchéng (冶阪城).
The *Shuǐ Jīng Zhù* (水經註) says: The old city of Héyáng (河陽) county is northwest of Yěbǎn (冶阪).
The *Wèi Tǔdì Jì* (魏土地記) says: Yěbǎnchéng (冶阪chéng),
formerly named Hàngzǔdù (漢祖渡),
is a strong and dangerous city,
facing Méngjīn (孟津) to the south,
forty-two *lǐ* (里) northwest of Luòyáng (洛陽).
Méng (盟),
read as Mèng (孟).
On the day Yǐchǒu (乙丑),
the Wèi (魏) ruler led his troops to cross north,
heading west to Hénèi (河內).
É Qīng (娥清), Zhōu Jǐ (周幾), and Lǘ Dàféi (閭大肥) patrolled the land reaching Húlù (湖陸).
The common people of Gāopíng (高平) gathered and shot at them.
Qīng (清) and the others completely attacked and destroyed all the counties of Gāopíng (高平),
wiping out several thousand households,
capturing and plundering over ten thousand people.
Zhèng Shùnzhī (鄭順之), Inspector of Yǎnzhōu (兗州), garrisoned Húlù (湖陸),
but with few troops, he dared not sally forth.
The Wèi (魏) ruler again sent Yīlóu Bá (伊樓拔), Inspector of Bìngzhōu (幷州), to assist Xī Jīn (奚斤) in attacking Hǔláo (虎牢).
Yīlóu (伊婁),
a barbarian compound surname.
Lóu (樓) is the same as Lóu (婁).
Many Wèi (魏) soldiers were killed,
and the generals and soldiers gradually became scattered.
In summer,
in the fourth month,
on the *dīngmǎo* day,
the Wei ruler went to Chénggāo,
cutting off the road from Hǔláo to the Jí River.
According to the *Běi Shǐ*: Hǔláo lacked water,
and within the city, they used ropes and buckets to draw water from the river.
The Wei ruler ordered connected ships to be fitted with *fénwēn* (mantlets) on top,
cutting off their water-drawing path.
He personally supervised the attack on the city,
but was ultimately unable to conquer it.
He then went to Luòyáng to view the Stone Classics.
The Stone Classics
were those written by Cài Yōng in the Later Hàn dynasty.
A detailed note can be found in Volume 57, under the fourth year of Xīpíng during Emperor Líng of Hàn.
Shūsūn Jiàn attacked Dōngyáng,
demolishing about thirty paces of its northern wall.
Diāo Yǒng asked for a swift entry,
but Jiàn refused,
and thus they failed to conquer it.
When he heard that Tán Dàojì and others were approaching,
Yǒng again said to Jiàn:
“The bandits fear the imperial army’s crack cavalry,
and will form a defensive *hánchén* (enclosed formation) with linked chariots.
*Hánchén*
means a square formation.
*Chén*
is read as *zhèn*.
The terrain is narrow everywhere,
and chariots cannot move abreast.
I ask to lead the five thousand recruited soldiers to hold the strategic passes and intercept them;
we will surely defeat them.”
At that time, the weather was hot,
and many Wei soldiers suffered from pestilence.
Jiàn said:
“More than half of the soldiers are sick with plague.
If we continue to hold out,
the soldiers will die out on their own.
Why do we need to fight again?
Returning with the whole army now
is the best plan.”
On the *jǐsì* day,
Dàojì’s army was at Línqú.
On the *rénshēn* day,
Jiàn and others burned their camp and equipment and fled.
Dàojì arrived at Dōngyáng,
but his provisions were exhausted,
so he could not pursue.
Zhú Kuí, seeing that Dōngyáng city was ruined
and indefensible,
moved his garrison to Bùqí city.
Bùqí county
belonged to Lángyé Commandery in the Former Hàn,
to Dōnglái Commandery in the Later Hàn,
and to Chángguǎng Commandery in the Jìn.
Rú Chún said: *Qí*
is pronounced *jī*.
Xián said: The old city of Bùqí
is in the southwest of modern Láizhōu’s Jìmò county.
Shūsūn Jiàn went from Dōngyáng towards Huátái.
Dàojì dispatched Wáng Zhòngdé towards Yǐnmǎo.
Dàojì stationed his army at Húlù.
Before Zhòngdé reached Yǐnmǎo,
he heard that the Wei army had already gone far,
so he returned to Dàojì.
Diāo Yǒng then remained to garrison Yǐnmǎo,
gathering over five thousand families of people from Qiáo, Liáng, Péng, and Pèi,
and establishing twenty-seven camps to lead them.
12 The Man king, Méi’ān, led dozens of chieftains to pay tribute to Wei.
Initially,
the various Man peoples originally lived between the Jiāng and Huái rivers.
Later, their tribes spread and multiplied,
extending over several prefectures,
east to Shòuchūn,
west to Bā and Shǔ,
north to Rǔ and Yǐng,
found almost everywhere.
During the Wei era, they were not much of a threat.
But by the Jìn,
they gradually became more numerous and prosperous,
and increasingly acted as brigands.
When Liú and Shí brought chaos to the Central Plains,
the various Man had no scruples,
and gradually moved north again.
South of Yīquè,
they filled the mountains and valleys.
According to history,
these Man peoples were descendants of Pánhù.
The character *fù*
is pronounced as *fú yòu fān* (a traditional fanqiè pronunciation guide).
13 The Heir Apparent of Hexī, Zhèngdé, attacked Jìnchāng
and conquered it.
Táng Qì, his brother Hé, and nephew Lǐ Bǎo all fled to Yīwú.
Táng Qì rebelled against Hexī at Jìnchāng.
See the second year of Yǒngchū in Emperor Wǔ’s reign.
Those who surrendered reached over two thousand families,
and they became vassals of Ròurán.
Ròurán made Qì the King of Yīwú.
14 Qín King Chìpán said to his retainers:
“Although Sòng now possesses Jiāngnán,
and the Xià people are powerfully entrenched in Guānzhōng,
neither is worth collaborating with.
Only the Wei ruler is heroic and martial through generations,
with worthy and capable individuals employed by him.
Moreover, a prophecy says,
‘To the north of Héngdài, there will be a True Man.’
I will lead my entire state to serve him.”
So he sent the Secretariat Director Mòzhě Āhú and others to meet the Wei ruler,
offering two hundred *jīn* of gold,
and also presenting a strategy for attacking Xià.
15 In the intercalary month,
on the *dīngwèi* day,
the Wei ruler went to Hénèi,
ascended Tàiháng,
and reached Gāodū.
Gāodū county had belonged to Shàngdǎng Commandery since the Hàn dynasty.
Liú Xù said: Táng’s Zézhōu Jìnchéng county
is the land of Hàn’s Gāodū county.
The character *xíng*
is pronounced *hù gāng fān*.
Shūsūn Jiàn went west from Huátái to join Xī Jīn,
and together they attacked Hǔláo.
Hǔláo was besieged for two hundred days,
with no day without battle.
The elite soldiers were almost all killed in battle,
while the Wei reinforcements kept increasing.
The Wei people destroyed its outer wall.
Máo Dézǔ built three more inner walls to resist them,
but the Wei people destroyed two of them again.
Dézǔ only held one wall,
resisting day and night.
The eyes of the generals and soldiers were all inflamed.
Dézǔ treated them with kindness,
and they never became disloyal.
At that time, Tán Dàojì’s army was at Húlù,
Liú Cuì’s army was at Xiàngchéng,
and Shěn Shūlí’s army was at Gāojiáo.
All feared the strong Wei army
and dared not advance.
On the *dīngsì* day,
the Wei people dug a tunnel to drain the wells within Hǔláo city.
The wells were forty *zhàng* deep.
The mountain terrain was steep,
making it impossible to defend against.
The people and horses in the city suffered from thirst and exhaustion.
The wounded no longer bled,
compounded by hunger and plague.
Wei continued its fierce assault.
On the *jǐwèi* day,
the city fell.
The generals and soldiers wanted to help Dézǔ escape,
but Dézǔ said:
“I swear to perish with this city.
It is not right for the city to fall and for my body to survive!”
The Wei ruler ordered his generals and soldiers:
“Whoever captures Dézǔ
must bring him alive.”
General Dàirén Dòu Dàitián captured Dézǔ and presented him.
Dòu
is a surname.
The *Hàn Shū* mentions Commandant Dòu Rúyì.
All were captured by Wei,
except for the Staff Officer Fàn
Dàojī, who led two hundred men to break through the siege and return south.
Two or three tenths of the Wei soldiers also died from plague.
Xī Jīn and others fully pacified the various commanderies and counties of Sī, Yǎn, and Yù prefectures,
appointing governors and magistrates to govern them.
At this time, all the territory of Sī Prefecture came under Wei control.
The territory of Yǎn Prefecture south of Húlù,
and the territory of Yù Prefecture south of Xiàngchéng,
were all held by Sòng.
Wei had not yet been able to fully pacify all the commanderies and counties.
