The people of Hénán settled down.
Xú Xiànzhī, Fù Liàng, and Xiè Huì, due to the loss of territory,
submitted memorials impeaching themselves.
An imperial edict ordered no inquiry.
16 Xú Xiànzhī’s nephew, the Administrator of Wú Commandery, Pèizhī, often participated in state affairs.
He formed a faction with Attendant Counselor Wáng Sháozhī, Chéng Dàohuì, and Secretariat Clerks Xíng Āntài and Pān Shèng.
At that time, Xiè Huì had been ill for a long time
and was unable to receive guests.
Pèizhī and others suspected him of feigning illness
and having ulterior motives.
So they claimed it was Xiànzhī’s intention and informed Fù Liàng,
wanting Liàng to draft an edict to execute him.
Liàng was then promoted to Central Secretariat Supervisor;
the Central Secretariat was in charge of imperial edicts.
He said: “The three of us received the dying emperor’s entrustment together.
How can we kill each other?
If you gentlemen indeed carry out this matter,
I will simply don my square cap and walk out through the Yèmén.”
The main south gate of the palace was called Duānmén;
the two gates on its sides were called the Left Yèmén and Right Yèmén.
17 In the fifth month,
the Wèi ruler returned to Píngchéng.
Kǎo Yì says: In the chronicle of the Later Wèi emperors:
"In the fifth month, on the day Gēngyín,
returned to Yànmén,"
"on the day Gēngyín,
the imperial carriage arrived from the southern tour."
One of these must be an error,
so neither is accepted here.
18 In the sixth month,
on the day Jǐhài,
Mù Guān, Prince Wénchéng of Yídū of Wèi, died.
19 On the day Bǐngchén,
the Wèi ruler went on a northern tour,
arriving at Cānhébēi.
20 In autumn,
in the seventh month,
Empress Mother Zhāng Fūrén was honored as Empress Dowager.
21 The Wèi ruler went to Sānhuìwūhóuquán.
Wèi Shōu’s Dìxíng Zhì says: Sìlú County of Xiùróng Commandery administered Xīnhuì City;
in the seventh year of Zhēnjūn, Sānhuì City was merged into it.
On the day Xīnchǒu,
he went to Mǎyì
to view the source of the Fèishui River.
22 The Rourán raided Héxī.
Mèng Xùn, Prince of Héxī, ordered his heir apparent Zhèngdé to attack them.
Zhèngdé advanced swiftly with light cavalry to engage in battle
and was killed by the Rourán.
Mèng Xùn then established his second son Xīng as heir apparent.
23 In the ninth month,
on the day Yǐhài,
the Wèi ruler returned to the palace.
He recalled Xī Jīn to Píngchéng,
leaving troops to guard Hǔláo;
he sent É Qīng and Zhōu Jǐ to garrison Fāngtóu;
the households commanded by Sīmǎ Chǔzhī were settled in the four commanderies of Rǔnán, Nányáng, Nándùn, and Xīncài.
Emperor Huì of Jìn had divided Rǔyīn to establish Xīncài Commandery,
and divided Rǔnán to establish Nándùn Commandery.
Wèi did not yet possess the territory of these four commanderies;
they were merely established as provisional administrative divisions.
24 In winter,
in the tenth month,
on the day Guǐmǎo,
the Wèi people expanded the outer wall of the Western Palace,
making its circumference twenty *lǐ*.
This was the Western Palace in Píngchéng,
built by Wèi ruler Guī in the first year of Tiāncì.
25 Regarding the death of Tūfà Nǔtán,
the account can be found in Volume 116, the tenth year of Yìxī during Emperor Ān of Jìn.
Nǔ is pronounced *nú wò*.
He had promised to settle him in the two commanderies of Fānhé and Xī'ān,
and also to lend him troops
to attack Qín,
avenge his father,
and recover his ancestral lands.
Hǔtái secretly agreed to this,
but the plan was leaked and consequently halted.
The empress of Qín ruler Chìpán
was Hǔtái's younger sister.
Chìpán treated her as before.
The empress secretly plotted with Hǔtái, saying:
"Qín was originally our enemy.
Although we are bound by marriage,
that was merely for expediency.
The death of the late king
was not by Heaven's will;
his dying wish not to avenge it
was for the sake of preserving his descendants.
How can a son
serve an enemy as a subject or concubine without thinking of revenge!"
So she conspired with the Wǔwèi general Yuè Zhìluòchéng to assassinate Chìpán.
The empress's sister, who was Chìpán's Left Lady,
learned of their plot and reported it.
Chìpán killed the empress and Hǔtái and more than ten others.
26 In the eleventh month,
Zhōu Jǐ of Wèi raided Xǔchāng.
Xǔchāng fell,
and Lǐ Yuándé, Administrator of Yǐngchuān, fled to Xiàng.
On the day Wùchén,
the Wèi people besieged Rǔyáng.
Wáng Gōngdù, Administrator of Rǔyáng, also fled to Xiàng.
Shěn Yuè says: Jìn Tàikāng Dìzhì and Wáng Yǐn's Dìdào do not mention Rǔyáng Commandery.
It should have been established by the Eastern Jìn by dividing Rǔnán.
Rǔyáng was an old Hàn county
belonging to Rǔnán Commandery.
The Wèi people razed Xǔchāng city,
destroyed Zhōngchéng,
established boundary markers, and then returned.
Zhōngchéng was in the territory of Tài Mountain.
They razed Xǔchāng to establish the boundary of Yù Province and destroyed Zhōngchéng to establish the boundary of Yǎn Province.
Huán (還) can be pronounced *cóng xuān* or as written.
27 On the day Jǐsì,
Wèi Tàizōng died
at the age of thirty-two.
On the day Rénshēn,
Shìzǔ ascended the throne.
Shìzǔ, whose personal name was Táo,
was the eldest son of Emperor Míngyuán.
Xiāo Zǐxiǎn says: Táo's courtesy name was Fólí.
In the twelfth month,
on the day Gēngzǐ,
Wèi buried Emperor Míngyuán at Jīnlíng.
This refers to Jīnlíng in Yúnzhōng.
According to the Běishǐ,
Emperor Dàowǔ was buried at Shènglè Jīnlíng;
it seems that all Wèi imperial tombs were called Jīnlíng.
Dù Yòu says: Hòuwèi's Shènglè County was in Yúnzhōng Commandery.
The Wèi ruler posthumously honored his mother, Imperial Consort Dù Guìpín, as Empress Mì.
Mì is a posthumous title.
He appointed Lú Lǔyuán, Duke of Xiāngchéng, as Zhōngshū Jiàn;
Liú Jié, Duke of Kuàijī, as Shàngshū Lìng;
and Wèi Juàn, Sīwèi Jiàn, Liú Kùrén, Sànqí Shìláng, and six others to divide the administration of the four departments.
Sīwèi Jiàn was an office established by Wèi
to manage the imperial guard.
This is another Liú Kùrén,
not the Liú Kùrén employed by Shíyìjiān.
Wèi is pronounced *yū wù*.
Sàn is pronounced *xī dǎn*.
Qí is pronounced *qí jì*.
The four departments were the Eastern, Western, Southern, and Northern departments.
He was a disciple of Gǔ Zhēn.
Wèi Gǔ Zhēn is mentioned in Volume 106, the tenth year of Tàiyuán during Emperor Xiàowǔ of Jìn.
He appointed the Dài native Luó Jié, Town General of Hénèi, as Shìzhōng and Wàidū Dàguān.
Wèi Shū Guānshì Zhì says: Among the surnames that entered the interior,
the Chìluó clan became the Luó clan.
Wèi had Wàidū Dàguān
and Nèidū Dàguān.
Jiàng (將) is pronounced *jí liàng*.
Jié was one hundred and seven years old at the time,
and his spirit remained vigorous.
Dù Yù says: Shuǎng means clear.
Shìzǔ trusted
and personally employed him, appointing him concurrently as Chángqiū Qīng,
supervising the inner palace, and allowing him to enter and exit the imperial bedchamber.
At one hundred and ten,
he was finally permitted to retire.
Whenever there was a major state affair,
the court would send a rider to consult him.
He died ten years later.
Cuī Hào, Zuo Guānglù Dàfū, deeply researched classics and arts,
and was skilled in institutions and regulations.
Since Wèi and Jìn,
Zuo and You Guānglù Dàfū ranked above Guānglù Dàfū
and were granted gold seals and purple sashes.
Yánjīng means to exhaust one's energy in research.
Imperial decrees and military documents
were all under his management.
Hào did not like the books of Lǎozi and Zhuāngzi,
saying:
"These are false and misleading theories,
which are not close to human nature."
To attribute one's theories to sages and worthies is called *jiǎo* (矯, to pretend);
when sages and worthies did not do such things, and one adds fictitious stories and slanders, that is called *wū* (誣, to falsely accuse).
Hǎo (好) is pronounced *hū dào*.
Jìn is pronounced *qí jìn*.
Confucius's teacher:
Shǐjì and Dàdài Jì both say that Confucius asked Lǎo Dān about rituals.
Dān is pronounced *tā gān*.
He particularly disbelieved in Buddhism,
saying:
"Why serve these Hu barbarian gods!"
When Shìzǔ ascended the throne,
many around him slandered Cuī Hào.
The emperor, having no choice,
ordered Hào to return to his residence as a private citizen.
However, he had always known his virtue,
and whenever there was a difficult issue,
he would summon him for advice.
Hào was slender, delicate, pure, and fair like a beautiful woman.
Xiān means fine;
yán means beautiful.
After returning to his residence,
he then cultivated the arts of diet and nourishing his nature.
At first,
Kòu Qiānzhī (寇謙之), a Daoist priest from Sōngshān (嵩山),
Zàn (讚)'s younger brother,
cultivated the arts of Zhāng Dàolíng (張道陵).
He claimed to have encountered Lǎozi (老子) descending,
who ordered Qiānzhī (謙之) to succeed Dàolíng (道陵) as the Celestial Master.
Zhāng Dàolíng (張道陵)
was a man of the Later Hàn (後漢) dynasty,
who practiced the Five Pecks of Rice Daoism (Wǔdǒumǐ Dào 五斗米道),
commonly known as the Celestial Masters (Tiānshī 天師).
The Daoist codes and precepts of today largely began here.
He also met the divine being Lǐ Pǔwén (李譜文),
who said he was Lǎozi (老子)'s great-grandson.
He bestowed upon him over sixty scrolls of diagrams, talismans, and true scriptures,
instructing him to assist the Tàipíng Zhēnjūn (太平真君) of the north;
he also revealed the method of the Heavenly Palace's Quiet Wheel (Tiāngōng Jìnglún zhī Fǎ 天宮靜輪之法),
a few chapters of which
were Lǐ Jūn (李君)'s own writing.
Qiānzhī (謙之) respectfully presented these writings to the Wèi (魏) emperor.
Many in the court and throughout the land did not believe it,
but Cuī Hào (崔浩) alone treated him as a master,
receiving his techniques.
He also presented a memorial praising and clarifying the matter, saying:
"Your servant has heard that when a sage king receives the Mandate of Heaven,
there must be heavenly responses.
The Hétú (河圖) and Luòshū (洛書) both convey messages through the patterns of insects and beasts.
When the Hér (河) produced the map,
Fúxī (伏羲) used its patterns to draw the Eight Trigrams;
when the Luò (洛) produced the book,
Yǔ (禹) obtained it to arrange the Nine Divisions.
Thus it is said:
'The dragon-map was given to Xī (羲),
the tortoise-book was bestowed upon Sǐ (姒).'
Moreover, the Shàngshū Zhōnghòu (尚書中候) states:
'Yáo (堯) sank a jade disc into the Luò (洛),
and a black tortoise bore a book,
with red patterns and vermilion characters on its back,
stopping by the altar.
Shùn (舜) performed rites at an altar by the Hér (河),
and a yellow dragon bore a rolled-out diagram from the water.'
The handwriting is brilliant,
the words and meaning are profound and subtle,
unmatched since ancient times;
how can one dismiss the command of the High Spirit (Shànglíng 上靈) with common worldly concerns!
Your servant secretly fears this."
The emperor was pleased,
and ordered an usher to offer jade, silk, and sacrificial animals to Sōngyuè (嵩嶽),
bringing in Qiānzhī (謙之)'s disciples who were in the mountains,
to honor the Celestial Master (Tiānshī 天師),
promote the new teachings,
and announce them throughout the realm.
A Celestial Master Daoist temple (Tiānshī Dàochǎng 天師道場) was established southeast of Píngchéng (平城),
with a five-story multi-tiered altar.
The Shuǐjīng Zhù (水經註) says: "To the south, the Shīshuǐ (濕水) flows past the east of Píngchéng (平城);
to the left of the water is a great Daoist altar,
built by Kòu Qiānzhī (寇謙之)."
The Shīshuǐ (濕水) is the same as the Lěishuǐ (灅水).
Each month, a feast (chúhuì 廚會) was held for several thousand people.
Your servant Guāng (光) says: The books of Lǎo (老) and Zhuāng (莊)
primarily aim to equate life and death,
and to take departure and arrival lightly.
Yet those who seek immortality
consume elixirs and cultivate themselves to achieve ascension (qīngjǔ 輕舉),
refining herbs and stones into gold and silver.
Gǔ Yǒng (谷永) said to Emperor Chéng (成) of Hàn (漢):
"All who speak of immortals in the world consuming inexhaustible elixirs,
rising high and ascending lightly,
climbing to the heavens and viewing inverted landscapes,
surveying Xuánpǔ (縣圃),
floating in Pénglái (蓬萊),
and transforming through alchemy (huángyě biànhuà 黃冶變化),
are all wicked people who mislead the masses,
employ heterodox methods,
harbor deceit and falsehood,
to deceive and defraud the rulers of the world."
"Consuming elixirs and cultivating oneself to achieve ascension" is what Gǔ Yǒng (谷永) referred to as "consuming inexhaustible elixirs and rising high and ascending lightly";
"refining herbs and stones into gold and silver" is what Gǔ Yǒng (谷永) referred to as "transforming through alchemy."
This is why Liú Xīn (劉歆)'s Qīlüè (七略) categorized Daoists as philosophers,
and immortals as technical practitioners (fāngjì 方技).
Because they were contradictory,
the Qīlüè (七lüè) could not combine them into one.
Talismanic water and incantations (fúshuǐ jìnzhòu 符水、禁呪) are the arts of Zhāng Dàolíng (張道陵).
Following them to this day,
their errors are grave indeed!
Why did Cuī Hào (崔浩), who disliked the books of Buddhism (Fó 佛) and Daoism (Lǎo 老), believe Qiānzhī (謙之)'s words?
In the past, Zāng Wénzhòng (臧文仲) sacrificed to Yuánjū (爰居),
and Kǒngzǐ (孔子) considered it unwise;
a sea bird, Yuánjū (爰居),避風 sheltered from the wind
and stopped outside the east gate of Lǔ (魯).
Zāng Wénzhòng (臧文仲) ordered the people of the state to sacrifice to it.
Kǒngzǐ (孔子) considered Zāng Wénzhòng (臧文仲) unwise in three things,
and sacrificing to Yuánjū (爰居) was one of them.
How great was this Yuánjū (爰居)!
The Three Hundred Poems (Shī Sānbǎi 詩三百),
can be summed up in one phrase:
"Thoughts without evil."
How can a gentleman not be cautious in choosing his methods!
Niè Chóngqí (聶崇岐) punctuated, Wáng Chóngwǔ (王崇武) proofread.
Sīmǎ Guāng (司馬光)
compiled by imperial decree.
Hòu (後) Xué (學) Tiān (天) Tái (台)
Tàizǔ Wénhuángdì (太祖文皇帝) Shàngzhīshàng (上之上)
His taboo name was Yìlóng (義隆),
his childhood name was Chē'ér (車兒),
the third son of Emperor Wǔ (武帝).
Yuánjiā (元嘉) First Year (Jiǎzǐ, 424 CE)
This year, the reign title was changed in August.
1 Spring,
First Month.
The Kǎoyì (考異) states: "In the Sòng Běnjì (宋本紀):
'On the first day of the First Month, guǐsì (癸巳),
there was a solar eclipse.'
The Sòngjì (宋紀) states
'Second Month, jǐsì (己巳),'
the Sònglüè (宋略) states
'Second Month, guǐsì (癸巳),'
and Lǐ Yánshòu (李延壽)'s Nánshǐ (南史) states
'Second Month, jǐmǎo (己卯) first day.'
All are errors.
According to the Chánglì (長曆),
the first day of the First Month of this year was dīngsì (丁巳), and the first day of the Second Month was dīnghài (丁亥).
The Hòu Wèishū Jì Zhì (後魏書紀、志) state that
there was no solar eclipse this year.
We follow this account now.
2 Bǐngyín (丙寅),
Mí (彌), the Shāng (殤) Prince of Āndìng (安定) of Wèi (魏), died.
3 Yíngyáng Wáng (營陽王) was undignified during mourning,
fond of being intimate with his attendants,
and played without restraint.
Fàn Tài (范泰), a retired Grand Master (Tèjìn Zhìshì 特進致仕), presented a memorial saying:
"Your servant humbly hears that Your Majesty sometimes practices military arts in the rear garden,
with drums and bugles in the palace,
their sounds heard outside.
Militarizing within the imperial women's quarters
and creating clamor within the palace gates
is not only insufficient to awe the Four Barbarians,
but merely gives rise to strange rumors far and near.
When Your Majesty ascended the throne,
you entrusted governance to your ministers,
truly matching the excellence of Gāozōng (高宗)'s three-year mourning period;
but instead you grew close to ignoble persons.
Your servant fears this is not the ultimate plan for the state,
nor the way to govern the world."
He did not listen.
Tài (泰)
was Níng (甯)'s son.
Fàn Níng (范甯),
Wāng (汪)'s son,
was favored by Emperor Xiàowǔ (孝武帝) for his Confucian scholarship.
Lúlíng Wáng (廬陵王) Yìzhēn (義真), the Governor of Nányùzhōu (南豫州),
was intelligent and fond of literature,
but his nature was frivolous and superficial.
He often associated with Xiè Língyùn (謝靈運), Left Guard Commander of the Crown Prince (Tàizǐ Zuǒwèilǜ 太子左衞率), and Yán Yánzhī (顏延之), Member of the Imperial Secretariat (Yuánwài Chángshì 員外常侍).
At the end of Cáo Wèi (曹魏),
the position of Yuánwài Sǎnqí Chángshì (員外散騎常侍) was established.
Lǜ (率),
pronounced suǒ lǜ.
He once said:
"On the day I achieve my ambition,
I will make Língyùn (靈運) and Yánzhī (延之) prime ministers,
and Huìlín (慧琳) the Military Governor of Xīyùzhōu (西豫州)."
Xīyùzhōu (西豫州) was Yùzhōu (豫州).
During the Sòng (宋), Nányùzhōu (南豫州) was governed from Lìyáng (歷陽),
and Yùzhōu (豫zhōu) from Shòuyáng (壽陽).
Shòuyáng (壽陽) was west of Lìyáng (歷陽),
hence Yùzhōu (豫zhōu) was also called Xīyùzhōu (西豫州).
He was Xuán (玄)'s grandson.
Língyùn (靈運)
was Xuán (玄)'s son Huán (瑍)'s son.
They did not abide by laws and regulations;
the imperial court merely regarded them as literary figures,
not considering them to have practical utility.
Língyùn (靈yùn) considered his talents suitable for participation in key governmental affairs,
and often felt resentful.
Yánzhī (延之)
was Hán (含)'s great-grandson.
Yán Hán (顏含) is mentioned in Volume 96, during Jìn (晉) Emperor Chéng (成)'s Xiánkāng (咸康) fourth year.
Xú Xiànzhī and others disliked Yìzhēn associating with Língyùn and others.
Yìzhēn’s former subordinate Fàn Yàn cautiously admonished him,
but Yìzhēn said:
“Língyùn is superficial and unlearned;
Yánzhī is narrow-minded and petty.
They are what Emperor Wén of Wèi referred to as ‘men of letters throughout history who generally do not guard their minor conduct.’
However,
it is merely what their nature dictates;
I cannot forget their words while appreciating them.”
Wù
means to awaken and enlighten.
Shǎng
means to commend and praise.
For criticizing and slandering the regents,
Língyùn was sent out as the Grand Administrator of Yǒngjiā,
and Yánzhī as the Grand Administrator of Shǐ’ān.
When Yìzhēn arrived at Lìyáng,
he made many demands.
The regents always judiciously weighed them and did not grant all.
Cái
means to regulate.
Liàng
means to measure.
Suǒ,
pronounced according to Shān Kè’s reading.
Liàng,
pronounced as liáng.
He often expressed dissatisfaction,
and also submitted a memorial requesting to return to the capital.
Cányì Cānjūn Hé Shàngzhī of Lújiāng repeatedly admonished him,
but he did not listen.
At that time, Xiànzhī and others had already secretly plotted to depose the Emperor,
and the next in line should have been Yìzhēn.
Thus, taking advantage of the rift between Yìzhēn and the Emperor,
they first presented a list of his crimes and transgressions,
deposed him as a commoner,
and exiled him to Xīn’ān Commandery.
The former Magistrate of Jíyáng, Zhāng Yuēzhī of Tángyì, submitted a memorial, saying:
Jíyáng County belonged to Lúlíng Commandery.
Now Jízhōu has Jíshuǐ County.
It was probably during the Wú dynasty that a county was established south of Jíshuǐ,
and thus named.
“The Prince of Lúlíng received the benevolent and compassionate treatment of the late Emperor in his youth,
and the affectionate and loving grace of Your Majesty in his maturity.
Therefore, what is in his heart he must speak,
and what he harbors he must clarify.
Liàng
means sincere,
clear,
and to guide.
It means that whatever Yìzhēn harbored in his heart,
he sincerely believed to be right,
and would certainly clarify and guide it,
without any evasion.
Shào,
pronounced according to Shī Zhào’s reading.
Zhǎng,
pronounced according to Zhī Liǎng’s reading.
This led him to incur the fault of arrogance and willfulness.”
It means that he might have committed acts that violated the duties of a subject,
leading to the crime of arrogance and willfulness.
“He truly possesses excellent virtues
and ought to be tolerated and nurtured,
recording his good deeds and concealing his flaws,
instructing him fully in the path of righteousness,
and advancing or withdrawing him gradually.
Now, to arbitrarily inflict humiliation and disgrace upon him,
and exile him to a distant commandery—
Bōrǔ
means to strip him of his title and reduce him to a commoner.
The decree has made those near and far disheartened and at a loss.
Your servant humbly reflects that the great Sòng dynasty is in its initial stages of establishment,
its roots and branches not yet numerous.
It is fitting to extensively establish imperial relatives and in-laws as bulwarks,
and to foster harmony and affection through the proper way.
Who among men is without fault?
The valuable thing is to be able to reform oneself.
As the beloved son of Emperor Wǔ and
Your Majesty’s admirable younger brother,
how can he be perpetually abandoned
for a single blemish?!”
When the memorial was submitted,
Yuēzhī was made a Cānjūn in the Liangzhōu Prefectural Office,
and soon after, he was killed.
4 In summer,
the fourth month,
on the day of Jiǎchén,
the Wèi ruler made an eastern tour to Dàníng.
5 Qín King Chìpán sent Zhènnán Jiāngjūn Jí Pí and others to lead an army of ten thousand infantry and cavalry to campaign south against the four states of Báigǒu, Chēfú, Cuī Tí, and Pángwéi.
All surrendered.
The state of Báigǒu still existed until the Táng dynasty;
it was probably inhabited by Qiāng tribes;
its territory bordered Dōnghuì Prefecture.
Chēfú, Cuī Tí, and Pángwéi are unidentifiable.
Shuài,
read as shuài.
Qí,
pronounced according to Qí Jì’s reading.
Jiàng,
pronounced according to Hù Jiāng’s reading.
6 Xú Xiànzhī and others considered that the Cìshǐ of Nányǎnzhōu, Tán Dàojì,
Shěn Yuē said: “When the Central Plains were in chaos,
many northern refugees moved south.
Emperor Chéng of Jìn established Nányǎn Prefecture,
with its temporary seat at Jīngkǒu;
Emperor Wén first delimited the region between the Jiāng and Huái rivers as its territory,
with its seat at Guǎnglíng.”
held sway over the palace and government,
and moreover possessed troops.
So they summoned Dàojì and the Cìshǐ of Jiāngzhōu, Wáng Hóng, to court.
In the fifth month,
both arrived in Jiànkāng,
and were informed of the plan to depose and enthrone a new emperor.
On the day of Jiǎshēn,
Xiè Huì, using the pretext that the roof of the Lǐngjūn mansion was damaged,
ordered all his household members to go outside,
and gathered his generals and soldiers inside the mansion.
He also had Zhōngshū Shèrén Xíng Āntài and Pān Shèng act as internal agents.
At night,
he invited Tán Dàojì to stay overnight with him.
Huì was agitated and could not sleep,
but Dàojì fell asleep as soon as he lay down.
Huì admired him for this.
He admired his ability to handle major affairs without altering his normal demeanor.
At that time, the Emperor had set up stalls in Huálínyuán,
personally engaging in buying and selling.
He also took pleasure in boating with his attendants.
In the evening,
he was cruising on the Tiānyuān Pond,
and fell asleep on the imperial boat.
At dawn on the day of Yǐyǒu,
Dàojì led his troops at the front,
with Xiànzhī and others following behind,
entering through the Yúnlóng Gate.
Āntài and others had already warned the palace guards,
so none offered resistance.
The Emperor had not yet risen when
the soldiers advanced and killed two attendants,
wounded the Emperor’s finger,
helped him out to the East Pavilion,
seized the imperial seals and ribbons,
made all the officials bow and take leave,
and escorted him to the former Crown Prince’s palace.
Shìzhōng Chéng Dàohuì advised Xiànzhī and others to enthrone the Emperor’s younger brother, Yìgōng, the Cìshǐ of Nányùzhōu.
Xiànzhī and others, however, considered Yìlóng, the Prince of Yídū, to have always enjoyed a good reputation,
and also many auspicious omens.
In the beginning of Jǐngpíng era,
a black dragon was seen in the west,
followed by five-colored clouds.
In the second year,
purple clouds appeared over the city of Jiānglíng,
and all who observed the astral phenomena believed them to be omens of an emperor,
who would arise in the west.
Moreover, from west of Jiānglíng to Shàngmíng,
and east to Jiāngjīn,
there were ninety-nine islets in between.
The Chǔ proverb says:
“When the islets reach one hundred,
a king shall emerge.”
At this time, an islet suddenly appeared naturally,
formed by the flowing currents and eddies.
All these were responses to the rise of the superior dragon.
They recounted the Emperor’s many transgressions,
deposed him as the Prince of Yíngyáng,
and had the Prince of Yídū succeed to the great imperial lineage,
pardoning all crimes below capital punishment.
They also issued an edict in the name of the Empress Dowager,
respectfully returning the imperial seals and ribbons.
Furthermore, they deposed the Empress as the Princess of Yíngyáng,
and moved the Prince of Yíngyáng to Wú.
Tán Dàojì was sent to guard the imperial court.
When the Prince arrived in Wú,
he stayed at Jīnchāng Pavilion.
In the sixth month,
on the day of Guǐchǒu,
Xiànzhī and others sent Xíng Āntài to assassinate him.
The Prince, being very strong,
broke out and ran towards Chāng Gate.
Jīnchāng Pavilion was inside Chāng Gate.
Sūn Quán’s records state: Chāngmén
was the western gate of the Wú outer city wall,
built by Fūchā;
because the heavenly gate connects to Chānghé,
it was named so.
Later, Lord Chūnshēn renamed it Chāng Gate.
Jīnchāng Pavilion was so called because it was inside the western gate.
Péi Zǐyě (裴子野) remarked: In ancient times, when a monarch raised his sons,
they were taught rhetoric by a master once they could speak,
and instructed in etiquette by a tutor when they could walk.
However, the education in the Sòng (宋) dynasty
was markedly different from this.
Indoors, they relied on servants and concubines;
outdoors, they kept close to attendants and runners.
The crown princes and imperial princes
had a shuài (帥) [commander]
and a shì (侍) [attendant].
These two positions
were both occupied by common functionaries.
In the Zuǒ Zhuàn (左傳), Shēn Wúyǔ (申無宇) said: "Scholars serve common functionaries;
servants serve attendants."
When the principles were transmitted to them,
and good and evil were conveyed,
none failed to follow them.
Their words did not touch upon ritual and righteousness;
their understanding did not reach back to the past or extend to the present.
The prudent could be encouraged to be parsimonious,
while the foolish might be enticed into wickedness.
Although there were masters and tutors,
they were often elderly grandees.
Although there were friends and literary companions,
they were often young men of wealthy families.
They merely filled the positions
and did not even associate with them.
A prince had one literary companion, one master, and one friend,
which was the ultimate Jìn (晉) system.
According to the Lǐ (禮):
"Fifty is called ài (艾) [aged],
serving in official government positions;
sixty is called qí (耆) [old],
directing others."
Kǒng Yǐngdá (孔穎達) said: "Ài (艾) means
that one's strength has already declined at fifty,
and one's hair is white like moxa."
Hè Yáng (賀瑒) said: "Qí (耆) means
to reach,
reaching the state of old age."
Shào (少) is read as "zhào (照)" in Shī (詩).
The Chángshǐ (長史) carried out affairs,
proclaiming teachings and commands.
Xíngshì (行事) means
to manage affairs of the prefecture and province.
They were often arbitrary and presumptuous,
secretly wielding power and authority.
The Nán Shǐ (南史) says: "Traditionally,
when discussing matters within the departments of the prefectural and provincial governments,
all matters discussed were first written on a slip;
afterwards it would say
'Respectfully noted,'
and below the date, it would also say
'Such-and-such official noted it.'
Therefore, prefectures and provinces established diǎnqiān (典籤) to manage this."
Originally fifth-rank officials,
they were changed to scholar-officials in the early Sòng (宋).
In the late Sòng (宋),
many young imperial princes were made regional governors.
The emperor at the time had close attendants lead the diǎnqiān (典籤),
and their authority thus became significant.
When the successor was young and immature,
and the lineage was filled with treachery,
even if evil and depraved individuals
arose naturally,
habit would make it commonplace,
and its influence would be far-reaching.
By the time of Tài Zōng (太宗),
he abandoned the entire realm,
which was also due to the influence of those close to him.
Alas!
Those who possess a state or a family,
take heed of this!
Péi Zǐyě (裴子野) thoroughly discussed the calamity of the Sòng (宋) dynasty's downfall.
The Tōng Jiàn (通鑑) records it here
to make those who possess a state or a family cautious from the very beginning.
7 Fù Liàng (傅亮) led the officials of the xíngtái (行臺) to greet the Yídū Wáng (宜都王) in Jiānglíng (江陵) with the imperial carriage.
The Cíbù Shàngshū (祠部尚書), Cài Kuò (蔡廓),
after the Jìn (晉) dynasty crossed the Jiāng (江),
first had the position of Cíbù Shàngshū (祠部尚書).
This position often shared duties with the Yòu Púyè (右僕射) [Right Grand Secretariat].
It was not permanently established;
the Yòu Púyè (右僕射) would act in its stead.
If the Yòu Púyè (右僕射) was vacant,
then the Cíbù Shàngshū (祠部尚書) would temporarily take charge of the right-hand affairs.
He fell ill and could not proceed.
Fù Liàng (傅亮) bade him farewell.
Cài Kuò (蔡廓) said:
"Yíngyáng (營陽) is in Wú (吳).
He should be offered ample provisions.
Should an misfortune suddenly occur,
you gentlemen will have the name of regicides.
Do you wish to establish yourselves in the world?
How can that be possible!"
At that time, Fù Liàng (傅亮) had already discussed with Xiànzhī (羨之) harming the Yíngyáng Wáng (營陽王).
He immediately sent a hurried message to stop it,
but it was too late.
Xiànzhī (羨之) was furious and said:
"To plot with someone
and then immediately turn around and betray them by speaking ill of them!"
Xuánbèi (旋背) is like
what modern people call zhuǎnbèi (轉背).
Bèi (背) is read as it is written.
The Kǎo Yì (考異) states: In the Běnjì (本紀) of the Sòng Nán Shǐ (宋南史),
below "In the second month, Yìzhēn (義真) was deposed and exiled to Xīn'ān (新安),"
it immediately says:
"The regents sent envoys to execute Yìzhēn (義真) in Xīn'ān (新安)."
The Sòng Yìzhēn Zhuàn (宋義真傳) says:
"On guǐwèi (癸未) of the sixth month,
Xiànzhī (羨之) and others sent envoys to kill Yìzhēn (義真) at his place of exile."
The Xiànzhī Zhuàn (羨之傳) also says:
"After the deposed emperor,
Yìzhēn (義真) was killed in Xīn'ān (新安),
and the emperor was killed in Wú Xiàn (吳縣)."
According to the Cháng Lì (長曆),
the first day of the sixth month was gēngyín (庚寅),
so there was no guǐwèi (癸未).
It was probably guǐchǒu (癸丑).
Xiànzhī (羨之), considering the importance of the Jīngzhōu (荊州) region,
feared that if the Yídū Wáng (宜都王) arrived, he might appoint different people.

So he immediately issued a lùmìng (錄命) [appointment order from the Secretariat] to appoint the Lǐngjūn Jiāngjūn (領軍將軍), Xiè Huì (謝晦), as acting Dūdū Jīng-Xiāng Děng Qī Zhōu Zhū Jūshì (都督荊‧湘等七州諸軍事) [Grand Coordinator of Military Affairs of Jīng (荊), Xiāng (湘), and other seven provinces] and Jīngzhōu Cìshǐ (荊州刺史) [Governor of Jīngzhōu (荊州)].
Lùmìng (錄命) means
an order issued by the Lù Shàngshū (錄尚書) [Director of the Imperial Secretariat] himself.
Elite troops and veteran generals
were all assigned to him.
This was how Xiànzhī (羨之), Fù Liàng (傅亮), and Xiè Huì (謝晦) planned for their own sakes,
but it did not save them from the punishment of deposition and regicide.
Yī (伊) and Huò (霍) acted with utmost public impartiality and sincerity,
but the record by Shī Chūn (師春) differs from the books.
Perhaps they did not envy Yī Yǐn (伊尹) and Huò Guāng (霍光) who could only preserve themselves but not their clans.
This is a great change of heaven and earth,
truly difficult for a minister to endure.
Jiāng (將) is read as "liàng (亮)" in the fanqiè.
In autumn,
seventh month,
the xíngtái (行臺) arrived in Jiānglíng (江陵).
A temporary gate was erected south of the city,
inscribed
"Dà Sīmǎ Mén" (大司馬門) [Gate of the Grand Marshal].
Fù Liàng (傅亮) led the officials to the gate to present a memorial,
offering the imperial seals and regalia.
The ceremony was very grand.
The Yídū Wáng (宜都王) was eighteen years old at the time.
He issued an edict saying:
"Unworthily and undutifully,
I have been mistakenly bestowed with this great mandate.
Reflecting on myself, I am filled with trepidation.
How can I possibly bear this!
I shall temporarily return to the imperial court
to express my sorrow at the imperial tombs,
and to convey my thoughts to worthy gentlemen.
I hope you will understand my heart
and not make excessive remarks."
The subordinate officials of the prefecture and province all declared themselves ministers
and requested to inscribe placards on all gates,
entirely following the palace regulations.
The king refused them all.
He ordered the gāngjì (綱紀) of the provinces, prefectures, and the state to pardon those under their jurisdiction who were currently undergoing punishment
and to remit outstanding debts.
Zhōu (州) refers to
Jīngzhōu (荊州);
fǔ (府) refers to
the Dūdū Fǔ (都督府);
guó (國) refers to
the Yídū Guó (宜都國);
gāngjì (綱紀) refers to
senior assistants and subordinate clerks.
Jiàn (見) is read as "xiánbiàn (賢遍)".
Bū (逋) means
to owe or
to be in debt.
Zé (責) is read as it is written,
and also as "zéxiè (仄懈)".
In the Hàn Shū Gāo Jì (漢書高紀): "Both families tore up the contracts and discarded the debts,"
without a tone mark.
In the Huáiyáng Wáng Zhuàn (淮陽王傳): "Zhāng Bó (張博) was responsible for debts," read as "zéxiè (仄懈)".
When the various generals and aides heard that the kings of Yíngyáng and Lúlín were dead,
they were all suspicious,
and advised Wáng not to go east.
Sīmǎ Wáng Huá said:
"The late emperor had great achievements for the realm,
and was obeyed by all within the four seas;
although the successor ruler was not disciplined,
people's expectations have not changed.
Xú Xiànzhī is a mediocre commoner,
Fù Liàng a common scholar,
it is clear they do not possess the ambition of Jìn Xuāndì or Wáng Dàjiāngjūn;
Wáng Dàjiāngjūn,
refers to Dūn.
They would not dare to immediately betray their virtue.
Fearing Lúlín's harsh judgment,
they will certainly not tolerate themselves in the future;
knowing Your Highness's magnanimity, sagacity, compassion, and benevolence,
which is known far and wide,
they will even go out of their way to respectfully welcome you,
hoping to demonstrate their virtue;
hoping to establish their virtue by settling the plan.
This is probably not the case.
Furthermore,
Xú Xiànzhī and the other five men,
sharing the same achievements and positions,
who among them would be willing to yield to another!
The five men,
refer to Xú Xiànzhī, Fù Liàng, Xiè Huì, Tán Dàojì, and Wáng Hóng.
Their scheme is bound to fail.
If the deposed ruler were still alive,
fearing future calamities,
they resorted to this killing;
this is likely due to an excessive desire to live,
how could they dare to harbor rebellious intentions all of a sudden!
They merely wish to grasp power to secure themselves,
relying on the young ruler.
Your Highness should simply drive forward with your six reins,
to fulfill the desires of Heaven and man."
Wáng said:
"Are you trying to be Sòng Chāng again! "
Chief Clerk Wáng Tánshǒu and Southern Man Colonel Dào Yànzhī all urged Wáng to proceed.
A family record states: Dào's ancestry is from Gāoyángshì,
a descendant of the Chu prime minister Qū Dào;
in the Later Hàn, there was Dōngpíng Prefect Dào Zhì.
Tán,
read tú hán fān.
Wáng then said:
"All of you have received the late emperor's dying instructions,
it is not permissible to betray justice.
Moreover, there are loyal ministers and old generals,
both inside and outside the court,
and now our military strength is sufficient to control matters,
what is there to doubt! "
Thereupon, he ordered Wáng Huá to be in charge of the rear and
remain to guard Jīngzhōu.
Wáng wanted Dào Yànzhī to lead the vanguard,
but Yànzhī said:
"If we are certain they will not rebel,
Liǎo,
means to know for sure.
Jiàng,
read jí liàng fān.
but if there is any doubt,
this army would not be reliable enough,
and it would further open up a source of suspicion and discord,
which is not how we should fulfill the hopes of those near and far. "
Yànzhī's words were indeed in line with great principles,
and he also knew that his talent was insufficient to control Tán Dàojì.
So, Yànzhī was sent to provisionally guard Xiāngyáng.
On the Jiǎxū day,
Wáng departed from Jiānglíng.
He granted an audience to Fù Liàng,
and wept bitterly,
moving everyone around him.
Afterward, he asked about the details of Yìzhēn and the young emperor's deposition and death,
and he cried with sobs,
so that those attending could not bear to look up.
Liàng's back was drenched in sweat,
unable to reply;
he then revealed his innermost thoughts to Dào Yànzhī, Wáng Huá, and others,
deeply ingratiating himself with them.
Wáng had his palace and provincial civil and military officials heavily guard him,
preventing the officials and numerous forces dispatched by the court from approaching his units.
Zhū Róngzǐ, the Staff Officer of the Central Army, stood with a sword outside the door of Wáng's boat,
not unbuckling his belt for several tens of days.
This was to guard against extraordinary events.
Chù,
read chāng lǚ fān.
8 The Wèi ruler returned to his palace.
9 Qín Wáng Chìpán sent his Crown Prince Mùmò, Commander of the Expeditionary North Mù Yìgān and others, with thirty thousand infantry and cavalry, to sortie from Diāoqú Valley,
attacking Báicǎolǐng and Línsōng Commandery in Hexi,
and defeated them all.
Shuǐjīngzhù: Southeast of Xīpíng Xiāngǔ Fortress is Báicǎolǐng.
Shuài,
read as shuài.
Qí,
read qí jì fān.
10 In the eighth month,
on the Bǐngshēn day,
the King of Yídū arrived in Jiànkāng.
All the ministers greeted him with bows at Xīntíng.
Xú Xiànzhī asked Fù Liàng:
"Who can Wáng be compared to?"
Liàng replied:
"Greater than Jìn Wén and Jǐng."
Xiànzhī said:
"He will surely understand my true loyalty."
Liàng said:
"Not so."
Liàng certainly knew he would not escape.
On the Dīngyǒu day,
Wáng visited Chūnínglíng,
and upon returning,
stopped at the Central Hall.
Jìn Xiàowǔ, considering the Imperial Academy was south of the Qínhuái River,
far from the imperial city,
temporarily used the Central Hall as the Imperial Academy,
and personally offered sacrifices to the Former Sages.
Thus, the Central Hall was also north of the Qínhuái,
but outside the imperial city.
The officials presented the imperial seal and sash,
Shòu,
pronounced shòu.
He then accepted them,
and immediately ascended the imperial throne in the Central Hall.
He entered the palace with the full imperial retinue,
and held court in the Great Ultimate Front Hall,
issued a great amnesty,
changed the era name,
and granted civil and military officials two ranks.
On the Wùxū day,
he paid respects at the Imperial Ancestral Temple.
An edict restored the former enfeoffment of the King of Lúlín,
and brought his coffin and his granddaughters Xiūhuá and Xiè back to Jiànkāng.
Sūn Xiūhuá,
was Yìzhēn's mother;
Xiè,
was Yìzhēn's sister.
Nán Shǐ states: Emperor Wǔ of Jìn adopted the system of Hàn and Wèi,
with Shū, Shūyuán, Shūyí, Xiūhuá, Xiūróng, Xiūyí, Jiéyú, Rónghuá, Chōnghuá,
these were the nine imperial concubines (Jǐupín),
their rank equivalent to the nine ministers.
Lǐ Yánshòu said: Guìpín was instituted by Emperor Wén of Wèi;
Fūrén was instituted by Emperor Wǔ of Wèi when he first established the state of Wèi;
Guìrén was instituted by Emperor Guāngwǔ of Hàn;
Jìn had three Fūrén,
their rank equivalent to the three dukes.
Shū was instituted by Emperor Míng of Wèi;
Shūyuán was instituted by Emperor Wén of Wèi;
Shūyí and Xiūhuá were instituted by Emperor Wǔ of Jìn;
Xiūróng was instituted by Emperor Wén of Wèi;
Xiūyí was instituted by Emperor Míng of Wèi;
Jiéyú and Rónghuá were old titles from the Former Hàn;
Chōnghuá was instituted by Emperor Wǔ of Jìn;
Měirén was instituted by Emperor Guāngwǔ of Hàn.
On the Gēngzǐ day,
acting Jīngzhōu Inspector Xiè Huì was made the permanent inspector.
As Huì was about to depart,
he bade farewell to Cài Kuò,
and privately asked him:
"Will I escape this?"
Kuò replied:
"You received the late emperor's dying mandate,
were entrusted with the state,
deposed the incompetent and established the enlightened,
which is entirely justifiable.
However, you killed two elder brothers and now face him from the north,
wielding the power to shake the ruler,
occupying a strategically important upstream position.
Judging the present by the past,
it will be difficult for you to escape."
Cài Kuò and his son were known for their uprightness and integrity in the Sòng dynasty.
Observing his unreserved and straightforward speech,
it seemed insufficient to preserve his life;
yet, he was able to live out his days with his reputation intact,
why was this?
It was probably because his conduct had always earned people's trust,
and his speaking on matters without evasion
also served to uphold his uprightness.
As for the one who asked him,
he was then troubled by gain and loss,
and sought a decision from him,
so listening to him naturally accorded with his heart,
and how could he dare to treat it as a taboo!
After departing,
he looked back at Shítou City and joyfully said:
"Now I have escaped!"
In the Guǐmǎo year,
Xú Xiànzhī was promoted to Sītú.
Wáng Hóng was promoted to Sīkōng.
Fù Liàng was granted the additional title of Kāifǔ Yítóng Sānsī.
Xiè Huì was promoted to the title of Wèi Jiāngjūn.
Tán Dàojì was promoted to the title of Zhēngběi Jiāngjūn.
Xiè Huì was promoted from Lǐngjūn Jiāngjūn.
Tán Dàojì was promoted from Zhènběi Jiāngjūn.
The relevant officials proposed that the imperial carriage should, as was customary, proceed to Huálín Yuán to hear lawsuits.
An imperial edict stated:
"My understanding of governance and punishments is still limited;
as before,
the two dukes may hear and investigate the cases."
The "two dukes"
referred to Xú Xiànzhī and Wáng Hóng.
The Emperor appointed Wáng Tánshǒu and Wáng Huá as Shìzhōng.
Tánshǒu also held the title of Yòuwèi Jiāngjūn.
Huá also held the title of Xiāoqí Jiāngjūn.
Zhū Róngzǐ was appointed Yòujūn Jiāngjūn.
Emperor Míng of Wèi had a Zuǒjūn Jiāngjūn.
Emperor Wǔ of Jìn established the Qiánjūn and Yòujūn,
and also established the Hòujūn,
making these the four armies.
Xiāoqí Jiāngjūn and Yóují Jiāngjūn
were both miscellaneous generals' titles from the Hàn dynasty;
Wèi established them as Zhongjūn.
During the Jìn dynasty,
the Lǐng, Hù, Zuǒwèi, Yòuwèi, Xiāoqí, and Yóují formed the Six Armies.
Xiāo
is pronounced "jiān yáo fān".
Qí
is pronounced "qí jì fān".
In the Jiǎchén year,
the Emperor's mother, Hú Jiéyú, was posthumously honored as Zhāng Huánghòu.
The Emperor's younger brother Yìgōng was enfeoffed as the Prince of Jiāngxià.
Yìxuān as the Prince of Jìnglíng.
Yìjì as the Prince of Héngyáng.
Yìxuān was also appointed Zuǒjiāngjūn,
and stationed at Shítóu.
Xú Xiànzhī and others wished to immediately appoint Dào Yànzhī to Yōngzhōu,
but the Emperor refused.
Yànzhī was summoned to be Zhōnglǐngjūn,
and entrusted with military affairs.
When Yànzhī traveled south from Xiāngyáng,
Xiè Huì had already arrived at his post,
fearing that Yànzhī would not pass through his territory.
When Yànzhī reached Yángkǒu,
he traveled on foot to Jiānglíng,
expressing deep sincerity.
Huì also established strong ties with him.
Yànzhī left his horse, a sharp sword, and a famous blade for Huì,
which greatly reassured Huì.
Ròurán's Héshengài Kèhán heard that Emperor Tàizōng of Wèi had died,
and leading sixty thousand cavalry, entered Yúnzhōng.
He massacred and plundered officials and common people,
and attacked and captured Shènglè Gōng.
Shíyìjiān, an ancestor of Wèi, first resided in Shènglè Gōng in Yúnzhōng,
and built Shènglè Chéng eight *lǐ* south of the old city.
Hé
is pronounced "hù gǔ fān".
Kè
follows "kān rù shēng".
Hán
has the sound "hán".
Jiāng
is pronounced "jí liàng fān".
Qí
is pronounced "qí jì fān".
Lè
has the sound "luò".
In three days and two nights, they reached Yúnzhōng.
Héshengài led his cavalry to surround the Wèi ruler over fifty layers deep,
with the cavalry pressing close to the horses' heads,
one after another like a wall.
The generals and soldiers were greatly frightened,
but the Wèi ruler's demeanor remained calm,
and thus the morale of the multitude stabilized.
Héshengài appointed his nephew Yú Zhìjīn as grand general;
the Wèi people shot and killed him.
Héshengài, frightened,
fled.
Shàngshū Lìng Liú Jié spoke to the Wèi ruler, saying:
"Dàtán relies on his large army
and will certainly return.
I request that after the harvest is complete,
we raise a large army in two divisions,
advancing simultaneously east and west to suppress him."
The Wèi ruler approved of this.
In the ninth month,
on the Bǐngzǐ day,
Lady Yuán was established as Empress.
She was the great-granddaughter of Dān.
Yuán Dān is mentioned in volume ninety-five, Emperor Chéng's Xiánkāng first year.
In winter,
in the tenth month,
Tuyuhun's Wēiwáng Āchái died.
Āchái had twenty sons.
When he was gravely ill,
he summoned his sons and younger brothers and said to them:
"My late father, the Cheqí,
for the sake of the great enterprise,
bypassed his son Shíqián and handed it to me.
How dare I show favoritism to Wěidài and forget the will of my late father!
'Late father'
refers to Shùluògān.
Shùluògān styled himself Cheqí Jiāngjūn,
and entrusted the state to Āchái,
as mentioned in volume one hundred eighteen, Emperor Ān of Jìn's Yìxī thirteenth year.
Wěi
is pronounced "yú guì fān".
You should
serve Mùguī as your lord."
Wěidài was
Āchái's eldest son;
Mùguī was Āchái's younger maternal brother, the son of his uncle Wūhétí.
When Wūhétí was established,
he married Shùluògān's mother,
and had two sons:
Mùguī and Mùlìyán.
Wěi
is pronounced "yú guì fān".
Guī
is pronounced "gū huí fān".
"Tí"
should be
"Dī".
Āchái then commanded his sons to each present an arrow.
He took one arrow and gave it to his younger brother Mùlìyán, instructing him to break it.
Mùlìyán broke it.
He then took nineteen arrows and asked him to break them,
but Mùlìyán could not break them.
Āchái then enlightened them, saying:
"Do you understand this?
A single arrow is easy to break,
but many arrows together are difficult to destroy.
You should unite your strength with one heart,
and then you can preserve the state and pacify the family."
After he finished speaking, he died.
Mùguī also possessed talent and strategy.
He appeased the displaced people of Qín and Liáng, as well as the Dī and Qiāng mixed tribes, totaling five to six hundred households.
His forces grew increasingly strong.
In the twelfth month,
the Wèi ruler ordered Ānjí Jiāngjūn Zhǎngsūn Hàn and Ānběi Jiāngjūn Wèi Juàn to attack Ròurán in the north.
The Wèi ruler himself led a contingent and encamped at Zuòshān.
Zuòshān is west of Píngchéng,
and east of the Dàhé.
Zuò
is pronounced "zé luò fān".
All the armies pursued them,
gaining great spoils and returning.
Hàn was
the son of Féi.
Zhǎngsūn Féi served Wèi ruler Guī,
and as a general,
frequently achieved meritorious deeds.
An edict appointed Yíngyángwáng's mother, Lady Zhāng, as Yíngyáng Tàifù.
Línyì King Fàn Yángmài plundered the commanderies of Rìnán and Jiǔdé.
Shěn Yuē said: Jiǔdé Commandery originally belonged to Jiǔzhēn.
Sūn Wú divided it to establish Jiǔdé Commandery.
During Suí and Táng, it was Huānzhōu.
Dàngchāng King Liáng Míhōng sent his son Míhuáng to visit the Wèi court.
Dàngchāng was
a distinct branch of the Qiāng people.
The Qiāng territory bordered Zhōngguó to the east,
and connected to the Western Regions to the west,
spanning several thousand *lǐ* in length.
Each had its own chiefs and commanders.
Their tribes and lands were divided
and not under unified control.
Dàngchāng was the strongest,
with over twenty thousand households of people;
the various other tribes feared them.
The *Běishǐ* states: Dàngchāng are likely descendants of Sānmiáo.
Dù Yòu said: Their territory extends from Qiúchí westward,
a thousand *lǐ* east to west;
and south of the Xí River, eight hundred *lǐ* north to south.
The land is mostly mountainous.
Dàng
is pronounced "tú làng fān".
Qiú
is pronounced "cí yóu fān".
Shuài

At first,

He left behind his heavy baggage
and advanced rapidly with thirty thousand light cavalry.
All the courtiers advised him, saying:
"The city of Tǒngwàn (統萬) is strong;
it cannot be taken in a day or night.
Now, if we attack with light forces,
we cannot conquer it by advancing, and we will have no supplies if we retreat.
It is better to go with the infantry and siege equipment all at once."
The Emperor said:
"In the art of war,
attacking a city is the lowest option;
it should only be used as a last resort.
If we advance with both infantry and siege equipment,
they will surely be frightened and defend stubbornly.
If the attack does not succeed promptly,
our provisions will be exhausted, and our soldiers will be weary.
There will be nothing to plunder outside,
and we will have no ground for advance or retreat.
It is better to go directly to their city with light cavalry.
When they see that the infantry has not yet arrived,
their guard will surely be relaxed.
We will show a weak formation to lure them out,
and they might come out to fight,
in which case they will be captured.
The reason for this
is that our soldiers are two thousand li from home,
and separated by a great river.
This is what is called 'placing them in a deadly situation to achieve life.'
When fighting far from home,
everyone fights to the death,
so their vanguard cannot be resisted.
They will have more than enough resolve for a decisive battle."
So he proceeded.
