to pacify Chāng before returning.”
Wèi Zhǔ did not permit it.
Jīn firmly requested again,
so he finally permitted it,
giving Jīn ten thousand soldiers
and sending General Liú Bá to deliver thirty
horses,
also leaving É Qīng and Qiū Duī to jointly attack Xià.
On the Xīnyǒu day,
the Wèi ruler returned east from Tǒngwàn,
appointing Chángshān Wáng Sù as Grand General Who Conquers the South (Zhēngnán Dàjiāngjūn) and acting-Immaculate Envoy (jiǎjié),
to garrison Tǒngwàn with Zhí Jīn Wú Huán Dài and Mò Yún.
The "Guānshì Zhì" (Official Family Register) of the Wèi Shū states that
among the various surnames that entered the interior,
the Wūwán clan became the Huán clan.
Dài was Mò Tí's younger brother.
Mò Tí is mentioned in Jin'ān Dì Yìxī fourth year, volume 114.
Qín Wáng Chìpán returned to Fúhǎn.
As Xià had been destroyed,
Chìpán therefore returned.
Fú
is pronounced fū.
In autumn,
in the seventh month,
on the Jǐmǎo day,
the Wèi ruler arrived at Zuòlǐng.
Zuòlǐng is the ridge of Zuòshān.
Zuò
is pronounced zuò.
(Hèlián Chāng) heard that Wèi had already conquered Tǒngwàn
and consequently fled.
Qín Wáng Chìpán said to his subordinates:
"I know that the Hèlián clan will surely fail.
I risked danger to submit to Wèi,
as recounted in the previous volume, Yíngyáng Wáng Jǐngpíng first year."
In the eighth month,
(Chìpán) sent his uncle, General of Far-Reaching Might (Píngyuǎn Jiāngjūn) Wòtóu and others, to pay tribute to Wèi.
On the Rénzǐ day,
the Wèi ruler returned to Píngchéng,
and distributed the spoils to the officials of the resident imperial secretariat, varying by rank.
The Wèi ruler's character:
he was robust, brave, and fierce.
When facing a city or arrayed battle,
he personally braved arrows and stones.
While his attendants fell dead or wounded one after another,
his expression remained natural.
Because of this, his generals and soldiers respected and submitted to him,
and all exerted their utmost strength.
His nature was frugal and unpretentious.
His clothing, chariots, food, and drink
were merely sufficient.
When his subordinates requested to further fortify the imperial city and repair palaces, he said:
"The Yì says: 'Kings and dukes establish defenses
to guard their states.'
This is from the comment on the hexagram Kǎn in the Yì.
Without grandeur and beauty,
there is no way to enhance authority."
This is mentioned in Han Gāodì seventh year, volume 11.
"The ancients said: 'Virtue, not defenses, is what matters.'
These are the words of Wú Qǐ.
How can it be about cities?
Currently, the world is not yet pacified,
and the people's strength is still needed.
Works of earth and construction
are something I have not yet undertaken.
This reply from Xiāo Hé
is not an elegant statement."
Yǎ means 'correct'.
It cannot be lightly wasted.
As for rewards,
they were all given to the families of those who died in service or performed meritorious deeds.
His relatives and favored nobles never received undue benefits.
When commissioning generals and dispatching armies,
he personally directed and stipulated their operations.
Those who violated his orders often met with defeat.
He was astute in judging people,
sometimes promoting scholars from among the ranks of common soldiers,
solely based on their talents and strengths,
regardless of their background.
He was keen and swift in listening and observing,
leaving no hidden truths among his subordinates.
Rewards were not withheld from the humble,
and punishments were not avoided for the noble.
Even those whom he loved greatly
were ultimately not excused.
He often said:
"Laws
are shared by me and the entire realm.
How dare I treat them lightly?"
However, his nature was cruel and ruthless,
decisive in killing.
Often, after killing, he would regret it.
Such as in the case of Cuī Hào.
Fù
is pronounced fú yòu.
In the ninth month,
on the Dīngyǒu day,
the people of Āndìng surrendered the city to Wèi.
As the Xià capital was already broken,
Āndìng also surrendered.
Jiàng
is pronounced hù jiāng;
the same applies below.
Dī Wáng Yáng Xuán sent General Fú Báizuò to besiege Qín Liángzhōu Governor Chūlián Fǔzhèng at Chìshuǐ.
Inside the city, provisions ran out,
and the people seized Fǔzhèng and surrendered.
Fǔzhèng reached Luògǔ
and then escaped back.
In winter,
in the tenth month,
Qín appointed Swift Cavalry General (Xiāoqí Jiāngjūn) Wú Hàn as General Who Pacifies the South (Píngnán Jiāngjūn) and Liángzhōu Governor,
to garrison Nánqiáng.
In the eleventh month,
the Wèi ruler sent Army Supervisor (Jūnsīmǎ) Gōngsūn Guǐ, concurrently Grand Herald (Dàhónglú),

holding the immaculate envoy's staff, to solemnly appoint Yáng Xuán as Commander-in-Chief of Military Affairs of Jīng, Liáng, and other four prefectures (Dūdū Jīng‧Liáng Děng Sìzhōu Zhū Jūnsì), Liángzhōu Governor, and King of Nánqín.
Xuán was enfeoffed as King of Nánqín to distinguish him from Qífú Chìpán.
Lú
is pronounced líng rú.
Xuán did not go out to welcome him.
Guǐ reprimanded him
and intended to return with the imperial edict.
Xuán, fearing, then went out to the suburbs to welcome him.
The Wèi ruler praised this
and appointed Guǐ as Minister (Shàngshū).
Guǐ
was the son of Gōngsūn Biǎo.
Biǎo died in Yíngyáng Wáng Jǐngpíng first year.
In the twelfth month,
Qín Liángzhōu Governor Wú Hàn was attacked by the local Qiāng
and led two thousand households back to Fúhǎn.
The Wèi ruler traveled to Zhōngshān.
On the Guǐmǎo day,
he returned to Píngchéng.
Edited by Niè Chóngqí, collated by Wáng Chóngwǔ.
Sīmǎ Guāng
Compiled by imperial decree.
Hòu Xué Tiāntái
Tàizǔ Wén Huángdì Shàng Zhī Zhōng
Yuánjiā fifth year (Wùchén, 428 CE)
In spring,
in the first month,
on the Xīnwèi day,
Wèi Jīngzhàowáng Lí died.
Jīngzhōu Governor Píngchéng Wáng Yìkāng
was intelligent and observant by nature,
and his duties in the prefecture were well-managed.
Zuǒ Guānglù Dàfū Fàn Tài said to Sītú Wáng Hóng:
"The affairs of the realm are weighty,
and positions of power are difficult to maintain.
Your brothers' prosperity is at its peak;
you should deeply cultivate humility and moderation.
This refers to Hóng and his younger brother Tánshǒu, who both held positions of power.
The emperor's second youngest brother
should be recalled to court
to participate in state affairs."
Hóng adopted his suggestion.
At that time, there was a severe drought and an epidemic.
Hóng submitted a memorial taking the blame and offering to resign,
but the emperor did not permit it.
Qín Shāngzhōu Governor and concurrently Administrator of Jiāohé (Lǐng Jiāohé Tàishǒu) Yáo Jùn rebelled
and surrendered to Héxī.
During the Jìn era,
Zhāng Zuò established Shāngzhōu in Dūnhuáng Commandery.
At that time, Dūnhuáng belonged to Héxī.
Chìpán probably appointed Jùn as titular Shāngzhōu Governor while he garrisoned Jiāohé.
Jiāo
is pronounced jiān yáo.
Jiàng
is pronounced hù jiāng.
(Chìpán) led three thousand cavalry to suppress him.
In the second month,
Sōng was captured by Tǔyùhún Yuánxù.
Wèi changed its era name to Shénjù.
5 Wèi’s Píngběi Jiāngjūn, Yù Juàn, attacked the Xià ruler at Shàngguī.
The Xià ruler retreated and garrisoned Píngliáng.
Xī Jīn advanced his army to Āndìng
and joined forces
with the armies of Qiū Duī and É Qīng.
Many of Xī Jīn’s horses died from plague,
and his soldiers lacked provisions,
so he deepened his encampment to secure himself.
He dispatched Qiū Duī to oversee grain collection from the populace.
The soldiers looted violently
and made no preparations for defense.
The Xià ruler ambushed them,
and Qiū Duī’s forces were defeated.
He returned to the city with a few hundred cavalry.
The Xià ruler, taking advantage of his victory,
came to the city walls daily to plunder.
With no fodder or pasture to be found,
the generals were troubled.
The Jiānjūn Shìyùshǐ, Ān Xié, said:
“We received an imperial edict to exterminate the bandits,
but now we are instead besieged by the bandits,
retreating to defend a desolate city.
If we are not killed by the bandits,
we will be executed according to the law.
There is no way out, whether we advance or retreat.
Yet, all you princes and dukes are at ease, never even making a plan?”
Xī Jīn, enfeoffed as Yíchéng Wáng,
was Sīkōng.
“Now our army has no horses,
and to fight cavalry on foot
will surely result in no victory.
We must wait for the relief cavalry from the capital to arrive and attack together.”
Ān Xié said:
“Now the fierce bandit is roaming free outside,
and our troops are exhausted and our provisions are depleted.
If we do not fight a decisive battle,
then death is imminent.
How can we wait for relief cavalry!
Rather than merely awaiting death,
to fight to the death,
would that not be preferable!”
Xī Jīn again used the scarcity of horses as an excuse.
Ān Xié said:
“If we gather the horses ridden by all the generals,
we can get two hundred.
I request to recruit brave warriors to sally forth and attack them.
Even if we cannot defeat the enemy,
we can at least break their morale.
Furthermore, Hèlián Chāng is impulsive and without strategy,
fond of bravery but reckless,
often personally coming out to challenge us.
Everyone recognizes him.
If we ambush him,
Chāng can be captured.”
Xī Jīn was still hesitant.
Ān Xié then secretly conspired with Yù Juàn and others,
selecting cavalry to await the opportunity.
Soon after, the Xià ruler came to attack the city,
and Ān Xié went out to engage him.
The Xià ruler himself came to the front of the formation to fight,
and the soldiers, recognizing his appearance,
rushed to him in contention.
It happened that there was a strong wind raising dust,
making the day dim.
The Xià ruler was defeated and fled.
Ān Xié pursued him;
the Xià ruler’s horse stumbled and he fell,
and he was then captured.
The Kǎoyì says: The Shíliù Guó Chūnqiū Chāocháo states:
“In the fifth month of Chéngguāng three,
they fought at Hēiqú
and were defeated by Wèi.
Chāng fled back with several thousand cavalry,
and Wèi’s pursuing cavalry also arrived.
Chāng’s Hénèi Gōng, Fèilián Wūtí, defended Gāopíng,
relocating seventy thousand households from various cities to Āndìng to make it the capital.
In the second month of four,
the Wèi army reached Āndìng,
and the three cities collapsed.
Chāng fled to Qínzhōu,
and Wèi’s Dōngpíng Gōng, É Qīng, pursued and captured him,
sending him to Wèi.”
This differs from the Hòuwèi Jì and Zhuàn;
we now follow the Hòuwèi Shū.
He was the son of Wèn.
Ān Tóng
was one of the Eight Dukes at the beginning of Yǒngxīng.
Xià’s Dà Jiāngjūn, Líng Sītú, and Píngyuán Wáng Dìng gathered the remaining several tens of thousands of troops
and fled back to Píngliáng.
He then ascended the imperial throne.
Dìng,
whose courtesy name was Zhígùn,
was the fifth son of Xià Wáng Bóbó.
He changed the era name to Shèngguāng.
In the third month,
on the Xīnsì day,
Hèlián Chāng arrived in Píngchéng.
The Wèi ruler housed him in the Western Palace,
providing him with replacement imperial articles for all the utensils inside the gate.
He also married his sister, Shǐpíng Gōngzhǔ, to him;
he was granted the title of Chángzhōng Jiāngjūn
and bestowed the noble rank of Huìjī Gōng.
Ān Xié was made Jiànjié Jiāngjūn
and bestowed the noble rank of Xīpíng Gōng;
Yù Juàn was made Níngběi Jiāngjūn
and advanced to the noble rank of Yúyáng Gōng.
The Wèi ruler often made Hèlián Chāng attend him at his side,
and they would hunt deer together on horseback,
venturing deep into mountain ravines.
Chāng had always been known for his bravery,
and all the generals deemed this to be ill-advised.
The Wèi ruler said:
“Heaven’s mandate has its own course;
what is there to fear!”
He continued to treat him personally as before.
Xī Jīn, considering himself the Grand Marshal,
felt deeply ashamed that Chāng had been captured by a mere subordinate.
He then abandoned his baggage train,
carrying three days’ rations,
and pursued the Xià ruler to Píngliáng.
É Qīng wanted to follow the river
(É Qīng probably intended to advance along the Jīngshuǐ River)
and intercept his path from the northern route.
Upon reaching Mǎmáo Lǐng,
(the ridge of Mǎmáo Shān),
it happened that a minor Wèi general, having committed a crime, defected to Xià
and reported that the Wèi army had little food and no water.
The Xià ruler then divided his forces to intercept Xī Jīn,
attacking him from front and rear simultaneously.
The Wèi army was utterly routed,
and Xī Jīn, É Qīng, and Liú Bá were all captured by Xià.
(Last year,
Wèi sent Liú Bá to attack Xià together with Xī Jīn.)
The Kǎoyì says: The Sòng Suǒlú Zhuàn states:
“In Yuánjiā five,
he sent the great general Tǔfá Jīn to campaign west to Cháng’ān,
capturing Hèlián Chāng alive at Āndìng,
enfeoffing Chāng as a duke,
and marrying his sister to him.
Chāng’s brother, Dìng, was in Lǒngshàng.
Tǔfá Jīn, emboldened by victory, attacked him with thirty thousand cavalry.
Dìng set an ambush in Lǒngshān’s Dànzhēng Gǔ,
defeated him,
beheaded Tǔfá Jīn,
and buried all his troops alive.
Dìng then led his forces back east
and recaptured Cháng’ān.
Táo again personally attacked,
but was unsuccessful,
so he divided his army to garrison major cities and returned.”
We now follow the Hòuwèi Shū.
Qiū Duī, who was guarding the baggage train at Āndìng,
hearing of Xī Jīn’s defeat,
abandoned the baggage train and fled to Cháng’ān,
fleeing with Gāoliáng Wáng Lǐ to Púbǎn.
The Xià people then re-took Cháng’ān.
The Wèi ruler was greatly enraged
and ordered Ān Xié to execute Qiū Duī,
take command of his troops,
and garrison Púbǎn to resist them.
6 Summer,
in the fourth month,
the Xià ruler sent an envoy to request peace with Wèi.
The Wèi ruler sent an imperial edict to persuade him to surrender.
7 On the Rénzǐ day,
the Wèi ruler went on a western tour;
on the Wùwǔ day,
he hunted west of the river.
(This is west of Jūnzǐ Jīn.)
8 In the fifth month,
Qín Wénzhāo Wáng Chìpán died.
Crown Prince Mùmò ascended the throne,
issued a general amnesty,
and changed the era name to Yǒnghóng.
9 Pínglù Lìng, Hénán Chéng Càn,
(Pínglù county had belonged to Dōngpíng Commandery since the Hàn dynasty.)
Hóng followed him,
repeatedly submitting memorials to make requests.
The emperor had no choice but to
in the sixth month,
on the Gēngxū day,
appoint Hóng as Wèijiāngjūn and Kāifǔ Yítóng Sānsī.
10On the Jiǎyín day,
the Wèi ruler went to Chángchuān.
(The Wèishū Dìjì states: In the eighth year of Tàicháng,
the Great Wall was built south of Chángchuān.)
11 Qín Wénzhāo Wáng was buried at Wǔpíng Líng.
His temple name was Tàizǔ.
In his last days, Qín Wáng promoted Yúanjī, the Right Chancellor, to Shìzhōng, Xiàngguó, Dūdū Zhōngwài Zhūjūn, and Lù Shàngshū Shì.
He promoted Qiāntún, the Zhènchén Dàjiāngjūn and Hézhōu Mù, to Piàojì Dàjiāngjūn.
The seat of Héchōu was Fúhǎn,
which was the capital of the Qífú clan.
驃,
Pǐmiào pronunciation.
騎,
Qíjiī pronunciation;
same below.
Duàn Huī had previously been stationed in Lèdū.
To guard Huánghé,
he appointed Mùyìgān, the Zhēngbèi Jiāngjūn, as Shàngshū Lìng and Chējì Dàjiāngjūn,
and Jípí, the Zhēngnán Jiāngjūn, as Shàngshū Púyè and Wèi Dàjiāngjūn.
Taking advantage of Qín's mourning, Héxī Wáng Méngxùn
attacked Qín's Xīpíng.
Qū Chéng, the Grand Administrator of Xīpíng, said to him:
"If Your Highness first takes Lèdū,
then Xīpíng will certainly be yours.
To submit
at the mere sight of the wind (i.e., without resistance)
is also what an enlightened ruler would despise."
Thereupon, Méngxùn released Xīpíng
and attacked Lèdū.
Xiàngguó Yúanjī led three thousand cavalry to relieve Lèdū.
Yúanjī marched from Fúhǎn to relieve Lèdū.
樂,
sound Luò.
When the Héxī forces arrived,
they attacked its outer city
and captured it.
They cut off its water supply,
and the city suffered from hunger and thirst,
with more than half dying.
Dōngqiāng Qítí followed Yúanjī to relieve Lèdū,
secretly conspiring with Héxī.
They lowered ropes to let their soldiers in,
and over a hundred men climbed the wall,
beating drums and shouting, then setting fire to the gate.
Yúanjī led his左右 to fight fiercely,
and the Héxī forces retreated.
Initially,
when Wénzhāo Wáng was seriously ill,
he said to Mùmò:
"After my death,
it will be good if you can merely secure the border.
Jūqú Chéngdū is highly regarded and trusted by Méngxùn.
You should return him."
At this point,
Mùmò sent an envoy to Méngxùn,
promising to return Chéngdū to seek peace.
Chéngdū was captured by Qín;
this event is described in Volume 119, Wǔdì Yǒngchū San Nián.
沮,
Zǐyú pronunciation.
使,
Shūlì pronunciation;
same below.
An envoy was sent to Qín to offer condolences and sacrifices.
Mùmò generously provided Chéngdū with resources and
dispatched General Wáng Fá to escort him.
Méngxùn was still suspicious,
so he sent Huīwǔ Jiāngjūn Jūqú Qízhēn to ambush Fá at Méntiān Lǐng,
capturing Fá and his three hundred cavalrymen and bringing them back.
Afterwards, he sent Shàngshū Láng Wáng Zhù to escort Fá back to Qín,
and also presented Mùmò with a thousand horses, brocade, woolen rugs, silver, and silk.
In autumn,
in the seventh month,
Mùmò sent Jìshì Lángzhōng Mǎ Ài to Héxī to return the courtesy.
12 The Wèi Lord returned to his palace.
In the eighth month,
he again went to Guǎngníng to visit the hot springs.
The Commentary on the Water Classic states: The old city of Xiàluò Xiàn,
Wèi's Yānzhōu Guǎngníng Xiàn,
was the seat of Guǎngníng Jùn.
The Wèi Tǔdì Jì states: Forty li southeast of Xiàluò City is Qiáo Shān.
Below the mountain are hot springs.
Above the springs are sacrificial halls,
with carved eaves and magnificent structures,
extending along the bank.
Stone pools spout water,
flowing gently below.
Though hot and cold seasons alternate,
this water remains perpetually hot;
it can cure a hundred ailments,
with people rushing to it like a stream.
復,
Fúyòu pronunciation.
Róurán Hésgāi Kèhán sent his son with over ten thousand cavalry to raid the Wèi border.
The Wèi Lord returned from Guǎngníng
and pursued them,
but did not catch them.
In the ninth month,
he returned to the palace.
In winter,
in the tenth month,
on the Jiǎchén day,
the Wèi Lord went on a northern tour.
On the Rénzǐ day,
he hunted at Niú Chuān.
13 Qín's Liángzhōu Mù, Qífú Qiānnián,
indulged in drink and was cruel and tyrannical,
neglecting government affairs.
Qín Wáng Mùmò sent an envoy to rebuke him.
Qiānnián, in fear,
fled to Héxī.
He fled to Héxī Wáng Méngxùn.
He was stationed in Huánghé.
14 Xúzhōu Cìshǐ Wáng Zhòngdé sent two thousand infantry and cavalry to attack Wèi's Jìyáng and Chénliú.
Jìyáng Xiàn,
from Hàn and Jìn onwards, belonged to Chénliú Jùn;
at this time, the seat of Chénliú Jùn was Jùnyí.
Dù Yòu said: The old city of Jìyáng Xiàn is southwest of Cǎozhōu Yuānqū Xiàn.
濟,
Zǐlǐ pronunciation.
Kǎoyì says: The Hou Wei Ji records
"Huáibèi Zhènjiāng."
According to the Nánshǐ,
Zhòngdé was then Ānbèi Jiāngjūn and Xúzhōu Cìshǐ.
The biography of Zhòngdé in the Sòng Shū is incomplete.
Furthermore,
the Sòng Shū, Nánshǐ Běnjì, Běishǐ Běnjì, and the biographies of various Sòng and Wèi officials, the Wèi Liú Yù biography, and the Sòng Suǒlú biography
all lack any mention of Wáng Zhòngdé's attack on Wèi in this year.
Only the Hou Wei Benji mentions it.
We follow it now.
15 The Wèi Lord returned to his palace.
16 In Wèi's Dìngzhōu, over two thousand households of Dīnglíng Xiānyú Táiyáng and others rebelled
and entered Xī Shān.
The Wèi Lord Guī established Ānzhōu at Zhōngshān in Huángshǐ Èr Nián,
and renamed it Dìngzhōu in Tiānxīng Sān Nián.
Xī Shān
is Qǔyáng Xī Shān.
In the intercalary month,
the Wèi Lord sent Zhènnán Jiāngjūn Shúsūn Jiàn to suppress them.
17 In the eleventh month,
on the Yǐwèi day (the first day of the month),
there was a solar eclipse.
18 The Wèi Lord went to Xīhé for a hunting expedition.
The Heshui River flows southwest of Hàn's Yúnzhōng Zhēnlíng Xiàn.
Píngchéng is to its northeast,
hence it is called Xīhé.
On the Jiǎshēn day,
he returned to the palace.
19 Héxī Wáng Méngxùn attacked Qín
and reached Pányí.
Qín's Xiàngguó Yúanjī and others led fifteen thousand cavalry to resist him.
Méngxùn returned to attack Xīpíng.
Zhēnglǔ Jiāngjūn Chūlián Fúzhèng and others led two thousand cavalry to relieve it.
20 Bìshū Jiān Xiè Língyùn,
considering his prominent family background and talent,
believed he should participate in current political affairs.
However, the Emperor only engaged him in literary matters,
and he merely attended banquets and discussions.
Wáng Tánshǒu, Wáng Huá, and Yīn Jǐngrén,
whose status had always been below Língyùn's,
were all appointed to important positions.
Língyùn was very displeased
and often feigned illness to avoid attending court or performing his duties.
Not attending court, not performing duties.
曇,
Túhán pronunciation.
朝,
Zhíyáo pronunciation.
He traveled over two hundred li
and did not return for ten days,
neither submitting a memorial
nor requesting leave due to emergency.
The Emperor did not wish to offend a senior official,
so he subtly hinted for Língyùn to resolve the situation himself.
Língyùn then submitted a memorial explaining his illness.
The Emperor granted him leave
to return to Kuàijī.
However, Língyùn continued his travels and drinking as before,
which was reported by the legal authorities.
He was consequently dismissed from office.
21 In this year,
the Lion King Chàlìmóhē and King Yuè'ài of Kapilavastu in Tiānzhú both sent envoys to present memorials and tribute.
The language of their memorials was all in the style of Buddhist teachings.
The Nánshǐ states: Shīzǐ Guó (Lion Kingdom)
is a country adjacent to Tiānzhú.
Its climate is mild and suitable,
with no distinction between winter and summer.
The five grains grow according to human planting,
without requiring specific seasons.
Tiānzhú has countries such as Kāpílì, Suōmálì, Jīntuólì, and Bólì,
all of which practice Buddhism.
剎,
Chūxiá pronunciation.
迦,
Gǔyá pronunciation,
also Jūgā pronunciation.
使,
Shūlì pronunciation.
22 Wèi's Zhènyuǎn Jiāngjūn, Píngshū Hóu Yān Fèng, passed away.
Yān Fèng served four generations of the Tuòbá clan.
1 In spring,
the first month,
Wáng Hóng (王弘) submitted a memorial requesting to resign his positions as governor of Yángzhōu (揚州) and director of the Department of State Affairs,
to bestow them upon Píngchéng Wáng Yìkāng (彭城王義康).
The "governor of Yángzhōu" and "director of the Department of State Affairs"
refer to the governor of Yángzhōu (揚州 Císhǐ) and the director of the Department of State Affairs (Lù Shàngshūshì).
On the day Guǐchǒu (癸丑),
Yìkāng (義康) was appointed Shìzhōng (侍中), Dūdū Yáng, Nánxú, Yǎn Sānzhōu Zhū Jūnshì (都督揚‧南徐‧兗三州諸軍事), Sītú (司徒), Lù Shàngshūshì (錄尚書事), and Lǐng Nánxúzhōu Císhǐ (領南徐州刺史).
In the second year of Yǒngchū (永初) of Wǔdì (武帝),
Xúzhōu (徐州) in Jīngkǒu (京口) was designated Nánxú (南徐),
while Xúzhōu (徐州) north of the Huái River was simply called Xú (徐).

Nánxú (南徐) administered commanderies such as Nánhǎidōng (南海東), Nán Lángxié (南琅邪), Jìnlíng (晉陵), Yìxīng (義興), Nán Lánlíng (南蘭陵), Nán Dōngguǎn (南東莞), Línhuái (臨淮), Huáilíng (淮陵), Nán Péngchéng (南彭城), Nán Qīnghé (南清河), Nán Gāopíng (南高平), Nán Píngchāng (南平昌), Nán Jìyīn (南濟陰), Nán Púyáng (南濮陽), Nán Tàishān (南泰山), Jìyáng (濟陽), and Nán Lǔjùn (南魯郡).
Together they assisted in court administration.
“Zuǒ” (佐)
means Cānyá (參佐),
referring to subordinate officials.
“Cháo” (朝)
is pronounced zhí yáo fān.
He intended to delegate great power,
and pushed every matter to Yìkāng (義康);
thus Yìkāng (義康) took sole charge of both internal and external affairs.
This laid the groundwork for Yìkāng (義康) to bring disaster upon himself through his monopolization of power.
Also, Jiāngxià Wáng Yìgōng (江夏王義恭) was appointed Fújun Jiāngjūn (撫軍將軍), Dūdū Jīng, Xiāng děng Bāzhōu Zhū Jūnshì (都督荊‧湘等八州諸軍事), and Jīngzhōu Císhǐ (荊州刺史).
Shìzhōng (侍中) Liú Zhàn (劉湛) was appointed Nánmán Xiàowèi (南蠻校尉),
acting as governor of the prefecture.
The Emperor wrote a letter to Yìgōng (義恭),
admonishing him:
“The world is difficult,
and the affairs of family and state are weighty.
Though it is called ‘maintaining what has been achieved,’
it is indeed not easy.
Rise or fall, safety or danger,
rests with us.
How can one not reflect upon the founding of the royal enterprise
and greatly fear the heavy burden?
To reflect on the difficulties of establishing the royal enterprise and to explore the principles of governance.
The proverb says: ‘His father splits the firewood,
but his son cannot bear the burden.’
“Yì” (易)
is pronounced yǐ chǐ fān.
“Hè” (荷)
is pronounced xià kě fān,
and also sounds as written.
Your nature is narrow and impetuous;
where your will is set,
your desire must be carried out.
“Zhì” (滯)
means doubt,
or accumulation.
“Biǎn” (褊)
is pronounced fāng miǎn fān.
You change by conforming to things;
this is a major fault,
and you should consider restraining it.
Wèi Qīng (衞青) treated scholars with courtesy
and commoners with kindness;
Xīmén Bào (西門豹) and Dǒng Ānyú (董安于) both corrected their natures and achieved excellence.
Xīmén Bào (西門豹) was naturally rigid and impetuous,
and always carried a leather strap to temper himself.
Dǒng Ānyú (董安于) was naturally broad-minded and relaxed,
and always carried a bowstring to admonish himself.
Excess in any one disposition leads to the same fault.
The story is found in volume sixty-nine, second year of Huángchū (黃初) of Wèi Wéndì (魏文帝).
You should deeply learn from this!
If circumstances differ from today,
and the heir is young and ignorant,
Lù Démíng (陸德明) said: “Méng (蒙)
means young and ignorant.”
You must exhaust the principle of respect and obedience.
At that time, the safety or danger of the realm
will depend entirely on the two of you.
Your personal expenses should not exceed three hundred thousand coins a month.
If you can save more,
it would be even better.
The official residences in Xīchǔ (西楚)
are generally known and studied;
I estimate there is no need to renovate them
or constantly seek new and exotic things.
The region east of the Yangtze River referred to Jīngzhōu (荊州) as Xīchǔ (西楚).
Difficulties are hard to foresee;
this is truly a challenge.
When inquiries arise,
be open-minded and exhaustive;
be careful not to let your joy or anger affect others.
If you can choose the good and follow it,
excellence will naturally return to you;
do not make decisions solely on your own authority,
priding yourself on the wisdom of independent judgment!
You should deeply cherish and guard titles and appointments;
do not carelessly bestow them upon others.
Especially regarding favors and rewards for close associates,
you should exercise discretion.
Though I may be somewhat lacking in kindness to those around me,
I hear that external opinions do not consider this a fault.
If you oppress others with your nobility,
they will not submit;
if you impose your authority on others,
they will not be displeased.
These are easy things to understand.
Music, entertainment, and pleasure trips
should not be excessive;
dice games, drinking, fishing, and hunting
should all be avoided.
“Pú” (蒲)
refers to dice games (Chūpú).
Everything should have limits;
extravagant clothes and unusual objects
should not be encouraged.
Furthermore, you should frequently summon and interview your subordinate officials.
“Zuǒshǐ” (佐史)
should be
“Zuǒlì” (佐吏).
Between the Jìn (晉) and Sòng (宋) dynasties,
provincial administrations commonly referred to their aides as Zuǒlì (佐吏).
“Shuò” (數)
is pronounced suǒ jué fān;
the same below.
Otherwise, we will not be close to each other;
if not close,
there will be no way to understand people's true feelings;
if people's true feelings are not understood,
how then can one know public affairs!”
Carefully examining this letter from Sòng Wéndì (宋文帝),
one can see why the governance of the region east of the Yangtze was praised as Yuánjiā (元嘉)
—there was indeed a reason for it.
“Fù” (復)
is pronounced fú yòu fān.
2 In summer, Jiǔquán Gōng Jùn (酒泉公雋) fled from Píngliáng (平涼) to Wèi (魏).
3 The Dīnglíng (丁零) Xiānyú Táiyáng (鮮于臺陽) and others requested to surrender to Wèi (魏).
The Wèi (魏) ruler pardoned them.
He pardoned them for their crime of rebelling and entering the Western Mountains last year.
4 Before Qín (秦) Chūlián Fǔzhèng (出連輔政) and others arrived at Xīpíng (西平),
Héxī Wáng Méngxùn (河西王蒙遜) captured Xīpíng (西平)
and seized the prefect Qū Chéng (麴承).
Méngxùn (蒙遜) had attacked Xīpíng (西平) last year.
5 In the second month,
Qín Wáng Mùmò (秦王暮末) established Lady Liáng (梁氏) as empress
and his son Wànzài (萬載) as crown prince.
6 In the third month,
on the day Dīngsì (丁巳),
Imperial Prince Shào (劭) was established as Crown Prince;
on the day Wǔwǔ (戊午),
a general amnesty was proclaimed.
7 On the day Xīnyǒu (辛酉),
Yīn Jǐngrén (殷景仁) was appointed Zuǒwèi Jiāngjūn (左衞將軍) and Zhōnglǐngjūn (中領軍).
Since Empress Zhāng (章太后) died early (Empress Zhāng (章太后), née Hú (胡), gave birth to the Emperor five years before
being condemned and granted death;
when the Emperor ascended the throne,
she was posthumously granted the title Zhāng (章)),
and Lady Sū (蘇氏) passed away,
the Emperor went to mourn and weep,
wishing to posthumously add titles and honors,
and had his close ministers discuss it.
Jǐngrén (景仁) considered there was no such precedent in classical rites,
so it was stopped.
8 Earlier,
Qín (秦) Shàngshū Lǒngxī Xīn Jìn (尚書隴西辛進) was accompanying Wénzhāo Wáng (文昭王) on a tour of Língxiāo Guān (陵霄觀)
when he shot a flying bird
and accidentally hit Qín Wáng Mùmò’s (秦王暮末) mother,
injuring her face.
When Mùmò (暮末) ascended the throne,
he asked his mother about the cause of her facial injury.
His mother told him the circumstances.
Mùmò (暮末) was enraged
and killed Xīn Jìn (辛進) and twenty-seven members of his five clans.
Historians say that Mùmò (暮末) perished through tyranny.
9 In summer,
the fourth month,
on the day Guǐhài (癸亥),
Shàngshū Zuǒpúyè Wáng Jìnghóng (尚書左僕射王敬弘) was appointed Shàngshūlìng (尚書令).
Línchuān Wáng Yìqìng (臨川王義慶) was appointed Zuǒpúyè (左僕射).
Lìbù Shàngshū Jìyáng Jiāng Yí (吏部尚書濟陽江夷) was appointed Yòupúyè (右僕射).
10 Earlier,
Wèi Tàizǔ (魏太祖) commanded Shàngshū Dèng Yuān (尚書鄧淵) to compile more than ten volumes of national records,
but it stopped before completion.
Shìzǔ (世祖) further commanded Cuī Hào (崔浩) and Zhōngshū Shìláng Dèng Yǐng (中書侍郎鄧穎) and others to continue and complete it,
which laid the groundwork for Cuī Hào (崔浩) to suffer disaster due to historical matters.
Yǐng (穎)
was Yuān’s (淵) son.
11 The Wèi (魏) ruler was about to attack Rouran (柔然).
He mustered his troops in the southern suburbs,
first offering sacrifices to Heaven,
and then arranging his formations.
All his close ministers, both inside and outside the court, did not wish to proceed;
Empress Bǎotài (保太后) firmly stopped him.
Only Cuī Hào (崔浩) encouraged him.
Shàngshūlìng Liú Jié and others jointly recommended Taishǐlìng Zhāng Yuān and Xú Biàn to speak to the Wèi lord, saying:
"This year's Jǐsì
is a year of three yin.
Of the heavenly stems, Jiǎ, Bǐng, Wù, Gēng, Rén are yang;
Yǐ, Dīng, Jǐ, Xīn, Guǐ are yin.
Of the earthly branches, Zǐ, Yín, Chén, Wǔ, Shēn, Xū are yang;
Chǒu, Mǎo, Sì, Wèi, Yǒu, Hài are yin.
Jǐ and Sì are both yin,
and the heavenly stem and earthly branch combine as Jǐsì,
making it a year of three yin.
Táibái (Venus) is in the west,
so it is not advisable to raise troops.
A northern expedition will surely fail;
even if victorious,
it will be disadvantageous to the emperor."
Many ministers then collectively supported them, saying:
"Yuān and the others once advised Fú Jiān against a southern expedition when they were younger.
Fú Jiān did not heed them and was defeated.
What they say is never wrong,
so we should not disregard it."
The Wèi lord was displeased,
and ordered Hào to debate with Yuān and the others in his presence.
Hào pressed Yuān and Biàn, saying:
"Yang represents virtue,
and yin represents punishment.
Therefore, during a solar eclipse, one cultivates virtue;
during a lunar eclipse, one cultivates punishment.
When a ruler employs punishment,
if it is minor, it is displayed in the market and court;
if it is major, it is arrayed in the fields.
Arrayed in the fields
means using weapons.
This statement originally comes from the 'Treatise on Punishments and Laws' in the Hànshū.
Jié (詰),
'qù jí' fan.
Cháo (朝),
'zhí yáo' fan.
This is precisely how punishment is cultivated.
I secretly observed the celestial phenomena,
and for several years now,
the moon has eclipsed Mǎo,
and it remains so even today.
The omen for this is:
'In three years, the Son of Heaven will utterly defeat the nations of Máotóu.'
The Rouran and Gāochē
are the people of Máotóu.
I ask Your Majesty not to doubt."
Yuān and Biàn retorted:
"The Rouran
are useless creatures from beyond the wilderness.
Their land cannot be cultivated for food,
and their people cannot be made subjects and servants.
They are light, swift, and inconstant,
difficult to capture and control.
Why the urgent haste
to weary soldiers and horses to attack them?"
Hào said:
"Yuān and Biàn speak of the Way of Heaven,
which is indeed their profession.
As for human affairs and circumstances,
these are beyond their knowledge.
This is merely common talk from the Hàn era,
from Hán Ānguó and Zhǔfù Yǎn to Yán Yóu;
their arguments were all like this.
They do not at all conform to practicality.
Why?
The Rouran were originally subjects of our nation's northern border,
but rebelled and left in the interim.
See Chapter 108, Jìn Xiàowǔ Tàiyuán nineteenth year.
Recovering their good people
to resume their former service is not useless.
People widely say that Yuān and Biàn are proficient in numerology,
and clearly determine success and failure.
I request to test them:
Before Tǒngwàn fell just now,
were there any signs of defeat?
If they did not know,
then they have no skill;
if they knew but did not speak,
then they are disloyal."
At that time, Hèlián Chāng was present,
and Yuān and the others, knowing they had never made such a statement,
were ashamed and could not reply.
The Wèi lord was greatly pleased.
After the assembly was dismissed,
some of the high officials criticized Hào, saying:
"Now the southern bandits are watching for a national weakness,
yet we abandon them for a northern expedition.
If the Rouran flee far away,
we will gain nothing in front,
and then face strong bandits behind.
How will we deal with them?"
Hào said:
"Not so.
If we do not first defeat the Rouran now,
we will have no means to confront the southern bandits.
The southerners, having heard that our nation captured Tǒngwàn,
harbor fear within,
and thus raise their voices and mobilize their forces to guard Huáinán.
By the time we defeat the Rouran,
and return,
the southern bandits will surely not have moved.
Moreover, they are infantry, and we are cavalry;
if they can come north,
we can also go south.
For them, it would be extremely difficult;
for us, it would not be laborious.
Furthermore, the north and south have different customs,
and land and water have different advantages.
Even if our nation were to yield Hénán to them,
they would not be able to hold it.
Cuī Hào's assessment of the Sòng people was accurate.
The emperor later repeatedly sent troops to contest Hénán,
ultimately exhausting himself.
Wú Lǚ Méng's unwillingness to take Wèi Xúzhōu
was precisely due to this concern.
Even with Liú Yù's heroism and brilliance,
after conquering Guānzhōng,
leaving his beloved son
assisted by good generals,
and tens of thousands of elite troops,
he still could not hold it,
and his entire army was annihilated.
The event is recorded in Chapter 118, Jìn Āndì Yìxī fourteenth year.
Jiāng (將),
'jí liàng' fan;
same below.
This continues to this day.
What's more, the present ruler and ministers of Yìlóng
are not comparable to Yù's time;
the emperor is heroic and mighty,
and our soldiers and horses are strong.
If they indeed come,
it would be like calves fighting tigers and wolves.
A young horse is called jú (駒),
a young ox is called dú (犢).
The Rouran rely on their remoteness,
believing our nation cannot control them,
and have been at ease for a long time.
Therefore, in summer they disperse their forces and release their livestock,
gathering only when autumn is fat.
Turning their backs on the cold and facing the warmth,
they come south to raid and plunder.
If we strike them when they are unprepared,
they will surely be terrified and scatter at the sight of dust.
Stallions protect mares,
and mares dote on their foals;
they will be difficult to control in their flight.
Without water and grass,
in no more than a few days,
they will surely gather and be exhausted,
and can be annihilated in one stroke.
A temporary hardship for lasting peace;
this opportunity must not be missed.
Zhàn (蹔),
same as zàn (暫).
The emperor's mind is already made up,
how can we stop him!"
Kòu Qiānzhī asked Hào:
"Can the Rouran truly be defeated?"
Hào said:
"They will certainly be defeated.
My only fear is that the generals will be petty,
looking back and forth,
unable to press deep into enemy territory with their victory,
thus preventing a complete victory."
Suǒsuǒ (瑣瑣)
means small and petty,
referring to small aspirations,
unable to achieve a complete victory in one go.
Previously, the emperor had sent a Wèi envoy back,
telling the Wèi lord:
"You must quickly return the land of Hénán to me!
Otherwise,
I will use all the strength of my generals and soldiers."
The Wèi lord was discussing an expedition against Rouran,
and hearing this,
laughed heartily,
and said to his officials:
"These small turtles and tortoises,
the southeast
is a marshy country,
hence they are slandered as small turtles and tortoises.
What can they possibly do!
Even if they can come,
if we do not first destroy the Rouran,
it would be waiting for the bandits to arrive,
suffering attacks from both front and back,
which is not a good strategy.
My decision is made."
On Gēngyín, the Wèi lord departed Píngchéng,
making Běipíngwáng Zhǎngsūn Sōng and Guǎnglǐnggōng Lóu Fúlián stay behind to guard.
The Wèi lord himself advanced eastward towards Hēishān,
and sent Píngyángwáng Zhǎngsūn Hàn westward towards Dà'éshān,
to meet together in the Rouran court.
12 In the fifth month,
on the *rénchén* day,
there was a solar eclipse.
13 Wáng Jìnghóng (王敬弘) firmly declined the post of Shàngshū Lìng (尚書令)
and submitted a memorial requesting to return east.
On the *guǐsì* day,
Jìnghóng (敬弘) was instead appointed Shìzhōng (侍中), Tèjìn (特進), and Zuǒ Guānglù Dàfū (左光祿大夫),
and granted permission to return east.
"Returning east" meant returning from Jiànkāng (建康) to Kuàijī (會稽).
14 On the *dīngwèi* day,
the Wèi (魏) ruler arrived at Mònán (漠南),
abandoned his baggage train,
and led light cavalry with spare horses to attack the Rourán (柔然),
reaching Lìshuǐ (栗水).
The Rourán (柔然) Hèshenggài Kèhán (紇升蓋可汗) had not prepared beforehand;
his people and livestock filled the plains,
and in fear and panic, they scattered,
unable to collect themselves.
*Shè* (攝)
means "to gather"
or "to organize and tidy."
They fled west, leaving no trace,
their destination unknown.
His younger brother Pǐlí (匹黎), who had previously governed the eastern part,
heard of the Wèi (魏) invasion
and led his troops, intending to join his brother.
He encountered Zhǎngsūn Hàn (長孫翰),
who intercepted and attacked him,
severely defeating him
and killing several hundred of his leaders.
15 The Xià (夏) ruler wanted to recapture Tǒngwàn (統萬),
and led his troops east to Hóuní Chéng (侯尼城).
Hóuní Chéng (侯尼城) was east of Píngliáng (平涼).
16 Héxī Wáng (河西王) Méngxùn (蒙遜) attacked Qín (秦).
Qín Wáng (秦王) Mùmò (暮末) left Xiàngguó (相國) Yuánjī (元基) to defend Fáohǎn (枹罕)
and moved to secure Dìnglián (定連).
Nán'ān Tàishǒu (南安太守) Zhái Chéngbó (翟承伯) and others held Hǎnkāi Gǔ (罕幵谷) in response to Héxī (河西).
Mùmò (暮末) attacked and defeated them,
advancing to Zhìchéng (治城).
Wèi Shōu's (魏收) *Dìxíng Zhì* (地形志) states: Líangzhōu (涼州) Dōngxíng Jùn (東陘郡) has Zhìchéng Xiàn (治城縣),
whose territory should be south of the Yellow River.
Also, Líangzhōu (涼州) has Jiànchāng Jùn (建昌郡),
which also has Zhìchéng Xiàn (治城縣).
Xī'ān Tàishǒu (西安太守) Mòzhě Yòujuàn (莫者幼眷) rebelled, occupying Qīanchuān (汧川).
This Qīanchuān (汧川) is not the Qīan (汧) of Fúfēng (扶風);
it should also be around Fáohǎn (枹罕).
*Qīan* (汧)
is pronounced like *kǒu jiān* (口堅).
He was defeated by Yòujuàn (幼眷)
and returned to Dìnglián (定連).
Méngxùn (蒙遜) arrived at Fáohǎn (枹罕)
and sent his heir apparent Xīngguó (興國) to attack Dìnglián (定連).
In the sixth month,
Mùmò (暮末) intercepted and attacked Xīngguó (興國) at Zhìchéng (治城),
capturing him, and pursued Méngxùn (蒙遜) to Tánjiāo (譚郊).
Tǔyùhún Wáng (吐谷渾王) Mùguī (慕璝) sent his younger brother Mòlìyán (沒利延) with five thousand cavalry to join Méngxùn (蒙遜) in attacking Qín (秦).
Mòlìyán (沒利延)
is Mùlìyán (慕利延);
the sounds of *mò* (沒) and *mù* (慕) are similar.
*Guī* (璝)
is pronounced like *gǔ huí* (古回).
He was utterly defeated.
17 After the Rourán (柔然) Hèshenggài Kèhán (紇升蓋可汗) had fled,
his tribes scattered in all directions,
hiding in mountains and valleys.
Diverse livestock were spread across the plains,
with no one to gather or look after them.
The Wèi (魏) ruler followed Lìshuǐ (栗水) westward
to Tuóyuán Shuǐ (菟園水),
divided his army to search and suppress them
over five thousand *lǐ* (里) east to west and three thousand *lǐ* (里) north to south,
capturing and killing a great many.
Various Gāochē (高車) tribes, capitalizing on the Wèi (魏) army's power,
raided and plundered the Rourán (柔然).
More than three hundred thousand Rourán (柔然) households surrendered to Wèi (魏) before and after,
and over one million warhorses were captured,
along with countless livestock and wagons,
filling the mountains and marshes;
their number was perhaps several million.
*Wáng* (亡) and *wú* (無) are interchangeable.
The Wèi (魏) ruler followed Ruòshuǐ (弱水) westward
to Zhuóxié Shān (涿邪山).
His generals, fearing that proceeding too deep might lead to an ambush,
advised the Wèi (魏) ruler to stop.
Kòu Qiānzhī (寇謙之) conveyed Cuī Hào's (崔浩) words to the Wèi (魏) ruler,
but the Wèi (魏) ruler did not comply.
In autumn,
in the seventh month,
he led his troops back east.
Upon reaching Hēishān (黑山),
he distributed the spoils to his officers and soldiers according to their rank.
Later, he received information from a surrendered person:
"The Kèhán (可汗) had been ill.
Hearing of the Wèi (魏) army's arrival,
he didn't know what to do,
so he burned his *qiónglú* (穹廬) [yurt],
loaded himself onto a cart,
and with several hundred men, entered the Southern Mountains.
His people and livestock were gathered in distress,
with no one to lead them.
They were separated by one hundred eighty *lǐ* (里);
if the pursuing troops had not arrived,
he would have slowly fled west,
and only in this way could he have escaped."
Later, he heard from a merchant from Líangzhōu (涼州):
"If they had advanced two more days,
they would have annihilated them all."
The Wèi (魏) ruler deeply regretted this.
Hèshenggài Kèhán (紇升蓋可汗), filled with indignation and grief,
died.
His son Wútí (吳提) succeeded him,
styling himself Chìlián Kèhán (敕連可汗).

On the 19th day of Jǐchǒu,
the Xià zhǔ sent his younger brother Wèi Yǐdài to attack Wèi's Fūchéng.
Wèi's Píngxī General, Duke of Shǐpíng Kuí Guī and others attacked him,
killing over ten thousand people.
Wèi Yǐdài fled.
The Xià zhǔ personally led tens of thousands of men to intercept and attack Kuí Guī east of Fūchéng.
He left his younger brothers, Duke of Shànggǔ Shè Gān and Duke of Guǎngyáng Dùluògū, to guard Píngliáng,
and sent an envoy to seek peace,
proposing to combine forces to destroy Wèi,
and remotely divide Hébĕi: from Mount Héng eastwards to belong to Sòng,
and westwards to belong to Xià.
The Wèi zhǔ, hearing of this,
prepared his army to attack Xià.
All the officials said:
"Liú Yìlóng's army is still in the middle of the river.
(Referring to the middle reaches of the Yellow River.)
The current invaders may not be overcome,
and if Yìlóng takes advantage of the emptiness to cross the river,
then we will lose Shāndōng."
(This Shāndōng refers to the area east of Mount Tàiháng and Mount Héng,
which is Hébĕi.)
The Wèi zhǔ replied:
"Yìlóng and Hèlián Dìng are remotely enticing each other,
echoing each other with empty boasts,
both eyeing our great nation.
Yìlóng waits for Dìng to advance,
and Dìng waits for Yìlóng to move forward.
Neither dares to enter first.
It's like two chickens tied together;
they cannot fly together,
and can do no harm.
I initially thought that when Yìlóng's army came,
they would station themselves in the middle reaches of the river,
advancing northward along two routes:
the eastern route towards Jìzhōu,
and the western route attacking Yè.
If this were the case,
then Your Majesty would have to personally attack them
without delay.
But now it is not so.
Their forces are arrayed east to west for two thousand *lǐ*,
with no more than a few thousand at any single point,
their formation divided and their strength weakened.
From this, we can see
the true feelings of these weaklings.
This is merely an attempt to secure the river and defend themselves;
they have no intention of crossing northward.
Hèlián Dìng's remaining roots are easy to destroy;
if we target him, he will surely fall.
After conquering Dìng,
we will march east from Tóngguān,
sweeping forward,
then our prestige will shake the southernmost regions,
and north of the Jiāng and Huái rivers there will be no place for even a blade of grass to stand.
This sagely strategy is uniquely conceived
and beyond the reach of ignorant commoners.
I implore Your Majesty not to doubt it."
On the day Jiǎchén,
the Wèi zhǔ proceeded to Tǒngwàn,
then surprised Píngliáng,
and appointed Wáng Jīn, the Wèibīng General, to garrison Púbǎn.
(Jīn
was the son of Jiàn.)
(Wáng Jiàn assisted Wèi zhǔ Guī in taking the Central Plains.)
From the first month,
Qín experienced no rain until the ninth month.
Many people migrated and rebelled.
In the winter,
tenth month,
Jìngláng Wáng Yìxuān was appointed Inspector of Nánxúzhōu,
still garrisoning Shítou.
(Yìxuān had previously garrisoned Shítou,
while the seat of Nánxúzhōu was Jīngkǒu.
Thus, he held the title of Inspector but was still garrisoning Shítou.)
On the 22nd day of Wùwǔ,
a mint was established
to cast four-zhū coins.
Dào Yànzhī and Wáng Zhòngdé established garrisons along the river
and returned to hold Dōngpíng.
(Dōngpíng Commandery was then administered from Xūchāng.)
On the *yǐhài* day,
Wèi’s Ān Jié (安頡) crossed the Hé (河) from Wěisùjīn (委粟津),
and attacked Jīnyǒng (金墉).
Jīnyǒng (金墉) had been neglected for a long time,
and also lacked provisions;
Dù Jì (杜驥) wanted to abandon the city and flee,
fearing punishment.
Initially,
Gāozǔ (高祖) had destroyed Qín (秦),
and moved its bells and stands to Jiāngnán (江南);
a large bell had sunk in the Luòshuǐ (洛水),
and the Emperor sent Yáo Sǒngfū (姚聳夫) with 1,500 men to retrieve it.
Jì (驥) deceived him, saying:
"Jīnyǒng City (金墉城) has been repaired and is complete,
and provisions are also sufficient;
what is lacking are men.
Now that the barbarian cavalry have crossed south,
we should join forces to resist them;
once this great achievement is made,
moving the bell will not be too late."
Sǒngfū (聳夫) agreed.
When he arrived,
he saw that the city was indefensible,
so he withdrew,
and Jì (驥) then fled south.
On the *bǐngzǐ* day,
Ān Jié (安頡) captured Luòyáng (洛陽),
killing over 5,000 soldiers.
Dù Jì (杜驥) returned
and told the Emperor:
"Originally, I intended to hold out to the death,
but Yáo Sǒngfū (姚聳夫) and the city quickly fled,
and morale was so disheartened
that it could no longer be restrained."
The Emperor was greatly enraged,
and executed Sǒngfū (聳夫) at Shòuyáng (壽陽).
Sǒngfū (聳夫) was brave and robust;
none of the lesser generals could match him.
Wèi’s (魏) armies north of the Hé (河) assembled at Qīnǚjīn (七女津).
Qīnǚjīn (七女津) should be on the northwest bank of Dōngpíng (東平).
They sent their subordinate general Wáng Pánlóng (王蟠龍) to sail upstream and seize their boats,
but Dù Chāo (杜超) and others attacked and killed him.
Ān Jié (安頡) and Longxiáng General Lù Hóu (陸侯) attacked Hǔláo (虎牢).
According to the *Běishǐ* (北史),
"Lù Hóu" (陸侯)
should be
"Lù Sì" (陸俟).
[Zhāng (章): The Jiǎ (甲) sixteen-line edition correctly writes
the Yǐ (乙) eleven-line edition is the same.] Xiáng (驤),
read as *sī jiāng* (思將).
On the *xīnsì* day,
they captured it;
Yǐn Chōng (尹沖) and the Grand Administrator of Xíngyáng (滎陽), Cuī Mó (崔模) of Qīnghé (清河), surrendered to Wèi (魏).
Qín (秦) King Mùmò (暮末), being pressed by Héxī (河西),
sent his officials Wáng Kǎi (王愷) and Wūnè Tián (烏訥闐) to request reception by Wèi (魏).
The Wèi (魏) people promised to enfeoff him with Píngliáng (平涼) and Āndìng (安定).
Mùmò (暮末) then burned his cities and towns,
destroyed his treasures,
and led 15,000 households
east towards Shàngguī (上邽).
When he reached Gāotiángǔ (高田谷),
Gāotiángǔ (高田谷) should be within the borders of Nán'ān (南安) Commandery,
not yet having reached Shàngguī (上邽).
When the matter was discovered,
Mùmò (暮末) killed them.
The Xià (夏) ruler, hearing that Mùmò (暮末) was approaching,
dispatched troops to resist him.
Mùmò (暮末) remained to defend Nán'ān (南安),
and his former territories all fell to the Tǔyùhún (吐谷渾).
From Yuànchuān (苑川) to Xīpíng (西平) and Báohǎn (枹罕) were all former territories of the Qǐfú (乞伏) clan.
In the eighth year of Jìn (晉) Xiàowǔdì’s (孝武帝) Tàiyuán (太元) reign,
the year of *guǐwèi*,
Qǐfú Guórén (乞伏國仁) occupied Lǒngxī (隴西),
and Nán'ān (南安) was also his territory.
In the eleventh month,
on the *yǐyǒu* day,
the Wèi (魏) ruler arrived at Píngliáng (平涼).
Xià (夏) Shànggǔ Duke Shè Gàn (社干) and others held the city fast;
the Wèi (魏) ruler sent Hèlián Chāng (赫連昌) to persuade them,
but they did not surrender.
So he sent Ānxī General Gǔ Bì (古弼) and others to lead troops towards Āndìng (安定).
The Xià (夏) ruler returned from Fūchéng (鄜城) to Āndìng (安定),
intending to lead 20,000 infantry and cavalry north to relieve Píngliáng (平涼),
and encountered Bì (弼).
Bì (弼) feigned retreat to lure him;
the Xià (夏) ruler pursued him,
and the Wèi (魏) ruler ordered high carts to charge and attack him,
severely defeating the Xià (夏) army,
beheading several thousand.
The Xià (夏) ruler fled back,
ascending Qúngūyuán (鶉觚原).
Qúngū (鶉觚) County
belonged to Běidì (北地) in the Former Hàn (漢),
and to Āndìng (安定) in the Later Hàn (漢) and Jìn (晉),
and had Qúngūyuán (鶉觚原);
in the first year of Táng (唐) Tiānbǎo (天寶),
it was renamed Língtái (靈臺) County,
belonging to Jīngzhōu (涇州).
Qún (鶉),
read as *shū lún* (殊倫).
Gū (觚),
pronounced *gū* (孤).
The Wèi (魏) troops then besieged him.
On the *rénchén* day,
Zhēngnán Great General Tán Dàojì (檀道濟) was additionally appointed Commander-in-chief of all expeditionary forces,
and led his troops to attack Wèi (魏).
On the *jiǎwǔ* day,
Wèi (魏) Shòuguāng Marquis Shúsūn Jiàn (叔孫建) and Rǔyīn Duke Zhǎngsūn Dàoshēng (長孫道生) crossed the Hé (河) and went south.
Dào Yànzhī (到彥之), hearing that Luòyáng (洛陽) and Hǔláo (虎牢) could not be held,
and that the armies were successively defeated and fleeing,
wanted to withdraw his troops.
Diànzhōng General Yuán Hùzhī (垣護之) wrote a letter to admonish him,
believing it was advisable to send Zhú Língxiù (竺靈秀) to assist Zhū Xiūzhī (朱脩之) in defending Huátái (滑臺),
and for him to personally lead the main army to approach Héběi (河北).
He further said:
"In the past, there were men who fought for years,
losing troops and lacking provisions,
yet still bravely advanced,
none willing to lightly retreat.
How much more so now, with Qīngzhōu (青州) bountiful,
the Jì (濟) and Cáo (漕) rivers flowing freely,
our soldiers and horses well-fed and rested,
and our power undiminished.
If we idly abandon Huátái (滑臺),
and passively lose our established enterprise,
how can this be the intention of the court in entrusting us with this duty?!"
"Shòu" (受)
should be
"Shòu" (授).
Hùzhī (護之) was
Miáo’s (苗) son.
Yuán Miáo (垣苗)
was a frontier general.
When Wǔdì (武帝) campaigned west to Cháng'ān (長安),
he ordered Miáo (苗) to garrison the junction of the Hé (河) and Jì (濟).
The common people called it Yuán Miáo City (垣苗城).
Ancestor, son, and grandson—three generations—all achieved fame at the frontier.
Yànzhī (彥之) wanted to burn his boats and flee on foot,
but Wáng Zhòngdé (王仲德) said:
"Luòyáng (洛陽) having fallen,
and Hǔláo (虎牢) undefended,
is a natural consequence.
Now the barbarians are still a thousand *lǐ* away from us,
and Huátái (滑臺) still has strong troops.
If we suddenly abandon our boats and flee south,
the soldiers will certainly scatter.
We should take the boats into the Jì (濟),
reach Mǎ'ěrgǔkǒu (馬耳谷口),
and then reconsider what is appropriate."
Mǎ'ěrgǔkǒu (馬耳谷口) is Mǎ'ěrgūan (馬耳關).
By this time, there was great unrest;
moreover, the generals and soldiers were sick with epidemic,
so they led their troops from Qīng (清) into the Jì (濟).
The *Shuǐjīng* (水經) says: The Jìshuǐ (濟水) flows northeast past the southern border of Ānmíntíng (安民亭) in Shòuzhāng (壽張) County,
and the Wènshuǐ (汶水) comes from the northeast to join it.
The commentary states:
The Jìshuǐ (濟水) then goes north,
and the Wènshuǐ (汶水) joins it,
which Dài Yánzhī (戴延之) called Qīngkǒu (清口).
Guō Yuánshēng’s (郭緣生) *Shùzhēngjì* (述征記) says: The Qīnghé (清河) first receives floodwaters,
then flows north into the Jì (濟),
or some say Qīng (清) is the Jì (濟) itself.
The *Yǔgòng* (禹貢) says: The Jì (濟) flows northeast and meets the Wèn (汶).
Now, the dried channel flows into a large marsh,
and north of the large marsh, Qīngshuǐ (清水) meets the Wèn (汶).
Jīng Xiāngfán (京相璠) says: Today, northeast of Jìběi (濟北) Dōng'ā (東阿) there is the old Qīngtíng (清亭),
which is what was called Qīng (清) in the Spring and Autumn period.
Therefore, the Jìshuǐ (濟水) was also known by the name Qīng (清),
also because its water was clear and deep,
thus sharing the appellation.
This is why King Yàn (燕王) said:
"I have heard that Qí (齊) has the clear Jì (濟) and the turbid Hé (河) as its defenses."
This is that same water.
They burned their boats and abandoned their armor,
marching on foot to Péngchéng (彭城).
Zhú Língxiù (竺靈秀) abandoned Xūchāng (須昌)
and fled south to Húlù (湖陸),
causing great turmoil in Qīng (青) and Yǎn (兗) provinces.
Chángshā King Yìxīn (義欣) was in Péngchéng (彭城);
his generals and subordinates feared that the Wèi (魏) army would arrive in great numbers,
and advised Yìxīn (義欣) to abandon the garrison and return to the capital,
but Yìxīn (義欣) refused to comply.
The Wèi troops attacked Jǐnán.
Jǐnán Commandery’s seat was Lìchéng.
In the second year of Tàikāng of Emperor Wǔ of Jìn,
Wǔjìn County was established by partitioning Dāntú and Qū'ā,
belonging to Jìnlíng Commandery;
after the southward migration,
it belonged to Nán Dōnghǎi Commandery.
Today, the towns of Bēnniú, Qīngchéng, and Wànsùi are all within its territory.
Chéngzhī ordered them to cease hostilities
and opened the city gates.
The masses said:
“The enemy is numerous and we are few;
why are you so disdainful of the enemy!”
Chéngzhī said:
“Now, holding out in a besieged city,
the situation is already critical;
if we again show weakness,
we will surely be massacred.
We must show strength to meet them.”
The Wèi people suspected an ambush,
and so they withdrew.
Chéngzhī
was the father of Xiāo Dàochéng.
The Wèi army besieged the Xià ruler for several days,
cutting off their water and fodder,
causing people and horses to suffer from hunger and thirst.
On the Dīngyǒu day,
the Xià ruler led his forces down Qūngūyuán.
Wèi Wǔwèi General Qiū Juàn attacked them,
and the Xià forces were utterly routed,
with over ten thousand dead.
The Xià ruler suffered a serious wound,
and fled alone on horseback,
gathered his remaining forces,
and drove fifty thousand civilians
west to secure Shàngguī.
The Wèi people captured Dānyánggōng Wūshìbá, Wǔlínggōng Tūgǔ, brothers of the Xià ruler, and over a hundred officials from dukes down to marquises.
On this day,
the Wèi troops, pressing their advantage, advanced to attack Āndìng.
Xià Dōngpínggōng Yǐdòu abandoned the city and fled to Cháng'ān,
driving several thousand households
west to Shàngguī.
On the Wùxū day,
Wèi Shūsūn Jiàn attacked Zhú Língxiù at Húlù.
Língxiù was thoroughly defeated,
with over five thousand dead.
Jiàn returned and garrisoned Fànchéng.
This was the city of Fàn County in Dōngpíng Commandery.
Dù Yòu said: Fàn County in Púzhōu
was the fief of Jìn Grandee Shì Huì.
On the Jǐhài day,
the Wèi ruler went to Āndìng;
on the Gēngzǐ day,
he returned,
overlooking Píngliáng,
dug trenches to besiege it,
comforted those newly submitted,
pardoned the people of Qín and Yōng,
and granted them seven years of tax exemption.
The Xià commander of Lǒngxī submitted to Wèi.
On the Xīnchǒu day,
Wèi Ān Jié supervised the various armies in attacking Huátái.
The King of Héxī, Méngxùn, sent Shàngshūláng Zōng Shū and others to pay tribute to Wèi.
The Wèi ruler hosted a banquet for them,
and held Cuī Hào’s hand to show Shū and others, saying:
“The Master Cuī you have heard of,
this is he.
The excellence of his talent and strategy
is unparalleled today.
I consult him on every action,
and he predicts success and failure,
as if matching a tally,
never once being wrong.”
Wèi appointed Shūsūn Jiàn as Dudū of the military affairs of Jì, Qīng, and other four prefectures.
Wèi had not yet obtained Qīngzhōu,
so Jiàn was made Dudū to manage it.
Wèi Shàngshū Kù Jié led five thousand cavalry to meet Qín King Mòmò.
Wèi Shū Guānshì Zhì: Among the northern surnames,
Kùnǔguān was later changed to Kù.
Shuài
is read as lǜ;

Qí

Mòmò followed him,
and Kù Jié led them back.
Over ten thousand Qiāng in Nán'ān rebelled against Qín,
electing Ānnán Jiāngjūn, Dudū of eight commanderies’ military affairs, and Guǎngníng Grand Administrator Jiāo Yí as their leader.
Wèi Shū Dìxíng Zhì: Guǎngníng Commandery’s seat was Zhāng County in Lǒngxī.

Mòmò requested aid from Dī King Yáng Nándāng.
Nándāng sent General Fú Xiàn to lead three thousand cavalry to relieve him.
Mòmò and Xiàn joined forces to attack the various Qiāng.
The various Qiāng were routed,
and Liàng fled back to Guǎngníng.
Mòmò advanced his army to attack him.
He sent a written order to Jiāo Yí to capture Liàng.
In the twelfth month,

Mòmò advanced Yí’s title to Zhènguó Jiāngjūn.
Qín Lüèyáng Grand Administrator, Hóngnóng Yáng Xiǎn, surrendered his commandery to Xià.
Emperor Wǔ of Jìn established Lüèyáng Commandery by partitioning Tiānshuǐ.
Jiàng

On the Xīnyǒu day,
Chángshā King Yìxīn was appointed Yùzhōu Cìshǐ,
garrisoning Shòuyáng.
Shòuyáng’s land was barren and its people dispersed,
its city walls dilapidated,
and bandits roamed openly;
Yìxīn managed it as appropriate,
and within his jurisdiction, the people settled peacefully,
nothing was picked up from the roads,
and the city and its granaries were complete and full,
thus becoming a prosperous march.
The Sháopí had long been abandoned;
Yìxīn repaired its dikes,
diverting river water into the reservoir,
irrigating over ten thousand qǐng of fields,
and there were no more droughts.
He diverted the water of the Féihé into the Sháopí.
Fù

Xià Shànggǔgōng Shègān and Guǎngyánggōng Duòluògū surrendered,

Guānzhōng Hóu Dòu Dàitián captured Xī Jīn, É Qīng, and others,

Xíng

who were stationed in the palace,

The Xià commanders of Cháng'ān, Línjìn, and Wǔgōng all fled,

Yǎnzhōu Cìshǐ Zhú Língxiù was executed for abandoning his army.
The emperor saw Yuán Hùzhī’s letter and praised it,

37 Péngchéng Wáng Yìkāng and Wáng Hóng were both Grand Secretaries (Lù Shàngshū).
Yìkāng was still resentful,
wanting to obtain Yángzhōu,
