Hóng, being old and ill,
repeatedly begged to retire.
Tánshǒu requested Wújùn for himself,
but the Emperor refused both requests.
Yìkāng said to someone:
"Grandee Wáng has been ill for a long time and cannot rise.
How can the Divine Land be governed while he lies in bed!"
Tánshǒu advised Hóng to cut his staff, civil and military, by half and give them to Yìkāng.
The Emperor allowed the transfer of two thousand men,
and Yìkāng was then pleased.
Punctuated by Niè Chóngqí, collated by Wáng Chóngwǔ.
Sīmǎ Guāng
compiled under imperial edict.
After learning at Tiāntái.
Tàizǔ Wénhuángdì, Part Two, Lower
Yuánjiā Eighth Year (Xīnwèi, 431)
1 Spring,
First Month.
On the day Rénwǔ, the first day of the month,
Yàn issued a great amnesty
and changed the reign title to Dàxīng.
2 On the day Bǐngshēn,
Tán Dàojì and others went from Qīngshuǐ to rescue Huátái.
Wèi's Shūsūn Jiàn and Zhǎngsūn Dàoshēng resisted them.
On the day Dīngyǒu,
Dàojì arrived at Shòuzhāng
and encountered Wèi's Ānpíng Gōng Yǐzhān Juàn.
According to Wèi's official history, the Shìzhì: Xiàndì ordered the descendants of his paternal uncle to adopt the surname Yǐzhān.
He heavily defeated him;
they fought their way to Gāoliáng Tíng,
and beheaded Wèi's Jìzhōu Cìshǐ Xífán Kùjié.
Wèi Míngyuándì, in the eighth year of Tàicháng,
established Jìzhōu,
with its seat of government in Què'áo Chéng.
濟,
read as "zǐ lǐ fān".
3 The Xià ruler attacked the Qín general Yáo Xiàn
and defeated him.
He then sent his paternal uncle, Běipíng Gōng Wéi Fá, to lead ten thousand men to attack Nán'ān.
At the end of last year, they protected Nán'ān.
People resorted to cannibalism.
Qín's Shìzhōng,
Zhēnglǔ Jiāngjūn Chūlián Fǔzhèng, Shìzhōng and Yòuwèi Jiāngjūn Qífú Yánzuò, and Lìbù Shàngshū Qífú Bábá climbed over the city wall and defected to Xià.
Qín Wáng Mùmò was desperate and exhausted;
he carried a coffin and surrendered.
The four rulers of the Qífú clan
perished after forty-nine years.
櫬,
read as "chū jìn fān".
降,
read as "hù jiāng fān".
Xīngguó was captured by Qín,
seen in scroll 6 of the previous volume.
沮,
read as "zǐ yú fān".
Tàizǐ Sīzhí,
in charge of impeaching palace officials and leading the commandery troops.
The Jìn Zhi does not have this office,
it should be an office established by the two Zhàos, Yàn, or Qín.
"Your Excellency bears the great favor of the state,
holding important responsibilities as a regional governor.
Now that the imperial court is overthrown,
how can you not lead your current troops to raise a righteous cause and eliminate the enemies!"
Yí said:
"Now that our sovereign has already fallen into the hands of the bandits,
it is not that I fear death and forget righteousness;
rather, if we pursue them with a large army,
it will hasten his death.
It is better to choose a worthy member of the royal clan,
elevate him as sovereign and then attack.
Perhaps we can succeed."
Kǎi then built an altar and swore an oath with the troops.
Within twenty days,
over ten thousand people responded.
Coincidentally, Yí died of illness,
Kǎi could not carry out the enterprise alone
and fled to Héxī.
4 Second Month.
On the day Wùwǔ,
Jiāng Yí, Shàngshū Yòu Púyè, was appointed Xiāngzhōu Cìshǐ.
5 Tán Dàojì and others advanced to Jìshàng.
In over twenty days,
they fought more than thirty battles with Wèi,
and Dàojì was victorious in most of them.
When the army reached Lìchéng,
Lìchéng County had belonged to Jìnán Jùn since the Hàn dynasty;
during the Sòng, it was the seat of the Jìzhōu Cìshǐ.
They burned grass and grain.
Dàojì's army lacked food
and could not advance.
Because of this, Ān Xié, Sīmǎ Chǔzhī, and others were able to concentrate their efforts on attacking Huátái.
The Wèi ruler again sent Chǔbīng Jiāngjūn Wáng Huìlóng to assist them.
Zhū Xiūzhī held out for several months,
but when provisions ran out,
he and his soldiers smoked rats to eat.
On the day Xīnyǒu,
Wèi conquered Huátái,
capturing Xiūzhī and Dōngjùn Tàishǒu Shēn Mó.
Dōngjùn had been governed from Báimǎ since the Hàn and Wèi dynasties;
Báimǎ
was the territory of Huátái.
Mó
was the great-grandson of Zhōng.
Shēn Zhōng is mentioned in Jìn Chéngdì Xiánhé Jiǔnián, scroll 95.
6 On the day Guǐyǒu,
the Wèi ruler returned to Píngchéng,
held a grand feast,
and reported to the ancestral temple.
Generals, commanders, and all officials were rewarded,
and soldiers were granted ten years of tax exemption.
This was to reward their achievements in campaigning north against Ròurán, west against Xià, and defending the south against Sòng.
將,
read as "jí liàng fān".
帥,
read as "suǒ lèi fān".
復,
read as "fāng mù fān",
meaning exemption from service;
the same applies to 復 below.
At this time, there were great floods in the southern border regions of Wèi,
and many people starved to death.
Shàngshū Lìng Liú Jié reported to the Wèi ruler, saying:
"Recently, border bandits have invaded,
and war chariots have been repeatedly deployed.
Heaven has assisted Your Sacred Wisdom,
and enemies have been vanquished everywhere.
Now that the difficulties are pacified,
all have received generous rewards.
However, the people of the commanderies and states,
though not participating in military campaigns,
diligently engage in farming and sericulture
to supply the army and the state.
This is truly the great foundation for governing the world
and what the state treasury relies upon.
Now, from the mountains eastward,
they have all suffered from floods.
Compassion should be shown
to extend your nurturing care."
The Wèi ruler followed his advice
and exempted the entire territory from one year's rent and taxes.
7 Tán Dàojì and others ran out of food
and withdrew from Lìchéng.
Some soldiers deserted to Wèi
and fully reported the situation.
The Wèi forces pursued them.
The army was panicking
and on the verge of collapsing.
Dàojì, during the night, made a noise as if counting tallies and measuring sand,
and covered the small amount of remaining rice with sand.
When dawn broke,
the Wèi army saw this
and thought Dàojì had abundant provisions.
They concluded the deserters had lied and executed them.
At that time, Dàojì's forces were small,
while the Wèi forces were very strong,
with cavalry surrounding them from four sides.
Dàojì ordered his soldiers to all wear armor,
while he himself rode in a carriage in white clothes,
leading his troops out slowly.
The Wèi people thought there was an ambush
and did not dare to approach,
gradually retreating.
Dàojì returned with his entire army intact.
The Inspector of Qīngzhōu, Xiāo Sīhuà, heard that Dàojìn had returned to Jìnán.
He wanted to abandon his post and ensure his safety.
Sòng Qīngzhōu was governed from Dōngyángchéng.
He did not comply.
On the day Dīngchǒu,
Sīhuà abandoned his post and fled to Píngchāng.
Píngchāng County
belonged to Lángxié during the Former Hàn dynasty,
and to Běihǎi during the Later Hàn dynasty.
The Dìzhì of the Jìn Tàikāng period states it belonged to Chéngyáng.
Emperor Huì divided it to establish Píngchāng Commandery.
The Wǔdài Zhì states: Jiāoxī County of Mìzhōu was formerly called Qiánzōu,
where Píngchāng Commandery was established.
Upon hearing this,
he also abandoned the city and fled.
The Wèi army ultimately did not arrive,
but the accumulated provisions in Dōngyáng had already been burned by the local people.
Sīhuà was summoned [to the capital] and punished,
and imprisoned in the Shàngfāng.
8. The King of Yàn established Lady Mùróng as Queen.
9. On the day Gēngxū,
Wèi's Ānjié and others returned to Píngchéng.
The Wèi ruler commended Zhū Xiūzhī for his integrity,
and married him to a daughter of the imperial clan.
This is to account for Xiūzhī's return from the north.
Qī (妻),
refers to Zǐxì Fān (子細翻).
Originally,
when the Emperor dispatched Dào Yànzhī,
he cautioned him, saying:
"If the northern country's troops move,
before they arrive,
proceed directly into the Hé;
if they do not move,
remain in Péngchéng and do not advance."
When Ānjié captured the Sòng prisoners,
the Wèi ruler first heard these words.
He said to his high-ranking officials:
"You all previously called my adoption of Cuī Hào's plan a mistake,
and, in your fear, strongly remonstrated.
Families that are always victorious
initially all consider themselves superior to others,
but when it comes to the ultimate outcome—
'ultimate outcome' (歸終)
refers to the extreme point of a situation."
Sīmǎ Chǔzhī submitted a memorial,
believing that all regions were now pacified,
and requested a large-scale expedition against Sòng.
The Wèi ruler, considering the troops had been long weary,
did not permit it.
He summoned Chǔzhī to be Sànqí Chángshì,
and appointed Wáng Huìlóng as the Administrator of Xíngyáng.
Although Wèi appointed an Administrator of Xíngyáng,
it actually regarded Hǔláo as a vital strategic point.
According to the Guānshì Zhì of the Wèishū: In the third year of Tàian of Gāozōng,
all tribal military protectors were first appointed as administrators.
It is likely that at this time, only Wáng Huìlóng was appointed as Administrator of Xíngyáng,
and it was not until the third year of Tàian that all were systematically changed.
Shǒu (守),
refers to Shì Yòu Fān (式又翻).
Huìlóng served in the commandery for ten years,
cultivating both agriculture and military affairs,
achieving great fame and accomplishments.
Over ten thousand households rallied and submitted to him.
The Emperor spread disinformation in Wèi,
saying,
"Huìlóng, believing his achievements were great but his position low,
intended to draw Sòng forces into an invasion,
and then seize Sīmǎ Chǔzhī and rebel."
Upon hearing this, the Wèi ruler
bestowed an imperial letter and seal upon Huìlóng, saying:
"Liú Yìlóng fears the general like a tiger,
and wishes to harm you;
I know this myself.
I imagine that such rumors
are not worth your concern."
The Emperor again sent an assassin, Lǚ Xuánbó, to kill him,
saying:
"If you obtain Huìlóng's head,
I will enfeoff you as a duke of two hundred households and reward you with a thousand bolts of silk."
Xuánbó pretended to be a defector,
requesting a private discussion with him.
Huìlóng suspected him,
and had someone search his bosom,
finding a small knife.
Xuánbó kowtowed and begged for death.
Huìlóng said:
"Each serves his own lord."
He released him.
His attendants remonstrated, saying:
"The Sòng people's plotting has not ceased.
If we do not kill Xuánbó,
we will have no means to deter future attempts."
Huìlóng said:
"Life and death are ordained by fate;
how can he harm me?
I rely on benevolence and righteousness as my shield,
so what do I have to worry about!"
Thus, he let him go.
The historian recounts this incident because Huìlóng served as Administrator of Xíngyáng until his death.
10. In summer,
the fifth month,
on the day Gēngyín,
the Wèi ruler went to Yúnzhōng.
11. In the sixth month,
on the day Yǐchǒu,
there was a general amnesty.
11. The Xià ruler killed Qǐfú Mùmò and five hundred members of his clan.
12. Fearing the pressure from the Wèi people, the Xià ruler
gathered over one hundred thousand Qín commoners—
Qín commoners
refers to the people of the Qǐfú clan that were acquired.
He fortified Jìhé,
intending to attack King Méngxùn of Héxī and seize his territory.
King Mùguī of Tǔyùhún sent the Inspector of Yìzhōu, Mù Lìyán, and the Inspector of Níngzhōu, Shí Qián,
leading thirty thousand cavalry.
Taking advantage of their crossing the river halfway,
they intercepted and attacked them,
capturing Xià ruler Dìng and returning with him.
The Hèlián clan, after three rulers and twenty-six years, was extinguished.
From then on, the Central Plains and the northwest regions
all came under Wèi rule.
Shuài (帥),
is read as Lǜ (率).
Qí (騎),
refers to Qí Jì Fān (奇寄翻).
Shí Qián
was the son of Shùluògān.
Shùluògān died in the thirteenth year of Yìxī of Emperor Ān of Jìn.
14. The Wèi border officials captured over twenty Rourán scouts.
The Wèi ruler gave them clothes and sent them away.
The Rourán were pleased and grateful.
In the intercalary month,
on the day Yǐwèi,
the Rourán Chìlián Kèhán sent envoys to Wèi.
The Wèi ruler treated them with great courtesy.
15. The Wèi ruler sent the Sànqí Shìláng Zhōu Shào to propose marriage,
and also to seek a matrimonial alliance.
The Emperor gave an evasive reply.
16. The Inspector of Jīngzhōu, Jiāngxià Wáng Yìgōng,
was gradually growing older and
wished to handle government affairs independently.
However, the Chángshǐ Liú Zhàn constantly restrained him,
creating a rift between them.
According to Sòng regulations: when a young prince governed a province,
the Chángshǐ usually acted on behalf of the provincial administration,
and all matters were decided by the acting official.
Yìgōng wanted to handle affairs independently, but Zhàn disagreed,
thus creating a rift.
Zhǎng (長),
refers to Zhī Liǎng Fān (知兩翻).
The Emperor sent someone to question and reprimand Yìgōng,
and also to mediate between them.
At this time,
Wáng Huá and Wáng Tánshǒu had both died.
The Língjūn Jiāngjūn Yīn Jǐngrén, who had always been on good terms with Zhàn,
reported to the Emperor that many worthy individuals of the time had passed away,
and requested to summon Zhàn to be Tàizǐ Zhànshì,
with the added title of Jǐshìzhōng,
to participate in government affairs together.
He appointed Zhāng Shào, the Inspector of Yōngzhōu, to replace Zhàn as Fǔjūn Chángshǐ and Nánmán Xiàowèi.
After some time,
Shào was impeached for engaging in private accumulation of wealth while serving as Inspector of Yōngzhōu.
The value of his illicit gains amounted to 2.45 million,
and he was sent to the Tíngwèi,
where he was sentenced to death.
In the fifth year of Yǒngjiā,
Shào was appointed Inspector of Yōngzhōu.
Yōng (雍),
refers to Yú Yòng Fān (於用翻).
Shù recalled Shào's old merits from the previous court:
when Emperor Wǔ was suppressing Huán Xuán,
Shào petitioned his father, Gǔ, to express his loyalty,
and also did not side with Liú Yì.
The Emperor personally issued an edict acknowledging his actions,
removed Shào from office,
and stripped him of his titles and land.
Shù said to his son, Zōng:
"The Sovereign commends Shào's early sincerity
and has especially shown leniency.
My words were coincidentally opportune,
which is why they were especially acknowledged.
If this matter were to be revealed,
it would be an encroachment upon the Sovereign's grace,
which is the greatest impropriety."
He then had Zōng burn the document in his presence.
Later, the Emperor said to Shào:
"Your acquittal
was largely due to Xiè Shù's efforts."
17. In autumn,
the seventh month,
on the day Jǐyǒu,
the Wèi ruler went to Héxī.
18. In the eighth month,
on the day Yǐyǒu,
King Méngxùn of Héxī sent his son Ānzhōu to serve at the Wèi court.
19 Mùguī, king of Tǔyùhún, sent Shìláng Xiè Tàiníng to present a memorial to the Wèi,
requesting to send Hèlián Dìng.
On the day Jǐchǒu,
the Wèi appointed Mùguī as Dà Jiāngjūn and King of Xīqín.
20 The Left Púyè, Prince Yìqìng of Línchuān, firmly requested to be relieved of his post;
on the day Jiǎchén,
Yìqìng was appointed Zhōngshūlìng,
with the office of Dānyáng Yǐn as before.
21 In the ninth month,
on the day Guǐchǒu,
the Wèi ruler returned to the palace.
On the day Gēngshēn,
Tàiwèi Zhǎngsūn Sōng was additionally appointed Zhùguó Dà Jiāngjūn;
the office of Zhùguó Dà Jiāngjūn began with this.
Zhēngxī Dà Jiāngjūn Zhǎngsūn Dàoshēng was made Sīkōng.
Dàoshēng was by nature pure and frugal;
he used one bearskin saddle flap
for several decades without changing it.
The Leìpiān says: A horse saddle flap is called shèn.
Shèn,
pronounced chāngyàn.
The Shǔ commentary says: it is for covering and protecting from mud.
"As wise as Cuī Hào,
as incorruptible as Dàoshēng."
22 The Wèi ruler wanted to select an envoy to go to Héxī.
Cuī Hào recommended Shàngshū Lǐ Shùn,
so Shùn was appointed Tàicháng,
and King Méngxùn of Héxī was appointed Shìzhōng, Dūdū Liángzhōu, Xīyù, Qiāng, Róng Zhū Jūnshì, Tàifù, Xíng Zhēngxī Dà Jiāngjūn, Liángzhōu Mù, and King of Liáng,
ruling the seven commanderies of Wǔwēi, Zhāngyè, Dūnhuáng, Jiǔquán, Xīhǎi, Jīnchéng, and Xīpíng.
The imperial decree stated:
"Rise and fall, survival and demise,
are to ascend and descend with Wèi.
To the north, reaching the Qióngfà;
to the south, reaching Yōng and Tīng;
to the west, covering Kūnlǐng;
to the east, reaching Héqǔ.
The Jīngdiǎn Shìwén says: Sīmǎ said: Qióngfà is the land without vegetation under the North Pole.
Note: Máo (hair) here means Cǎo (grass).
Geographical texts say: mountains use grass and trees as their hair.
Yōng refers to the land of Shàngyōng in Wèixīng.
Tīng is a mountain.
Kūnlǐng refers to Kūnlún.
Héqǔ is the bend of the river in Shuòfāng.
Tīng is pronounced the same as Mín.
Bèi is pronounced píyì.
To assist the imperial house.
Establish generals and ministers, various qīng, and hundreds of officials,
to be provisionally appointed according to imperial prerogative.
Erect the emperor's banners and flags,
with guards and clearings for entry and exit,
following the precedents of the feudal kings in the early Hàn dynasty."
23 On the day Rénshēn,
the Wèi ruler issued an edict saying:
"Now that the two enemies have been crushed,
we shall put away military matters and cultivate civil affairs,
restore neglected offices,
and bring forth reclusive talents.
Lú Xuán of Fànyáng, Cuī Chuò of Bólíng, Lǐ Líng of Zhàojùn, Xíng Yǐng of Héjiān, Gāo Yǔn of Bóhǎi, Yóu Yǎ of Guǎngpíng, Zhāng Wěi of Tàiyuán, and others,
are all descendants of distinguished individuals,
adorning the Zhōu state.
"Zhōu"
should be
"Zhōu" (州).
[Note: The Jiǎshíxíngběn correctly has
"Zhōu" (州);
the Yǐshíxíngběn is the same;
the Kǒngběn is the same.]
'I shall lead you with a halter.'
This is from the Jiǔ'èr line of Yì Jīng, Zhōngfú hexagram.
Fully instruct the zhōu and commanderies to send them with propriety."
Consequently, Xuán and others, as well as several hundred people sent by the zhōu and commanderies who arrived, were ranked and appointed.
Cuī Chuò firmly declined on account of his elderly mother.
Xuán and the others were all appointed Zhōngshū Bóshì.
Xuán
was the great-grandson of Chén.
After the Yǒngjiā era of the Jìn,
Lú Chén wandered between the Shí family,
and after Rǎn Mǐn's defeat,
he died in battle.
Chén
is pronounced shírén.
He was Shùn's paternal cousin.
Xuán's maternal uncle Cuī Hào,
whenever he spoke with Xuán,
would always sigh and say:
"Facing Zǐzhēn makes my nostalgic feelings even deeper."
Lú Xuán's
courtesy name was Zǐzhēn.
He was skilled at discerning family names and clans.
Xuán stopped him and said:
"Indeed, the initiation and establishment of affairs
each have their opportune time;
how many people
are willing to do this?
You should think thrice."
Hào did not follow,
and thus incurred the displeasure of the multitude.
24 At first,
Emperor Zhāochéng of Wèi initially established laws and decrees:
Shíyìjiān was posthumously honored as Emperor Zhāochéng.
"Those who commit rebellion or treason shall have their families exterminated;
for other offenses punishable by death, they may offer gold or horses to redeem their crime;
murderers may offer cattle, horses, and burial implements to the victim's family to settle the matter;
those who steal official property shall compensate it fivefold;
for private property,
they shall compensate it tenfold."
Bèi means to compensate,
nowadays people often say péibèi.
There was no suffering from prolonged interrogation and extensive implication,
and the people within the borders were content.
When Tàizǔ entered the Central Plains,
Emperor Dàowǔ's temple name was Tàizǔ.
He ordered the Sāngōng Láng Wáng Dé to revise and standardize the laws,
striving for simplicity.
Details can be found in Volume 110, Year 2 of Lóng'ān in the reign of Emperor Ān of Jìn.
Yì is pronounced yǐchǐ.
Punishments were excessive and cruel;
details can be found in Volume 111, Year 4 of Lóng'ān in the reign of Emperor Ān of Jìn.
Bèi is pronounced píyì.
The bureaucratic language was also abstruse.
Emperor Míngyuán's temple name was Tàizōng.
In the tenth month,
on the day Wùyín,
Shìzǔ ordered Cuī Hào to revise the laws and decrees,
abolishing the five-year and four-year punishments,
and adding one-year punishments.
Those who practiced witchcraft were to
carry a black ram and hold a dog, and be drowned in a deep pool.
It was initially ordered that officials of the ninth rank and above could have their punishments remitted with their official titles.
Hàn officials were ranked by their stone salaries,
while Wèi and Jìn first established the order of official ranks.
Postpartum women were to be judged only after one hundred days.
A dengwen drum was hung to the left of the palace gate for the wronged to reach the emperor.
The Yu laws had those with lawsuits shake a drum-bell;
the Zhōu Lǐ states: a Jiā Stone was placed on the left to pacify troubled commoners.
All these were means to convey grievances.
The dengwen drum meant that
the wronged could go to the palace gate and beat the drum,
and their case would be heard immediately.
25 The Wèi ruler went to Mònán.
In the eleventh month,
on the day Bǐngchén,
Mòfú Kùgān of the Northern Chìlè
(the chieftain of Gāochē was called Mòfú).
The Kǎoyì says: the Hòuwèishū and Běishǐ annals both write
"Chìlè",
while the Dèng Yuān biography all writes
"Gāochē".
Note: Gāochē is another name for Chìlè.
drove several million deer
to the Wèi ruler's temporary residence.
The Wèi ruler held a great hunt and bestowed the game upon his accompanying officials.
On the day Dīngchǒu in the twelfth month,
he returned to the palace.
26 In this year,
the King of Liáng changed his era name to Yìhé.
27 Fàn Yángmài, king of Línyì, raided Jiǔdé,
and the Jiāozhōu troops repelled him.
Jiǔdé commandery,
anciently the state of Yuèshāngshì,
was Huānzhōu during the Suí and Táng dynasties.
1 In spring,
the first month,
on the day Bǐngwǔ,
the Wèi ruler honored Bảo Tàihòu Dòu Shì as Huáng Tàihòu,
and honored his wet nurse as his mother,
which was not proper according to ritual.
His son Huǎng was made Huáng Tàizǐ;
a general amnesty was declared;
and the era name was changed to Yánhé.
2 The King of Yàn made Wáng Rén, the son of Empress Mùróng, the crown prince.
3 In the third month,
on the day Gēngxū,
Wèi Jiāngjūn Wáng Hóng was promoted to Tàibǎo,
and additionally appointed Zhōngshū Jiān.
On the day Dīngsì,
Zhēngnán Dà Jiāngjūn Tán Dàojì was promoted to Sīkōng,
and returned to guard Xúnyáng.
Dàojì had returned from Lìchéng to Jiànkāng, and was again sent back to guard Xúnyáng.
4 On the *rénshēn* day,
Mùguī (慕璝), King of Tǔyùhún (吐谷渾), sent Hèlián Dìng (赫連定) to Wèi (魏).
The Wèi (魏) people killed him.
Mùguī (慕璝) submitted a memorial, saying:
"Your servant has captured the usurping rebel,
and presented the victory to the royal court.
Although my rank and title are high, my territory has not been expanded.
Although my chariots and banners are adorned, my wealth is insufficient for rewards.
I wish for your imperial scrutiny."
The Wèi (魏) ruler sent it down for discussion.
The high officials believed:
"What Mùguī (慕璝) delivered was only Dìng (定) himself.
The people beyond the frontier are all under his control,
yet he is insatiably greedy,
and cannot be granted this."
The Wèi (魏) ruler then issued an edict, saying:
"The lands of Jīnchéng (金城), Bāohǎn (枹罕), and Lǒngxī (隴西) obtained by the King of Xīqín (西秦),
I have already granted them to him.
This is a division of territory;
why should it be expanded again?
When Xīqín (西秦) arrives respectfully,
silk and cotton will be provided according to the frequency of his envoys,
and increased as circumstances require.
It is not a one-time grant that ceases there."
From then on, Mùguī's (慕璝) tributary envoys to Wèi (魏) gradually became fewer.
5 The Wèi (魏) *fāngshì* Qí Xiān (祁纎) proposed changing Dài (代) to Wànnián (萬年),
making the Dài (代) Prefect into the Wànnián (萬年) Prefect,
and the Dài (代) Magistrate into the Wànnián (萬年) Magistrate.
Cuī Hào (崔浩) said:
"In ancient times, Emperor Tàizǔ (太祖) responded to heaven's mandate
and simultaneously called himself Dài (代) and Wèi (魏), following the example of Yīn (殷) and Shāng (商).
Emperor Kù (帝嚳) resided in Bó (亳).
His son Qì (契) was enfeoffed in Shāng (商).
From Qì (契) to Tāng (湯), there were eight relocations.
Tāng (湯) first established his capital in Bó (亳),
residing in the place of the former king,
thus it was called Bó Yīn (亳殷).
Therefore, they were called both Yīn (殷) and Shāng (商).
We are destined to enjoy prosperity for ten thousand *yì* years,
and do not need to assume a name to add to it.
What Xiān (纎) has heard
is not of correct meaning.
The old designation should be restored."
The Wèi (魏) ruler followed him.
6 In summer,
in the fifth month,
on the *rénshēn* day,
Wáng Hóng (王弘), the Civil and Resplendent Duke of Huáróng (華容), passed away.
Hóng (弘) was intelligent and thoughtful,
but frivolous and lacked solemnity.
By nature, he was narrow-minded and
enjoyed humiliating others,
which made people look down upon him.
Although he held a high and prominent position,
he did not engage in accumulating wealth;
when he passed away,
his family had no surplus assets.
The emperor, hearing of this,
specially bestowed a million coins
and a thousand *hú* of rice.
7 The Wèi (魏) ruler reviewed his troops in the southern suburbs,
planning to attack Yān (燕).
8 The emperor sent the envoy Zhào Dàoshēng (趙道生) to Wèi (魏) to establish relations.
9 In the sixth month,
on the *wùyín* day,
Yìkāng (義康), Prince of Péngchéng (彭城), who was *Sītú* and Inspector of Nánsúzhōu (南徐州), was reassigned to lead as Inspector of Yángzhōu (揚州).
Upon Wáng Hóng's (王弘) death,
Yìkāng (義康) first took charge of Yángzhōu (揚州).
10 An edict was issued to divide Qīngzhōu (青州) and establish Jìzhōu (冀州).
Sòng (宋) Jìzhōu (冀州) comprised the nine commanderies of Guǎngchuān (廣川), Píngyuán (平原), Qīnghé (清河), Lèlíng (樂陵), Wèijùn (魏郡), Héjiān (河間), Dùnqiū (頓丘), Gāoyáng (高陽), and Bóhǎi (勃海),
all provisionally established between the Hé (河) and Jì (濟) Rivers.
11 Mùguī (慕璝), King of Tǔyùhún (吐谷渾), sent his *Sīmǎ* Zhào Xù (趙敍) to offer tribute,
and also to report a victory.
He reported the victory of capturing Hèlián Dìng (赫連定).
*Guī* (璝) is pronounced like *gǔhuí*.
12 On the *gēngyín* day,
the Wèi (魏) ruler attacked Yān (燕).
He ordered太子 Huǎng (晃) to oversee the affairs of the *shàngshū*.
At this time, Huǎng (晃) was only five years old.
He also sent the Left *Púyè* Ān Yuán (安原) and Chóng (崇), Prince of Jiànníng (建寧), etc., to garrison the Mònán (漠南) to guard against the Rourán (柔然).
13 On the *xīnmǎo* day,
the Wèi (魏) ruler sent the *Sànqí Chángshì* Dèng Yǐng (鄧穎) to establish relations.
14 On the *yǐwèi* day,

Mùguī (慕璝), King of Tǔyùhún (吐谷渾), was appointed *Dūdū* of the military affairs of Xīqín (西秦), Hé (河), and Shā (沙) three prefectures, *Zhēngxī Dàjiāngjūn*, and Inspector of Xīqín (西秦) and Hé (河) two prefectures.
His noble title was advanced to Prince of Lǒngxī (隴西).
Mùguī (慕璝) was also ordered to return all the southern generals and soldiers who had previously been captured by Xià (夏),
numbering over one hundred and fifty people.
Those who were defeated and captured by Xià (夏) under Liú Yìzhēn (劉義真).
In addition, Yáng Nándāng (楊難當), Inspector of Běiqínzhōu (北秦州), was promoted to *Zhēngxī Jiāngjūn*.
Nándāng (難當) appointed his nephew Bǎozōng (保宗) as *Zhènnán Jiāngjūn*,
to guard Dàngchāng (宕昌).
Dàngchāng (宕昌) was the land of Dàngzhōu (宕州) during the Suí (隋) and Táng (唐) dynasties.
*Dàng* (宕) is pronounced like *túlàng*.
He also guarded Shàngguī (上邽).
Bǎozōng (保宗) plotted to attack Nándāng (難當);
the plot was exposed,
and Nándāng (難當) imprisoned him.
15 On the *rènyín* day,
Yìgōng (義恭), Prince of Jiāngxià (江夏), was appointed *Dūdū* of the military affairs of Nányǎn (南兗) and other six prefectures, *Kāifǔ Yítóng Sānsī*, and Inspector of Nányǎnzhōu (南兗州).
Yìqìng (義慶), Prince of Línchuān (臨川), was appointed *Dūdū* of the military affairs of Jīng (荊), Yōng (雍) and other seven prefectures, and Inspector of Jīngzhōu (荊zhōu).
Yìxuān (義宣), Prince of Jìnglíng (竟陵), was appointed *Zhōngshū Jiān*.
Yìjì (義季), Prince of Héngyáng (衡陽), was appointed Inspector of Nánxúzhōu (南徐州).
Previously,
Gāozǔ (高祖) considered Jīngzhōu (荊zhōu) to be of critical importance in the upper reaches,
with vast territory and resources,
possessing half of the court's wealth and military power.
Therefore, his dying edict commanded his sons to reside there.
The Emperor considered Yìqìng (義慶) to be an excellent member of the imperial clan,
and also that Prince Lìwǔ (烈武) had great merit for the state.
Prince Dàoguī (道規) of Línchuān (臨chuān) was posthumously honored as Prince Lìwǔ (烈武).
16 In autumn,
in the seventh month,
on the *jǐwèi* day,
the Wèi (魏) ruler arrived at Rúshuǐ (濡水).
The *Shuǐ Jīng* states: Rúshuǐ (濡水) comes from beyond the frontier,
passes through the counties of Lìngzhī (令支), Féirú (肥如), Hǎiyáng (海陽) in Liáoxī (遼西), and then enters the sea.
*Rú* (濡) is pronounced like *nǎiguān*.
On the *gēngshēn* day,
Xī Jīn (奚斤), the *Āndōng Jiāngjūn*, was dispatched to mobilize over ten thousand civilians from Yōuzhōu (幽州) and Dīnglíng (丁零) people from Mìyún (密雲).
Wèi Shōu (魏收) said: In the second year of Huángshǐ (皇始) of Emperor Dàowǔ (道武),
Mìyún (密雲) Commandery and Mìyún (密雲) County were established,
with its seat in Tíxié (提攜) City,
originally the land of Tíxī (厗奚) County during the Hàn (漢) dynasty.
Mèng Kāng (孟康) said: *Tí* (厗) is pronounced *tí*.
He was to exit via the southern route
and rendezvous at Hélóng (和龍).
When the Wèi (魏) ruler arrived at Liáoxī (遼西),
the King of Yān (燕) sent his *Shìyùshǐ* Cuī Pìn (崔聘) to present cattle and wine to reward the army.
On the *jǐsì* day,
the Wèi (魏) ruler arrived at Hélóng (和龍).
17 On the *gēngwǔ* day,
Yīn Jǐngrén (殷景仁), the *Lǐngjūn Jiāngjūn*, was appointed *Shàngshū Púyè*.
Liú Zhàn (劉湛), the太子 *Zhànshì*, was appointed *Lǐngjūn Jiāngjūn*.
18 Liú Dàojì (劉道濟), Inspector of Yìzhōu (益州),
who was Zuì's (粹) younger brother,
trusted the *Chángshǐ* Fèi Qiān (費謙), *Biéjià* Zhāng Xī (張熙), and others.
They accumulated wealth and created benefits,
harming governance and the people.
They established official foundries,
prohibited common people from casting,
and sold ironware at high prices.
Merchants lost their livelihoods,
and lamentations filled the roads.
The displaced person Xǔ Mùzhī (許穆之)
changed his surname and personal name to Sīmǎ Fēilóng (司馬飛龍),
claiming to be a close relative of the Jìn (晉) imperial family.
He went to seek refuge with the Dī (氐) king Yáng Nándāng (楊難當).
Nándāng (難當), capitalizing on the people's grievances,
provided Fēilóng (飛龍) with troops
to harass Yìzhōu (益州).
Fēilóng (飛龍) gathered Shǔ (蜀) people,
obtaining over a thousand men.
They attacked and killed the Magistrate of Bāxīng (巴興).
Shěn Yuè (沈約) said: The Magistrate of Bāxīng (巴興),
Xú Zhì (徐志) did not note its establishment,
possibly established by the Lǐ (李) family,
and belonged to Suìníng (遂寧) Commandery.
Sòng Bái (宋白) said: Bāxīng (巴興) County was established in the eleventh year of Yǒnghé (永和) of Jìn (晉).
The Western Wèi (魏) changed its name to Chángjiāng (長江) County.
During the Táng (唐) dynasty, it belonged to Suìzhōu (遂州).
In the Tàishǐ (泰始) era of Emperor Xiàowǔ (孝武) of Jìn (晉),
Yīnpíng (陰平) Commandery was established.
By the Yǒngchū (永初) era of Emperor Wǔ (武),
it was again divided into Southern Yīnpíng (南陰平) and Northern Yīnpíng (北陰平).
This is Southern Yīnpíng (南陰平).
During the Suí (隋) dynasty, Southern Yīnpíng (南陰平) was merged into Luò (雒) County.
Sòng Bái (宋白) said: Wénzhōu (文州) was ancient Yīnpíng (陰平).
During the Warring States period, it was occupied by the Dī (氐) and Qiāng (羌) people.
In the Hàn (漢) dynasty, it was Yīnpíng (陰平) Dao.
During the Wèi (魏) and Jìn (晉) dynasties, it was Yīnpíng (陰平) County, Yīnpíng (陰平) Commandery.
At the end of Yǒngjiā (永嘉),
Wáng Jiàn (王鑒), the Administrator, surrendered the commandery to Lǐ Xióng (李雄).
The Jìn (晉) people then all migrated to Shǔ (蜀) and Hàn (漢).
Their Dī (氐) and Qiāng (羌) people all belonged to Yáng Màosōu (楊茂搜).
This commandery no longer received the imperial calendar,
therefore, the various records in the *Nán Shǐ* (南史) do not list it.
Among the Jìn (晉) people who took refuge in Shǔ (蜀),
they still established Southern and Northern Yīnpíng (陰平) in Yìzhōu (益州).
Those who took refuge in Hánzhōng (漢中) also established Southern and Northern Yīnpíng (陰平) in Liángzhōu (梁州).
Today's Yīnpíng (陰平) County in Jiànzhōu (劍州)
is the Northern Yīnpíng (陰平) Commandery of Yìzhōu (益州).
Dào Jì wished to appoint Bó Dī Nú and Liáng Xiǎn from Wǔchéng as Staff Officers and Supervisors.
Sūn Miǎn said: Bó
is a surname.
Dī Nú and others, along with Zhào Guǎng from their locality, instigated the people of the county,
falsely claiming that His Highness Sīmǎ was still in Yángquán Mountain,
gathering several thousand people,
and leading them towards Guǎnghàn.
Shěn Yuē said: Shǔ was divided to establish Yángquán County,
subordinate to Guǎnghàn Commandery.
During the Suí dynasty, it was merged back into [the larger county].
All were defeated and died.
Táng Pín from Bāxī gathered a crowd to support them.
Zhào Guǎng and others advanced to attack Fúchéng,
and captured it.
Thereupon, the administrators of the commanderies of Fúlíng, Jiāngyáng, and Suìníng all abandoned their cities and fled.
In the land of Shǔ, both the immigrant (qiáo) and native (jiù) populations rebelled.
Shěn Yuē said: Suìníng Commandery
is mentioned in the Yǒngchū Jùn Guó Zhì.
It is probably believed to have been established at the end of the Jìn dynasty by dividing Guǎnghàn,
and became Suìzhōu during the Táng dynasty.
Shǒu
is also read shǒu.
The same applies to tàishǒu below.
The administrator of Yàn Shíchéng, Lǐ Chóng, and those of ten other commanderies surrendered to Wèi.
Shíchéng County
belonged to Yòuběipíng in the Former Hàn dynasty.
Yàn divided it to establish Shíchéng Commandery.
In the eighth year of Zhēnjūn of Wèi,
Jiàndé Commandery was established at Báiláng,
with Shíchéng as a county,
subordinate to it.
Xiáng
is read Hùjiāng.
Chóng
was the son of Jì.
See Lǐ Jì in volume 100, fourth year of Shēngpíng of Jìn Mùdì.
Qiàn
is read Qīyàn.
In the eighth month,
the King of Yàn sent tens of thousands of men to sally forth and fight.
Qíu, Duke of Chānglí of Wèi, and others, defeated them.
There must be a missing character
after "Gōngqiū".
The Yàn Minister Gāo Shào led over ten thousand families to secure Qiānghú Gù.
On the day Xīnsì,
the Wèi ruler attacked Shào
and beheaded him.
The General of Pacifying the East, Hè Duōluó, attacked Dàifāng.
The General of Garrisoning the Army and Prince of Yǒngchāng, Jiàn, attacked Jiàndé.
The General of Agile Cavalry and Prince of Lèpíng, Pī, attacked Jìyáng.
All were captured.
In the ninth month,
on the day Yǐmǎo,
the Wèi ruler led his troops back west,
relocating three thousand families from the six commanderies of Yíngqiū, Chéngzhōu, Liáodōng, Lèlàng, Dàifāng, and Xuántú to Yōuzhōu.
The Wǔdài Zhì states: The Later Wèi established Yíngzhōu at Hélóngchéng,
administering commanderies such as Jiàndé, Jìyáng, Liáodōng, Lèlàng, and Yíngqiū,
and counties such as Lóngchéng, Dàxīng, Yǒnglè, Dàifāng, Dìnghuāng, Shíchéng, Guǎngdū, Yángwǔ, Xiāngpíng, Xīnchāng, Pínggāng, Liǔchéng, and Fùpíng.
It is probable that since Mùróng, the Yàn state
established commanderies and counties in Liáoxī,
which were later either abolished or merged.
Whether they were commanderies or counties
cannot all be verified.
For example, Xuántú Commandery should also have been established in Liáoxī.
Piào
is read Pǐmiào.
Qí
is read Qíjì.
Lèlàng
is pronounced Luòláng.
Tú
is read Tóngdū.
The Yàn Minister Guō Yuān advised the King of Yàn to offer terms and send a daughter to Wèi,
begging to become a dependent state.
The King of Yàn said:
"Having committed offenses previously,
our enmity is now deep.
Surrendering means certain death;
it is better to uphold our principles and plan anew."
When the Wèi ruler besieged Hélóng,
many of his palace guards were in the battle formation.
Chén
is the same as zhèn.
Zhū Xiūzhī, the garrison commander of Yúnzhōng, conspired with southerners to ambush and kill the Wèi ruler,
then enter Hélóng,
and return south by sea.
He informed the General of Championing the Army, Máo Xiūzhī,
but Máo Xiūzhī did not agree,
so he stopped.
Later, the plot was exposed, and Zhū Xiūzhī fled to Yàn.
The Wèi forces repeatedly attacked Yàn,
so the King of Yàn dispatched Xiūzhī to return south to seek aid.
Xiūzhī sailed by sea to Dōnglái,
then returned to Jiànkāng,
and was appointed Attendant-in-ordinary of the Palace Gate.
Zhào Guǎng and others advanced to attack Chéngdū.
Liú Dàojì defended the city behind its walls.
The bandit multitude had been encamped for a long time
and had not seen Sīmǎ Fēilóng,
and wished to disperse.
Guǎng feared this and
took three thousand men and feather banners to Yángquán Temple.
Feathers were used as ceremonial instruments,
hence it was called "feather banners".
Upon arrival,
he said to the Daoist monk Chéng Dàoyǎng from Báohǎn:
"You need only claim to be Fēilóng,
and you will enjoy wealth and honor;
otherwise, your head will be cut off!"
Dàoyǎng, terrified, agreed.
Guǎng then put Dàoyǎng forward as the King of Shǔ, General-in-chief of Chariots and Cavalry, and Inspector of the two provinces of Yì and Liáng,
changed the reign title to Tàishǐ,
and appointed all officials.
Dàoyǎng's younger brother Dàozhù was appointed General of Agile Cavalry and Prince of Chángshā,
garrisoning Fúchéng.
Zhào Guǎng, Bó Dī Nú, Liáng Xiǎn, and their associates Zhāng Xún and Yán Xiá were all appointed generals.
They escorted Dàoyǎng back to Chéngdū.
The multitude reached over a hundred thousand,
surrounding the city on all four sides.
They sent someone to tell Dàojì:
"Just send Fèi Qiān and Zhāng Xī,
and we will withdraw on our own."
Dàojì dispatched the Staff Officer of Central Army, Péi Fāngmíng, and Rèn Làngzhī, each leading over a thousand men to sally forth and fight,
but all were defeated and returned.
In winter,
the eleventh month,
on the day Yǐsì,
the Wèi ruler returned to Píngchéng.
On the day Rénzǐ,
Zhēn Fǎchóng of Zhōngshān, the Lesser Minister of Finance, was appointed Inspector of Yìzhōu,
replacing Liú Dàojì.
Zhēn
is read Zhīrén.
Originally,
the King of Yàn's principal consort, Lady Wáng,
bore Chánglè Gōng Chóng,
who was the eldest among his brothers.
When he ascended the throne,
he established Lady Mùróng as queen,
so Lady Wáng could not be established,
and Chóng was also demoted,
and sent to garrison Féirú.
Yàn appointed the Inspector of Yōuzhōu to garrison Féirú,
which was in the region of Liáoxī.
"Now the state is about to perish,
and everyone, wise or foolish, knows it.
The king has again accepted the slander of Queen Mùróng,
and my brothers and I will soon die."
So they fled together to Liáoxī,
persuading Chóng to surrender to Wèi.
Chóng agreed.
At that time, the Wèi ruler sent the Gentleman Attendant Wáng Dé to recruit Chóng.
"Jǐshìláng"
is written
"Jǐshìzhōng" in the Běishǐ.
Shuō
is read Shūruì.
Jiàng
is read Hùjiāng;
the same applies below.
On the day Jǐchǒu,
Chóng sent Miǎo to Wèi
to request the surrender of the entire commandery.
The King of Yàn, hearing this,
sent his general Fēng Yǔ to besiege Chóng at Liáoxī.
The Wèi ruler summoned prominent scholars who had not yet served.
Many prefectures and commanderies forcibly dispatched them.
The Wèi ruler, hearing this,
issued an edict,
"ordering local officials to respectfully persuade them with courtesy,
Shēn
means 'repeatedly'.
Zhòng
is read Zhílóng.
Shǒu
is read Shìyòu.
and not to force their dispatch."
Originally,
the Emperor designated his youngest son Shào as the heir of Lúlíng Xiàoxiàn Wáng.
Yìzhēn's posthumous title was Xiàoxiàn.
Shào
is read Shīzhào.
On the day Gēngyín,
Shào was enfeoffed as the Prince of Lúlíng,
and Lǎng as the Prince of Nánfēng County.
Péi Fāngmíng and others again sallied forth to attack Chéng Dàoyǎng's camp,
defeated it,
and burned their accumulated supplies.
The rebel leader Yáng Mèngzǐ 楊孟zǐ 楊孟子 of Jiāngyáng 江陽, leading over a thousand men, encamped south of the city.
Jiāngyáng 江陽,
was merged into Lóngshān Xiàn 隆山縣 of Yángzhōu 陽州 during the Suí 隋 dynasty.
(Liú Dàojì 劉道濟) sent a letter to persuade Mèngzǐ 孟子,
inviting his envoy to enter the city to meet Liú Dàojì 劉道濟.
Dàojì 道濟 had been appointed Principal Clerk (Zhǔbù 主簿).
He set a date to attack the rebels.
Zhào Guǎng 趙廣 learned of his plan,
and Mèngzǐ 孟子 became frightened,
leading his subordinates to flee to Jìnyuán 晉原.
Wén Zhòngxīng 文仲興, the Administrator of Jìnyuán 晉原, joined him in resisting the siege.
Zhào Guǎng 趙廣 dispatched Bó Dǐnú 帛氐奴 to attack Jìnyuán 晉原,
and defeated them.
Lǐ Xióng 李雄 divided Shǔjùn 蜀郡 to form Hànyuán Jùn 漢原郡.
Emperor Mù of Jìn 晉穆帝 later renamed it Jìnyuán Jùn 晉原郡,
with its seat in Jiāngyuán Xiàn 江原縣.
In the Táng 唐 dynasty, it became Jìnyuán Xiàn 晉原縣 of Shǔzhōu 蜀州.
Sòng Bái 宋白 said: "Jìnyuán Xiàn 晉原縣 was originally the land of Jiāngyuán Xiàn 江原縣 of the Hàn 漢 dynasty.
Lǐ Xióng 李雄 established Jiāngyuán Jùn 江原郡,
and the Jìn 晉 dynasty changed it to Duōróng Xiàn 多融縣,
and then again to Jìnyuán 晉原,
naming it after Jìnyuán Shān 晉原山 on its border."
Péi Fāngmíng 裴方明 again sallied forth to attack the rebels,
fighting repeatedly,
and defeating them.
The rebels then suffered a great rout.
Chéng Dàoyǎng 程道養 gathered seven thousand men,
and returned to Guǎnghàn 廣漢.
Zhào Guǎng's 趙廣 other generals, with over five thousand men, returned to Fúchéng 涪城.
Previously,
Zhāng Xī 張熙 had persuaded Dàojì 道濟 to sell the grain from the granaries.
Therefore, from the end of the ninth month when the city was besieged until the twelfth month,
all food stores were exhausted.
Fāngmíng 方明 led two thousand men out of the city to seek food,
but was defeated by the rebels,
returning alone on horseback.
The rebel forces gathered in large numbers again.
Fāngmíng 方明 scaled the wall at night by rope.
Dàojì 道濟 prepared food for him,
but he wept and could not eat.
Dàojì 道濟 said:
"You are no true hero!
Why lament a minor defeat?
The rebel power is already waning,
and the imperial troops will arrive soon.
Just let you return,
what is there to fear from the rebels!"
He immediately reduced his personal guards to reinforce Fāngmíng 方明.
The rebels spread rumors outside the city,
saying
"Fāngmíng 方明 is dead,"
causing great fear within the city.
Dàojì 道濟 lit torches at night
and brought Fāngmíng 方明 out to show the populace,
and then the people were pacified.
Dàojì 道濟 brought all his wealth to the Northern Archery Hall (Běi Shètáng 北射堂)
and ordered Fāngmíng 方明 to recruit men.
At that time, some in the city rumored that Dàojì 道濟 had died,
so no one responded.
Liáng Xiézhī 梁攜之 advised Dàojì 道濟 to send over thirty attendants and personal servants out, saying:
Liáng Xiézhī 梁攜之,
is probably Liáng Jùnzhī 梁儁之,
the character "xié 攜"
is a mistake.
"My illness has slightly improved,
you may all return home to rest."
Once the attendants had left,
the city was pacified,
and over a thousand people daily answered the call to arms.
In the beginning of 27 (the 27th year of the reign period),
Xiè Hùn 謝混 of Jìn 晉 married Princess Jìnlíng 晉陵.
Princess Jìnlíng 晉陵
was the daughter of Emperor Xiàowǔ of Jìn 晉孝武.
See Volume 116, Yìxī 義熙 8th year of Emperor Ān of Jìn 晉安帝.
The princess entrusted all of Hùn's 混 household affairs to Hùn's 混 cousin, Hóngwēi 弘微.
Hùn's 混 family had served as prime ministers for generations,
and had a thousand servants.
He only had two daughters,
who were several years old.
Hóngwēi 弘微 managed their livelihood for them,
and every coin and foot of silk was meticulously recorded in ledgers.
Nine years later, Gāozǔ 高祖 ascended the throne,
and the princess's title was demoted to Lady Dōngxiāng 東鄉君,
and she was permitted to return to the Xiè 謝 family.
Upon entering the gate,
the houses and granaries
were no different from before,
and the fields were cultivated and expanded,
even more so than in the past.
Lady Dōngxiāng 東鄉君 sighed and said:
"The Minister (Púyè 僕射) in his lifetime valued this son,
and can be said to have known men;
the Minister's spirit is not lost!"
Hùn 混 served the Jìn 晉 dynasty as Minister of Personnel (Shàngshū Zuǒ Púyè 尚書左僕射).
In that year,
Lady Dōngxiāng 東鄉君 died.
Both public and private opinion held that the wealth and property should go to the two daughters,
and the fields, houses, and servants should belong to Hóngwēi 弘微.
Hóngwēi 弘微 took nothing,
and buried Lady Dōngxiāng 東鄉君 with his own official salary.
Hùn's 混 son-in-law, Yīn Ruì 殷叡, was fond of gambling (Chūpú 摴蒱).
When he heard that Hóngwēi 弘微 had taken none of the property,
he seized the shares of his wife's younger sister, his paternal aunt, and his two maternal aunts to repay his gambling debts.
All the women in the family were influenced by Hóngwēi's 弘微's deference
and did not dispute it at all.
Someone criticized him, saying:
"The accumulated wealth of the Xiè 謝 family for generations,
used to repay Lord Yīn's 殷君 gambling debts in a single day,
this is utterly unreasonable,
nothing could be greater.
You watch and say nothing,
it is like throwing away objects into the rivers and seas to be called incorruptible.
Even if one establishes a pure reputation but causes hardship within the family,
it is also something I would not approve of."
Hóngwēi 弘微 said:
"Relatives contending for wealth is extremely vulgar.
Now, the women in the family can still remain silent,
how can I guide them to contend?
The shares are many, and the common share is small;
it will not lead to lack.
After I die,
what concern will it be to me?"
In 28 (the 28th year of the reign period), Tūfà Bǎozhōu 禿髮保周 fled from Liáng 涼 to Wèi 魏.
For Bǎozhōu's 保周 flight to Liáng 涼, see Volume 116, Yìxī 義熙 10th year of Emperor Ān of Jìn 晉安帝.
In 29 (the 29th year of the reign period), Lǐ Shùn 李順 of Wèi 魏 again served as an envoy to Liáng 涼.
King Méngxùn 蒙遜 of Liáng 涼 sent his Central Army Colonel (Zhōngbīng Xiàoláng 中兵校郎) Yáng Dìngguī 楊定歸 to say to Shùn 李順:
"I am old and often ill,
my waist and hips are not strong,
and I cannot prostrate myself.
If I feel a little better in three to five days,
I will meet you."
Shùn 李順 said:
"The King's old age and illness
are known to the court;
how can he presume to be at ease
and not see the imperial envoy!"
The next day,
Méngxùn 蒙遜 invited Shùn 李順 into the courtyard.
Méngxùn 蒙遜 sat with legs splayed (jīzuò 箕坐), leaning on an armrest,
showing no sign of rising.
Shīgǔ 師古 said: "It means sitting with both legs stretched out,
shaped like a winnowing basket (jī 箕)."
"Yǐn 隱",
pronounced yú jìn (於靳翻).
(Shùn 李順 said:) "I did not expect this old man to be so disrespectful!
He does not fear his own downfall and dares to insult Heaven and Earth.
His soul has departed,
why should I see him!"
He grasped his staff and was about to leave.
The King of Liáng 涼 sent Dìngguī 定歸 to chase and stop him,
saying:
"As the Grand Master (Tàicháng 太常) is so understanding of my old age and illness,
'yǎ 雅'
means 'always' or 'originally.'
Therefore, I dared to be at ease."
Shùn 李順 said:
"Duke Huán of Qí 齊桓公 united the feudal lords nine times
and brought order to the realm once.
The Son of Heaven of Zhōu 周 天子 bestowed sacrificial meat,
ordering him not to prostrate himself,
yet Duke Huán 桓公 still dared not neglect the etiquette of a subject,
prostrating himself to receive it.
Duke Huán of Qí 齊桓公 gathered the feudal lords at Kuíqiū 葵丘.
The King sent Zǎi Kǒng 宰孔 to bestow sacrificial meat.
The Marquis of Qí 齊侯 was about to prostrate himself.
Kǒng 孔 said:
'The Son of Heaven, considering the伯舅 (bójiù, paternal uncle or senior uncle-in-law) old and infirm,
has especially honored him with this gift,
so there is no need to prostrate yourself.'
(The Marquis) replied:
'The majesty of Heaven is not far from my face.
How dare I, Xiǎobái 小白, presume upon the Son of Heaven's command not to prostrate myself?
I fear that I might stumble and fall below,
bringing shame upon the Son of Heaven;
how dare I not prostrate myself!'
He prostrated himself
and ascended to receive it.
You are not equal to Duke Huán of Qí 齊桓;
although the court highly respects you,
there is no decree exempting you from bowing.
To suddenly act so arrogantly,
how can this be a blessing for the state!"
Méngxùn 蒙遜 then rose
and bowed to receive the decree.
Upon his return,
the Wèi Zhǔ asked him about the affairs of Liáng.
Shùn said:
"Méngxùn has controlled Héyòu
for over thirty years.
In the fifth year of Lóng'ān of Emperor Ān of Jìn (401 CE), Méngxùn killed Duàn Yè
and usurped his state.
By now, it has been thirty-one years.
He roughly understands strategy and change,
and has pacified and gathered the remote and uncivilized tribes;
the common people fear and obey him.
Although he cannot leave plans for his descendants,
he is still sufficient to see out his own lifetime.
However, ritual is the carriage of virtue,
and reverence is the foundation of the self.
Méngxùn is without ritual and irreverent.
In my humble opinion,
he will not live another year."
The Wèi Zhǔ said:
"After the change of generations,
when will it be destroyed?"
Shùn said:
"I have briefly seen Méngxùn's sons;
they are all mediocre talents.
I hear that the Administrator of Dūnhuáng, Mùjiàn,
has a roughly established character and disposition.
The one who succeeds Méngxùn
must be this person.
However, compared to his father,
everyone says he is inferior.
This is probably what Heaven uses to provide for a sagely and enlightened ruler."
Kǎo Yì says: According to the Hòu Wèi Shū,
when Shùn first presented the imperial edict to appoint Jǔqú Méngxùn as Liángzhōu Mù,
there was already the matter of Méngxùn not bowing and Shùn's discussion of Mùjiàn upon his return.
According to the Nán Shǐ,
after Shùn returned from presenting the imperial edict to Méngxùn,
he was appointed Dūdū Sì Zhōu, Cháng'ān Zhèn Dūdà Jiāng, and Kāifǔ,
and was summoned to be Sì Bù Shàngshū,
with the addition of Chángshì.
In the early Yánhé period, he was sent to Liáng,
and only then did the matters of not bowing occur.
Now, based on Shùn's saying,
"he will not last another year" (lit. "not again a week/year");
the next year Méngxùn died,
and the Emperor said:
"Your prediction of Méngxùn's death
is proven true."
Therefore, we follow the Nán Shǐ.
"Zhèn is about to undertake a campaign in the east"
means he was planning to attack Yān.
"As you have said,
it will not be more than a few years from now,
which is not too late."
In the beginning,
the Bhikkhu Tánwúchèn from Jìbīn,
claimed he could make ghosts cure diseases,
and also possessed secret arts.
The Běi Shǐ says: Tánwúchèn claimed he could make ghosts heal diseases,
and enable women to have many children.
Jì,
pronounced jì.
Tán,
pronounced tú hán fān.
Chèn,
pronounced chǔ zèn fān.
Zhì,
pronounced zhí zhī fān.
He was called
a "sage,"
and all the imperial concubines and daughters-in-law went to receive his arts.
The Wèi Zhǔ heard of this,
and sent Lǐ Shùn to summon him.
Méngxùn kept him and would not send him,
and then killed him.
The Wèi Zhǔ was thus angered at Liáng.
Méngxùn was licentious, tyrannical, and cruel;
the common people suffered under him.
This laid the groundwork for Wèi to destroy Liáng.
1. In the spring,
first month,
on the day Yǐmǎo,
the Wèi Zhǔ dispatched Yǒngchāng Wáng Jiàn to lead all armies to rescue Liáoxī.
This was because Féng Chóng was besieged.
2. On the day Jǐwèi,
a general amnesty was granted.
3. On the day Bǐngyín,
Wèi appointed Lè'ān Wáng Fàn as Dūdū Qín, Yōng, děng Wǔ Zhōu Zhū Jūnfù, Wèi Dà Jiāngjūn, Kāifǔ Yítóng Sān Sī, and Cháng'ān Zhèn Dūdà Jiāng.
Dūdà Jiāng was also above Zhèn Dà Jiāng.
Yōng,
pronounced yú yòng fān.
Jiāng,
pronounced jí liàng fān;
same below.
He further selected the virtuous former Píngxī Jiāngjūn Cuī Huī and Zhēngběi Dà Jiāngjūn Yànmén Zhāng Lí as his deputies,
to jointly guard Cháng'ān.
Huī,
was Hóng's younger brother;
Cuī Hóng was Cuī Hào's father.
Huī was dedicated to the greater good,
and Lí was pure, restrained, and fair.
Their administration and laws were simple and lenient,
with light corvée and low taxes,
and Guānzhōng consequently became peaceful.
4. In the second month,
on the day Gēngwǔ,
the Wèi Zhǔ appointed Féng Chóng as Dūdū Yōu, Píng, Dōngyí Zhū Jūnfù, Chējì Dà Jiāngjūn, Yōu, Píng Èr Zhōu Mù,
ennobled him as Liáoxī Wáng,
recorded his state's Shàngshū matters,
granted him ten commanderies of Liáoxī as his income,
and authorized him to provisionally appoint officials from Shàngshū, Cìshǐ, Zhēnglǔ downwards.
From Zhēnglǔ downwards, all miscellaneous generals could be provisionally appointed.
Qí,
pronounced qí jì fān.
5. Wèi's Píngliáng Xiūtú Zhēngxī Jiāngjūn Jīn Yá,
(sentence break).
Tú,
pronounced zhí yú fān.
Wèi established Jīngzhōu in Āndìng Jùn,
with its seat in Línjīng Chéng.
Yá and Zǐyù raised troops to attack Pǔ,
but failed to overcome him,
and retreated to defend Húkōng Gǔ.
This is the location of Húkōng Bǎo.
(Wèi troops) attacked Yá and others,
and captured them all.
The Wèi Zhǔ summoned Lù Sī to be Sànqí Chángshì,
then sent him out to be Huáihuāng Zhèn Dà Jiāng.
Huáihuāng Zhèn was one of the six garrisons established by Wèi for the surrendered Gāochē.
Sàn,
pronounced xì dān fān.
Qí,
pronounced qí jì fān.
The Gāochē Zhū Mòfú complained that Sī was too strict and ungenerous,
and requested the former garrison commander Láng Gū.
The Wèi Zhǔ recalled Sī,
and replaced him with Gū.
After Sī arrived,
he spoke to the Emperor, saying:
"Within a year,
Láng Gū will surely be defeated,
and the Gāochē will surely rebel."
The Emperor was angry,
severely reprimanded him,
and ordered him to retire to his residence as Jiànyè Gōng.
The next year,
the Zhū Mòfú indeed killed Láng Gū and rebelled.
The Emperor was greatly alarmed,
immediately summoned Sī and asked him:
"How did you know that would happen?"
Sī said:
"The Gāochē do not understand the proper etiquette between superiors and inferiors.
Therefore, I governed them with authority
and controlled them with laws,
wishing to gradually instruct and guide them,
so they would know their proper limits.
However, the Zhū Mòfú disliked my actions,
complained that I was ungenerous,
and praised Gū.
When I was removed due to my 'fault,'
and Gū was reinstated to the garrison,
pleased by their praise,
he further sought a good reputation,
and exclusively treated them with leniency and forgiveness.
People without manners
easily become arrogant and presumptuous.
Within a year,
there would be no distinction between superior and inferior.
Gū would be unable to tolerate this,
and would surely once again try to regulate them with laws.
If this happens,
then the hearts of the multitude will be resentful and dissatisfied,
and trouble and rebellion will surely arise."
When Wèi Péi Qián left Dàijùn and the Wūhuán rebelled,
the situation was also like this.
Duì,
pronounced zhí lèi fān.
"Although your body is short,
how far-reaching is your thought!"
That same day, he was reinstated as Sànqí Chángshì.
6. On the day Rénwǔ,
the Wèi Zhǔ went to Héxī,
and sent the acting Sànqí Chángshì Sòng Xuān to offer tribute,
and also to propose marriage for Crown Prince Huǎng;
the Emperor gave an equivocal answer.
7. Liú Dàojì died.
Liáng Jùnzhī, Péi Fāngmíng, and others secretly buried his body behind the study,
and faked Dàojì's instructions to respond to memorials.
Even his mother and wife did not know.
Chéng Dàoyǎng ascended an altar at Huǐjīn Qiáo to sacrifice to Heaven in the suburbs.
Fāngmíng led three thousand men to attack him.
Dàoyǎng and his forces were utterly defeated,
and retreated to defend Guǎnghàn.
The Jīngzhōu Cìshǐ, Línchuān Wáng Yìqìng, appointed Bādōng Tàishǒu Zhōu Jízhī as Dūdū Bāxī děng Wǔ Jùn Zhū Jūnfù,
leading two thousand men to rescue Chéngdū.
8 In the third month,
the fugitive Sīmǎ Tiānzhù surrendered to Wèi.
He claimed to be the son of Yuánxiǎn, the heir apparent of Huìjī Commandery of Jìn.
The Wèi people appointed him as the Inspector of Qīng and Xú Prefectures and Duke of Dōnghǎi.
9 On the day Rénzǐ,
the Wèi ruler returned to the palace.
10 Zhào Guǎng and others advanced from Guǎnghàn to Pí.
Pí County had belonged to Shǔ Commandery since the Hàn Dynasty.
Shīgǔ said: Pí
is pronounced 'pí'.
Zhōu Jízhī and Péi Fāngmíng combined their forces to attack Pí,
capturing it.
They then advanced to attack Guǎng and others at Guǎnghàn.
Guǎng and others fled back to Fú and Wǔchéng.
In summer,
in the fourth month,
on the day Wùyín,
the mourning period for Liú Dàojì officially began.
11 The Emperor heard that Zhēn Fǎhù, the Inspector of Liáng and Nánqín Prefectures, was not governing effectively,
and had lost the harmony of the Dī and Qiāng peoples.
So he appointed Xiāo Sīhuà, who was in exile, as the Inspector of Liáng and Nánqín Prefectures.
The "Kǎo Yì" states: Sīhuà's biography says:
"Yáng Nándāng raided Hànzhōng,
so Sīhuà was appointed."
According to the basic annals and the biography of Dī Hú,
Nándāng's raid on Hànzhōng was in the eleventh month.
Fǎhù was Fǎchóng's elder brother.
12 Liáng King Méngxùn was severely ill.
The people of the state deliberated together,
and, considering that the heir apparent Pútí was young and weak,
they established Pútí's elder brother, Dūnhuáng Administrator Mùjiàn, as the heir apparent.
He was given the added titles of Grand Controller of Internal and External Affairs, Grand General, and Supervisor of the Secretariat.
Méngxùn died,
and was posthumously given the title King Wǔxuān and the temple name Tàizǔ.
Mùjiàn ascended the throne as King of Héxī,
issued a general amnesty,
and changed the era name to Yǒnghé.
He established his son Fēngtán as the heir apparent,
and gave him the added titles of General Who Guards the Army and Supervisor of the Secretariat.
He sent an envoy to request investiture from Wèi.
Mùjiàn was intelligent and fond of learning,
gentle, refined, and magnanimous,
which is why the people of the state established him.
Previously,
the Wèi ruler had sent Lǐ Shùn to escort King Wǔxuān's daughter to be his consort.
Coincidentally, Méngxùn died.
Mùjiàn, claiming it was his late father's dying wish,
sent his younger sister, Princess Xīngpíng, to Wèi, escorted by Vice-Chancellor Sòng Yáo.
She was appointed Right Zhāoyí.
Lǐ Yánshòu said: The Wèi ruler added the positions of Left and Right Zhāoyí.
The Wèi ruler said to Lǐ Shùn:
"Your words that Méngxùn would die have now been proven true.
And you also said Mùjiàn would be enthroned;
how marvelous!
My conquest of Liáng Prefecture
will also not be far off."
Thereupon, he bestowed a thousand bolts of silk,
a carriage with four horses,
promoted him to General Who Pacifies the West,
and treated him with even greater favor.
All matters of government, large or small, were discussed with him.
Lǐ Shùn was favored and treated with distinction because his predictions came true,
but he also believed that for Liáng to be secretly punished
showed how difficult it was to be a minister!

(The Wèi ruler) sent Shùn to formally invest Mùjiàn as Controller of Military Affairs of Liáng, Shā, and Hé Prefectures and the Western Regions' Qiāng and Róng peoples, General of Chariots and Cavalry, Administrator with the Same Rights as the Three Ducal Ministers, Inspector of Liáng Prefecture, and King of Héxī.
Sòng Yáo was appointed Right Chancellor to the King of Héxī.
Mùjiàn, feeling he received a reward without merit,
detained Shùn
and submitted a memorial requesting an "ān" or "píng" title.
This means he requested one of the titles, either General Who Pacifies the West or General Who Subdues the West.
Mùjiàn honored Liú Bǐng of Dūnhuáng as National Preceptor,
personally bowed to him,
and ordered all officials and subordinates to face north and receive his teachings.
13 In the fifth month,
on the day Jǐhài,
the Wèi ruler went to the north of the mountain.
This was the north of Wǔzhōu Mountain.
14 Fàn Yángmài, the King of Línyì, sent an envoy to present tribute,
and requested to administer Jiāozhōu.
An imperial edict replied that the distance was too great,
and refused the request.
15 Péi Fāngmíng advanced his army towards Fúchéng,
defeated Zhāng Xún and Táng Pín,
captured Chéng Dàozhù,
and executed Yán Xiá.
Thereupon, Zhào Guǎng and others all dispersed in flight.
16 In the sixth month,
Jiàn, Prince Yǒngchāng of Wèi, and Ān Yuán, Left Director of the Imperial Secretariat, led the various armies to attack Hélóng.
General Lóu Bó separately led five thousand cavalry to besiege Fánchéng.
The "Wèi Shū Guānshì Zhì" states: Among the surnames brought into the interior,
the Hèlóu clan was changed to the Lóu clan.
The character '將'
is pronounced 'liàng' (jiàng);
the same applies below.
They collected over three thousand households and returned.
17 On the day Xīnsì,
the Wèi people dispatched ten thousand soldiers from Qín and Yōng Prefectures
to build a small city within Cháng'ān City.
18 In autumn,
in the eighth month,
Féng Chóng submitted a memorial requesting permission to persuade his father to surrender.
The Wèi ruler did not allow it.
19 In the ninth month,
Zhēn Fǎchóng, Inspector of Yì Prefecture, arrived in Chéngdū,
arrested Fèi Qiān,
and executed him.
Chéng Dàoyǎng and Zhāng Xún led over two thousand households and fled into Qīshān.
This is the mountain in Qī County of Guǎnghàn Commandery.
Shīgǔ said: Qī
is pronounced 'qī',
also 'qiānsī' (qiānxī).
They constantly emerged from time to time to plunder.
20 On the day Wùwǔ,

the Wèi ruler sent Cuī Zé, acting Grand Master of the Imperial Clan, with a staff of authority to appoint Dī King Yáng Nándāng as Grand General Who Conquers the South, Administrator with the Same Rights as the Three Ducal Ministers, Governor of Qín and Liáng Prefectures, and King of Nánqín.
Zé
was the son of Chěng.
Cuī Chěng returned to Wèi from Yān,
but was killed by Wèi ruler Guī for his insolence.
Zé
is pronounced 'shìgé' (zé).
21 Yáng Nándāng, taking advantage of Xiāo Sīhuà's delayed arrival and Zhēn Fǎhù's impending descent,
raised an army and attacked Liáng Prefecture.
He captured Bái Mǎ,
took Zhāng Fàn, Administrator of Jìnchāng, captive.
The Bái Mǎ garrison was north of the Miànshǔi,
which is Yángpíng Pass.
When Huán Wēn of Jìn pacified Shǔ,
he established Jìnchāng Commandery west of Shàngyōng with migrants from Bá and Hàn.
He also attacked Jiāmēng,
and captured Fàn Yánlǎng, Administrator of Jìnshòu.
In the fifteenth year of Tàiyuán of Emperor Xiàowǔ of Jìn,
Zhōu Fù, Inspector of Liáng Prefecture, submitted a memorial to divide Zǐtóng and establish Jìnshòu Commandery,
which was the ancient land of Jiāmēng.
Jiā is pronounced 'jiā'.
In the eleventh month,
on the day Dīngwèi,
Fǎhù abandoned the city and fled to the west city of Yángchuān.
Later, Northern Wèi established Yángchuān Commandery in Xīxiāng County of Hànzhōng.
This was probably because there was a river called Yángshuǐ in that area,
so it was called Yángchuān.
Yáng
is pronounced 'xiáng',
or as written.
He appointed his Sīmǎ Zhào Wēn as Inspector of Liáng and Qín Prefectures.
22 On the day Jiǎyín,
the Wèi ruler returned to the palace.
23 In the twelfth month,
on the day Jǐsì,
Wèi issued a general amnesty.
24 On the day Xīnwèi,
the Wèi ruler went to the north of Yīnshān.
25 Lú Xuán, General of Níngshuò of Wèi, came to pay a diplomatic visit.
26 Xiè Língyùn, former Supervisor of the Imperial Secretariat,
was fond of traveling in mountains and marshes.
(After) five years,
Língyùn was dismissed from office,
hence "former" is used.
'好' (hǎo) is pronounced 'hàodào' (hào).
His followers numbered several hundred,
felling trees and clearing paths.
The common people were alarmed and disturbed,
thinking they were mountain bandits.
Mèng Yǐ, Administrator of Huìjī, had a grudge against Língyùn.
He memorialized that Língyùn had rebellious intentions
and raised troops for self-defense.
Língyùn went to the palace gate to explain himself.
The Emperor appointed him Administrator of Línchuān.
Língyùn indulged in his travels and disregarded his duties in the commandery,
for which he was impeached by the relevant authorities.
In this year,
the Minister of Works sent Zhèng Wàngshēng, an assistant from the provincial government, to arrest Língyùn.
Língyùn seized Wàngshēng,
raised troops, and escaped.
He composed a poem saying:
"When Hàn fell, Zǐfáng rose;
when Qín became emperor, Lǔ Lián was ashamed."
Língyùn considered his family to have been ministers of Jìn for generations,
hence he composed this poem.
