Shěn Liàng, the Chief Clerk of the Western Section of Yángzhōu, suggested
that alcohol consumes grain and is insufficient to relieve hunger.
(Since the Jìn dynasty, the ducal administration was divided into Eastern and Western Sections,
each with its own clerks and chief clerks.)
The Emperor approved his suggestion.
(Liàng was the son of Línzǐ.)
(Shěn Línzǐ rendered meritorious service in campaigns with Emperor Wǔ.)
18 In autumn,
seventh month,
the Wèi Emperor hunted at Gùyáng.
(North of Gùyáng is Guānglù Pass,
the northern frontier of Hàn Wǔyuán.)
(Shīgǔ says: Gù (稒),
pronounced Gù.)
19 On Jǐmǎo,
Wèi’s Pī, King of Lèpíng, and others arrived at Hélóng;
the King of Yān presented cattle and wine to entertain the army
and offered 3,000 suits of armor.
Qū Yuán reproached him for not sending a hostage prince,
then plundered 6,000 men and women
and returned.
20 In the eighth month,
on Bǐngxū,
the Wèi Emperor went to Héxī;
in the ninth month,
on Jiǎxū,
he returned to the palace.
21 Wèi’s Left Minister, Ān Yuán, Duke of Héjiān,
was arrogant and indulged in wanton behavior, relying on the Emperor’s favor.
Someone accused Ān Yuán of plotting rebellion;
in winter, tenth month,
on Guǐmǎo,
Ān Yuán was executed with his entire clan.
22 On Jiǎchén,
the Wèi Emperor went to Dìngzhōu;
in the eleventh month,
on Yǐchǒu,
he went to Jìzhōu;
on Jǐsì,
he hunted at Guǎngchuān;
on Bǐngzǐ,
he went to Yè.
23 Wei often attacked Yān,
and Yān became increasingly precarious,
with everyone, high and low, anxious and fearful.
Tàicháng Yáng Fù advised the King of Yān to quickly send the crown prince to serve as a hostage.
The King of Yān said,
"I cannot bear to do this yet.
If the situation becomes critical,
I will temporarily rely on Gāolì in the east to plan a future move."
Yáng Fù said,
"Wei has mobilized the whole world to attack a corner;
there is no reason they will not succeed.
Gāolì is untrustworthy;
though they may initially be friendly,
in the end, I fear they will cause trouble."
The King of Yān did not listen,
and secretly sent Shàngshū Yáng Yī to request Gāolì to welcome him.
This laid the groundwork for the King of Yān being killed by Gāolì.
Lì,
pronunciation is "lì" (力知翻).
24 Dānyáng Yǐn Xiāo Mózhī submitted a memorial, saying:
"The influence of Buddhism has spread throughout Zhōngguó,
and has already lasted for four dynasties.
The four dynasties
are Hàn, Wèi, Jìn, and Sòng.
Bèi,
pronunciation is "bèi" (皮義翻).
There are thousands of temples.
However, recently,
devotion has become superficial and trivial,
not valuing sincerity as paramount,
but rather prioritizing extravagance and competition.
Timber, bamboo, bronze, and colored silks
are endlessly wasted;
this has no relation to the deities
and only burdens human affairs.
If no preventative measures are taken,
this trend of decadence will not cease.
I request that from now on, whoever wishes to cast bronze statues or build pagodas and monasteries
must all submit a detailed report,
and may only proceed after receiving approval."
The emperor decreed to follow this.
Mózhī
was Sī Huà's paternal uncle.
25 Wèi Qínzhōu Cìshǐ Xuē Jǐn attacked Tǔmògǔ,
and annihilated them.
26 Yáng Nándāng released Yáng Bǎozōng from prison.
The matter of imprisoning Bǎozōng
is found in the ninth year [of Yuánjiā].
The Shuǐ Jīng Zhù states: Gǔshuǐ originates from the southeast of Shàngguī, flowing into the mountain of Gǔzhī,
then northeast past Dǒngtíng;
Yáng Nándāng made his nephew Bǎozōng garrison Dǒngtíng,
which is this pavilion.
The characters "Dǒng" and "Tóng" are similar.
Kǎo Yì says: The Hòu Wèishū writes
"Xūntíng".
The Sòngshū writes
"Tóng",
and we follow this now.
Punctuation by Niè Chóngqí, collated by Wáng Chóngwǔ
Sīmǎ Guāng
Compiled by imperial decree
Hòu Xué Tiān Tái
Tàizǔ Wénhuángdì Zhōng Zhī Shàng
Yuánjiā Thirteenth Year (Bǐngzǐ, 436 CE)
1 Spring,
First month,
Guǐchǒu (first day of the month),
The Emperor was ill
and did not hold court assemblies.
2 Jiǎyín,
The Wei ruler returned to the palace.
3 Second month,
Wùzǐ,
The King of Yān sent envoys to pay tribute to Wei,
requesting to send a hostage.
The Wei ruler did not permit it.
The King of Yān repeatedly requested to send a hostage but did not follow through,
so the Wei ruler knew his deception
and therefore did not permit it.
Rénchén,
More than ten envoys were sent to the eastern states of Gāolì and others to issue a proclamation.
It informed them of the King of Yān's crimes,
so they could not communicate with him;
and if anyone fled,
they were not to provide refuge.
4 Sīkōng, Jiāngzhōu Cìshǐ, Yǒngxiū Gōng Tán Dàojì.
In the Zhongping era of Emperor Ling of Han,
Yǒngxiū County was established,
belonging to Yùzhāng Commandery.
In the ninth year of Kaihuang of Sui,
it was merged into Jiànchāng County.
His prestige was very high,
and his close confidants had all experienced hundreds of battles.
His sons also possessed talent and spirit,
so the court was suspicious and fearful of him.
The Emperor had been ill for a long time without recovering.
Liú Zhàn persuaded Sītú Yìkāng,
believing
that "should the imperial carriage one day pass away,
Dàojì would no longer be controllable."
Shuō,
pronunciation is "shuō" (輪芮輸).
Fù,
pronunciation is "fù" (扶又翻);
the character "復" below has the same pronunciation.
Yìkāng spoke to the Emperor,
who summoned Dàojì to court.
His wife, Lady Xiàng, said to Dàojì,
"The Xìngpǔ states
that descendants of the Qí surname became the state of Xiàng."
Xiàng,
pronunciation is "xiàng" (式亮翻),
also as written.
"Your eminent achievements,
have always been dreaded since ancient times.
Now you are summoned without cause,
disaster will surely befall you."
Upon his arrival,
he was detained for several months.
When the Emperor's illness slightly abated,
Jiàn,
as written.
He had already descended to the islet.
Dàojì was about to return to Jiāngzhōu,
and his boat had already descended to Qínhuái Zhǔ.
Coincidentally, the Emperor's illness recurred.
Yìkāng falsely issued an imperial edict summoning Dàojì to a send-off ceremony,
and then arrested him.
Third month,
Jǐwèi,
An imperial edict was issued stating:
"Dàojì secretly distributed gold and goods,
and enticed brigands.
Taking advantage of Our illness,
he planned to unleash his malevolent intentions."
He was arrested and handed over to the Tíngwèi,
and he, along with his son Jǐshì Huángmén Shìláng Zhí and ten others, were executed.
Only his grandsons, who were children, were spared.
Only the grandsons who were children were pardoned.
Tán Dàojì's two confidantes
possessed courage and strength;
people at the time compared them to Guān Yǔ and Zhāng Fēi.
Guān Yǔ and Zhāng Fēi.
When Dàojì was arrested,
he was furious,
his eyes blazing like torches.
He tore off his cap, threw it to the ground, and said,
"You are destroying your Great Wall of ten thousand Lǐ!"
When the Wei people heard of this,
they rejoiced, saying,
"With Dàojì dead, there is no need to fear those Wú fellows anymore."
This laid the groundwork for the later Wei incursions,
and the Emperor's longing for Dàojì.
Gēngshēn,
A general amnesty was granted;
Zhōngjūn Jiāngjūn Nánqiáo Wáng Yìxuān was appointed Jiāngzhōu Cìshǐ.
5 Xīnwèi,
Wèi Píngdōng Jiāngjūn É Qīng and Ānxī Jiāngjūn Gǔ Bì led ten thousand elite cavalry to attack Yān.
Píngzhōu Cìshǐ Tuòbá Yīng commanded the various armies of Liáoxī to join them.
6 The Dī King Yáng Nándāng declared himself Great Qín Wáng,
and changed the era name to Jiànyì.
He appointed his wife as Queen,
and the crown prince as太子,
establishing all officials according to the Son of Heaven's system;
nevertheless, he continued to pay tribute to Sòng and Wei without interruption.
7 Summer,
Fourth month,
Wei's É Qīng and Gǔ Bì attacked Yān's Báiláng Chéng,
and captured it.
Báiláng County
belonged to Yòuběipíng Commandery during the Hàn dynasty.
Yān regarded Báiláng Chéng as an important stronghold
and established Bìngzhōu there.
Later, Wei incorporated it into Guǎngdū County of Jiàndé Commandery.
There are Báiláng Shān
and Báiláng Shuǐ.
Gāolì sent its general Gě Lú Mèngguāng with tens of thousands of troops to accompany Yáng Yī to Hélóng to welcome the King of Yān.
Last year,
Yān sent Yáng Yī to request Gāolì to welcome him.
Línchuān is
east of Hélóng Chéng.
[The King of Yān] opened the city gate to admit Wei troops.
Kǎo Yì states: The Hòu Wèi Gǔ Bì Zhuàn writes
"Minister Gǔ Ní",
but we follow the Shíliù Guó Chūnqiū Chāo here.
He did not enter.
Then he personally led troops to attack the King of Yān.
The King led Gāolì troops to enter through the East Gate
and fought Gǔ Bì below the palace gate.
Gǔ Bì was struck by a stray arrow and died.
Gě Lú Mèngguāng entered the city,
ordered his soldiers to shed their worn-out robes,
and take the fine weapons from Yān's armory to equip themselves,
and extensively plundered the city.
In the fifth month,
on the *yǐmǎo* day,
Yān Wáng led the households from Lóngchéng eastward,
burning the palaces and halls.
The fire did not extinguish for ten days.
He ordered the women to wear armor and stay in the middle,
while Yáng Yī and others commanded elite troops to stay on the outside.
Gě Lú and Méng Guāng led cavalry to guard the rear.
They advanced abreast,
stretching over eighty *lǐ* front to back.
Gǔ Bì's subordinate general, Gāo Gǒuzǐ, led cavalry intending to pursue them,
but Bì was drunk
and drew his sword to stop him,
so Yān Wáng was able to escape.
When the Wèi Zhǔ heard of this,
he was enraged.
He had Bì and É Qīng brought in a caged cart to Píngchéng,
and both were demoted to gatekeepers.
On the *wùwǔ* day,
the Wèi Zhǔ sent the Sanqí Chángshì Fēng Bō as envoy to Gāolí,
ordering them to send Yān Wáng.
8 On the *dīngmǎo* day,
the Wèi Zhǔ traveled to Héxī.
9 In the sixth month,
an edict ordered the Níngshuò Jiāngjūn Xiāo Wāng zhī to lead troops to attack Chéng Dàoyǎng.
The army reached Qīkǒu.
The Qī Jiāng originates from present-day Tóngchuān Fǔ Tóngshān Xiàn,
passes through Suíníng Fǔ Chángjiāng Xiàn, and merges with the Fú Shuǐ;
this is called Qīkǒu.
Qī
is pronounced *qī*.
Dàoyǎng's army was defeated
and retreated into Qī Shān.
10 Regarding Hèlián Dìng's westward migration,
the details can be found in the eighth year of the previous volume.
In autumn,
the seventh month,
the Wèi Zhǔ sent the Piàojí Dàjiāngjūn Lèpíng Wáng Pī and Shàngshū Lìng Liú Jié to oversee the Héxī and Gāopíng armies to attack him,
first dispatching the Píngdōng Jiāngjūn Cuī Zé with an imperial edict to persuade Yáng Nándāng.
11 The Wèi Sanqí Shìláng Yóu Yǎ came to make an alliance.
According to the *Xìngpǔ* (Genealogy of Surnames), the son of Zhèng Gōngzǐ Yǎn was Zǐ Yóu,
whose descendants later adopted Yóu as their surname.
In Wèi, it was a prominent surname in Guǎngpíng.
12 On the *jǐwèi* day,
the Linglíng Wáng Tàizhǔ Shì passed away.
She was posthumously honored as Jìn Gōngsī Huánghòu
and buried according to Jìn rites.
13 In the eighth month,
the Wèi Zhǔ hunted in Héxī.
14 The Wèi Zhǔ sent Guǎngpíng Gōng Zhāng Lí to dispatch twelve thousand troops from Dìngzhōu to open up the Shuōquán Dao.
Shuōquán is in Língqiū.
According to the *Wèi Shōu Dìxíng Zhì*, Língqiū Jùn had Shuōquán Xiàn.
During the Suí dynasty, Língqiū was abolished as a county,
and Shuōquán was merged into it.
Shuō
is pronounced *suō*.
15 In the ninth month,
on the *gēngxū* day,
Wèi Lèpíng Wáng Pī and others arrived at Luèyáng.
Yáng Nándāng was afraid
and requested to accept the imperial edict,
withdrawing his defending troops from Shàngguī to Hùchí.
The generals debated, saying:
"If we do not punish their chieftains,
after the army returns,
they will surely gather and cause trouble again.
Moreover,
the large army has traveled far;
if we do not seize something,
we will have nothing to replenish military provisions
or reward the officers and soldiers."
Pī was about to agree,
but the Zhōngshū Shìláng Gāo Yǔn, who was assisting Pī in military affairs,
advised against it, saying:
"If we follow the generals' plan,
it will harm their intention to submit.
Once the main army returns,
their rebellion will surely be swift."
Pī then stopped,
comforting those who had newly submitted,
not harming even a single autumn hair.
Qín and Lǒng thus became peaceful.
Nándāng made his son Shùn the Yōngzhōu Cìshǐ
to garrison Xiàbiàn.
16 Gāolí did not send Yān Wáng to Wèi,
but sent envoys to present a memorial,
stating
that they "would both submit to the royal transformation along with Féng Hóng."
The Wèi Zhǔ considered Gāolí to have defied the edict
and deliberated on attacking them, intending to dispatch cavalry from Lǒngyòu.
Liú Jié said:
"The new people of Qín and Lǒng
should first be given preferential treatment and exemption from taxes and labor.
'New people'
refers to the newly submitted people.
'Exemption'
is pronounced *fù*.
Only then should they be employed."
Lèpíng Wáng Pī said:
"Hélóng has just been pacified;
it is advisable to extensively cultivate agriculture and sericulture to enrich military provisions,
and then advance.
Then Gāolí can be destroyed in one fell swoop."
The Wèi Zhǔ then stopped.
17 On the *guǐchǒu* day,
the imperial son Jùn was enfeoffed as Shǐxīng Wáng,
and Jùn as Wǔlíng Wáng.
18 In winter,
the eleventh month,
on the *jǐyǒu* day,
the Wèi Zhǔ traveled to Gūyáng,
herding wild horses in Yúnzhōng
and establishing a wild horse park.
In the intercalary month,
on the *rénzǐ* day,
he returned to the palace.
19 In the beginning,
when Gāozǔ conquered Cháng'ān—
the details can be found in volume 118, Jìn Āndì's Yìxī thirteenth year—
although the *yízhàng* (armillary sphere) was completed,
it did not incorporate the Seven Luminaries.
The sun, moon, and five planets are called the Seven Luminaries.
An edict ordered the Tàishǐ Lìng Qián Lèzhī to recast the *húnyí* (armillary sphere).
It was six *chǐ* and eight *fēn* in diameter,
rotated by water,
and the central stars at dusk and dawn corresponded with the heavens.
In the first month of spring,
at dusk,
Cān was central;
at dawn,
Wěi was central.
In the second month of spring,
at dusk,
Hú was central;
at dawn,
Jiànxīng was central.
In the third month of spring,
at dusk,
Qīxīng was central;
at dawn,
Qiānniú was central.
In the first month of summer,
at dusk,
Yì was central;
at dawn,
Wùnǚ was central.
In the second month of summer,
at dusk,
Kàng was central;
at dawn,
Wēi was central.
In the third month of summer,
at dusk,
Huǒ was central;
at dawn,
Kuí was central.
In the first month of autumn,
at dusk,
Jiànxīng was central;
at dawn,
Bì was central.
In the second month of autumn,
at dusk,
Qiānniú was central;
at dawn,
Zīxuē was central.
In the third month of autumn,
at dusk,
Xū was central;
at dawn,
Liǔ was central.
In the first month of winter,
at dusk,
Wēi was central;
at dawn,
Qīxīng was central.
In the second month of winter,
at dusk,
Dōngbì was central;
at dawn,
Zhěn was central.
In the third month of winter,
at dusk,
Lóu was central;
at dawn,
Dī was central.
'Recast'
is pronounced *gēng*.
20 Ròurán broke off peaceful relations with Wèi
and encroached upon Wèi's borders.
Ròurán had been at peace with Wèi;
see the eighth year of the previous volume.
21 Tùyùhùn Huì Wáng Mùguī passed away.
His younger brother Mùlìyán succeeded him.
1 In spring,
the first month,
on the *wùzǐ* day,
Wèi Běipíng Xuān Wáng Zhǎngsūn Sōng passed away.
2 On the Xīnmǎo day,
a general amnesty was declared.
3 In the second month,
on the Yǐmǎo day,
the Wèi Lord went to Yōuzhōu.
In the third month,
on the Dīngchǒu day,
the Wèi Lord appointed Jūqú Hún (南平王渾), the Prince of Nánpíng, as Grand General Zhen Dōng (鎮東大將軍) and Yítóng Sānsī (儀同三司),
to garrison Hélóng.
On the Jǐmǎo day,
he returned to the palace.
4 The Emperor dispatched Sànqí Chángshì (散騎常侍) Liú Xībó (劉熙伯) to Wèi to discuss the presentation of tribute.
However, the mission was halted due to the death of the Emperor's daughter.
Wèi had been requesting a marriage alliance for ten years, as recorded in the previous scroll.
5 In summer,
in the fourth month,
Zhào Guǎng (趙廣), Zhāng Xún (張尋), Liáng Xiǎn (梁顯) and others each led their multitudes and surrendered;
a separate general, Wáng Dào'ēn (王道恩), beheaded Chéng Dàoyǎng (程道養),
and sent his head,
completely pacifying the remaining rebels.
Nine years earlier,
Zhào Guǎng and others had rebelled,
and now they were finally pacified.
Shuài (帥)
is read as lǜ.
Jiàng (降)
is read as hú jiāng fān.
Jiàng (將)
is read as jí liàng fān.
On the Dīngwèi day,
Zhōu Jízhī (周籍之) was appointed Inspector of Yìzhōu (益州刺史) with the title of Auxiliary General of the State (輔國將軍).
6 The Wèi Lord, seeing that many civil officials were corrupt,
especially the commanderies' governors and county magistrates,
who were officials close to the people.
In the fifth month,
on the Jǐchǒu day,
he issued an edict allowing officials and commoners to report any governors or magistrates who did not follow the law.
Consequently, cunning and treacherous individuals exclusively sought out the shortcomings of the administrators,
coercing those in office,
and acting arrogantly in the neighborhoods;
yet the senior officials all lowered themselves to accommodate them,
and their avarice and indulgence remained unchanged.
7 On the Bǐngshēn day,
the Wèi Lord went to Yúnzhōng.
8 In autumn,
in the seventh month,
on the Wùzǐ day,
Yuán Jiàn (永昌王健), the Prince of Yǒngchāng, and others from Wèi attacked the remaining rebels of the Shāhú (山胡) Báilóng (白龍) in Xīhé,
and annihilated them.
9 In the eighth month,
on the Jiǎchén day,
the Wèi Lord went to Héxī;
in the ninth month,
on the Jiǎshēn day,
he returned to the palace.
10 On the Dīngyǒu day,
the Wèi Lord dispatched envoys to appoint Mùlìyán (慕利延), the King of Tǔyùhún, as Grand General Zhen Xī (鎮西大將軍) and Yítóng Sānsī (儀同三司),
and re-enfeoffed him as Prince of Xīpíng.
11 In winter,
in the tenth month,
on the Guǐmǎo day,
the Wèi Lord went to Yúnzhōng;
in the eleventh month,
on the Rénshēn day,
he returned to the palace.
12 The Wèi Lord again dispatched Sànqí Shìláng (散騎侍郎) Dǒng Wǎn (董琬) and Gāo Míng (高明) with much gold and silk to the Western Regions,
to recruit and pacify nine kingdoms.
When Wǎn and others reached Wūsūn,
its king was very pleased,
saying:
"The two kingdoms of Pòluònà (破落那) and Zhěshé (者舌)
Pòluònà
is the Hàn Dàyuān Kingdom,
14,450 lì from Dài.
Zhěshé
is the Hàn Kāngjū Kingdom,
15,450 lì from Dài.
There is simply no path to reach them ourselves,
so now your excellencies should pass by and pacify them."
He then sent guides and interpreters to escort Wǎn to Pòluònà,
and Míng to Zhěshé.
Neighboring countries, hearing of this,
vied to send envoys to follow Wǎn and others to present tribute,
totaling sixteen kingdoms.
From then on, annual tribute continued without interruption.
13 The Wèi Lord married his younger sister, Princess Wǔwēi (武威公主), to Mùjiān (牧犍), the King of Héxī.
The King of Héxī sent Sòng Yáo (宋繇) to present a memorial to Píngchéng to express his gratitude,
and to inquire what title was appropriate for the Princess.
The Wèi Lord had his ministers deliberate on it,
and they all said:
"A mother is honored by her son,
and a wife's rank follows her husband's title.
According to the principle of the Spring and Autumn Annals,
a mother is honored by her son.
The Book of Rites states: A woman has no rank
and follows her husband's rank.
The Princess should be called Queen in her own country,
but in the capital, she should be called Princess."
The Wèi Lord followed their advice.
Initially,
Mùjiān had married the daughter of Láng Wǔzhāo Wáng (涼武昭王).
When the Wèi Princess arrived,
Lady Lǐ and her mother, Lady Yǐn, moved to Jiǔquán.
Soon after,
Lady Lǐ died.
Lady Yǐn caressed her,
but did not weep,
saying:
"Your country is ruined, your family destroyed,
your death now is too late."
Mùjiān's younger brother, Wúhuì (無諱), who was garrisoned in Jiǔquán,
said to Lady Yǐn:
"The queen's grandsons are in Yīwú."
Lǐ Bǎo (李寶) had fled to Yīwú,
as seen in Scroll 119, year one of Yíngyáng Wáng Jǐngpíng (營陽王景平).
Lady Yǐn, not understanding his intention,
deceived him, saying:
"My children and grandchildren are scattered,
relying on a foreign land;
I have not much life left,
I shall die here,
and will not become a ghost of the felt-dwelling people again."
Not long after,
she secretly fled to Yīwú.
Wúhuì sent cavalry to pursue and catch her.
Lady Yǐn said to the pursuing cavalry:
"Jǔqú Jiǔquán (沮渠酒泉) allowed me to return north,
why are you chasing me again!
You may take my head and go,
I will not return."
The pursuing cavalry dared not press her,
and turned back.
Lady Yǐn died in Yīwú.
Historians say Lady Yǐn was righteous and resolute.
Dài (紿)
is read as dàng hǎi fān.
Jǐ (幾)
is read as jū qǐ fān.
Fù (復)
is read as fú yòu fān.
Qí (騎)
is read as qí jì fān.
Zú (卒)
is read as zǐ xù fān.
Mùjiān sent General Jǔqú Pángzhōu (沮渠旁周) to present tribute to Wèi.
The Wèi Lord sent Shìzhōng (侍中) Gǔ Bì (古弼) and Shàngshū (尚書) Lǐ Shùn (李順) to bestow clothing upon his attendants,
and also to summon Crown Prince Fēng Tán (封壇) to serve at court.
In this year,
Mùjiān sent Fēng Tán to Wèi,
and also dispatched envoys to Jiànkāng,
presenting various books and the Jiǎyín Yuánlì (甲寅元曆) compiled by Zhào (趙) of Dūnhuáng,
and also requesting several dozen kinds of miscellaneous books.
The Emperor gave them all.
When Lǐ Shùn returned from Héxī,

Bó was skilled in archery,

When the Wèi Lord [Tàiwǔdì] was campaigning in the west,

From Píngchéng, he escorted the Wèi Lord west to the Hé [River].
"Wú Tí and Mùjiān have long been closely allied.
When he hears that I am attacking Mùjiān,

Ròurán's Chìlián Kèhán's personal name is Wú Tí.
I send you to assist the Crown Prince.
Once the harvest is complete,
immediately dispatch troops to Mònán [South of the Desert],

luring them to penetrate deep,

and there will be no failure.
Liángzhōu is far away,

Do not disobey my words!"
Shòu kowtowed and accepted the order.
Shòu deeply trusted Gōngsūn Zhì, a Doctor of the Secretariat,

Shòu and Zhì both believed in divination,

Zhì [Gōngsūn Zhì]

Běizhèn

Empress Dòu [Tàihòu]

Hearing this, Chìlián [Kèhán]

In winter,
in the tenth month,
on the Xīnyǒu day

During the reign of Emperor Xiàopíng,

When the usurper Wáng Mǎng held power,

significantly correcting and standardizing the ancient script.
At that time, there were six types of writing: the first was Gǔwén,

the second was Qíjì,

the third was Zhuànshū,

the fourth was Zuǒshū,

the fifth was Miàozhuàn,

The script from Kǒngzǐ's wall

Also,
Mǎrquise Běipíng Zhāng Cāng presented the Zuǒshì Zhuàn of the Spring and Autumn Annals,
whose script style was similar to that of the Kǒng clan,

In the Later Hàn dynasty, Cáo Xǐ of Fúfēng was known as a master of Zhuàn [seal script],
differing slightly from Lǐ Sī's method but being very refined and skillful.
From then on, later scholars
all followed his method.
Furthermore, an imperial edict ordered Palace Attendant Jiǎ Kuí to revise old texts.
Various arts and different techniques,
and all aspects of royal instruction,
anything that could benefit the state,
were diligently collected.
Kuí was also the teacher of Xǔ Shèn of Rǔnán in ancient script studies.
Later, Shèn lamented the curiosity of people of his time

Therefore, he compiled the Shūowén Jiězì in fifteen chapters.
Starting with the radical 'yī' (一) and ending with 'hài' (亥),
each had its category.
It can be said that he grouped things by class and neatly divided them,
making them diverse yet without exceeding bounds.
Elegant and substantial,
it is most worthy of discussion.
Zuǒ Zhōngláng Jiāng Cài Yōng adopted the methods of Lǐ Sī and Cáo Xǐ to create various ancient and modern forms.
An imperial edict ordered the erection of stone tablets at the Imperial Academy,

The standard script used for these inscriptions

Later, the Hóngdū [Academy] was opened,

At that time, among those who presented seal script from various regions,
none surpassed Yōng.
In the early Wèi period,

Comparing them to Xǔ Shèn's work,
in terms of ancient and modern forms and usage,
there were both successes and failures.
Hándān Chún of Chénliú also lived at the same time as Yī.
He was broadly learned in ancient matters and skilled in the arts,
especially proficient in the Cāngjié Piān, the Guǎngyá, and Xǔ Shèn's explanations of characters,
as well as the eight styles and six types of writing.
He thoroughly investigated their principles,
was as famous as Yī,

He also erected the Three-Style Stone Classics to the west of the Hàn tablets,
whose inscriptions were brilliant and clear,
proclaiming the three styles anew.
Compared to the Shūowén,
the zhuàn and lì scripts were largely the same, but the ancient characters differed slightly.
There were also Wéi Dàn of Jīngzhào
and Wèi Jì of Hédōng.
Both families were renowned for their seal script.
At that time, the inscriptions on palace and terrace plaques and precious artifacts
were all in Dàn's hand.
They were passed down to his descendants,
and their excellence was praised through generations.
During the Jìn dynasty, Lǚ Chén submitted the Zìlín in six volumes.
Examining its content and purpose,
it was based on Xǔ Shèn's Shūowén but arranged according to chapters and sentences,
subtly distinguishing ancient, Zhòuwén, peculiar, and confusing characters.
The characters followed correct Lìshū,
without deviating from the intent of Zhuànshū.
Chén's younger brother, Jìng,
separately emulated the method of the sound categories (Shēnglèi) by Lǐ Dēng, the former Director of the Left Bureau.

assigning the sounds gōng, shāng, jué [AS-FBED] lù, zhǐ, and yǔ each to a chapter.

were like those of Lǔ and Wèi [i.e., different dialects],

sometimes differing.
The Imperial Wèi inherited the decline of a hundred kings [dynasties],
succeeding the legacy of the Five Elements.
As times changed and customs shifted,
written characters also changed.
Seal forms became erroneous,
and clerical script lost its authenticity.
Vulgar and crude scholarly practices
were further overlaid with artificial embellishments.
Debaters,
based on their own ideas, created doubts,
perplexing the age,
making it difficult to correct.

"追 (zhuī) [to pursue] becomes 歸 (guī) [to return],"

all of which did not accord with Kǒngzǐ's ancient texts, Shǐ Zhòu's Dàzhuàn, Xǔ Shèn's Shūowén, or the characters on the Stone Classics.
Alas!
Written characters are
the foundation of the Six Classics

They are what the ancients used to instruct the present,

Your servant's sixth-generation ancestor, Qióng,

At that time, they both received high praise.
However, the ancestor encountered the chaos in Luòyáng

For several generations, this craft was passed down,

In the Tàiyán era of Shìzǔ,
Mùlìyán pledged allegiance.
My deceased ancestor, Wénwēi, journeyed back to the country,

I, relying on the foundation of six generations,

I hope this will reduce the need to consult numerous texts and bring uniformity to the realm of characters."
An imperial edict approved the request.

In the ninth year,
the emperor made Láng, the son of Jiāngxià Wáng Yìgōng, King of Nánfēng,
to continue the sacrifices for the King of Yíngyáng,
and made his mother the Nánfēng Tài.
Zhào Guǎng and Zhāng Xún
again conspired to rebel and were
executed.
In the fourteenth year,
Guǎng and Xún surrendered and
arrived at Jiànkāng,
then again plotted rebellion.
Fù,
read as "fú yòu fān" (tone note);
the same applies to fùnéng, fùnà, bùfù, and wúfù below.
Spring,
first month,
on the day Jǐyǒu,
Jǔqú Wúhuì raided Wèi's Jiǔquán.
Yuán Jié thought lightly of him
and went out of the city to speak with him.
On the day Rénzǐ,
Wúhuì captured Jié and besieged Jiǔquán.
Second month,
Wèi sent acting Tōngzhí Chángshì Xíng Yǐng to visit.
Sànqí Chángshì
was an office of the Qín dynasty.
At the end of Cao Wèi,
Yuánwài Sànqí Chángshì were added.
In the tenth year of Tàishǐ of Jìn Wǔdì,
two Yuánwài officials were made Tōngzhí with the Sànqí Chángshì,
hence they were called Tōngzhí Sànqí Chángshì.
Yǐng was acting as an envoy,
not holding a regular office.
Third month,
Jǔqú Wúhuì captured Jiǔquán.
Summer,
fourth month,
on the first day Wùwǔ,
there was a solar eclipse.
On the Gēngchén day,
Jǔqú Wúhuì plundered Wèi's Zhāngyè.
Tùfǎ Bǎozhōu garrisoned Shāndān.
Shāndān county
belonged to Zhāngyè Commandery during the Hàn dynasty,
and later to Xī Commandery after a division.
In the Táng dynasty, it belonged to Gānzhōu.
Jūyán Hǎi was within the county's borders.
On the Bǐngxū day,
the Wèi ruler dispatched the Grand General Fǔjūn, Prince Yǒngchāng Jiàn, to oversee his generals and suppress him.
Sītú Yìkāng exclusively managed the court's authority.
The Emperor had been suffering from a lingering illness for years,
and any mental exertion would trigger it,
often bringing him to the brink of death.
Yìkāng diligently attended to him,
not allowing any medicine to be administered until he had personally tasted it,
sometimes staying awake for successive nights.
All internal and external affairs were decided and implemented solely by him.
He enjoyed official duties,
scrutinizing documents and records,
leaving nothing unexamined.
Because of this, the Emperor entrusted many affairs to him.
Whatever he proposed
was always approved.
Officials from Fangbó downwards
were all selected by Yìkāng.
Even major matters of life and death
were sometimes decided by "Lù Mìng".
Yìkāng held the position of Lù Shàngshū,
hence his commands were called "Lù Mìng".
Duàn,
Dīng luàn fān.
Officials and commoners flocked to him.
Every morning, hundreds of carriages would regularly be at the gates of his mansion.
Yìkāng wholeheartedly received them,
never showing weariness.
He also possessed a strong memory.
Anything he saw or heard
he would never forget throughout his life.
He liked to demonstrate his intelligence
by recalling things in crowded public settings.
Capable and experienced scholars
often received his special attention.
He once said to Liú Zhàn:
"What are people like Wáng Jìnghóng and Wáng Qiú capable of, after all?
To simply obtain wealth and honor by sitting idly,
how can that be explained!"
Wáng Jìnghóng was calm and indifferent, with a great reputation.
Wáng Qiú was refined, noble, and serene.
Both held the position of Bā Zuò due to their family prestige,
and did not concern themselves with documents and records.
This is why Yìkāng said so.
Jiě,
Hù mǎi fān.
Not understanding the broader picture,
he attracted all talented and capable court officials to his own mansion.
Only those of his mansion staff who were ineffective or displeased him were then transferred to be Tái officials.
Since the Jìn and Sòng dynasties, the imperial court was referred to as Tiāntái.
Wǔ,
Wǔ gù fān.
He no longer maintained the formality between ruler and minister,
acting on his own impulses,
without any suspicion or precaution.
He privately kept over six thousand servants,
not reporting them to the court.
Offerings from all directions
were first presented to Yìkāng with the best quality, and then the lesser ones were supplied for the Emperor.
The Emperor once ate gān (a type of citrus) in winter.
The gān resembled oranges but were larger.
Their skin was yellower than oranges,
and their taste sweeter than oranges.
Yìkāng said:
"This year's gān are especially good."
He sent someone back to the Eastern Mansion to fetch gān,
providing the Emperor with those three inches in diameter.
Lǐngjūn Liú Zhàn had a rift with Púyè Yīn Jǐngrén.
The matter is detailed in the previous volume, twelfth year.
Yìkāng's power was already great.
Zhàn increasingly exalted him,
no longer showing the respect due from a subject to a ruler.
The Emperor gradually became displeased.
When Zhàn first entered court,
the Emperor treated him with great favor and courtesy.
Zhàn was skilled in discussing governance,
conversant with historical events of previous dynasties,
and adept at narrating and analyzing principles.
Zhì,
refers to the ultimate point.
Lǐ,
refers to literary principles.
It means narrating their ultimate points
and also organizing their literary principles.
Zhì,
Zhí lì fān.
Ān,
Wū hán fān.
Whenever he entered the Yúnlóng Gate,
the charioteer would immediately unhitch the carriage,
and the attendants and honor guards would disperse as they pleased.
He would not leave until evening,
this being a regular occurrence.
In his later years, he incited and fanned Yìkāng.
If a horse is running and its whip is urged, it is called qū;
if a fire is raging and its flames are fanned, it is called shān.
He once said to a close associate:
"When Liú Bān returned to the palace from the west,
I would talk with him
and constantly watch the time,
fearing he would leave soon.
Now, when he comes in,
I also watch the time,
annoyed that he doesn't leave."
Zhàn's
given name was Bānhǔ,
so he was referred to as Bān.
Bǐ,
Pí zhì fān,
meaning near.
Yīn Jǐngrén secretly told the Emperor:
"The Prince Regent's power is too great.
This is not beneficial for the state and its altars.
He should be restrained somewhat!"
The Emperor secretly agreed.
Sītú Zuǒ Chángshǐ Liú Bīn,
was a relative of Zhàn.
Grand General Cóngshì Zhōngláng Wáng Lǚ,
was the grandson of Mì.
Wáng Mì recognized Emperor Wǔ during his humble beginnings.
Around the Jìn and Sòng transition,
he held prominent official positions.
Jìjiǔ Lǔ Jùn Kǒng Yìnxiù,
all gained favor with Yìkāng through flattery and sycophancy.
Seeing the Emperor often ill,
they all said:
"Should the Emperor pass away one day,
it would be appropriate to establish an older ruler."
The Emperor once fell gravely ill
and had Yìkāng prepare a will.
He summoned Yìkāng to his residence
and tearfully told Zhàn and Jǐngrén.
Zhàn said:
"The world is difficult.
How can an infant ruler manage it!"
Yìkāng and Jǐngrén both did not reply.
Kǎo Yì states: Nán Shǐ believes Yìkāng said this,
and Zhàn and Jǐngrén both did not reply.
However, although Yìkāng did not understand the broader picture,
how could he dare to say such a thing himself?
Zhàn always wanted to promote Yìkāng,
how could he hear it and not reply?
We now follow Sòng Shū and Sòng Luè.
"Yìcáo",
Nán Shǐ has "Yícáo",
which should be followed.
Cáo Wèi established twenty-three Láng,
and Yícáo was one of them.
The matter of establishing Emperor Kāng is in Volume 97.
Suǒ,
Shān kè fān.
When the Emperor recovered,
he vaguely heard about it.
Meanwhile, Bīn and others secretly plotted,
wishing that the grand enterprise would ultimately fall to Yìkāng.
They then formed factions,
spied on the imperial palace,
and if anyone did not align with them,
they would surely frame them in a hundred ways.
They also gathered Jǐngrén's shortcomings,
or fabricated differences to tell Zhàn.
From then on, the power of the ruler and the regent diverged.
Yìkāng wanted to appoint Liú Bīn as Dānyáng Yǐn.
During a conversation,
he informed the Emperor, stating Bīn's poverty.
Before he finished speaking,
the Emperor said:
"Let him be Wú Jùn."
Later, Huìjī Tàishǒu Yáng Xuánbǎo requested to return.
Yìkāng again wanted to replace him with Bīn,
and reported to the Emperor, saying:
"Yáng Xuánbǎo requested to return.
I wonder who should be Huìjī?"
The Emperor had not yet decided on a candidate at the time,
and blurted out:
"I have already appointed Wáng Hóng."
Since the autumn of the previous year,
the Emperor no longer visited the Eastern Mansion.
Historians say that the Emperor had already become distant and wary of Yìkāng,
but Yìkāng was greedy for power
and misled by flatterers,
unable to retire.
Fù,
Fú yòu fān;
same below.
In the fifth month,
on the day Guǐsì,
Liú Zhàn (劉湛) was dismissed from office due to the mourning for his mother.
Zhàn (湛) knew that his crimes and transgressions were already manifest,
and there was no way to save himself.
He said to his confidants:
"This year I will surely fail.
In ordinary times, I relied on my eloquence to contend,
and thus managed to delay;
but now that I am in such a dire situation,
to say that mother and son are parting ways,
it means that human reason is exhausted, and I am suffering immense bitterness.
How long can this misfortune last!"
The Kǎoyì (考異) says: The Nánshǐ (南史) states,
"Zhàn (湛) concealed armed men in his chamber,
waiting for the Emperor to visit to offer condolences.
The plot was leaked again,
and the Emperor eventually did not go."
The Sòngshū (宋書) has no such incident.
We consider that if Zhàn's (湛) plot were leaked,
he would have been immediately executed;
how could he have been spared for another half a year!
We now follow the Sòngshū (宋書).
On the 7th, Yǐsì,
Jǔqú Wúhuì (沮渠無諱) again besieged Zhāngyè (張掖),
but failed,
and retreated to defend Línsōng (臨松).
Línsōng Commandery (臨松郡) and Línsōng County (臨松縣)
must have been established by the Jǔqú (沮渠) clan;
later, Yǔwén Zhōu (宇文周) abolished them and merged them into Zhāngyè (張掖).
Fù (復),
pronounced fú yòu;
the same below.
Only with an edict to placate him.
In the sixth month,
on the day Dīngchǒu,
Wèi (魏) Imperial Grandson Jùn (濬) was born.
A general amnesty was declared,
and the era name was changed to Tàipíng Zhēnjūn (太平真君).
This was based on Kòu Qiānzhī's (寇謙之) divine scripture which said,
"Assisting the Northern Tàipíng Zhēnjūn (太平真君),"
hence the name.
Kòu Qiānzhī's (寇謙之) divine scripture is mentioned in Volume 119, in the section on Yíngyángwáng Jǐngpíng (營陽王景平) first year.
The 9th, Crown Prince Shào (劭) went to Jīngkǒu (京口) to pay respects at the imperial tombs.
Sītú Yìkāng (司徒義康) and Jìnglíngwáng Dàn (竟陵王誕) and others accompanied him.
The Nányǎnzhōu (南兗州) Inspector, Jiāngxiàwáng Yìgōng (江夏王義恭), met him from Jiāngdū (江都).
In autumn,
the seventh month,
on the day Jǐchǒu,
Wèi (魏) Prince Yǒngchāng (永昌王) Jiàn (健) defeated Tūfà Bǎozhōu (禿髮保周) at Fānhé (番禾);
Bǎozhōu (保周) fled,
and General Ānnán (安南將軍) Wèi Juàn (尉眷) was sent to pursue him.
On the 11th, Bǐngshēn,
Wèi (魏) Empress Dowager Dòu (竇) passed away.
On the 12th, Rénzǐ,
Empress Yuán (袁) passed away.
The Crown Prince Shào's (劭) murderous and rebellious intentions began to sprout here.
On the 13th, Guǐchǒu,
Tūfà Bǎozhōu (禿髮保周), driven to desperation, committed suicide.
In the eighth month,
on the day Jiǎshēn,
Jǔqú Wúhuì (沮渠無諱) sent his Middle Commandant Liáng Wěi (梁偉) to Wèi (魏) Prince Yǒngchāng (永昌王) Jiàn (健) to request surrender,
returning Jǐuquán Commandery (酒泉郡) and the captured generals and officers, including Yuán Jié (元絜).
The Wèi (魏) ruler ordered Wèi Juàn (尉眷) to remain and garrison Liángzhōu (涼州).
In the ninth month,
on the day Rénzǐ,
Empress Yuán (元) was buried.
The 15th, The Emperor, considering that the animosity between himself and Sītú Péngchéngwáng Yìkāng (司徒彭城王義康) was already evident
and would lead to disaster and rebellion,
in winter,
the tenth month,
on the day Wùshēn,
arrested Liú Zhàn (劉湛) and handed him over to the Grand Judge.
An edict was issued exposing his crimes and evils,
and he was executed in prison.
His sons Àn (黯), Liàng (亮), and Yǎn (儼), along with his partisans Liú Bīn (劉斌), Liú Jìngwén (劉敬文), Kǒng Yìnxiù (孔胤秀), and eight others were also executed.
Five others, including Shàngshū Kùbù Láng (尚書庫部郎) Hé Mòzǐ (何默子), were exiled to Guǎngzhōu (廣州).
Cáo Wèi (曹魏) established twenty-three Shàngshū Láng (尚書郎),
and Kùbù (庫部) was one of them.
On this day,
Yìkāng (義康) was ordered to enter the palace for the night
and stay in the Zhōngshūshěng (中書省).
That evening,
Zhàn (湛) and his associates were apprehended separately.
Qīngzhōu (青州) Inspector Dù Jì (杜驥) commanded troops within the palace to guard against unforeseen events.
People were dispatched to convey the imperial decree, informing Yìkāng (義康) of the charges against Zhàn (湛) and others.
Yìkāng (義康) submitted a memorial to resign his position.
An imperial edict appointed Yìkāng (義康) as Jiāngzhōu (江州) Inspector,
with his titles of Shìzhōng (侍中) and Dàjiāngjūn (大將軍) remaining as before,
and sent him to garrison Yùzhāng (豫章).
Previously,
Yīn Jǐngrén (殷景仁) had been ill in bed for five years.
Jǐngrén (景仁) fell ill in the twelfth year of the previous volume.
However, secret letters were exchanged,
numbering in the tens daily,
and all matters, great and small, concerning court politics
had to be consulted with him;
his traces and movements were so meticulous
that no one could discern their limits.
On the day Zhàn (湛) was arrested,
Jǐngrén (景仁) ordered his clothes and hat to be dusted off,
and those around him did not understand his intention.
That night,
the Emperor went out to the Yánxiántáng (延賢堂) in the Huálínyuán (華林園)
and summoned Jǐngrén (景仁).
Jǐngrén (景仁) still claimed a foot ailment,
and was carried on a small bed to his seat;
the arrangements for execution and punishment
were entirely entrusted to him.
Previously,
Tán Dàojì (檀道濟) had recommended Shěn Qìngzhī (沈慶之) of Wúxīng (吳興) as loyal, prudent, and skilled in military affairs.
The Emperor assigned him to lead the guard at the eastern Yèmént (掖門).
Liú Zhàn (劉湛), as the Commander of the Guards,
once said to him:
"You have been in the office for many years;
it's about time we discussed your promotion."
Shěng (省),
refers to the commander's office.
Bǐ (比),
pronounced pí mèi.
Meaning, it's time to discuss and arrange for him.
I have been in the office for ten years,
and I should naturally be promoted;
I don't need to trouble you with this again!"
On the evening Zhàn (湛) was arrested,
the Emperor opened the gate and summoned Qìngzhī (慶之).
Qìngzhī (慶之) entered in military attire with his trousers tied up.
The Emperor said:
"Why are you dressed so hastily?"
Qìngzhī (慶之) replied:
"When the team leader is called in the middle of the night,
according to the military system of Jiangnan,
a commander is called a duìzhǔ (隊主) or jūzhǔ (軍主).
A duìzhǔ (隊主) is the commander of a team;
a jūnzhǔ (軍主) is the commander of an army.
The historian says Shěn Qìngzhī (沈慶之) had discernment and strategy.
kill him.
The General of Agile Cavalry (驍騎將軍) Xú Zhànzhī (徐湛之)
was the son of Kuízhī (逵之).
Xú Kuízhī (徐逵之)
was Emperor Wǔ's (武帝) beloved son-in-law,
who died in the rebellion of Sīmǎ Chǔzhī (司馬楚之) and Lǔ Zōngzhī (魯宗之).
Xiāo (驍),
pronounced jiān yáo.
Qí (騎),
pronounced qí jì.
The Emperor held a deep grudge against him.
When Yìkāng (義康) was defeated,
Zhànzhī (湛之) was arrested,
and his crime warranted death.
His mother, Princess Kuàijī (會稽公主),
was the eldest legitimate child among the siblings,
and had always been treated with respect by the Emperor;
all family matters, big or small,
were consulted with her before action was taken.
When Gāozǔ (高祖) was of humble status,
he once personally cut reeds in Xīnzhōu (新洲),
wearing a patched cloth jacket and padded gown.
Nà (納),
same as nà (衲).
After he became noble,
he gave it to the Princess, saying:
"If future generations become extravagant and immoderate,
you can show them this garment."
By this time,
the Princess entered the palace to see the Emperor,
weeping bitterly,
no longer observing the etiquette of a subject or concubine,
and threw the patched clothes, contained in a brocade pouch, onto the ground,
saying:
"Your family was originally poor and humble;
this was made by my mother for your father.
Now that you have enough to eat,
do you immediately want to kill my son!"
The Emperor then pardoned him.
The Minister of Personnel, Wáng Qiú,
who was Lǚ’s paternal uncle,
was known for his simplicity and integrity,
and was highly esteemed by the Emperor.
Lǚ was by nature ambitious and covetous of gain.
This means Lǚ was eager to advance and fond of profit.
Wáng Qiú repeatedly admonished him,
but he did not listen.
On the night Liú Zhàn was executed,
Lǚ, barefoot and in distress, went to Wáng Qiú.
Wáng Qiú ordered his attendants to fetch shoes for him
and first offered him warm wine,
saying:
"What did I tell you on normal days?"
Lǚ was too terrified to answer.
Wáng Qiú calmly said:
"Your Àfù is here,
what do you have to worry about!"
People in Jiāngnán called their paternal uncle (shūfù or bófù) Àfù,
and also used it to refer to themselves when speaking to their nephews.
À
is pronounced wū-gé.
Lǚ was spared death
but was banished to his home.
According to the Nán Shǐ,
when the Emperor was first the Prince of Yídū,
he considered Wáng Qiú a friend,
and esteemed his simplicity and integrity.
Thus, he had known him for a long time.
Yìkāng was then in power,
and people vied to gain his intimacy.
Only the Chief Clerk of the Minister of Works, Jiāng Zhàn, was early able to distance himself,
requesting to be dispatched as the Administrator of Wǔlíng.
Tán Dàojì once sought a marriage alliance for his son with Jiāng Zhàn,
but Jiāng Zhàn firmly declined.
Tán Dàojì then, through Yìkāng, pressed the request,
but Jiāng Zhàn’s refusal became even firmer.
Thus, he was not implicated in the troubles of the two dukes.
The Emperor heard of this and praised him.
Jiāng Zhàn
was Yí’s son.
Jiāng Yí had been favored and employed at the beginning of the Yuánjiā era.
The Prince of Péngchéng, Yìkāng, remained in the palace for more than ten days.
When he saw the Emperor to take his leave,
he immediately descended to the sandbank.
The Emperor only wept bitterly in front of him,
saying nothing else.
The Emperor sent the Buddhist monk Huìlín to see him.
Yìkāng said:
"Does this disciple have a chance to return?"
Huìlín said:
"I regret that Your Grace did not read several hundred scrolls of books!"
Previously,
Xiè Shù, the Administrator of Wúxìng,
was Yù’s younger brother.
See Xiè Yù in volume 115, Yìxī 5th year of the Jìn Emperor Ān.
He offered beneficial advice several times;
but died early.
When Yìkāng was stationed in Jiānglíng,
Xiè Shù served as his General of Agile Cavalry’s Chief Clerk and Administrator of Nánjùn.
When Yìkāng became Chancellor,
Xiè Shù again served as the Minister of Works’ Senior Chief Clerk of the Left.
Shù
is pronounced suǒ-jiǎo.
(Yìkāng) was about to be moved south from Jiànkāng to Yùzhāng.
"In the past, Xiè Shù only advised me to retreat,
while Liú Bān only advised me to advance.
Now Liú Bān lives and Xiè Shù is dead,
so my defeat is fitting!"
The Emperor also said:
"If Xiè Shù were alive,
Yìkāng surely would not have come to this."
Xiāo Bīn, the Sīmǎ of the General Who Conquers the Barbarians, was appointed Yìkāng’s Consulting Military Advisor,
concurrently serving as the Administrator of Yùzhāng.
All matters, great or small,
were entrusted to him.
Xiāo Bīn
was Mózī’s son.
See Xiāo Mózī in volume 12, 12th year.
Yìkāng’s favored attendants
were all allowed to accompany him;
their provisions were generous,
and gifts and correspondence were continuous.
All important court affairs were reported to him.
After a long time,
the Emperor gathered with Princess Kuàijī for a banquet,
which was very joyful.
The Princess rose,
bowed twice, and kowtowed,
overcome with sorrow.
The Emperor did not understand her intention
and rose to help her up.
The Princess said:
"Chēzi will surely not be tolerated by Your Majesty by year’s end.
I particularly plead for his life now."
Yìkāng’s
courtesy name was Chēzi.
The Emperor also shed tears,
pointed to Jiǎngshān, and said:
"There will definitely be no such worry.
If I violate this oath today,
I will have betrayed Chūnínglíng."
Gāozǔ was buried in Chūnínglíng,
which was on Jiǎngshān.
He also wrote:
"My sister of Kuàijī remembered her brother during the banquet.
The remaining wine is now sealed and sent."
Thus, for the rest of the Princess’s life,
Yìkāng remained unharmed.
Your servant Guāng says: The Emperor Wén’s fraternal affection for Yìkāng
was indeed profound at the beginning;
yet it ended in the loss of brotherly joy
and a breach of the loyalty between sovereign and minister.
Tracing the origin of this disorder,
it was precisely due to Liú Zhàn’s insatiable ambition for power.
The Shī Jīng says:
"The greedy ruin their kind."
This is from the poem Sāngróu by Ruì Liángfū.
Bài
is pronounced bǔ-mài.
The General Who Attacks the South, Governor of Yánzhōu, the Prince of Jiāngxià, Yìgōng, was appointed Minister of Works and Director of the Department of State Affairs.
On wùyín,
the Prince of Línchuān, Yìqìng, was appointed Governor of Nányánzhōu;
Yīn Jǐngrén was appointed Governor of Yángzhōu,
remaining Grand Master of Ceremonies and Minister of Personnel as before.
Yìgōng, chastened by Péngchéng’s defeat,
although serving as Director-General,
merely carried out official documents,
which then put the Emperor at ease.
Péngchéng
refers to Yìkāng.
Other accounts confirm this;
however, Yìgōng was extravagant
and always in need of more,
so the Emperor also gave him separate funds,
amounting to ten million annually.
In the eleventh month,
on dīnghài,
the Wèi ruler went north of the mountains.
After Yīn Jǐngrén was appointed Governor of Yángzhōu,
his lingering illness worsened.
The Emperor issued an edict that no carriage sounds were allowed on the roads of Xīzhōu for his sake.
On guǐchǒu,
he passed away.
In the twelfth month,
on guǐhài,
Wáng Qiú, Grand Master of Guanglu, was appointed Grand Master of Ceremonies.
On wùchén,
the Prince of Shǐxīng, Jùn, was appointed Governor of Yángzhōu.
At this time, Jùn was still young,
so all provincial affairs were entrusted to Fàn Yè, the Chief Clerk of the Rear Army, and Shěn Pú, the Chief Clerk.
Fàn Yè
was Tài’s son;
Shěn Pú
was Línzǐ’s son.
Fàn Tài was admired and cherished by Gāozǔ.
Línzǐ had rendered meritorious service as a general under Gāozǔ.
Shěn Yǎnzhī, a Director of the Bureau of Personnel, was appointed General of the Right Guard,
jointly overseeing the imperial guards.
Yú Bǐngzhī was also appointed Director of the Bureau of Personnel,
both participating in confidential matters.
Shěn Yǎnzhī
was Jìngzhī’s great-grandson.
Shěn Jìng died defending Luòyáng
to clear his father, Chōng, of the crime of rebellion.
Fàn Yè possessed extraordinary talent,
but was cold-hearted and shallow in conduct,
often violating moral principles,
and was despised by the scholarly class.
He was impulsive and competitive by nature,
believing his talents were not fully utilized,
and was often discontented and unfulfilled.
This laid the groundwork for Fàn Yè's later conspiracy.
"Fàn Yè’s ambitions are unusual.
I request that he be sent out as Governor of Guǎngzhōu.
If he remains within the capital and a crisis erupts,
we will inevitably have to execute him,
and frequent executions
are not a credit to the state."
The Emperor said:
"Just having executed Liú Zhàn,
if we now also remove Fàn Yè,
people will say that you gentlemen cannot tolerate talent,
and that I believe slanderous words.
As long as we all know his true nature,
he cannot cause harm."
In this year,
Wáng Huìlóng, the Wèi General Who Pacifies the South, died.
Lǚ Xuánbó remained guarding his tomb
and never left for the rest of his life.
Wáng Huìlóng did not kill Lǚ Xuánbó;
see volume 8, 8th year.
20 The Wèi chủ wanted to make Yī Bō 尚書 (Shàngshū),
and enfeoff him as Jùn Gōng.
Bō declined, saying:
“The duties of a Shàngshū are onerous,
and the ducal title is extremely weighty.
These are not suitable for a young and foolish person like me to receive.”
The Emperor asked him what he desired.
He replied:
“The Central and Secretariat departments have many literary scholars.
Zhōng and Mì
refer to the Zhōngshū Shěng and Mìshū Shěng.
Please let me join their ranks.”
The Emperor approved of this,
and made him Zhōnghùjūn Jiāngjūn and Mìshūjiān.
21 Dà Qín Wáng Yáng Nándāng again claimed the title of Wǔdū Wáng.
In the thirteenth year,
Nándāng styled himself Dà Qín Wáng.
1 In spring,
the first month,
on the day Guǐmǎo,
Wèi appointed Qúqú Wúhuì as Zhēngxī Dàjiàngjūn, Liángzhōu Mù, and Jiǔquán Wáng.
2 Péngchéng Wáng Yìkāng arrived in Yùzhāng
and resigned from his post as Cìshǐ.
He resigned from the position of Jiāngzhōu Cìshǐ.
On the day Jiǎchén,
Yìkāng was appointed Dūdū of the military affairs of Jiāng, Jiāo, and Guǎng provinces.
The former Lóngxiáng Cānjūn, Bādōng Fú Lìngyù, went to the imperial court and presented a memorial,
stating:
“In the past, Yuán Àng advised Hàn Wéndì, saying: ‘If Huáinán Wáng were to die from exposure to frost and dew on the road,
Your Majesty would bear the reputation of having killed your brother.’
Wéndì did not heed this,
and later regretted it to no avail.
See volume fourteen, Wéndì’s sixth year.
The beloved son of the previous dynasty,
and Your Majesty’s younger brother –
if there were any errors or transgressions,
one should only enumerate his good and bad points,
and guide him with proper principles.
How can one trust suspicious rumors
and suddenly dismiss him,
sending him far away to the southern frontier!
Even commoners in the wilds
all feel sorrow for Your Majesty.
The past events of Lúlíng
are sufficient as a lesson and warning.
See volume one hundred and twenty, the first year.
To suddenly perish in the south –
though I am humble and insignificant,
I am secretly ashamed for Your Majesty.
Your Majesty only knows that a bad branch should be cut,
but how can you not know that cutting a branch harms the tree!
I earnestly wish that Your Majesty would immediately summon Yìkāng back to the capital region,
so that brothers may live in harmony,
and ruler and ministers may be in accord.
Then the hopes of the four seas will be fulfilled,
and the path of rumors will be cut off.
Why must it be Sītú Gōng and Yángzhōu Mù before Péngchéng Wáng can be properly placed?
If what I have said is detrimental to the state,
I request to suffer severe punishment to atone to Your Majesty.”
When the memorial was presented,
he was immediately arrested and sent to Jiànkāng prison,
and granted death.
Péi Zǐyě commented: A ruler who acts virtuously
is like clouds moving and rain falling,
from which all things receive blessings;
but when he acts wickedly,
it is like the sky splitting and the earth shaking,
which terrifies all things.
Who does not know it,
who does not see it!
How can killing one person
or silencing one mouth
repel or
eliminate it?
These are all due to an inability to overcome anger, which only exacerbates the illness.
Even with Tàizǔ’s magnanimity,
he still blocked his ears to the execution of Péngchéng Wáng;
from then on,
who dared to speak easily!
Zhèng Xuán said: Yóu
means 'to use.'
Yì
is pronounced with the sound of chì.
Rarely are straightforward and honest words heard.
Is it that the spirit of integrity
is ashamed of ancient times in this era?
Or is it that the penal policies of the kings of the time caused it to be so?
Zhāng Yuē perished at the hands of powerful ministers.
The event is found in volume one hundred and twenty, the first year.
The cauldron punishments of Sòng—
Alas,
how terrifying!
3 Wèi Xīnxīng Wáng Jùn was dissolute and lawless.
In the third month,
on the day Gēngxū,
his rank was demoted to Gōng.
Jùn’s mother had previously been disgraced and died,
and Jùn harbored resentment
and had rebellious intentions;
when the matter was discovered,
he was granted death.
4 On the day Xīnhài,
Wèi granted Yùjiǔlǘ Qǐlièguī the title of Shuòfāng Wáng,
and Qúqú Wànnián the title of Zhāngyè Wáng.
In the sixteenth year,
Wèi captured Qǐlièguī,
and Qúqú Wànnián also surrendered Gūzāng to Wèi in that same year.
5 In summer,
the fourth month,
Qúqú Táng’ér rebelled against Qúqú Wúhuì;
Wúhuì left his younger cousin Tiānzhōu to guard Jiǔquán,
and he and his younger brother Yíde led troops to attack Táng’ér.
Táng’ér was defeated and died.
Wèi considered Wúhuì to be a continuous border threat,
so on the day Gēngchén,
they dispatched Zhènnán Jiāngjūn Xī Juàn to attack Jiǔquán.
6 In autumn,
the eighth month,
on the day Xīnhài,
Wèi dispatched Sànqí Shìláng Zhāng Wěi to come as an envoy.
7 In the ninth month,
on the day Wùxū,
Wèi Yǒngchāng Wáng Jiàn died.
8 In winter,
the eleventh month,
on the day Wùzǐ,
Wáng Qiú died.
On the day Jǐhài,
Dānyáng Yǐn Mèng Yǐ was appointed Shàngshū Púshè.
9 The food in Jiǔquán city was exhausted,
and over ten thousand people starved to death.
Qúqú Tiānzhōu killed his wife to feed his soldiers.
On the day Gēngzǐ,
Wèi’s Xī Juàn captured Jiǔquán,
seized Tiānzhōu,
sent him to Píngchéng,
and killed him.
Qúqú Wúhuì was short of food,
and also feared the might of the Wèi army,
so he planned to cross the quicksand westward,
and sent his younger brother Ānzhōu to attack Shànshàn in the west.
The king of Shànshàn wanted to surrender,
but a Wèi envoy happened to arrive
and persuaded him to resist;
Ānzhōu could not overcome them
and retreated to garrison the Eastern City.
This refers to the Eastern City of the Shànshàn kingdom.
10 The Dī king Yáng Nándāng mobilized his entire nation to invade,
intending to occupy the land of Shǔ,
and sent his Jiànzhōng Jiāngjūn Fú Chōng to go out through Dōngluò to resist the Liángzhōu army;
The Wǔdài Zhì states: Yìchéng Jùn, Jǐnggǔ Xiàn,
was formerly Báishuǐ Xiàn. Later, the Hòu Zhōu abolished Dōngluò Jùn and incorporated it.
I understand Báishuǐ Xiàn
to have belonged to Guǎnghàn in the Hàn,
Zǐtóng in the Jìn,
and Jìnshòu at that time,
thus Dōngluò was within Jìnshòu’s borders.
Zhēndào
was the son of Huáijìng.
Liú Huáijìng is mentioned in volume one hundred and eleven, Jìn Āndì, Lóng’ān third year.
He captured Jìnshòu Tàishǒu Shēn Tǎn,
and then besieged Fúchéng;
The Tàishǒu of Báxī and Zǐtóng, Liú Dàoxī, held the city firmly,
and Nándāng attacked it for more than ten days
but could not take it,
so he returned.
Dàoxī
was the younger brother of Dàochǎn.
In the twelfth month,
on the day Guǐhài,
an edict ordered Lóngxiáng Jiāngjūn Péi Fāngmíng and others to lead three thousand armored soldiers,
and also dispatched troops from Jīng and Yōng provinces to suppress Nándāng,
all under the command of Liú Zhēndào.
Péi Fāngmíng
was a good general from Yìzhōu.
Chéng Dàoyǎng
had repeatedly distinguished himself in battles during Zhào Guǎng’s rebellion,
hence he was employed.
This laid the groundwork for pacifying Qiúchí in the following year.
Xiáng
is pronounced sī jiàng fān.
Shuài
is read as lǜ.
Yōng
is pronounced yú yòng fān.
The Kǎoyì states: The Dī Hú Zhuàn records
“In the nineteenth year, in the first month, Fāngmíng and others were dispatched,”
but we follow the Dìjì here.
11 Jìnníng Tàishǒu Cuàn Sōngzǐ rebelled,
and Níngzhōu Cìshǐ Xú Xún suppressed him.
In Jìn Huìdì’s Yǒng’ān second year,
seven western counties of Jiànníng were separated to form Yìzhōu Jùn.
By Huáidì’s reign,
it was renamed Jìnníng Jùn.
12. The Mán of Tiānmén, led by Tián Xiàngqiú and others, revolted,
and defeated Lóuzhōng.
Shěn Yuē said: Lóuzhōng County
did not exist during the Two Hàn dynasties.
It appears in the Dìzhì of Tàikāng in the Jìn dynasty.
I suspect it was established by Wú,
and belonged to Tiānmén Commandery.
Lóu,
pronunciation Láng Hóu fān.
13. Kòu Qiānzhī of Wèi spoke to the Wèi emperor, saying:
"Now Your Majesty, with the True Lord governing the world,
establishes the ritual of the Jìnglún Tiāngōng.
Since ancient times,
this has never happened.
You should ascend and receive the divine talismans to manifest your sagely virtue."
The Emperor followed his advice.

under imperial command.

Yuánjiā Nineteenth Year (Rénwǔ, 442)
1. Spring,
First month,
Jiǎshēn (day),
the Wèi emperor prepared the imperial carriage,
and went to the Taoist altar to receive the talismans.
His banners and flags were all green.
From then on, every emperor upon ascension received the talismans.
What was received here
is what Taoist priests today call fǎlù.
The Suízhì says: The method for Taoist priests to receive the Tao is,
first they receive the Wǔqiānwénlù,
next they receive the Sāndònglù,
next they receive the Dòngxuánlù,
next they receive the Shàngqīnglù.
The lù are all written on plain silk,
recording the names of officials and assistant scribes of the various heavenly bureaus.
There are also various talismans interspersed among them,
with strange and bizarre writings
that the world does not recognize.
Lù,
pronunciation Lóng Yù fān.
The Shuǐjīngzhù says: The Jìnglúngōng is northeast of the Taoist altar,
and the Taoist altar is on the west bank of the Léishuǐ, east of Píngchéng.
(The purpose was) to connect with the heavenly spirits above.
Cuī Hào advised the emperor to do this,
but the cost was enormous, in the tens of thousands,
and it was not completed after a year.
Crown Prince Huǎng admonished, saying:
"The paths of heaven and man are different;
the distinction between high and low is fixed,
and they cannot be connected.
This is an inevitable principle.
Now, exhausting the treasury
and wearying the common people
for a useless endeavor,
what purpose will it serve?
If it must be as Qiānzhī says,
please use the height of the ten-thousand-ren-high eastern mountain."
This refers to the eastern mountain of Píngchéng.
The emperor did not comply.
2. Summer,
Fourth month,
Jǔqú Wúhuì led over ten thousand households,
abandoned Dūnhuáng and moved west to join Jǔqú Ānzhōu.
Before he arrived,
Bǐlóng, the King of Shànshàn, feared him,
and led his people to flee to Qiěmò.
His heir apparent surrendered to Ānzhōu.
Wúhuì then occupied Shànshàn.
More than half of his soldiers died of thirst while passing through the Liúshā desert.
Lǐ Bǎo, from Yīwú, led two thousand troops and occupied Dūnhuáng.
He repaired the city and its administration,
and resettled the former inhabitants.
When Jǔqú Mùjiān fled,
see volume 121, year 16.
Jiān,
pronunciation Jū Yán fān.
He called himself Grand Administrator.
Táng Qì, pressed by the Rourán,
led his forces west towards Gāochāng,
intending to seize its territory.
The Rourán dispatched their general Āruò to pursue and attack him.
Qì was defeated and died.
In the first year of Jǐngpíng, King of Yíngyáng,
Qì and Lǐ Bǎo had both fled to Yīwú.
At that time, Jǔqú Ānzhōu was stationed at Héngjiéchéng.
Hē attacked and captured it,
and also captured the two cities of Gāoníng and Báilì.
Lǐ Yánshòu said: The kingdom of Gāochāng has forty-six garrisons,
including Jiāohé, Tiándì, Gāoníng,
Báirèn, Héngjié, etc.
The rest are not fully listed.
"Báilì",
should be
"Báirèn".
3. Jiǎxū (day),
the emperor, having recovered from illness,
issued a general amnesty.
4. Fifth month,
Péi Fāngmíng and others arrived in Hànzhōng,
and with Liú Zhēndào and others, divided their troops to attack Wǔxīng, Xiàbiàn, and Báishuǐ,
and captured them all.
"Xiàbiàn",
in the Hànshū is written
"Xiàbiàn".
Bìng,
pronunciation Pí Xiàn fān.
The Yuánfēng Jiǔyùzhì says: Jiējī Zhānglì County has Lángāozhèn.
According to the Wǔdàizhì,
Zhānglì County was Shímén County of Wǔxīng Commandery in the Later Wèi.
Xiāo Zǐxiǎn said: Northwest of Wǔxīng is Lángāosù,
two hundred *lǐ* from Qiúchí.
"Fú",
is probably meant to be
"Fú";
the Yáng and Fú clans
are both of the Dī ethnic group.
Fāngmíng and Hóngzǔ fought at Zhuóshuǐ.
Zhuóshuǐchéng is southeast of Shànglù County,
and northwest of Wǔjiēchéng.
Lì Dàoyuán said: Zhuóshuǐ is Báishuǐ.
Wǔjiēchéng was the former seat of Xiàbiàn County.
Hóngzǔ was beheaded;
Hē retreated and fled.
He was pursued to Chìtíng,
and defeated again.
Nándāng fled to Shàngguī;
his nephew, General Jiànjié Bǎochì, was captured.
Nándāng had made his son Hǔ the Inspector of Yìzhōu,
stationed at Yīnpíng.
Hearing that Nándāng had fled,
Hǔ led his troops back,
reaching Xiàbiàn.
Fāngmíng sent his son Sùzhī to intercept and attack him,
capturing Hǔ,
sending him to Jiànkāng,
where he was executed.
Qiúchí was pacified.
Hú Chóngzhī, the Auxiliary General of the State, was made Inspector of Běiqínzhōu,
to guard the territory.
Yáng Bǎochì was established as the successor of Yáng Xuán,
and made to guard Qiúchí.
Yáng Nándāng deposed Xuán's son Bǎozōng and usurped the throne,
see volume 121, year 6.
Autumn, Seventh month,
Liú Zhēndào was appointed Inspector of Yōngzhōu,
and Péi Fāngmíng was appointed Inspector of Liáng and Nánqín two prefectures.
Fāngmíng declined the appointment.
Kǎoyì says: In Zhēndào's biography,
this event occurred after Hú Chóngzhī's death;
in the Dīhú biography,
Chóngzhī died in the second month of the following year;
thus, Zhēndào's biography is mistaken.
Bǐngyín (day),
the Wèi emperor sent General Ānxī Gǔ Bì,
Kǎoyì says: The Sòng Suǒlǔ Biography writes
"Tǔxī Àibì",
and the Dīhú Biography writes
"Tǔxī Bì".
This was probably his old surname.
We now follow the Hòuwèishū.
with Yáng Bǎozōng, King of Wǔdū, to enter from Qíshān in the south.
Bǎozōng fled to Wèi, see volume 121, year 16.
They all converged on Qiúchí.
He also sent Sīmǎ Wénsī, King of Qiáo, to oversee the various armies of Luò and Yù to advance south towards Xiāngyáng.
In the second year of Jǐngpíng, King of Yíngyáng,
Wèi captured Hénán,
established Luòzhōu at Luòyáng,
and Yùzhōu at Hǔláo.
Qū,
pronunciation Qī Yù fān;
same below.
A letter was sent to Xúzhōu,
stating that they were avenging Yáng Nándāng.
5. Jiǎxū (day), the last day of the month,
there was a solar eclipse.
6 When Táng Qìzhī attacked Kàn Shuǎng,
the *Kǎoyì* says: The Sòng *Dīhú Zhuàn* writes
"Quē Shuǎng."
We now follow the *Hòuwèi Shū*.
He wanted to join them in attacking Qì.
In the eighth month,
Wúhuì led his forces toward Gāochāng;
by the time they arrived,
Qì had already died,
and Shuǎng closed the gates and resisted them.
In the ninth month,
Wúhuì ordered Wèi Xīngnú to launch a night attack on Gāochāng,
and they slaughtered its city.
The *Kǎoyì* says: In the *Sòng Shū*,
"Wèi Xīngnú"
is written as
"Wèi Liáo."
We now follow the *Hòuwèi Shū*.
Wúhuì occupied Gāochāng
and sent his *Chángshì* Fàn Jùn with a memorial to Jiànkāng.
An imperial edict appointed Wúhuì as *Dūdū Liáng-Hé-Shā Sānzhōu Zhūjūnshì*, *Zhēngxī Dàjiāngjūn*, *Liángzhōu Cìshǐ*, and King of Héxī.
The *Kǎoyì* says: In the Sòng *Běnjì*,
the enfeoffment and titles are in the sixth month,
while in the biography they are at the end of the ninth month.
We now follow the biography.
7 In winter,
the tenth month,
on the *Jǐmǎo* day,
the Wèi established Imperial Prince Fúluó as the King of Jìn,
Hàn as the King of Qín,
Tán as the King of Yān,
Jiàn as the King of Chǔ,
and Yú as the King of Wú.
8 On the *Jiǎshēn* day,
Rórán sent envoys to Jiànkāng.
9 In the twelfth month,
on the *Xīnsì* day,
Lú Lǔyuán, the Filial King Xiāngchéng of Wèi, died.
10 On the *Bǐngshēn* day,
an imperial edict commanded that the Temple of Kǒngzǐ and the schoolhouses in Lǔjùn be repaired,
and that five households near the tomb be exempted from taxes and labor services to provide for sweeping and cleaning.
11 Lǐ Bǎo sent his younger brother Huáidá and his son Chéng with a memorial to Píngchéng;
the Wèi people appointed Bǎo as *Dūdū Xīchuí Zhūjūnshì*,
*Yuǎnbiān Rìchuí*.
Officials of the fourth rank and below were permitted to grant provisional appointments based on imperial authority.
12 Liú Dàochǎn, the *Cìshǐ* of Yōngzhōu and Marquis Xiāng of Jìn'ān, died.
Dàochǎn was skilled at governance,
the people were settled in their occupations,
and both rich and poor were prosperous;
for this reason, there was a folk song called the "Xiāngyáng Lègē."
The mountain barbarians (*shānmán*), who had been uncontrollable before, all came out,
forming villages along the Miǎn River,
and their households and populations became numerous and thriving.
When he died,
the barbarians followed his cortege to the mouth of the Miǎn.
Not long after,
the Dī barbarians launched a major movement.
Dàochǎn died not long before the Dī barbarians revolted,
because later people could not tolerate or accommodate them.
Miǎn (沔),
pronounced *mí yǎn fān*.
Jī (幾),
pronounced *jū qǐ fān*.
This was unfavorable;
an imperial edict commanded Jiànwēi Jiāngjūn Shěn Qìngzhī to replace him,
who killed over ten thousand of the barbarians.
13 The Wèi ruler ordered *Shàngshū* Lǐ Shùn to classify and rank the Dī officials,
and grant them titles;
Shùn accepted bribes,
and his grading was unfair.
In this year,
Xú Jié, a native of Liángzhōu, reported this,
and the Wèi ruler was enraged,
also because Shùn had protected and sheltered the Jǔqú clan
and deceived the state to its detriment;
the matter is found in the sixteenth year of the previous volume.
1 In spring,
the first month,
Wèi Pí Bàozǐ attacked Lèxiāng,
and generals Wáng Huànzhī and others were defeated and perished.
The Wèi army advanced to Xiàbiàn,
and generals Qiáng Xuánmíng and others were defeated and killed.
In the second month,
Hú Chóngzhī fought the Wèi at Zhuóshuǐ;
Chóngzhī was captured by the Wèi,
and the remaining troops fled back to Hànzhōng.
General Jiāng Dàozǔ's army was defeated,
and he surrendered to Wèi;
Wèi then took Qiúchí.
Yáng Bǎochì fled.
2 On the *Bǐngwǔ* day,
the Wèi ruler went to the south of Héngshān;
in the third month,
on the *Gēngshēn* day,
he returned to the palace.
3 On the *Rénxū* day,
the state of Wūluòhóu sent envoys to Wèi.
The state of Wūluòhóu is north of the state of Dìdòugān,
over 4,500 *lǐ* from Dài.
Dìdòugān is over 1,000 *lǐ* west of Shìwéi,
Shìwéi is north of Wùjí,
and Wùjí is north of Gāolí;
thus Wūluòhóu is an Eastern Yi state.
Shǐ (使),
pronounced *shū lì fān*.
When Wèi was in the northern wilderness,
they carved a temple into a rock,
northwest of Wūluòhóu,
to worship their ancestors,
seventy *chǐ* high and ninety *bù* deep.
When the envoys from Wūluòhóu arrived in Wèi,
they reported that the stone temple was still there in its entirety,
so the Wèi ruler sent *Zhōngshū Shìláng* Lǐ Chǎng to the stone temple to offer sacrifices,
carved the prayer text onto the wall, and returned;
it was over 4,000 *lǐ* from Píngchéng.
4 Qí, Duke of Héjiān of Wèi, and Yáng Bǎozōng, King of Wǔdū, were stationed opposite each other at Luògǔ.
Luògǔ (雒谷),
is Luògǔ (駱谷);
the *Běishǐ* writes
"Luò" (駱).
They were ordered to close off the passes and fortify themselves to rebel against Wèi.
Someone informed Qí of this.
In summer, the fourth month,
Qí enticed and captured Bǎozōng,
sent him to Píngchéng,
and killed him.
Former *Zhèndōng Sī Fú Dá*,
above
"Sī" (司)
there should be the character
"Jūn" (軍);
otherwise,
below
"Sī" (司)
there should be the character

"Sī" (司)
there is indeed the character
Kǒng's edition is the same;
Zhāng's collation is the same.]
Fú Dá and others were all officials and subordinates of the Yáng clan.
Rèn (任),
pronounced *rén*.
Fěi (朏),
pronounced *fū wěi fān*.
They occupied Báiyá.
Eighty *lǐ* northeast of present-day Dà'ānjūn there is Báiyá.
Dà'ānjūn was ancient Jiāmén territory.
The *Kǎoyì* says: The Sòng *Dīhú Zhuàn* states:

Thus, the *Sòng Shū* is erroneous.
They advanced to besiege Qiúchí,

8 In the fifth month,
Wèi Gǔ Bì dispatched troops from Shàngguī, Gāopíng, and Qiānchéng to attack Yáng Wéndé.
"岍城"

Pí Bàozǐ led the Guānzhōng armies to Xiàbiàn.

Bì sent someone to tell Bàozǐ,
"The Sòng people are ashamed of their defeat
and will surely return.
After the army returns,
it will be difficult to raise it again.
It is better to train the troops and accumulate strength to await them.
Before autumn or winter,
the Sòng army will surely arrive.
By waiting at ease for the weary,

Bàozǐ followed his advice.
Wèi appointed Bàozǐ as the Defender of Qiúchí.
Yáng Wéndé sent an envoy to request aid.
In autumn,
the seventh month,
on the guǐchǒu day,

Wéndé garrisoned Jiālú Chéng.
The Wǔdài Zhì states: Wǔdū Commandery's Pándī County

Wèi also established Wǔyáng Commandery and Jiālú County,

Later, a county was established here.
Many Dī people from Wǔdū and Yīnpíng submitted to him.
9 On the jiǎzǐ day,
former Inspector of Yōng Province Liú Zhēndào, and

The Sòng people overlooked merits and recorded faults,
slaying their own good generals;

下 (xià)
is pronounced xiá jià.
10 In the ninth month,
on the xīnsì day,

On the jiǎchén day,

He divided his army into four routes: Prince Lè'ān Fàn and Prince Jiànníng Chóng each commanded fifteen generals and departed via the eastern route;
Prince Lèpíng Pī oversaw fifteen generals and departed via the western route;
the Wèi ruler himself took the central route;
and Prince Zhōngshān Chén oversaw fifteen generals as the rear guard.
The Wèi ruler arrived at Lùhún Gǔ.
Lùhún Gǔ is the valley of Lùhún Hǎi.
It was originally inhabited by the Gāochē Yuánhé tribe.
Its land is directly northwest of Píngchéng,
and to its east is the Ruòluò Shuǐ.
可 (kě)
is pronounced from kān, entering tone.
汗 (hán)
is pronounced hán.
"The enemy does not expect the great army to arrive suddenly.

Shàngshū Lìng Liú Jié strenuously advised against it,

If they came out to open ground,
they might be surrounded.
It would be better to wait for all the armies to gather.
須 (xū)
means to wait.
Huǎng said,
"The thickness of the dust

How could there be such dust over the camp?"

The Rouran fled.
He pursued them to Shí Shuǐ
but could not catch them and returned.
Shí Shuǐ is north of the Ègēn Hé.
還 (huán)
is pronounced xuán,
also as is.
"The Rouran did not realize the Wèi army had arrived.

The Wèi ruler deeply regretted this.
This laid the groundwork for Wèi to execute Liú Jié, Prince Zhōngshān Chén, and others.
They had all conspired with the Crown Prince.
Sīmǎ Chǔzhī separately led troops to oversee military provisions.
Zhènběi Jiāngjūn Fēng Tá wáng (fled) and surrendered to the Rouran,
persuading the Rouran to attack Chǔzhī to cut off the army's food supply.
Soon after, there was a report in the army of missing donkey ears.
The generals did not understand the reason.
Chǔzhī said,
"This must be thieves who sent spies into the camp

The thieves will arrive soon;
we should quickly prepare for them."
He then cut down willows to build a city,
and poured water over it to make it freeze.
As soon as the city was built, the Rouran arrived.
The ice was hard and slippery,

11 In the eleventh month,
General Jiāng Dàoshèng and Yáng Wéndé combined forces of twenty thousand to attack Wèi's Zhuóshuǐ Garrison.
Wèi's Pí Bàozǐ and Héjiān Gōng Qí came to its rescue.
Dàoshèng was defeated and died.
12 On the jiǎzǐ day,
the Wèi ruler returned.
Arriving at Shuòfāng,
he issued an edict ordering the Crown Prince to assist in managing all affairs of state
and to oversee all government matters.
The Kǎoyì states: The Sòng Suǒlǔ Zhuàn says:
"Huǎng was not on good terms with the ministers Cuī and Kòu.
Cuī and Kòu slandered him.
Xuángāo, a Buddhist monk, had magical arts.
Huǎng sent him to pray for blessings

Fólí dreamed that his ancestors were both angry,
pointing daggers at him and saying, 'Why do you believe slander

Fólí awoke with a start

succession is of great importance.
The Crown Prince's succession

From now on,
no matter how great or small the matter,

The details of the event differ slightly.
We now follow the Hòuwèi Shū.
"All meritorious officials who have toiled for a long time
should all return to their residences with their titles,
attend court at appropriate times,
feast before Us,
discuss principles, and present strategies,
but they should no longer be burdened with difficult duties.
Instead, select worthy and outstanding individuals to fill all official positions."
In the twelfth month,
on the dīng
mǎo day,
the Wèi ruler returned to Píngchéng.
This was after his expedition against the Rouran.
1 In spring,
the first month,
on the jǐhài day,
the Emperor plowed the ceremonial field and issued a great amnesty.
2 On the rényín day,
the Wèi Crown Prince began to oversee all government matters.
He ordered Shìzhōng and Zhōngshū Jiàn Mù Shòu, Sītú Cuī Hào, Shìzhōng Zhāng Lí, and Gǔ Bì to assist the Crown Prince in deciding various governmental affairs.
All who submitted memorials addressed themselves as 'your servant,'
and the ceremony was the same as that for memorials.
Gǔ Bì was a person who was
loyal, cautious, and straightforward.
He once requested that the Upper Valley (Shànggǔ) imperial park, which was too vast,
be reduced by more than half to be given to the poor.
He entered to see the Wèi ruler
to present this matter.
According to the biography of Gǔ Bì in the Běishǐ:
"At that time, the people of Shànggǔ submitted a petition,
saying that the imperial park was excessively large,
leaving people without land for their livelihood,
and that it should be reduced by more than half and given to the poor."
However, Shànggǔ was very far from the capital of Dài,
and Wèi never established an imperial park in that area.
Rather, Emperor Dàowǔ built the Lùyuàn park south of the Nántái Terrace,
extending north to the Great Wall,
east encompassing Báidēng,
and connecting to the Xīshān mountains,
covering tens of li in circumference.
In the sixth year of Tiānxīng,
he visited Nánpíngchéng,
and surveyed the Huángguāduī hill on the back of Xiàwūshān mountain south of the Lěi River to build a new city.

palaces and pavilions were built south of the Lěi River,
canals were dug and ponds excavated,

This is what was referred to as "too vast,"
and it was not in Shànggǔ.
The Běishǐ should be considered correct.
"見" (jiàn)
is pronounced xián biàn.
The ruler's mind was not on Gǔ Bì.
Bì attended him for a long time,

Suddenly, he stood up,
grabbed the end of the bed,
pulled it down from the platform,
boxed the ruler's ears,
hit him on the back,
and said:
"The court is not being governed,

The emperor lost his composure,
put down the game of go, and said:
"Not listening to your report

what crime has the bed committed!
Leave it!"
Bì then fully reported the situation,
and the emperor approved all his requests.
Bì said:
"As a minister, to be so disrespectful,
my crime is great."
He went out to the Gōngchē gate,
removed his cap, and went barefoot to beg for punishment.
The emperor summoned him in

"I have heard that during the construction of altars (shè),
if one stumbles and falls while building,
(The note in Shǔ says: 'to stumble and fall down.')

If that is the case, what crime have you committed!
Put on your cap and shoes and resume your duties.
If something benefits the state (shèjì)
and the common people,
exert all your strength to do it,

The Crown Prince (Tàizǐ) instructed the people in farming and sowing.
He had those without oxen borrow oxen from others for plowing and sowing,
and in return, they would weed their fields as compensation.
Generally, for every twenty-two mú plowed and sown, seven mú would be weeded.
This was roughly the standard.
He had the people mark their names at the head of their fields to know their diligence or laziness,
and forbade drinking and gaming.
As a result, cultivated land greatly increased.

The sons of artisans and merchants,

4 In the second month,
on the day of Xīnwèi,
Chén, Prince of Zhōngshān of Wèi, and Xuē Biàn, the Imperial Chancellor of the Inner Capital (Nèidū Zuò Dàguān),

"坐" (zuò)

were executed at the south of the capital for failing to meet the appointed time for a planned attack on Rouran.
Previously,

At the end of Yǒngchū reign of Emperor Gāozǔ of Sòng,

"蠕" (rú)

Cuī Hào strongly urged the Wèi ruler to proceed,

Jié was ashamed that his advice was not taken

The Wèi ruler had arranged a rendezvous with his generals at Lùhúgǔ valley,

When the emperor was traveling north,

Jié heard that Zhāng Sōng, the Right Assistant of the Imperial Secretariat (Shàngshū Yòuchéng), had a book of prophecies (túchèn) at his home.
He asked:

Do I have a name in it?"

When the emperor heard of this,

They searched Sōng's home

The matter implicated Dí Lín, Duke of Nánkāng.
Jié, Sōng, and Lín were all exterminated to the third degree of kinship (yí sāzú),

Jié, while in a position of power,
enjoyed wielding authority and privilege.
When generals defeated enemies,
all the spoils they obtained were divided with Jié.
After his death,
his household was confiscated,
and his wealth amounted to tens of millions.
The emperor would grit his teeth every time he spoke of it.
On the *Guǐyǒu* day,
LéPíng Lìwáng Pī died of sorrow.
Initially, the Wèi ruler built a White Platform,

Looking around, no one could be seen.
He ordered the diviner Dǒng Dàoxiù to consult the oracle.
Dàoxiù said:
"Great auspiciousness."
Pī secretly showed a joyful expression.

Dàoxiù should have said: 'Being excessively high leads to arrogance.

These are the words from *Yì* *Qián* upper nine and the *Wényán*.
亢 (*kàng*)

A king cannot but be cautious.
If he had done so,

On the *Gēngchén* day,
the Wèi ruler visited Lú.
Since the division and separate rule of the Southern and Northern dynasties,

In the third month,

In summer,

Wèi Shìzhōng, Tàizǎi, and Yángpíng Wáng Dù Chāo was killed by his subordinate.

孤帥 (*gū shuài*)

to

Since Wèi entered the Central Plains,

In autumn,

雍 (*yōng*)

In the eighth month,
on the *Yǐchǒu* day,
the Wèi ruler hunted in Héxī.
Shàngshūlìng Gǔ Bì remained behind to guard.

"As a minister,
I should not allow the ruler to indulge in hunting.

means 'joy'.

Now the Rúrú are strong,
