I provide stout horses for the army

This is foresight for the nation;

Moreover, I did this myself,

When the emperor heard this,

"To have such a minister

He bestowed upon him a set of clothes,
衣一襲 (*yī yī xí*)
means one set of clothes,

and ten deer.
Another day,

An edict ordered the Shàngshū to dispatch five hundred carts to transport the game.

The Wèi ruler said to his attendants:

The emperor said:

The Wèi ruler sent Yuánwài Sànqí Chángshì Gāo Jì to make a formal visit.
19th year, *wùchén* day:
Huáng Dé-jì (衡陽王), Yì-jì (義季), the Inspector of Jīngzhōu (荊州), was made General-in-Chief for Pacifying the North (征北大將軍), *Kāifǔ Yítóng Sānsī* (開府儀同三司), and Inspector of Nányánzhōu (南兗州).

means 'to warn' or 'to command'.
Yì-jì's
childhood name was *Shī-hù*.
Now I intend to grant this,
replacing him with you.
Although *Shī-hù* has no extraordinary achievements,
he cleanses himself and practices frugality (*jié yòng* 節用) —
*Jié* (絜)
is the same as *jié* (潔) —
he does not act wantonly towards his subordinates,
and his reputation is well-known in the Western lands.
He is held in high regard by both officials and commoners.
Commentators have not yet discussed moving him.
This present change
is because you and *Shī-hù* are of the same generation and age,
and I wish to test your respective abilities.
If you go,
and there is even one thing you do less well than him,
then it will cause significant obstruction in the Western lands.
The *Jiāngzuǒ Liùcháo* (江左六朝) commentary states: 'Jīngchǔ (荊楚) was considered the Western lands (*Xīxià* 西夏) during the Six Dynasties period in the lower Yangtze region.'
*Xià* (夏)
is pronounced *hù yǎ fān* (戶雅翻).
Responsibility will surely fall upon me.
This refers to the occasion of transfer and replacement,
where the wrong person was entrusted.
Do not cause people to criticize again!"
When Yì-xuān arrived at his post,
he diligently pushed himself,
and affairs were managed properly.
*gēngchén* day:
The Eldest Princess Huìjī passed away.
20th year: The Tùyùhùn (吐谷渾) chieftain Chìlìyán (叱力延) and others requested assistance from Wèi (魏) to attack Mùlìyán (慕利延), the King of Tùyùhùn.
The Wèi ruler dispatched Jìnwáng (晉王) Fúluó (伏羅) to lead the various armies to attack them.
21st year, 9th month,
*jiǎchén* day:
Jǔqú Ānzhōu (沮渠安周) was made Administrator-in-Chief of the military affairs of Liáng (涼), Hé (河), and Shā (沙) three prefectures, Inspector of Liángzhōu, and King of Héxī (河西).
22nd year, *dīngwèi* day:
The Wèi ruler went to Mònán (漠南),
intending to attack the Rouran (柔然).
However, Chìlián Kèhán (敕連可汗) of the Rouran had already fled far away,
so the attack was called off.
Chìlián soon died,
and his son Tǔhèzhēn (吐賀真) succeeded him,
adopting the title Chǔluó Kèhán (處羅可汗).
Wèi Shōu (魏收) said: "Chǔluó
means 'only' in Wèi language."
*Kě* (可)
is pronounced *cóng kān rù shēng* (從刊入聲).
*Hán* (汗)
is pronounced *hán* (寒).
23rd year: Jìnwáng Fúluó of Wèi arrived at Lèdū (樂都).
He led his troops along a secret path to attack Tùyùhùn,
reaching Dàmǔqiáo (大母橋).
Mùlìyán, the King of Tùyùhùn, was greatly alarmed
and fled to Báilán (白蘭).
Mùlìyán's nephew Shíyín (拾寅) fled to Héxī.
The Wèi army beheaded over five thousand enemies.
Mùlìyán's younger cousin Fúniàn (伏念) and others led thirteen thousand households to surrender to Wèi.
Mùlìyán had violated Āchái's (阿柴) "broken arrow" admonition,
which encouraged him to invite foreign invaders,
leading to his people rebelling and his relatives abandoning him.
This was indeed his just deserts.
*Cóng* (從)
is pronounced *cái yòng fān* (才用翻).
*Shuài* (帥)
is read as *shuài* (率).
*Jiàng* (降)
is pronounced *hù jiāng fān* (戶江翻).
24th year, winter,
10th month,
*jǐmǎo* day:
Xú Qióng (徐瓊), General of the Left Army (左軍將軍), was made Inspector of Yánzhōu (兗州).
Shēn Tián (申恬), an Assistant in the General-in-Chief's staff (大將軍參軍), was made Inspector of Jìzhōu (冀州).
The seat of Yánzhōu was moved to Xūchāng (須昌).
Shěn Yuè (沈約) said: "When Wǔdì (武帝) pacified Hénán (河南),
Yánzhōu's administration was in Huátái (滑臺).
In the 13th year of Yuánjiā (元嘉) under Wéndì (文帝), it was in Zōushān (鄒山),
and it was also temporarily administered from Péngchéng (彭城).
This is yet another move from Péngchéng to Xūchāng."
Lìxià (歷下)
is Lìchéng (歷城).
This refers to Mó's (謨) younger brother.
25th year, 12th month:
The Wèi ruler returned to Píngchéng (平城).
26th year:
Lǐ Bǎo (李寶), the Governor of Shāzhōu (沙州), paid tribute to Wèi.
The Wèi people kept him,
making him *Wàidū Dàguān* (外都大官).
This laid the foundation for the prosperity and power of the Lǐ clan.
*Cháo* (朝)
is pronounced *zhí yáo fān* (直遙翻).
27th year: Hé Chéngtiān (何承天), the Palace Aide to the Crown Prince (*tàizǐ shuàigēng lìng* 太子率更令), compiled the *Yuánjiā Xīnlì* (元嘉新曆, New Calendar of Yuánjiā),
and submitted it to the throne.
He determined the sun's position by observing the opposition of a lunar eclipse.
When the sun and moon are in direct opposition, their light obscures each other, allowing for this determination.
He found that during the time of Yáo (堯), the winter solstice sun was at 10 degrees of Xūnǚ (須女).
This was deduced from the *Yáodiǎn* (堯典)
passage
"When the day is shortest, the star is Mǎo (昴)."
Furthermore, he measured shadows and calibrated the two solstices,
finding a discrepancy of more than three days.
This also employed the method of measuring solstice shadows as described in the *Zhōulǐ* (周禮).
Thus, he established a new method,
moving the winter solstice forward by three days and five *shí* (時).
The sun's position
shifted four degrees from the old calculation.
Moreover, the moon has periods of acceleration and deceleration.
In the old calendar, when the conjunction of the sun and moon (*héshuò* 合朔) was calculated,
lunar eclipses did not fall on the new moon or full moon.
There should be
the character
"*rì*" (日, sun)
before
"*yuè shí*" (月食, lunar eclipse).
This was to correct the days of the new moon and full moon.
*Yíng* (贏)
is sometimes written as
*yíng* (盈).
Calendar methods involve 'major remainders' (*dàyú* 大餘) and 'minor remainders' (*xiǎoyú* 小餘).
The *Shǐjì Lìshū* (史記曆書) states:
The major remainder
pertains to the day;
the minor remainder
pertains to the month.
The circumference of the heavens is 365 and one-quarter degrees per day.
The sun travels one degree per day,
completing a full circuit in twelve months.
A year has twelve months, totaling 354 days.
Dividing this by six gives 300 days for five six-day cycles,
with 54 days remaining as the major remainder.
The circumference of the heavens is 365 degrees.
Dividing by *liùjiǎ* (六甲) (60), gives six times 60, which is 360,
with 5 remaining as the major remainder.
The minor remainder is the fraction of a day less than one-quarter.
When this fraction
reaches 32, it forms one day.
Odd days constitute the major remainder,
and odd fractions constitute the minor remainder,
accumulating to form intercalary months.
Qín Lèzhī (錢樂之), the Director of the Grand Astrologer's Office (太史令), and others memorialized,
agreeing with everything Hé Chéngtiān had submitted,
except for the moon having frequent three large and
frequent two small cycles.
This differed significantly from the old method,
and they suggested adhering to the old method.
The Emperor
approved the imperial edict.
1st year, spring,
1st month,
*xīnmǎo* day (the first day of the month):
The new calendar began to be implemented.
Originally,
Hàn (漢) scholar Jīng Fáng (京房) believed that among the twelve *lǜ* (律, pitches), *zhōnglǚ* (中呂) produced *huángzhōng* (黃鍾) one note higher,
but it was not a full nine *cùn* (寸).
He further developed this into sixty *lǜ*.
Qín Lèzhī further developed it into three hundred sixty *lǜ*,
with one pipe for each day.
Hé Chéngtiān put forward the argument
that the generation of pitches, one from another,
by adding or subtracting one-third,
was a simple method of the ancients,
just like the ancient calendar where the circumference of the heavens was 365 and one-quarter degrees.
However, Jīng Fáng did not understand this
and mistakenly devised sixty *lǜ*.
He then proposed a new system of *lǜ*,
where *línzhōng* (林鍾) was six *cùn* and one *lí* (釐) long.
Then, starting from *zhōnglǚ*, one could still obtain twelve *huángzhōng*s,
and the cyclical modulation of notes and rhymes would be perfectly aligned.
Thus, the sixty *lǜ* would be complete.
The transformation from twelve *lǜ* to sixty
is similar to the transformation from the eight trigrams to sixty-four.
The names of the sixty *lǜ* are detailed in the *Xù Hànshū Bǔzhì* (續漢書補志).
2nd year, *rénchén* day:
Wǔlíngwáng (武陵王) Jùn (駿) was made Inspector of Yōngzhōu (雍州).
The Emperor wished to plan for the regions of Guān (關) and Hé (河),
and therefore stationed Jùn at Xiāngyáng (襄陽).
3 The Wèi主 dispatched Sànqí Chángshì Sòng Yīn to come and offer tribute.
4 In the second month,
the Wèi主 went to Shàngdǎng,
then west to Tǔjīng,
to suppress rebellious Hú,
relocating them to various prefectures and counties.
5 On the day Jiǎxū,
Imperial Prince Yī was made the King of Dōnghǎi,
and Chǎng was made the King of Yìyáng.
6 In the third month,
on the day Gēngshēn,
the Wèi主 returned to the palace.
7 A Wèi edict stated:
"All cases of doubtful judgment shall be submitted to the Zhōngshū,
to be decided by the principles of the classics."
8 In summer,
the fourth month,
on the day Gēngxū,
the Wèi主 dispatched Zhēngxī Dàjiāngjūn Gāoliáng Wáng Nà and others to attack Tǔyùhún King Mùlìyán at Báilán.
Qínzhōu Cìshǐ, a native of Dài, Fēng Chìwén, and Ānyuǎn Jiāngjūn Yǐ Wūtóu attacked Mùlìyán's nephew, Shíguī, at Páohǎn.
9 When Héxī fell,
the people of Shànshàn, whose territory bordered Wèi,
were greatly alarmed,
saying:
"If we allow their envoys to pass,
they will learn the strengths and weaknesses of our state,
and our downfall will be swift."
So they closed off the Wèi route.
(This means they cut off Wèi's route to the Western Regions.)
(The character 使 [shǐ]
is pronounced like shū lì.
The same applies below.)
(The character 斷 [duàn]
is pronounced like dīng guǎn.)
They would often plunder and rob them.
Consequently, the Western Regions were cut off for several years.
The Wèi主 dispatched Sànqí Chángshì Wàn Dùguī to mobilize troops from Liángzhōu westward to attack Shànshàn.
10 In the sixth month,
on the day Rénchén,
the Wèi主 conducted a northern inspection tour.
11 The Emperor planned to attack Wèi.
He abolished Nányùzhōu and merged it into Yùzhōu,
appointing
Nányùzhōu Cìshǐ Nánpíng Wáng Shuò as Yùzhōu Cìshǐ.
In the second year of Gāozǔ Yǒngchū,
the land east of the Huái River was divided to form Nányùzhōu,
with its seat in Lìyáng;
the land west of the Huái River was Yùzhōu,
with its seat sometimes in Shòuyáng,
sometimes in Rǔnán.
(Shuò
is pronounced like shì yuē.)
12 In autumn,
the seventh month,
on the day Jǐwèi,
Shàngshū Púyè Mèng Yǐ was appointed Zuǒ Púyè,
and Zhōnghùjūn Hé Shàngzhī was appointed Yòu Púyè.
13 When Wǔlíng Wáng Jùn was about to proceed to his garrison,
at that time, the various Man tribes along the Miǎn River were still committing piracy,
obstructing water and land routes.
Jùn divided his army and dispatched Fǔjūn Zhōngbīng Cānjūn Shěn Qìngzhī to ambush and attack them,
achieving a great victory.
When Jùn arrived at his garrison,
the Man tribes cut off the post roads,
intending to attack Suíjùn.
Suíjùn Tàishǒu, Lǐu Yuánjǐng of Hédōng, recruited six or seven hundred men,
ambushed them,
and thoroughly defeated them.
Thereupon, the various Man tribes were pacified,
and over seventy thousand people were captured.
The Mǐnshān Man were the strongest.
(The Shuǐ Jīng Zhù states: The river originates from the Dàhóng Mountain southeast of Càiyáng County,
which is southwest of Suíjùn and northeast of Jìnglíng,
its base spanning
over one hundred lí in circumference.
The Mǐnshǔi flows from the north side of this mountain,
so people at the time considered it to be guided by the Mǐnshǔi,
and also called it Mǐnshān.)
(Mǐn
is pronounced like yún.)
Over thirty thousand people were captured,
and over ten thousand were relocated to Jiànkāng.
14 When Tǔyùhún Shíguī heard that the Wèi army was approaching,
he abandoned the city and fled by night.
In the eighth month,
on the day Dīnghài,
Fēng Chìwén entered Páohǎn,
relocated a thousand households of its people back to Shàngguī,
and left Yǐ Wūtóu to guard Páohǎn.
15 Wàn Dùguī reached Dūnhuáng,
left his baggage train,
and with five thousand light cavalry crossed the Liúshā Desert,
surprising Shànshàn.
On the day Rénchén,
Shànshàn King Zhēndá came out with his hands bound and surrendered.
Dùguī left troops to garrison the area,
and went with Zhēndá to Píngchéng,
thus reopening communication with the Western Regions.
16 The Wèi主 went north of Yīnshān,
mobilized one-third of the troops from various prefectures,
ordering each to be on high alert in their respective prefectures,
awaiting further orders.
(Xū
means to wait.)
He ordered them to graze livestock in the north,
to bait the Rourán.
17 On the day Rén Yín,
Wèi Gāoliáng Wáng Nà's army arrived at Níng
tóuchéng.
(Níngtóuchéng should be northeast of Báilán.)
Bèináng, the son of Tǔyùhún Mùguī, engaged them in battle.
Nà defeated him;
Bèináng fled.
Zhōngshān Gōng Dù Fēng led elite cavalry in pursuit,
crossing Sānwēi
and reaching Xuěshān.
(Lì Dàoyuán states: Sānwēi Mountain is south of Dūnhuáng County.)
All were sent to Píngchéng.
(Qífú Chénglóng, after Hèlián Dìng's defeat, was captured by Tǔyùhún.)
They killed their king,
occupied their territory,
and tens of thousands died.
18 In the ninth month,
on the day Guǐyǒu,
the Emperor held a farewell banquet for Héngyáng Wáng Yìjì at Wǔzhàng Gāng.
(This was to see Yìjì off to garrison Nányǎn.)
(Dù Yòu says: Wǔzhàng Gāng is outside Guǎngmòmén, in Xuānwǔchǎng.
A temporary palace and comfortable seat were set up there,
hence the name.)
He ordered his sons not to eat yet,
but to wait for the meal prepared at the gathering place.
As the day wore on,
and they had not yet arrived,
they showed signs of hunger.
The Emperor then said:
"You, my sons, have grown up in abundance and ease,
and have not seen the hardships of the common people.
Today I make you experience hunger,
so that you may know how to manage things with frugality."
Péi Zǐyě's commentary states: Excellent indeed was the instruction of Tàizǔ!
Extravagance arises from having too much,
and frugality from having too little.
If one desires them to be humble and constrained,
there is nothing better than poverty and low status!
Accustom them to danger and hardship,
and it will be advantageous to entrust them with responsibilities;
be aware of their true nature,
and it will be easy to personally oversee them.
If Tàizǔ could have adhered to this instruction,
refined their aspirations and conduct,
lowered their ritual ranks,
and after their education was complete and their virtue established,
then entrusted them with governance,
they would have been neither remiss nor negligent,
and their influence could have spread throughout the Jiǔfú.
(The Zhōu system of Jiǔfú consisted of: Hóufú, Diànfú, Nánfú, Cǎifú, Wèifú, Mánfú, Yífú, Zhènfú,
[and Fānfú],
each five hundred lí.)
(They were called 'fú' because their duty was to serve the Son of Heaven.)
Gāozǔ, desiring to secure his lineage,
greatly established his sons in infancy;
later generations followed suit,
successively occupying key regional posts.
(This refers to Yìzhēn, Yìkāng, Yìgōng, and Yìxuān all successively holding regional commands.)
(Qiáng
is pronounced like jū liǎng.)
(Bǎo
is pronounced like bǎo.)
Towards the end of Shēngmíng,
dozens of people were strangled in their beds.
(This refers to Míng Dì killing all the sons of Xiàowǔ,
and at the time of the abdication from Sòng to Qí, the Xiāo clan exterminated the Liú clan.)
(Yàn
is pronounced like yān.)
Since this was not the right way,
they were early given power over the people.
(The Zuǒ Zhuàn states: Jìn Shī Kuàng said:
"Heaven's love for the people is profound;
how could it allow one man to oppress the people?")
19 In the Wèi (魏) common folk, a rumor spread,
"The one who destroys Wèi (魏) is Wú (吳)."
Gài Wú (蓋吳), a Lúshuǐ Hú (盧水胡), gathered a multitude and rebelled at Xìngchéng (杏城).
Gài Wú (蓋吳)
was a branch of the Lúshuǐ Hú (盧水胡) from Āndìng (安定) who resided in Xìngchéng (杏城).
Gài (蓋),
pronounced like "gě" in ancient times.
He had a multitude of over ten thousand people.
He dispatched his confederate Zhào Wǎn (趙綰) to come
and submit a memorial, offering his allegiance.
In winter,
the tenth month,
on the day of wùzǐ (戊子),
the Vice General of Cháng'ān (長安) Garrison, Tuòbá Gē (拓跋紇), led his troops to suppress Wú (吳).
Gē (紇) was defeated and died.
Wú's (吳) multitude grew even stronger,
and the people all crossed the Wèi (渭) River and fled to the Southern Mountains.
These were the Southern Mountains of Cháng'ān (長安).
An order was issued for General Shūsūn Bá (叔孫拔) to take command of the forces from Bìng (幷), Qín (秦), and Yōng (雍) three prefectures and garrison them north of the Wèi (渭) River.
20 In the eleventh month,
Wèi (魏) mobilized the people of Jìzhōu (冀州) to build a pontoon bridge at Quèqiáo (碻磝) Ford.
21 Gài Wú (蓋吳) dispatched his separate commander Bái Guǎngpíng (白廣平)
to raid Xīnpíng (新平) to the west.
All the various Hú (胡) tribes in Āndìng (安定) gathered their forces to respond to him.
He also divided his troops to raid Línjìn (臨晉) and Bādōng (巴東) to the east.
"Bā" (巴)
should be
Over thirty thousand people drowned in the river.
Wú (吳) again sent troops to raid to the west,
reaching Cháng'ān (長安).
General Shūsūn Bá (叔孫拔) fought them north of the Wèi (渭) River,
thoroughly defeating them,
and beheading over thirty thousand.
Xuē Yǒngzōng (薛永宗) of the Hédōng Shǔ (河東蜀) gathered a multitude to respond to Wú (吳).
Those Shǔ (蜀) people who migrated to Hédōng (河東)
were called Hédōng Shǔ (河東蜀).
Those residing in Jiàngjùn (絳郡) were called Jiàng Shǔ (絳蜀).
Those residing in Chǐshuǐ (赤水) in Guānzhōng (關中) were called Chǐshuǐ Shǔ (赤水蜀).
Wénxǐ (聞喜) County
belonged to Hédōng Jùn (河東郡).
In the Spring and Autumn period, it was Qǔwò (曲沃), where Jìn Wǔgōng (晉武公) resided.
Qín (秦) changed its name to Zuǒyì (左邑).
Hàn Wǔdì (漢武帝) heard of the defeat of Nányuè (南越) here,
and changed its name to Wénxǐ (聞喜).
Later, Wèi (魏) divided it to belong to Jiàngjùn (絳郡).
The magistrate was anxious and at a loss for a plan.
Péi Jùn (裴駿), a person from the county, led the local strongmen to attack them,
and Yǒngzōng (永宗) withdrew.
The Wèi (魏) ruler ordered Xuē Jǐn's (薛謹) son, Bá (拔), to assemble his clan and villagers,
"clan" referring to Xuē's (薛) relatives,
"villagers" referring to the people from the same village,
to cut off the path of transit for the two bandits.
The "two bandits" referred to Xuē Yǒngzōng (薛永宗) and Gài Wú (蓋吳).
"Cut off" (斷),
pronounced like "duàn".
On the day of gēngwǔ (庚午),
the Wèi (魏) ruler sent Diànzhōng Shàngshū (殿中尚書) Tuòbá Chǔzhí (拓跋處直) and others to lead twenty thousand cavalry to suppress Xuē Yǒngzōng (薛永宗).
Diànzhōng Shàngshū (殿中尚書) Yǐ Bá (乙拔) led thirty thousand cavalry to suppress Gài Wú (蓋吳).
Jìn (晉) established the Diànzhōng Shàngshū (殿中尚書),
which, along with Lìbù (吏部), Wǔbīng (五兵), Tiáncáo (田曹), Dùzhī (度支), and Zuǒmín (左民), formed the Six Bureaus.
Dù Yòu (杜佑) stated: In the early Wèi (魏) dynasty,
there were five Shàngshū (尚書): Diànzhōng (殿中), Yuèbù (樂部), Jiàbù (駕部), Nánbù (南部), and Běibù (北部).
Diànzhōng (殿中) managed the palace's military horses and granaries.
Yuèbù (樂部) managed performing arts, musicians, and ushers.
Jiàbù (駕部) managed cattle, horses, donkeys, and mules.
Nánbù (南部) managed the various prefectures and commanderies in the southern border regions.
Běibù (北部) managed the various prefectures and commanderies in the northern border regions.
The Wèi Shū Guānshì Zhì (魏書官氏志) states: Among the assimilated clans,
the Yǐfú (乙弗) clan was changed to the Yǐ (乙) clan.
Chǔ (處),
pronounced like "chǔ".
"Lead" (將),
pronounced like "jiàng".
"Cavalry" (騎),
pronounced like "jì";
same below.
The Guānshì Zhì (官氏志) states: Among the assimilated clans,
the Ruòkǒuyǐn (若口引) clan was changed to the Kòu (寇) clan.
Offices were established and officials appointed.
22 On the day of xīnwèi (辛未),
the Wèi (魏) ruler returned to the palace.
He returned from Yīnshān (陰山).
23 Wèi (魏) selected twenty thousand elite cavalry from six prefectures.
The six prefectures were Jì (冀), Dìng (定), Xiāng (相), Bìng (幷), Yōu (幽), and Píng (平).
"Elite" (驍),
pronounced like "xiāo".
They raided north of the Huái (淮) and Sì (泗) Rivers,
and resettled the people of Qīng (青) and Xú (徐) to fill Héběi (河北).
24 On the day of guǐwèi (癸未),
the Wèi (魏) ruler made a western tour.
25 In the beginning,
Kǒng Xīxiān (孔熙先) from Lǔguó (魯國) was widely learned in literature and history,
and also proficient in various divination arts.
He possessed talents and ambitions for political maneuvering.
He served as Yuánwài Sǎnqí Shìláng (員外散騎侍郎),
but was not recognized by his contemporaries,
feeling frustrated and discontented.
His father, Mò (默), when serving as the Governor of Guǎngzhōu (廣州),
was convicted of corruption.
Grand General Péngchéng Wáng Yìkāng (彭城王義康) rescued him from punishment.
When Yìkāng (義康) was transferred to Yùzhāng (豫章) –
Yìkāng's (義康) transfer
is mentioned in Volume 17 of the previous scroll –
he also believed that according to astronomical phenomena and prophetic diagrams,
the Emperor would inevitably die an unnatural death,
due to internecine strife among relatives;
and that the son of heaven would emerge from Jiāngzhōu (江州).
Seeing Fàn Yè (范曄) was discontented,
he wished to involve him in his conspiracy,
but Xīxiān (熙先) was never highly regarded by Yè (曄).
Crown Prince Zhōngshèrén (太子中舍人) Xiè Zōng (謝綜),
who was Yè's (曄) nephew –
the position of Crown Prince Zhōngshèrén (太子中舍人) was established in the fourth year of Xiánníng (咸寧) of Jìn (晉) (278 CE),
for those with excellent talent and learning,
sharing the responsibility of literary work with the Zhōngshùzǐ (中庶子),
with duties similar to the Huángmén Shìláng (黃門侍郎),
ranked below the Zhōngshùzǐ (中庶子) and above the Xǐmǎ (洗馬) –
Zōng (綜) introduced Xīxiān (熙先) to Yè (曄).
Xīxiān's family was wealthy,
and he often gambled with Yè,
so he deliberately played poorly
to lose money to him.
Yè not only profited from his wealth
but also admired his literary and artistic talents;
consequently, their relationship became close and intimate.
Xīxiān then calmly persuaded Yè, saying:
"The Grand General is sagacious and intelligent,
with both men and gods devoted to him.
He lost his position in the southern border,
which refers to his transfer to Yùzhāng.
I, your humble servant, received my late father's dying command
to repay the Grand General's kindness with my life.
Recently, public sentiment has been agitated,
and celestial phenomena have been anomalous.
This is what is called the arrival of opportune timing,
which cannot be pushed away.
If we align with the hearts of heaven and men,
unite the heroic and exceptional,
with internal and external forces responding in kind,
and act from within our midst;
then, by executing those who oppose us
and upholding the enlightened sage,
issuing commands to the world,
who would dare not comply!
I, your humble servant, request to use my seven-foot body
and three-inch tongue
to achieve deeds and accomplish tasks, then attribute them to you gentlemen.
What do you, venerable sir, think of this? "
Yè was greatly astonished.
Xīxiān said:
"In the past, Máojiè dedicated himself to Wèi Wǔ,
and Zhāng Wēn exhaustively deliberated with Sūn Quán.
Those two individuals
were both outstanding talents of the state.
Were their words and actions flawed,
leading to disaster and disgrace?
Rather, it was because they were incorruptible, upright, and firm,
and could not be tolerated for long.
Máojiè's story can be found in Volume 67, in the 21st year of Jiàn'ān of Emperor Xiàn of Hàn.
Zhāng Wēn's affair
can be found in Volume 69, in the 5th year of Huángchū of Emperor Wén of Wèi.
行,
read as xià mèng fān;
same as xià nèi xíng.
玷,
read as duō tiǎn fān.
Their bond with the two lords was not deep,
and their excellent reputation among people
surpassed that of other ministers.
Slanderers had cast sidelong glances at them
for a long time.
To compete shoulder to shoulder
- how could one succeed in that?
It means competing shoulder to shoulder with the powerful figures of the time,
where glory and profit lie,
a prize for all to contend for,
making it impossible to achieve one's ambitions.
朝,
read as zhí yáo fān.
See Volume 17.
Would it lead to resentment for a hundred generations?
What they contended for was merely the priority of glory, fame, power, and profit.
By the end,
they feared only that they had not been deeply enough ensnared,
or that their downfall had not been brought about early enough;
even the slaughter of a hundred family members
would still be considered insufficient.
This is enough to make one's heart turn cold with dread and fear;
how could it be merely distant matters recorded in books!
Now, to establish a great achievement,
uphold the virtuous and wise,
plan difficult tasks from an easy position,
replace danger with safety,
enjoy great benefits,
and acquire lofty renown,
grasping and possessing it all at once—
how can one abandon it and not take it! "
Yè still hesitated and was undecided.
Xīxiān said:
"There is something even more significant than this,
which I, a fool, have not dared to mention yet."
Yè asked:
"What is it?"
Xīxiān said:
"Your venerable sir's family has been distinguished and prominent for generations.
Yè's great-grandfather Wāng, grandfather Níng, and father Tài
all had renowned conduct.
People treat you like dogs and pigs,
yet your venerable sir does not feel ashamed,
and wishes to die for them;
is this not bewildering! "
Yè's family lacked internal political influence,
so Xīxiān used this to provoke him.
Yè remained silent, not responding,
but his intent to revolt was decided.
Yè and Shěn Yǎnzhī were both favored by the Emperor.
When Yè arrived first,
he would surely wait for Yǎnzhī to enter together.
When Yǎnzhī arrived first,
he was often admitted alone,
and Yè resented this.
Yè had served as a subordinate in Yìkāng's administration multiple times,
and during this period, he offended Yìkāng.
Xiè Zōng and his father Shù
were both held in high regard by Yìkāng,
and Zōng's younger brother Yuē married Yìkāng's daughter.
Zōng, as Yìkāng's secretarial aide,
returned from Yùzhāng
and conveyed Yìkāng's intention to Yè,
seeking to resolve their past animosity
and restore their former good relations.
Zhòng Chéngzǔ, a clerk in the Grand General's office,
was favored by Yìkāng.
Hearing of Xīxiān's plot,
he secretly allied himself with them.
Xú Zhànzhī, the Governor of Dānyáng,
was always beloved by Yìkāng.
Chéngzǔ thus used this connection to approach Zhànzhī,
informing him of the secret plan.
The Buddhist monk Fǎlüè and the nun Fǎjìng
were both grateful for Yìkāng's past kindness
and maintained contact with Xīxiān.
Fǎjìng's brother-in-law, Xǔ Yào,
commanded a troop stationed in the imperial palace (tái).
In Jiangnan, the imperial palace was called tái.
When Fǎjìng went to Yùzhāng,
Xīxiān entrusted her with a letter
expounding on prophecies and omens.
Thereupon, they secretly assigned positions
and sought out those they disliked,
listing them all for execution.
They itemized the names,
wishing to put to death
all those they had always disliked.
They declared:
"The traitorous minister Zhào Bófú unleashed soldiers and violated the imperial procession,
bringing disaster to the Heir Apparent.
Zhào Bófú was then the General of the Imperial Guard,
so they intended to attribute the crime of regicide to him.
The phrase 'bringing disaster to the Heir Apparent' means they intended to kill Crown Prince Shào as well.
Immediately behead Bófú and his associates.
We now send the Protector-General Zāng Zhì to respectfully present the imperial seal and ribbon, and welcome the Prince of Péngchéng to ascend the imperial throne."
The North Star is the celestial pole,
hence the imperial throne is referred to as the celestial pole.
璽,
read as sī shì fān.
綬,
read as yīn shòu.
Yè also forged a letter from Yìkāng to Zhànzhī,
ordering the execution of corrupt officials around the ruler,
and publicized it among his confederates.
When the Emperor was feasting at Wǔzhànggāng,
Yè and others planned to start the rebellion on that very day.
Xǔ Yào, attending the Emperor,
tapped his sword and looked at Yè.
'Tapping the sword' means drawing the sword slightly out of its scabbard.
Soon after, the gathering dispersed,
and Xú Zhànzhī, fearing the plot would fail,
secretly reported their scheme to the Emperor.
The Emperor ordered Zhànzhī to thoroughly investigate and uncover the full details,
obtaining their manifestos and lists of appointed names,
and submitted them.
The Emperor then ordered the relevant officials to arrest and thoroughly interrogate them.
That night,
he summoned Yè and placed him in the guesthouse.
The guesthouse was where visitors from all directions stayed when they came for an audience;
it was subordinate to the Director of Guest Reception.
All confessed their crimes.
The Emperor sent an envoy to question Yè,
but Yè still covertly resisted;
Xīxiān heard of this
and laughed, saying:
"All the dispositions, manifestos, and letters
were created by Fàn,
so why is he still resisting like this now?"
The Emperor showed Yè his handwriting,
and he then fully recounted the whole affair.
The next day,
the armed guards sent them to the Court of Judicial Review (Tíngwèi).
*Zhàngshì* (仗士)
refers to soldiers who carry weapons.
Their words and demeanor were unyielding.
The Emperor (Shàng) was surprised by their talent,
and sent someone to console and encourage them, saying:
"With your talent, to be stuck in the Bureau of Books (Jíshūshěng),
*Sànqí Shìláng* (散騎侍郎),
is an official in the Bureau of Books.
Xiāo Zǐxiǎn (蕭子顯) said: From *Sànqí Shìláng* to *Tōngzhí Yuánwài* (通直員外), *Gěishìzhōng* (給事中), *Fèngcháoqǐng* (奉朝請), and *Fùmǎ Dūwèi* (駙馬都尉),
all are positions within the Bureau of Books.
This is my fault towards you."
He also reprimanded the former Minister of Personnel (Lìbù Shàngshū) Hé Shàngzhī (何尚之), saying:
"To make Kǒng Xīxiān (孔熙先) a *Sànqí Láng* (散騎郎) when he was nearly thirty,
why wouldn't he become a rebel!"
Xīxiān submitted a memorial from prison to express gratitude for the Emperor's (Shàng) grace,
and also presented a prophecy (túchèn),
strongly warning the Emperor (Shàng) about the calamity among his kin,
saying:
"I hope you will not abandon us,
but keep us in the Central Secretariat (Zhōngshū).
If we die as prisoners,
perhaps we can still be posthumously recorded,
so that even in the underworld,
we might somewhat atone for our offenses."
Yè (曄) wrote a poem in prison, saying:
"Though I have no *Jī Shēng*'s (嵇生) zither,
I hope to be like Xiàhóu (夏侯) in countenance."
Jī Kāng (嵇康) was killed by King Wén (Wénwáng) of Jìn (Jìn),
and at the moment of his death,
he looked at the shadow of the sun,
asked for a zither and played it.
Xiàhóu Xuán (夏侯玄) was killed by King Jǐng (Jǐngwáng) of Jìn (Jìn),
and when he went to the East Market,
his expression did not change.
However, the Emperor (Shàng) pursued a thorough investigation of their case,
which lasted for two weeks,
and Yè (曄) gained renewed hope for survival.
A jailer joked with him, saying:
"There are rumors outside that the Grand Tutor to the Crown Prince (Zhànshì) might be imprisoned for a long time."
When Yè (曄) heard this,
he was both surprised and delighted.
Zōng (綜) and Xīxiān (熙先) laughed at him, saying:
"The Grand Tutor to the Crown Prince (Zhànshì) in the past would roll up his sleeves, glare angrily,
leap onto his horse, and look around,
considering himself a hero of his age;
now in this chaotic turmoil,
he is so afraid of death!
Yè (曄) was the Grand Tutor to the Crown Prince (Tàizǐ Zhànshì),
hence the稱 (chēng) him.
*Chēn* (瞋),
pronounced as *qī rén fān*.
As subjects plotting against their sovereign,
how can you have the face to want to live!"
In the twelfth month,
on the day of *Yǐwèi* (乙未),
Yè (曄), Zōng (綜), Xīxiān (熙先) and their sons, younger brothers, and confederates were all executed.
Yè's (曄) mother went to the market,
weeping and reprimanding Yè (曄), striking Yè's (曄) neck with her hand,
but Yè's (曄) expression showed no shame;
when his sister and concubines came to bid farewell,
Yè (曄) wept profusely with sorrow.
Zōng (綜) said:
"Uncle is far from matching Xiàhóu's (夏侯) countenance."
Yè (曄) collected his tears and stopped.
Xiè Yuē (謝約) was not involved in the rebellious plot.
Seeing his elder brother Zōng (綜) associating with Xīxiān (熙先),
he often advised him, saying:
"This person is frivolous in his actions and curious about the unusual,
not adhering to the Way,
sharp in his actions but without restraint."
*Yánwújiǎntōngyě* (言無檢東也).
*Hào* (好),
pronounced as *hūdào fān*.
*Jìn* (近),
pronounced as *qíjìn fān*.
Zōng (綜) did not listen and failed.
Zōng's (綜) mother, seeing her son and his younger brothers fall into rebellion,
alone did not go out to watch.
Yè (曄) said to Zōng (綜):
"Sister not coming now
is better than many others."
When Yè's (曄) household was confiscated,
musical instruments and cherished possessions
were all rare and beautiful,
and his concubines were laden with pearls and jade.
His mother's residence was simple and humble,
with only one cabinet filled with firewood;
his younger brothers had no quilts in winter,
and his uncle wore simple cotton clothes.
Péi Zǐyě (裴子野) commented: "Indeed, those with extraordinary talent
must aspire to soaring positions;
*chōng* (沖),
same as *chōng* (翀),
flying high.
An ancient saying goes:
'Once it flies, it soars to the sky.'
Then they fall below the ordinary level.
*Chángjūn* (常均) means 'ordinary.'
To guide them with propriety,
how rarely does it happen!
Liú Hóngrén (劉弘仁) and Fàn Wèizōng (范蔚宗),
Liú Zhàn (劉湛),
whose courtesy name was Hóngrén (弘仁).
Fàn Yè (范曄),
whose courtesy name was Wèizōng (蔚宗).
*Wèi* (蔚),
pronounced as *yúwù fān*.
They prided themselves on their talent and served rebellion,
destroying generations of refined conduct
in a single morning.
What was previously called wisdom
turned out to be the means of their own destruction."
Xú Zhànzhī (徐湛之) did not fully disclose much of what he knew,
and was implicated by Yè (曄) and others' confessions,
but the Emperor (Shàng) pardoned him and did not investigate further.
Zāng Zhì (臧質),
son of Xī (熹),
Zāng Xī (臧熹)
was the younger brother of Zāng Táo (臧燾).
Zhì (質) was related to the imperial family through marriage,
and was a maternal cousin to the Emperor (Dì).
He was on very good terms with Yè (曄).
When Yè (曄) was defeated,
Zhì (質) was made Governor of Yìxīng (Yìxīng Tàishǒu).
The proper authorities memorialized to strip Péngchéng Wáng Yìkāng (彭城王義康) of his noble title,
and hand him over to the Court of Judicial Review (Tíngwèi) for punishment.
On the day of *Dīngyǒu* (丁酉),
an imperial edict (zhào) ordered Yìkāng (義康) and all his children, male and female, to be reduced to commoners,
removed from the imperial clan registry,
and exiled to Ānchéng (Ānchéng Jùn);
Shěn Shào (沈卲), General Who Pacifies the North (Níngshuò Jiāngjūn), was appointed Minister of Ānchéng (Ānchéng Xiàng),
leading troops to guard him.
Shào (卲)
was Pú's (璞) elder brother.
While in Ānchéng (Ānchéng), Yìkāng (義康)
read about the affairs of Liè Wáng Liú Cháng (淮南厲王長) of Huáinán (Huáinán),
and put down his book, sighing:
"Such things have existed since ancient times,
but I did not know,
so it is fitting that I am punished."
On the day of *Gēngxū* (庚戌),
Zhào Bófú (趙伯符), former Inspector of Yùzhōu (Yùzhōu Cìshǐ), was appointed General of the Imperial Guard (Hùjūn Jiāngjūn).
Bófú (伯符)
was the nephew of Empress Xiàomù (Xiàomù Huánghòu).
Emperor Gāozǔ's (Gāozǔ) grandmother, Lady Zhào (Zhào Shì), was posthumously honored as Empress Xiàomù (Xiàomù Huánghòu);
the Empress's (Hòu) younger brother was Lúnzhī (倫之).
Originally, in the regions east of the river (Jiāngzuǒ), there was no music for the two suburban sacrifices,
and although there were "ascending songs" (dēnggē) in the ancestral temple,
there were no "two dances" (èrwǔ) either.
That year,
the southern suburban sacrifice (Nánjiāo) first featured "ascending songs" (dēnggē).
The *Lǐjì Jiāo Tèshēng* (禮記郊特牲) says: 'When the sacrificial wine is offered, the musicians ascend and sing to express virtue.'
The singers are above,
the gourds and bamboo instruments below,
valuing the human voice.
The "two dances" (èrwǔ)
are the civil dance (wénwǔ) and the military dance (wǔwǔ).
The offices of General Who Pacifies the South (Ānnán) and General Who Pacifies the South (Píngnán) of Wèi (Wèi) sent a dispatch to Yǎnzhōu (Yǎnzhōu),
referring to the two general's offices, Ānnán (安南) and Píngnán (平南).
They also wanted to hunt in Jùqū (具區).
The *Zhōuguān Zhífāngshì* (周官職方氏) says: 'The marsh in Yángzhōu (Yángzhōu) is called Jùqū (具區).'
Shī Gǔ (師古) said: 'Jùqū (具區) is in Wú (Wú).'
"If states are established based on territory,
then how could they establish Xú (Xú) and Yáng (Yáng) there
without their own land?
We also know that you wish to hunt in Jùqū (具區)
and observe the customs of the southern country.
If you open guest houses and decorate residences,
then the relevant officials will be present;
when Hū Hán (呼韓) entered Hàn (Hàn),
that ceremony has not faded,
and the provisions and gifts were always abundant."
*Kuì* (饋)
means to offer food.
*Kuìxì* (饋餼)
means to offer guests raw food, hay, and grain.
The *Shīzhuàn* (詩傳) says: 'Sacrificial meat is called *xì* (餼).'
pronounced as *xǔjì fān*.
Spring,
first month,
on the day of *Gēngshēn* (庚申),
Mèng Yǐ (孟顗), Minister of the Left (Shàngshū Zuǒpúshè), was dismissed.
2 On the day Wùchén,
the Wèi ruler's army reached Dōngyōngzhōu,
and approached Xuē Yǒngzōng's stronghold.
Cuī Hào said:
"Yǒngzōng does not yet know Your Majesty has come personally,
so the morale of his forces is lax.
Now the north wind is swift and strong,
we should attack them urgently."
The Wèi ruler followed his advice.
On the day Gēngwǔ,
they surrounded his stronghold.
Yǒngzōng came out to fight,
was greatly defeated,
and he and his family all drowned themselves in the Fénshuǐ River.
According to the 'Biography of Xuē Āndū' in the Nánshǐ,
the various Xuē families resided in Hédōng Fényīn,
and were a powerful clan for generations.
They abandoned the city and came to surrender.
On the day Xīnwèi,
the Wèi ruler went south to Fényīn,
crossed the Hé River,
and reached the Luòshuǐ bridge.
This is the Luòshuǐ River in Huáyīn.
It is what the Shǐjì refers to in the first year of Qín Xiàogōng as
"Wèi built a long wall from Zhèng along the Luò."
The Emperor considered that there was no grain or fodder north of the Wèi River,
and wished to cross to the south of the Wèi River,
and proceed west along the Wèi River;
he asked Cuī Hào about this,
who replied:
"Indeed, when striking a snake, one must first strike its head;
if the head is broken, the tail cannot wag.
Now Gài Wú's camp is sixty *lǐ* from here.
With light cavalry heading there,
we can arrive in one day.
Once there, breaking it is certain.
After defeating Wú,
marching south to Cháng'ān will also take no more than one day.
The fatigue of one day
will not cause significant harm.
If we take the southern route,
Wú will slowly enter the northern mountains,
and cannot be subdued quickly."
The Emperor did not follow his advice,
and went from south of the Wèi River towards Cháng'ān.
On the day Gēngchén,
he arrived at Xìshuǐ.
When Wú's forces heard of this,
they all dispersed into the mountains of Běidì.
The character 'dì'
is superfluous.
The Emperor regretted this.
In the second month,
on the day Bǐngxū,
the Emperor arrived in Cháng'ān.
On the day Bǐngshēn,
he went to Zhōuzhì,
passed through Chéncāng,
returned,
and went to Yōngchéng,
executing all commoners and non-Han people who had colluded with Gài Wú in the places he passed through.
Yǐbá and other armies greatly defeated Gài Wú at Xìngchéng.
Wú again sent an envoy to submit a memorial requesting aid.
An edict appointed Wú as Dūdū Guān-Lǒng Zhūjūnshì, Yōngzhōu Cìshǐ, and Běidì Gōng,
and ordered the two prefectures of Yōng and Liáng to dispatch troops to garrison their borders,
to provide vocal support for Wú;
an envoy was sent to bestow Wú with one hundred twenty-one seals,
to allow Wú to grant them as appropriate.
3 Initially,
Línlìp King Fàn Yángmài,
although he sent
envoys to pay tribute,
continued his piracy,
and his
tribute was also meager and crude.
The Emperor dispatched the Jiāozhōu Cìshǐ Tán Hézhī to suppress him.
Zōng Què of Nányáng,
came from a family of scholars and plain living.
Què's uncle Shàowén,
was of noble character and did not serve in office;
all his sons and nephews,
all loved classical texts.
He often said,
"I wish to ride the long wind and break through ten thousand *lǐ* of waves."
When Hézhī was campaigning against Línlìp,
Què bravely volunteered to join the army.
An edict appointed Què as Zhènwǔ Jiāngjūn,
and Hézhī sent Què as the vanguard.
Yángmài, hearing that the army had set out,
sent an envoy to request the return of the Rìnán people he had plundered,
and offered to pay ten thousand *jīn* of gold
and one hundred thousand *jīn* of silver.
The Emperor decreed to Hézhī:
"If Yángmài truly shows sincerity,
you may permit him to submit."
Hézhī reached Zhūwú Shù.
Zhūwú County,
since the Hàn dynasty, belonged to Rìnán Commandery;
at that time, a garrison was established in its territory.
Sòng Bái said: "Hàn Rìnán Commandery was governed from Zhūwú,
and going another four hundred *lǐ* south reached the state of Línlìp."
"Fǔ" refers to the Jiāozhōu Cìshǐ's residence.
Hézhī then advanced his army and besieged Línlìp general Fàn Fúlóng at Qūsùchéng.
The Shuǐjīngzhù states: "The Lúróngshuǐ River originates from the high mountain south of Qūsùchéng in Lúróng County, Rìnán,
flows east past the north of Qūsùchéng.
Línlìp's weapons and military equipment were all inside the city."
The character 'jiàng'
is pronounced as 'liàng'.
Zōng Què secretly led his troops to intercept Píshādá,
and defeated him.
4 The Wèi ruler and Cuī Hào both trusted and respected Kòu Qiānzhī,
and upheld his teachings.
Hào had always disliked Buddhism,
and frequently spoke to the Wèi ruler,
believing that Buddhism was false and extravagant,
and a harmful waste for the world,
and that it should all be abolished.
When the Wèi ruler attacked Gài Wú,
and reached Cháng'ān,
he entered a Buddhist temple.
The Buddhist monks offered wine to his accompanying officials;
the accompanying officials entered their rooms,
and found a large quantity of weapons.
They reported this to the Emperor,
who angrily said:
"These are not for monks' use.
They must be colluding with Gài Wú,
intending to cause rebellion!"
He ordered the relevant officials to investigate and execute all the monks in the temple,
and examine their property.
They found a large amount of brewing equipment,
and tens of thousands of items deposited by regional governors, prefects, and wealthy individuals,
and also cave dwellings used to hide women.
Hào then persuaded the Emperor to execute all the monks in the world,
and destroy all scriptures and images.
The Emperor agreed.
Kòu Qiānzhī and Hào strongly debated,
but Hào did not yield.
First, all monks in Cháng'ān were executed,
and scriptures and images were burned and destroyed.
An imperial edict was also sent to Liútái and to all four directions,
ordering them to universally adopt the Cháng'ān method.
When the Wèi King was on campaign,
the Crown Prince remained in charge,
hence Píngchéng was called Liútái.
'Xià'
is pronounced as 'xiá-jià'.
"In ancient times, the degenerate rulers of the Later Hàn dynasty,
believed in and were deluded by falsehoods, disrupting the natural order.
Buddhist teachings entered China from the time of Emperor Míng of Hàn.
King Yīng of Chǔ was the first to favor it,
and it was not until Emperor Huán that people began to serve the Buddha.
This has never happened before.
Its extravagant and grand claims,
do not conform to human nature,
and in later generations,
none were not deluded by it."
"Mù wú cháng zhǔ" means one cannot distinguish between black and white,
hence 'xuàn' (dizzy/deluded).
"Ritual and righteousness have been greatly destroyed,
and within the nine regions,
everything has been reduced to ruins."
"Jū" means exhausted.
"To eliminate falsehood and establish truth,
to restore the governance of Xī and Nóng,
all of it must be completely swept away,

The Emperor was concerned about the Wèi raids

Hé Chéngtiān, the Imperial Censor-in-chief, submitted a memorial,

"Generally, the strategies to guard against the Xiongnú
are no more than two types: warriors devote themselves to plans of conquest,
while scholars advocate treaties of peace and alliance.
If we now wish to emulate Wèi Qīng and Huò Qùbì,
unless we extensively farm the Huái and Sì river basins,
internally strengthen Qīng and Xú,
so that the people have surplus savings
and the fields have stored grain,

to sweep them away in one fell swoop,
then it is not worth doing.
If we merely wish to send armies to pursue and attack,
to avenge their incursions,
then they will surely flee on light cavalry,
unwilling to engage in battle;
we would incur huge expenses in vain,
without harming them,

would then become endless.
This is the lowest of strategies.
Securing the border and holding firm

I humbly observe that the hegemonies of Cáo and Sūn,

Cáo and Sūn refer to Cáo Cāo and Sūn Quán.

In summary,
there are four such strategies: First, move the distant closer.
Currently, the former inhabitants of Qīng and Yǎn, and the newly surrendered people of Jìzhōu,
who are at the border, number over thirty thousand households.

Second, build more cities and towns to house the newly resettled families,
provide them with capital for expenses,

one city of a thousand households

Third, assemble carts and oxen to transport provisions and weapons.
Zuǎn means to compile and gather.

Suppose the city cannot be held,

In case of an urgent levy,

Fourth, assess weapons per adult male.
Every two thousand warriors,
according to their aptitude and ability,

They should engrave their names on them.
Upon returning, they should deposit them in the arsenal;

Within a few years,
military provisions will be largely prepared.

those located within the state's domain.

Their grievances are also deep.
In my estimation,
it is not as easy as simply using those local people.
If we now guide and lead the people based on what benefits them,
our army will be strong without the enemy being forewarned.
The state will be rich and the people not toiled,
compared to restoring the original military units
who merely consume grain from the granaries,
these cannot be compared in the same year. "

do you wish me to wield it against your own person?"
The Wèi 魏 ruler was greatly enraged,
and made an iron bed,
placing iron spikes upon it,
saying:
"If I break the city and capture Zhì 質,
he shall be seated upon this."
Zhì 質 again wrote to the Wèi 魏 troops, saying:
"Tell all the officers and common people among the barbarians: the letter Fólí 佛貍 sent,
treats you thus."
Using the Wèi 魏 ruler's letter which said that if his soldiers died in battle, it would only reduce the bandits in the country,
he then used it to alienate them;
there is no stratagem closer to this.
When the Wèi 魏 ruler received this letter from Zhì 質,
how could he not regret the previous letter he sent to Zhì 質?
"Why bring about your own destruction?
How can you not know how to turn misfortune into good fortune!"
The people of the Central Plains originally followed the orthodox calendar of Hàn 漢 and Jìn 晉,
hence they were called "people of the orthodox calendar".
"Behead Fólí 佛貍,
be enfeoffed as a marquis of ten thousand households,
and be granted ten thousand bolts each of plain cloth and silk."
This refers to the reward scale established by the Sòng 2 臺 court.
Fó 佛,
is pronounced like Bì 弼.
The Wèi people used hook-chariots to hook the city towers.
Inside the city, ropes were tied to the towers,
and hundreds of people shouted and pulled them,
preventing the chariots from retreating.
When night fell,
soldiers were lowered in buckets to emerge,
cut off the hooks,
and captured them.
The next morning,
they again attacked the city with battering rams.
The city's earth walls were solid and dense,
and each time they reached
the wall, they would break.
This means the battering rams struck the body of the city wall.
The Wèi people then engaged in hand-to-hand combat to scale the city walls,
taking turns to relieve each other.
They fell and then ascended again,
with none retreating.
Tens of thousands were killed or wounded,
and the corpses piled up to be level with the city walls.
They attacked for three *xún* (thirty days) in total,
but did not capture it.
It so happened that there was a widespread epidemic in the Wèi army.
Someone reported that Jiànkāng had dispatched a naval force to enter the Huái River from the sea.
The naval force descended the Jiāng River from Jiànkāng,
exited the Jiāng River to the sea,
then turned at Jiǎojiǎo to enter the Huái River.
In the second month,
on the *bǐngchén* day, which was the first day of the month,
the Wèi ruler burned his siege equipment and retreated.
The people of Xūyí wanted to pursue them,
but Shěn Pú said: "Our troops are not numerous now.
Although we can defend the city,
we cannot sally forth to battle.
Instead, we should arrange our boats and ships,
making it appear as if we intend to cross north."
This means to make it appear as if they intended to cross the Huái River from Xūyí to the north to pursue and intercept their rear.
"The plan does not need to be actually carried out."
Zāng Zhì, as Pú was the city's commander,
ordered him to submit an open memorial.
An open memorial meant
writing about the victory,
and submitting it openly
so that everyone in the world would know about it.
*Shàng*,
read *shí zhǎng* *fān*.
He attributed the credit to Zhì.
Upon hearing this,
the emperor commended him even more.
Having already praised Pú for his merit,
he now commended him even more for his humility.
When the Wèi army passed Péngchéng,
Jiāngxià Wáng Yìgōng was terrified and dared not attack.
Someone reported:
"The barbarians are driving over ten thousand southern captives,
and tonight they will encamp at Ānwáng Pí,
several tens of *lǐ* from the city.
If we pursue them now,
we can capture them all."
All the generals requested to go,
but Yìgōng forbade it.
The next day,
an imperial envoy arrived,
conveying the emperor's order for Yìgōng to pursue immediately with all his might.
The Wèi army was already far away,
so Yìgōng then dispatched the Zhenjūn Sīmǎ, Tán Hézhī, towards Xiāochéng.
The Wèi people had already heard of this,
and they killed all the captives they were driving before leaving.
Chéng Tiānzuò escaped and returned.
Tiānzuò was captured by Wèi; see volume 26 above.
The Wèi people utterly destroyed the six provinces of Nányǎn, Xú, Yǎn, Yù, Qīng, and Jì.
They destroyed the population of the six provinces,
but the cities in these six provinces were never lost in defense.
Able-bodied men were immediately decapitated or mutilated,
and infants were impaled on spears,
danced with as entertainment.
In every commandery and county they passed through,
the land was left barren, with nothing remaining.
When spring swallows returned,
they nested in trees.
Houses and homes were burned and destroyed,
so the swallows had nowhere to return,
hence they nested in trees.
Everyone in the country condemned this.
Whenever the emperor ordered a general to lead an army,
he would always give them detailed regulations.
Even the time for engagement
had to await an imperial edict.
Consequently, the generals hesitated,
none daring to make their own decisions.
Furthermore, the commoners of the Jiāngnán region
easily advanced and retreated lightly.
This was the reason for their defeat.
From this point, villages became desolate,
and the administration of Yuánjiā declined.
Historians mention the disaster of frequent military campaigns.
On *guǐyǒu*,
an edict was issued to provide relief to the people of commanderies and counties affected by the invasion,
and their taxes and levies were remitted.
On *jiǎxū*,
Grand Commandant Yìgōng was demoted to General of Agile Cavalry and concurrently *Kāifǔ Yítóng Sānsī*.
On *wùyín*,
the Wèi ruler crossed the Hé River.
From the *bǐngchén* day when the army retreated from Xūyí,
it took twenty-three days to cross the Hé River.
On *xīnsì*,
Zhenjūn Jiāngjūn Wǔlíng Wáng Jùn was demoted to North Zhonglangjiang.
On *rénwǔ*,
the emperor went to Guāpù.
On this day,
martial law was lifted.
Previously,
Wèi Central Secretariat student Lú Dùshì,
son of Xuán,
in the fourth year of Wèi Shénjiā,
Lú Xuán was summoned.
He hid at the house of Zhèng Pí of Gāoyáng.
The matter of Cuī Hào is found in volume 27 above.
Gāoyáng County,
belonged to Zhuó Commandery in the Former Hàn dynasty,
to Héjiān Kingdom in the Later Hàn,
and was later divided to Gāoyáng Commandery in the Jìn dynasty.
He was captured and interrogated.
Pí warned his son, saying:
"A gentleman sacrifices his life to achieve *rén*."
This is recorded as Confucius's words in the Analects.
His son obeyed his father's command;
the officials burned his body with fire,
but he ultimately did not speak and died.
When the Wèi ruler reached the Jiāng River,
the emperor sent Diànshàng Jiāngjūn Huáng Yánnián as an envoy to Wèi.
Since the Jìn dynasty, there had been Diànzhōng Jiāngjūn;
Diànshàng Jiāngjūn was likely established by Sòng.
*Shǐ*,
read *shū lì* *fān*.
"Lú Dùshì is a fugitive;
he should have arrived there by now."
Yánnián said:
"We have not heard of Dùshì in the capital."
The Wèi ruler then pardoned Dùshì and his clansmen who had fled and whose properties had been confiscated.
This means all of Dùshì's clansmen who had fled and whose families had been confiscated were pardoned.
The Wèi ruler appointed him Zhongshu Shilang.
*Kǎoyì* states: In the biography of Liǔ Yuánjǐng in Sòng,
"Yuánjǐng's cousin Guāngshì,
who had previously remained in his hometown,
was appointed by the *suǒlǔ* as Zhéchōng Jiāngjūn and Héběi Tàishǒu,
and enfeoffed as the Baron of Xīlíng.
Guāngshì's brother-in-law was Sītú Cuī Hào,
a minister of the barbarians.
In the 27th year of Yuánjiā,
the barbarian ruler Tuòbá Tàodì invaded Rǔ and Yǐng to the south.
Hào secretly harbored alternative plans.
Guāngshì united righteous men from Héběi to conspire with Hào,
but the plot was exposed and they were executed.
Many prominent families in Hédōng were implicated in the conspiracy and annihilated.
Guāngshì fled south and escaped,
and Tàizǔ appointed him Zhènwǔ Jiāngjūn."
This differs from the Wèi account.
We now follow the Wèi records.
In the third month,
on *yǐyǒu*,
the emperor returned to the palace.
On *jǐhài*,
the Wèi ruler returned to Píngchéng.
The Wèi ruler crossed the Hé River on *wùyín*,
and traveled twenty-two days to reach Píngchéng.
The *Zuǒzhuàn* states: "Whenever the duke goes forth, he reports to the temple;
when he returns, he holds a banquet,
and bestows cups to commend meritorious service;
this is the ritual."
It also says: "After three years, an army is mobilized.
Upon entering, they hold a grand review;
upon returning, they hold a banquet,
to count military resources."
Dù Yù's commentary says: "They drink at the temple
to count chariots, men, weapons, and what was captured."
*Jìnjī*
refers to the thousand-*lǐ* radius around Píngchéng.
*Jiàng*,
read *hù jiāng* *fān*.
Initially,
the Lord of Wèi passed Píngchéng,
and sent someone to tell the people in the city:
"When your food is exhausted, you may leave.
We will return when the wheat ripens."
When the time came,
Jiāngxià Wáng Yìgōng discussed whether to cut down the wheat and trim the sprouts,
and move the common people into fortified settlements.
Zhèn Jūn Lùshì Cānjūn Wáng Xiàosūn said:
"Bái Shì Liù Tiē says: The Zhōuzhǔbù and Jùndūyóu
are both now Lùshì Cānjūn.
I note that when Jìn Lángyé Wáng Ruì was Dūdū Yángzhōu,
he appointed Chén Yún as Lùshì Cānjūn.
At that time, there were still Zhōuzhǔbù and Dūyóu officials,
which was in line with ancient practices;
while the duty of the Lùshì
was to rectify errors
and supervise seals.
The barbarians will not be able to return,
so we are already safe;
if they do return,
this plan cannot be implemented either.
The common people are confined within the inner city,
suffering from hunger for a long time.
In the spring month,
they rely on foraging in the wilderness for sustenance;
once they enter the fortified settlements,
death by starvation will quickly follow.
If the people know they will surely die,
how can they be controlled?
If the barbarians are sure to come,
cutting the wheat will not be too late."
Everyone present fell silent,
no one daring to contradict him.
Chángshǐ Zhāng Chàng said:
"Xiàosūn's proposal
indeed has merit."
Xún means
to investigate principles,
or to employ.
Zuǒzhuàn says: "He will employ the army."
It also says,
"Daily employ weapons."
Dù Yù's commentary all states: Xún,
means to employ.
He continued:
"Secretary Wáng's proposal cannot be overturned."
Biéjià Wáng Zǐxià said:
"This argument is truly so."
Chàng clasped his tablet and addressed Jùn:
Bǎn is
a hand-tablet.
Officials clasping their tablets to report to the Prefect
showed reverence.
"Your subordinate wishes to order Xiàosūn to impeach Zǐxià."
The Lùshì Cānjūn was responsible for impeachment,
hence this statement.
Dàn is
pronounced tu-dan.
"What fault does Biéjià Wáng have?"
Chàng said:
"Cutting the wheat and relocating the people
can be called a major proposal,
and the safety of an entire region
depends on this matter.
Zǐxià is personally the head of the province;
the Zhōubiéjià ranks to the right of the other officials,
hence referred to as the head of the province.
Yet upon hearing Yuánsì's words,
he replied with laughter and agreement.
To curry favor with those around you,
how can you serve your lord?!"
Zǐxià and Yuánsì were both greatly ashamed,
and Yìgōng's proposal was consequently dropped.
3 Initially,
Lǔ Zōngzhī fled to Wèi.
In the 11th year of Yìxī of Emperor Ān of Jìn,
Lǔ Zōngzhī fled from Xiāngyáng to Qín,
and in the 13th year,
Qín fell and he fled to Wèi.
He was garrisoned at Chángshè,
always wishing to return south;
because he had previously killed Liú Kāngzǔ and Xú Zhànzhī's father.
Liú Kāngzǔ's father was Qiánzhī,
Xú Zhànzhī's father was Dázhī,
both killed by Lǔ Guǐ in the 11th year of Yìxī.
After Guǐ died,
his son Shuǎng inherited his father's official title and peerage.
Shuǎng was young but had military talent,
and he and his younger brother Xiù were both favored by the Lord of Wèi.
Later, both brothers committed offenses,
and the Lord of Wèi interrogated and rebuked them.
Shuǎng was coarse and committed many errors when under the influence of alcohol,
and Xiù, after inspecting the case of the Yè people's rebellion,
returned late due to illness,
and both were interrogated and rebuked by the Lord of Wèi.
Qí is
pronounced qù-jí.
Returning with the Lord of Wèi from Guāpù,
they reached Húlù,
and Shuǎng requested:
"Your servant has an enemy in the south,
and whenever an army comes,
I always fear disaster will befall our ancestral tombs."
Shuǎng's grandfather and father were both buried in Chángshè.
The Lord of Wèi granted his request.
When Shuǎng arrived at Chángshè,
he killed several hundred Wèi garrison soldiers,
and led his troops and over a thousand willing followers to flee to Rǔnán.
From Chángshè to Rǔnán is less than three hundred *lǐ*.
Shuài,
read as shuài.
Shuǎng sent Xiù to Shòuyáng,
bearing a letter to Nánpíng Wáng Shuò to request surrender.
When the Emperor heard of it,
he was greatly pleased,
and appointed Shuǎng as Sīzhōu Cìshǐ,
garrisoned at Yìyáng.
Shěn Yuē said: The Sīzhōu Cìshǐ
was the Hán Sīlì Xiàowèi.
Since the Jìn era south of the river,
it had fallen into barbarian hands.
Although during Yǒnghé and Tàiyuán,
royal rule briefly reached it,
by Tàihé and Lóng'ān,
it was again submerged.
Emperor Wǔ pacified Guān and Luò in the north,
and Hénán was settled.
A Sīzhōu Cìshǐ was appointed,
governing Hǔláo,
and administering the three actual commanderies of Hénán, Xíngyáng, and Hóngnóng.
In the early Jǐngpíng era of Emperor Shào,
Sīzhōu was again lost.
In late Yuánjiā,
a provisional one was established,
governing Rǔnán.
Thereafter, it governed Yìyáng,
administering Yìyáng, Suíyáng, Ānlù, and Nánrǔnán commanderies.
Kǎoyì says: Sònglüè states
"Xíngyáng Tàishǒu",
now following Sòngshū.
I believe the Emperor likely appointed Xiù as Yǐngchuān Tàishǒu
because the Xiù brothers surrendered from Yǐngchuān.
The rewards and gifts were very generous.
The Wèi people destroyed their ancestral tombs.
Xú Zhànzhī believed this was a long-term strategic calculation
and a special act of encouragement and acceptance,
so he dared not rashly express private resentment,
and begged to live in seclusion in the countryside;
this was not permitted.
4 A Qīngzhōu commoner, Sīmǎ Shùnzé, claiming to be a close relative of the Jìn imperial house,
gathered a crowd and proclaimed himself King of Qí.
The Liángzōu Garrison Commander Cuī Xūnzhī went to the provincial capital.
In the fifth month,
on the *yǐyǒu* day,
Shùnzé took advantage of the emptiness to attack Liángzōu City.
Liángzōu County belonged to Jìnán Commandery in the Hán dynasty;
it was abolished by Jìn;
Sòng established the Liángzōu Garrison,
as the seat of the Píngyuán Tàishǒu.
Shuǐjīngzhù: The Jì River flowed east past Guǎn County, then north past Liángzōu County,
and then northeast past Línjì County.
Examining and comparing,
its location was likely within the boundaries of Táng Qízhōu Línjì County.
He also gathered a crowd and proclaimed himself King of Āndìng to respond to him.
5 On the *rěnyín* day,
Wèi issued a great amnesty.
6 On the *jǐsì* day,
Jiāngxià Wáng Yìgōng was appointed Sīzhōu Cìshǐ of Nányǎnzhōu,
transferred his garrison to Xūyí,
and his supervision of military affairs for twelve more provinces was increased.
7 On the *wùshēn* day,
Shàngshū Zuǒpúshè Hé Shàngzhī was appointed Shàngshū Lìng,
and Tàizǐ Zhànshì Xú Zhànzhī was appointed Púshè and Hùjūn Jiāngjūn.
Jìnzhì states: From Wèi and Jìn until south of the river,
when two Púshè were appointed, they were divided into Left and Right;
or sometimes only one was appointed,
simply called Shàngshū Púshè;
if the Lìng position was vacant,
the Left Púshè became the head of the department;
if both Left and Right were vacant,
then a Shàngshū Púshè was appointed to take charge of the Left's duties.
Now, Zhànzhī was likely holding the position of Shàngshū Púshè concurrently with Hùjūn Jiāngjūn.
Zhànzhī was
the Emperor's nephew,
son of Princess Kuàijī.
The Emperor deferred to him in all matters.
An imperial edict ordered Zhànzhī and Shàngzhī to jointly receive petitions and complaints.
Although Shàngzhī was Lìng,
all court affairs fell to Zhànzhī.
8 In the sixth month,
on the *rénxū* day,
Wèi changed its era name to Zhèngpíng.
9 The Lord of Wèi ordered Tàizǐ Shàofù Yóu Yǎ and Zhōngshū Shìláng Hú Fānghuí and others to revise the laws and regulations,
adding and deleting many provisions,
totaling three hundred and ninety-one articles.
In the 10th year [of the Yuánjiā era of Emperor Wén of Sòng],
Wèi太子Tàizǐ Huǎng, overseeing the state,
largely trusted his左右zuǒyòu (attendants)
and also managed farms and orchards,
collecting their profits.
Gāo Yǔn admonished him, saying:
"Heaven and Earth are impartial,
hence they can cover and support;
a king is impartial,
hence he can tolerate and nourish.
Now, Your Highness is the heir apparent of the state,
a model for all regions;
yet you establish private fields,
raise chickens and dogs,
and even engage in peddling and market trading,
competing with the people for profit.
'Chán' (廛) refers to an empty space in the market;
another explanation states it is
a dwelling.
The Shuōwén (說文) says: 'Chán' (廛) is one and a half mù (畝),
the dwelling of a family.
Kǒng Yǐngdá (孔穎達) says: 'If market chán (市廛) are not taxed,
chán (廛) refers to official residences
where merchants stop to store their goods;
only the dwelling place is taxed,
not the goods sold in the market.'
An empty space within the city is called chán (廛);
an empty space within the city walls is called sì (肆).
According to the Zàishī (載師): 'To assign land within the state based on chánlǐ (廛里).'
Zhèng Xuán's (鄭玄) commentary says: 'Chánlǐ (廛里) refers to settlements and villages;
chán (廛) is the area where people reside.'
Sīnóng (司農) says: 'Chán (廛) is an empty space in the market not yet occupied by a sì (肆),
or an empty space within the city not yet occupied by a dwelling.'
Suí Rén (遂人) allocates land to the people,
where one chán (廛) is one hundred mù (畝) of land.
The Shī (詩) says: 'Why take three hundred chán (廛) of grain?'
The commentary says: 'The dwelling of one common man is called chán (廛).'
This refers to a common man's hundred mù (畝) of land.
Yáng Zǐ (揚子) says: 'To have one chán (廛) of land'
refers to a dwelling of one hundred mù (畝),
which is consistent with the Shī (詩) commentary.
The meaning of chán (廛) as land
and chán (廛) as market space
are different;
each has its proper application.
This cannot be hidden or covered up.
Indeed, the world
is Your Highness's world;
you are rich in all four seas.
What could you seek and not find,
that you would compete with peddlers and hawkers for such tiny profits?
In the past, when Guó (虢) was about to perish,
the gods bestowed upon it land and fields.
(The note refers to an earlier entry.)
(The event is found in volume 57, Guānghé (光和) first year.)
(Cáng, sound cú làng.)
Such a past lesson is truly
to be feared.
King Wǔ (武王) loved Zhōu Gōng (周公), Shào Gōng (召公), Qí (齊), and Bì (畢),
and thereby became king of all under Heaven.
(The Shǐjì (史記) 'Zhōu Jì' (周紀) states: 'King Wǔ (武王) ascended the throne,
Tàigōng Wàng (太公望) was his master,
Zhōu Gōng Dàn (周公旦) was his assistant,
Shào Gōng (召公), Bì Gōng (畢公) and others attended the royal army,
and with one battle, the world was greatly pacified.')
(Wáng, sound yú kuàng.)
[Jié (桀) and Zhòu (紂)] thereby lost their states.
Fēi Lián (飛廉) was mighty,
È Lái (惡來) was swift;
father and son both served Zhòu (紂) with their talents and strength.
È Lái (惡來) was good at slandering and defaming,
which caused the feudal lords to become increasingly alienated.
(Sàng, sound xī làng.)
Recently, those attending to Your Highness
are probably not the chosen ones of the court.
I hope Your Highness will dismiss the sycophants and the wicked,
and draw close to the loyal and upright;
as for the fields and gardens you possess,
distribute them to the poor;
and for the goods you sell,
collect and distribute them in due time.
(Shōu, means to store the goods;
sàn, means to distribute them to the poor.
Another explanation says: 'To collect and distribute them in due time' means
at harvest time, if the people's labor can repay their debts, then collect it;
if goods are stagnant,
then when the people desire them, distribute them.)
Then good renown will arrive daily,
and criticism and censure can be eliminated."
[Tàizǐ Huǎng (太子晃)] did not listen.
Although the Crown Prince was meticulous in governance,
the Zhongchángshì (中常侍) Zōng Ài (宗愛)
was of a treacherous and violent nature,
often acting unlawfully.
The Crown Prince disliked him.
The Jǐshìzhōng (給事中) Qiúní Dàoshèng (仇尼道盛) and the Shìláng (侍郎) Rèn Píngchéng (任平城)
(Shìláng (侍郎) refers to Jǐshì Huángmén Shìláng (給事黃門侍郎).
Qiúní (仇尼) is a double surname,
originating from Túhé (徒河).
Rèn, sound Rén.)
were quite influential
and all disagreed with Zōng Ài (宗愛).
Zōng Ài (宗愛), fearing exposure by Dàoshèng (道盛) and others,
consequently fabricated accusations against them.
The Wèi Emperor (魏主) was enraged
and had Dàoshèng (道盛) and others executed at the Dūjiē (都街).
(Dūjiē (都街) is the metropolitan street.)
The Emperor was extremely angry.
On the day Wùchén (戊辰),
the Crown Prince died of grief.
Kǎoyì (考異) states: The Sòng Suǒlǔ Zhuàn (宋索虜傳) says:
"When Táo (燾) reached Ruǎnán Guā Bù (汝南瓜步),
Huǎng (晃) secretly sent people to seize many captives and spoils from the camps.
When Táo (燾) returned,
he heard about it and conducted a thorough search.
Huǎng (晃) was afraid and plotted to kill Táo (燾).
Táo (燾) then feigned death,
had his close attendants summon Huǎng (晃) to receive the coffin,
and seized him on the way;
upon reaching the capital,
he was caged in an iron cage,
and soon after killed."
Xiāo Zǐxiǎn's (蕭子顯) Qí Shū (齊書) also says:
"Huǎng (晃) plotted to kill Fó Lí (佛貍),
and was killed."
The Sòng Lüè (宋略) says:
"After Táo (燾) invaded the south,
Huǎng (晃) indulged in licentious acts within [the palace]
and plotted to kill Táo (燾).
Táo (燾) learned of this,
returned and feigned death,
summoning Huǎng (晃) to receive the coffin.
When Huǎng (晃) arrived,
he was seized,
caged in an iron cage,
beaten three hundred times,
and dragged into a thicket of thorns to be killed."
Also, the Suǒlǔ Zhuàn (索虜傳) says:
"Huǎng's (晃) younger brother, Qín Wáng Wūyìgàn (秦王烏奕旰),
jointly managed state affairs with Huǎng (晃);
Huǎng (晃) resented him
and accused him of greed and cruelty.
Táo (燾) whipped him two hundred times
and sent him to garrison Páohǎn (枹罕)."
These are all errors from hearsay in Jiāngnán (江南).
We now follow the Hòu Wèi Shū (後魏書).
On the day Rénshēn (壬申),
[the Crown Prince] was buried at Jīnlíng (金陵),
and posthumously titled Jǐngmù (景穆).
The Emperor later realized the Crown Prince was innocent
and deeply regretted it.
This laid the groundwork for Zōng Ài (宗愛)'s assassination of the Emperor.
In the 11th year [of the Yuánjiā era of Emperor Wén of Sòng],
in autumn,
seventh month,
on the day Dīnghài (丁亥),
the Wèi Emperor (魏主) went to Yīnshān (陰山).
In the 12th year [of the Yuánjiā era of Emperor Wén of Sòng],
Xiāo Bīn (蕭斌), the inspector of Qīng (青) and Jì (冀) provinces,
dispatched Zhènwǔ Jiāngjūn (振武將軍) Liú Wǔzhī (劉武之) and others
to attack Sīmǎ Shùnzé (司馬順則) and Sīmǎ Bǎinián (司馬百年),
both of whom they beheaded.
On the day Guǐhài (癸亥),
Liángzōu (梁鄒) was pacified.
In the 13th year [of the Yuánjiā era of Emperor Wén of Sòng],
Xiāo Bīn (蕭斌) and Wáng Xuánmó (王玄謨) were both dismissed from office for their defeat.
The Emperor asked Shěn Qìngzhī (沈慶之):
"Bīn (斌) wanted to execute Xuánmó (玄謨), but you stopped him,
why?"
He replied:
"All the generals who fled
were afraid of punishment.
If they surrendered and died,
the generals would flee and scatter,
therefore I stopped him."
(Qìngzhī's (慶之) admonition against executing Xuánmó (玄謨) is found in the previous volume, last year.)
In the 14th year [of the Yuánjiā era of Emperor Wén of Sòng],
in the ninth month,
on the day Guǐsì (癸巳),
the Wèi Emperor (魏主) returned to Píngchéng (平城);
in winter, tenth month, on the day Gēngshēn (庚申),
he again went to Yīnshān (陰山).
In the 15th year [of the Yuánjiā era of Emperor Wén of Sòng],
the Emperor sent an envoy to Wèi (魏),

In the 16th year [of the Yuánjiā era of Emperor Wén of Sòng],
on the day Jǐsì (己巳),
Chángsūn Dàoshēng (長孫道生), Jìng Wáng (靖王) of Shàngdǎng (上黨) in Wèi (魏),
passed away.
17th day of the twelfth month,
on the *dīngchǒu* day,
the Wèi ruler enfeoffed Jǐngmù Tàizǐ's son, Jùn, as Prince Gāoyáng.
Soon after, it was deemed that as an imperial grandson and the legitimate heir,
he should not be made a princely vassal,
so it was stopped.
Observing this,
it is clear that Wèi Shìzǔ's intention to establish his grandson as heir was fixed.
Jùn was exceptionally intelligent and perceptive,
and the Wèi ruler loved him,
always keeping him by his side.
Prince Qín Hàn was moved to be Prince Dōngpíng;
Prince Yān Tán to be Prince Línhuái;
Prince Chǔ Jiàn to be Prince Guǎngyáng;
Prince Wú Yú to be Prince Nán'ān.
Hàn and the others were all sons of the Wèi ruler.
The relocation of kings of states to be kings of commanderies
should be investigated.
18th day, the Emperor ordered Shěn Qìngzhī to move several thousand households of refugees from Péngchéng to Guābù.
The General of the Northern Expedition's aide-de-camp, Chéng Tiānzuò, moved several thousand households of refugees from Jiangxi to Gūshú.
The refugees from Péngchéng and Jiangxi
were all those who had fled south from the Wèi invaders.
19th day, the Emperor appointed the Minister of Personnel, Wáng Sēngchuò, as Attendant-in-ordinary.
Sēngchuò

Tánshǒu had assisted in government at the beginning of Yuánjiā.
(The character "曇" [Tán]

Everyone considered him a man of national talent.
He was fond of learning,
had a profound mind,

He was married to the Emperor's daughter, Princess Dōngyáng Xiàn.
While in the Ministry of Personnel,
he was well-acquainted with people

When he became Attendant-in-ordinary,
he was twenty-nine years old,
profound and possessed of great composure and measure.
With composure, one can manage affairs;

(The character "沈" [Shěn]

The Emperor was quite concerned about future matters,

wished to entrust him with great responsibilities,

"Hé Yǔzhī"

20th day, Táng Hé came to court in Wèi,

1st day of spring,
first month,
more than five thousand households of Sòng people acquired by Wèi who were in Zhōngshān plotted rebellion,

The provincial army

He was forty-five years old.

As the imperial grandson, Jùn, was young and immature,
Zōng Ài wished to establish an elder ruler.
He summoned Prince Qín Hàn

A secret chamber

He could not be deposed.
The debate continued for a long time without resolution.
Zōng Ài, knowing this,

He falsely claimed that Empress Hèlián had ordered the summoning of Yán and others.
Empress Hèlián

They did not suspect anything

Ài had previously positioned thirty eunuchs armed with weapons in ambush within the forbidden palace.
When Yán and the others entered,
they were bound in succession

Prince Qín Hàn was killed in Yǒngxiàng, and Yú was enthroned.
A general amnesty was declared,

The Empress was honored as Empress Dowager.
Ài was appointed Grand Marshal, Grand General, Grand Tutor, Supreme Commander of all military affairs inside and outside the capital, and Head of the Imperial Secretariat,
and enfeoffed as Prince Fèngyì.
The historians describe the chaos in Wèi.
3rd day, on the *gēngwǔ* day,
the imperial son Xiūrrén was established as Prince Jiàn'ān.
4th day, third month,
on the *xīnmǎo* day,
Wèi buried Tàiwǔ Huángdì at Jīnlíng.
He was buried at Jīnlíng in Yúnzhōng.
5th day, the Emperor, upon hearing of Wèi Shìzǔ's demise,

The Emperor consulted his close officials.
The Crown Prince's Chief Secretary, Hé Yǎn, believed that

The Emperor did not heed him.
Yǎn

Summer,
fifth month,

an imperial edict stated:

It is hereby ordered that the offices of the General of Agile Cavalry and the Minister of Works
(At this time, Prince Jiāngxià Yìgōng had his title lowered to General of Agile Cavalry

Prince Nánqiáo Yìyí was stationed in Jiānglíng
and promoted to Minister of Works.
The character "驃" [piào]

The character "騎" [qí]

respond from east and west.
Those who return to righteousness and achieve merit

Thereupon, the General of the Household, Xiāo Sīhuà, was dispatched to supervise the Governor of Jìzhōu, Zhāng Yǒng, and others towards Quèqiáo.
Lǔ Shuǎng, Lǔ Xiù, and Chéng Tiānzuò led forty thousand armored soldiers from Jīngzhōu to advance through Xǔ and Luò.

The character "將" [jiāng]

Yǒng

Zhāng Yù,
courtesy name Màodù,

The Emperor, due to his dissenting opinions,

Qīngzhōu Cìshǐ Liú Xìngzǔ memorialized,

"Hénán is suffering from famine.

Detaining the large army

Now, the pseudo-commander has just died,

There is suspicion and turmoil within their country,

I foolishly believe we should drive straight to Zhōngshān

The population is still abundant,

This makes it easy to obtain resources.
This means obtaining resources from the enemy,
which makes the task easy.
Yì,
pronounced like yì, dì.
They will surely respond immediately.
If the central plains are shaken,
the area south of the Yellow River

Your servant requests to dispatch seven thousand soldiers from Qīng and Jì,
send a general to lead them,
and penetrate directly into their heartland.
If the vanguard achieves victory,
Zhāng Yǒng and the Hénán armies
should all cross the river at once,
so that both reputation and reality are achieved.
Simultaneously establish governors and prefects,
comfort and pacify those newly attached,
defend against Tàiháng to the west,
and block Jūndū to the north.
The intention is to deploy troops by relying on the mountainous terrain

Háng,
pronounced like háng.
Sài,
pronounced like sài.
Bestow appointments according to what is appropriate.
'Bestow appointments'

For those who did not hold office but could gather people to respond to the Sòng army,
they should first be granted office.
The people will feel a hundredfold gratitude.
This means their gratitude will be a hundred times greater than usual.
Peace and unity can be expected;
meaning the pacification of Hénán and Hénán-běi,
and the achievement of unification can be expected.
There will not be great damage."
He also urged: "Please hurry with the preparations,

The Emperor's intention was only to secure Hénán,

Liú Xìngzǔ's words

however, the best strategy

He received the imperial decree in secret and conveyed the strategy to the generals,
which was to be announced when the time was right.
6 Shàngshū Lìng Hé Shàngzhī, citing old age, requested to resign his

Fāngshān is northeast of Jiànkāng.
There is the Fāngshān Dài [weir],

It is called Fāngshān [Square Mountain]

Afterwards, imperial edicts urged him to return to office several times.
In the sixth month,
on the day wù shēn of the first quarter,
Hé Shàngzhī resumed his duties.
Yùshǐ Zhōngchéng Yuán Shú compiled a "True Hermits' Biography" about ancient hermits who had the conduct but not the reputation [of hermits] to mock him.
"Having the conduct but not the reputation"
refers to people like the gatekeeper, the basket-carrier, the broom-carrier, the two old men of Yěwáng, and the old man of Hànyīn.
7 In autumn,
in the seventh month,
Zhāng Yǒng and others arrived at Què’áo

The Kǎoyì says: The Sònglüè states:
"On the day rén chén of the seventh month,

Below this, it also mentions

According to the Chánglì,
the first quarter of this month was dìng chǒu.
The fourth day was gēng chén,
the sixth day was rén wǔ,

It is suspected that Yǒng arrived at Què’áo on gēng chén or rén wǔ,

8 On rén chén,
Rǔyīn Wáng Hún was transferred to be Wǔchāng Wáng,

9 Earlier,
Pān Shú gave birth to Shǐxīng Wáng Jùn.

We now follow Jùn's main biography.
Because Shú was favored by the Emperor,

Empress Yuán posthumously named her Yuán.
The Empress died in the seventeenth year.
Huì,
pronounced like huì.
Because of this, Tàizǐ Shào deeply disliked Shú and Jùn.
Jùn, fearing future calamity,
went out of his way to serve Shào,

The female shaman Yán Dàoyù from Wúxìng,
Yán Dàoyù
was a female shaman.
Her husband was a bandit,
and she was consequently confiscated to the Xīguān.
She commanded spirits and ghosts;
through Dōngyáng Gōngzhǔ's maid Wáng Yīngwǔ, she gained access to the princess's household.
Dàoyù told the princess:

One night, as the princess slept,
she saw a flowing light, like a firefly,

She opened it and saw
two blue pearls.
From then on, the princess, Shào, and Jùn were all deluded by her.
Shào and Jùn both had many faults,
and were repeatedly reprimanded by the Emperor.
They asked Dàoyù to pray,
hoping their faults would not reach the Emperor's ears.
Dàoyù said:
"I have already made representations to Heaven on your behalf,

Shào and others revered her,

They carved a jade image of the Emperor

Shào appointed Tiānyǔ as a duìzhǔ [squad leader].
After Dōngyáng Gōngzhǔ died,
Yīngwǔ was due to be married out.
Shào and Jùn feared that the matter would be leaked.
They feared that the witchcraft and curse would be revealed.
As Yīngwǔ had always been favored by Jùn,

When the Emperor heard that Tiānyǔ was leading a squad,

"Are the squad leaders and deputies you employ

Shào, frightened,

Jùn replied:
"If that person's actions do not cease,

According to this,
the plot to assassinate [the Emperor]

Shào was in the capital,
Jùn was in Jīngkǒu,

A careful examination of the letter's meaning shows
