Its origins were gradual.
This letter, however, affirmed their rebellious plot,

They often referred to the Emperor as
"that person"

"the person."
They referred to Jiāngxià Wáng Yìgōng as

Yīngwǔ had an illicit affair with Tiānyǔ.

Chén Qìngguó was afraid

He ordered the authorities to thoroughly investigate the matter.
Dàoyù fled,

Previously,
Jùn, from Yángzhōu,

(Before,

(Shào,

"When one ought to act decisively but fails to,

and defeated him.
(Dù Yù said: East of Xiángāo is Dàsuǒ Chéng.)
(Jīng Xiāngfán said: Jīng Xiàn has Dàsuǒ Tíng;
Xiǎosuǒ Tíng.
The Dà and Xiǎo Suǒ families, brothers, lived there,
hence the names Dà and Xiǎo.)
(Kuòdì Zhì says: Xíngyáng is Dàsuǒ Chéng;
Xiǎosuǒ Gùchéng is four lǐ north of Xíngyáng Xiàn.)
Hearing of the defeat and retreat at Quèqiáo,
he and Liǔ Yuánjǐng both led their troops back.
Xiāo Dàochéng, Mǎ Wāng, and others, hearing that Wèi reinforcements were approaching,
returned quickly to Qiúchí.
On Jǐchǒu,
an imperial edict relieved Xiāo Sīhuà of Xúzhōu,
and he was newly appointed Jìzhōu Cìshǐ,
garrisoned at Lìchéng.
The Emperor, seeing that his generals had repeatedly been dispatched without achieving success,
and that Zhāng Yǒng and others could not be solely blamed,
bestowed an imperial edict upon Sī Huà, saying:
"Since the barbarians have gained an advantage,
and it is now the depth of winter,
if they dare to throw their lives away,
my brothers and sons will personally take responsibility for dealing with them.
This means that none of the generals can be relied upon.
This can be shown to Zhāng Yǒng and Shēn Tǎn."
He had it shown to Yǒng and Tǎn,
intending to incite and encourage them.
"Had I known earlier that these generals were like this,
I would regret not having driven them with drawn blades.
Now, what is the use of regret!"
These were also words of indignation.
He followed this course.
13. Wèi Nán'ān Yǐnwáng Yú, having been established out of proper succession –
Yú was established by Zōng Ài as a younger son,
which was not the proper succession.
According to the Shìfǎ: "one who holds the throne but does not shine" is called "Yǐn".
– wished to win over the hearts of the people;
but within a month,
the treasury was depleted.
He also indulged in heavy drinking, music, and hunting,
neglecting state affairs.
Zōng Ài became Zǎixiàng,
overseeing the Sānshěng.
The Wèi, for example, considered the Shàngshū, Shìzhōng, and Zhōng Mìshū as the Sānshěng,
just as today the Shàngshū, Ménxià, and Zhōngshū are considered the Sānshěng.
He summoned high officials from his seat,
and his arbitrary power grew daily.
Yú was troubled by this,
and planned to seize his power.
Ài was enraged.
In winter,
the tenth month,
on the *bǐngwǔ* day which was the first day of the month,
Yú secretly performed a night sacrifice at the Dōng Miào.
The Wèishū states: In the fourth year of Míngyuán Dì Yǒngxīng,
the Tàizǔ Dàowǔ temple was erected on Báidēng Shān,
where sacrifices were offered once a year,
with grand offerings;
there was no fixed month.
Additionally, west of Báidēng Shān, at the former dwelling place of Tàizǔ,
the Zhāochéng Xiànmíng Tàizǔ temple was erected,
where the emperor personally sacrificed, usually at the turn of the ninth and tenth months,
using horses, cattle, and sheep as offerings.
Báidēng was east of Píngchéng,
hence it was called Dōng Miào.
Yú kept it secret,
having been on the throne for only just over 220 days.
The Yǔlín Láng has existed
since the Hàn dynasty.
A Hàn Yǔlín Láng held a rank equivalent to 300 *dàn* of grain,
from which one can generally infer the rank of a Lángzhōng.
The Wèi appointed Liú Ní as Yǔlín Lángzhōng,
who, together with the Diànzhōng Shàngshū, commanded the palace guard.
Thus, their positions were presumably more important than in the Hàn court.
Ài was startled and said:
"You are a great fool!
If the Imperial Grandson were to be enthroned,
could you forget the events of the Zhèngpíng era!"
The death of Jǐngmù Tàizǐ
occurred in the first year of Wèi Zhèngpíng.
The first year of Zhèngpíng was the previous year.
"If so,
whom should we enthrone now?"
Ài said:
"Wait until we return to the palace,
then we shall choose a worthy among the various princes to enthrone."
Ní feared Ài would make a move,
so he secretly reported the situation to Diànzhōng Shàngshū Yuán Hè.
Hè, who at the time was commanding the palace guard together with Ní,
then plotted with Nánbù Shàngshū Lù Lì, saying:
"Zōng Ài first enthroned Nán'ān,
then killed him.
Now he does not wish to enthrone the Imperial Grandson;
this will be detrimental to the state."
Thus, he and Lì finalized their plan
to jointly enthrone the Imperial Grandson.
Lì
was the son of Sì.
Historians say that Lù Sì and his son both possessed wisdom and strategy,
and were loyal to Hòu Wèi.
On the *wùshēn* day,
Hè and Shàngshū Zhǎngsūn Kěhóu strictly guarded the palace,
and sent Ní and Lì to welcome the Imperial Grandson from the imperial park.
The Wèi capital Píngchéng had a Deer Park.
Upon entering Píngchéng,
Hè and Kěhóu opened the gates to admit him.
Ní rushed back to the Dōng Miào,
shouting:
"Zōng Ài has murdered Nán'ān Wáng,
an act of great rebellion and impiety!
The Imperial Grandson has already ascended the great throne!
There is an imperial edict
that all palace guards return to the palace!"
The multitude all shouted "Long live!",
then seized Zōng Ài, Jiǎ Zhōu, and others,
led their troops in,
and enthroned the Imperial Grandson as emperor.
The emperor's tabooed given name was Jùn,
the legitimate grandson of Tàiwǔ Huángdì
and the eldest son of Jǐngmù Tàizǐ.
Xiāo Zǐxiǎn said: Jùn's
courtesy name was Wūléi Zhílè.
The Běishǐ states: In the second year of Wèi Tàiwǔ Dì Shǐguāng,
the Dōnggōng was renamed Wànshòu Gōng,
and the Yǒng'ān and Ānlè palaces were built.
The reign era was changed to Xīng'ān.
Kǎoyì says: The Sòng Suǒlǔ Zhuàn states:
"Táo, seeing Wūyìgàn's military prowess,
appointed him crown prince.
When Táo died,
the favored eunuch Zōng Ài enthroned Kěbózhēn as empress.
Zōng Ài and Bózhēn, fearing danger from Yìgàn,
falsely accused and killed him and enthroned themselves,
naming the reign Chéngpíng.
Bózhēn was timid
and not supported by the people.
Huàng's son Jùn, whose courtesy name was Wūléi Zhíqín,
was always beloved by Táo.
The Yàn Wáng said to the people:
'Bózhēn is not legitimate
and should not be enthroned;
Zhíqín is the legitimate grandson
and should be enthroned.' So they killed Bózhēn and Zōng Ài and enthroned Jùn as ruler,
naming the reign Zhèngpíng."
This differs from the Hòu Wèishū.
It also says it was in the twenty-eighth year.
Both are errors in the Sòngshū.
All were subjected to the Five Punishments
and their three familial exterminated.
14. The Wǔshuǐ Mán of Xīyáng revolted.
The Shuǐjīng Zhù states: The Qí Shuǐ originates from the northern mountains of Qíchūn Xiàn in Jiāngxià.
The river initially receives the Xī Shuǐ,
then its branches flow southwest,
passing through Qí Shān,
emerging from the Man territory,
hence this water group is called the Wǔshuǐ Mán.
The Five Waters
refer to the Bā Shuǐ, Qí Shuǐ, Xī Shuǐ, Chìtíng Shuǐ, and Xīguī Shuǐ.
The Mán tribes relied on the rugged mountains and rivers,
and for generations engaged in plunder and violence.
Shěn Qìngzhī of Sòng subjugated them in the regions around Xīyáng,
referring to these Wǔshuǐ Mán.
All suffered from their affliction.
The Nánshǐ says: The Mán tribes resided in deep and inaccessible areas,
their communities thriving.
To the north, they bordered the Huái and Rǔ rivers;
to the south, they extended to the Jiāng and Hàn rivers,
covering thousands of *lǐ*.
This formed the basis
for Shěn Qìngzhī to use his troops against the Mán to assist Wǔlíng Wáng Jùn in his uprising.
15. The Wèi appointed Piàojì Dàjiāngjūn Tuòbá Shòulè as Tàizǎi, Dūdū Zhōngwài Zhūjūn, and Lù Shàngshū Shì.
Shòulè
was a descendant of Tuòbá Xīlù.
He was also granted the Yítóng Sānsī rank.
This was in reward for his achievement in establishing the succession.
Shòulè and Kěhóu, due to their struggle for power,
were both granted death.
16. On the *guǐwèi* day,
Wèi Guǎngyáng Jiǎnwáng Jiàn and Línhuái Xuānwáng Tán both died.
17. On the *jiǎshēn* day,
Wèi's mother Lǘ Shì died.
According to the Běishǐ,
the Wèi ruler's mother was of the Yùjiǔlǘ Shì clan, and was the younger sister of Hédōng Wáng Pí.
18When Wèi Nán'ān Wáng Yú was enthroned,
Gǔ Bì was made Sītú,
and Zhāng Lí was made Tàiwèi.
When Gāozōng was enthroned,
Bì and Lí's discussions did not accord with the imperial will,
so they were demoted to Wàidū Dàguān.
They were found guilty of uttering resentful words,
and their family members accused them of sorcery,
so they were both executed.
Gǔ Bì and Zhāng Lí
were trusted and important officials of Wèi Shìzǔ.
When Zōng Ài committed regicide,
they could not expose his crime and punish him;
when Nán'ān was enthroned,
they immediately held high official positions.
Even if they were not guilty of sorcery,
their crime was certainly not pardonable by death.
被,
read Píyì.
19On the day Rén'yín,
Lúlíng Zhāowáng Shào passed away.
20Wèi posthumously honored Jǐngmù Tàizǐ as Jǐngmù Huángdì,
and the imperial consort mother, Lǘ Shì, as Gōng Huánghòu,
and honored the wet nurse, Cháng Shì, as Bǎotàihòu.
21Wáng Jǐngwén of the Lǒngxī Túgē rebelled against Wèi,
appointing kings and marquises.
Wèi Tǒngwàn Zhènjiāng Nányáng Wáng Huìshòu and Wàidū Dàguān Yú Luòbá commanded the forces of four prefectures to suppress and pacify him.
The four prefectures
refer to Qín, Yōng, Hé, and Liáng.
This refers to the great boundary between Zhào and Wèi during the Warring States period.
22In the twelfth month,
on the day Wùshēn,
Wèi buried Gōng Huánghòu at Jīnlíng.
23In Wèi Shìzǔ's later years,
the ban on Buddhism was gradually relaxed.
The Wèi ban on Buddhism is seen for twenty-three years in 124 juan.
When Gāozōng ascended the throne,
many officials requested its restoration.
On the day Yǐmǎo,
an edict was issued, permitting
each prefecture, commandery, and county where people resided
to build one Buddhist temple.
People who wished to become Shāmén
were allowed to leave home (舍俗為僧謂之出家, meaning 'leaving secular life to become a monk is called 'leaving home').
Forty people in small prefectures.
Thus, the Buddhist temples that had been destroyed earlier
were mostly repaired.
Fótú
is also Fútú,
or some say: Fótú
is a Buddhist temple.
Shī Xián was appointed Dàorén Tǒng.
Dàorén Tǒng
is like the Sòng's Dūsēnglù;
northerners called it Sēngzǒngshè.
The Wèi Shū says: Shāmén Shī Xián,
originally a royal family member from the country of Jìbīn,
entered the monastic life at a young age,
traveled east to Liángzhōu,
and came to Dài after Liángzhōu was pacified.
When Buddhist law was abolished,
Shī Xián pretended to be a physician and returned to secular life,
but he upheld his monastic principles without change.
On the day of restoration,
he immediately returned to being a Shāmén
and became Dàorén Tǒng.
In the early Hépíng era,
Shī Xián passed away,
and Tán Yào succeeded him,
with the title changed to Shāmén Tǒng.
24On the day Dīngsì,
Wèi appointed Lèlíng Wáng Zhōu Niǔ as Tàiwèi,
Nánbù Shàngshū Lù Lì as Sītú,
and Zhènxī Jiāngjūn Dù Yuánbǎo as Sīkōng.
Lì, by virtue of his merit in welcoming and enthroning the emperor,
received the emperor's deep trust,
and no court official surpassed him.
He was granted the title Píngyuán Wáng.
Lì declined, saying:
"Your Majesty,
as the legitimate heir of the state,
the lineal imperial grandson (故曰正統, hence called 'legitimate heir'),
offering loyalty and support
is the constant duty of a minister and a son.
I dare not appropriate the功 of Heaven"
慆,
meaning the same as 叨,
greedy.
He declined three times.
The Wèi ruler did not permit it.
Lì said:
"My father served the previous court,
and his loyalty and diligence were evident."
Lù Sī served Shìzǔ,
exercising authority in the northern garrisons,
and his achievements were notable in Guānzhōng.
桑榆 (mulberry and elm),
late years.
The Emperor said:
"As the ruler of the world,
how could I not make your father and son two kings?!"
On the day Wùwǔ,
his father, Jiànyè Gōng Sī, was advanced in rank to Dōngpíng Wáng.
Kǎoyì says: The Wèi Jì says
"Wùshēn."
However, since there is Dīngsì above
and Guǐhài below,
Wùshēn should not be in between;
perhaps
the character
"Wùwǔ"
was mistaken.
Regarding the restoration of his descendants,
Lì strongly declined to accept.
The Emperor admired him even more.
Dōng'ān Gōng Liú Ní was appointed Shàngshū Púyè,
and Xīpíng Gōng Yuán Hè was appointed Zhēngběi Jiāngjūn,
both elevated to the rank of king.
The Emperor distributed rewards to his officials,
and said to Yuán Hè:
"Take whatever you wish."
Hè declined, saying:
"The north and south are not yet submissive;
the state treasury must not be emptied."
Meaning that Wèi had Sòng in the south
and Rourán in the north,
and preparations could not be relaxed for a single day;
the state treasury was for military and national expenses,
and should not be emptied for rewards.
He then took one warhorse.
Showing his desire to exert effort on the frontiers.
When Gāozōng was enthroned,
Gāo Yǔn was involved in the planning,
and Lù Lì and others all received generous rewards,
but Yǔn did not.
Yǔn never spoke of it throughout his life.
Gāo Yǔn did not boast of his merit,
and later his position and treatment were greatly elevated.
How could Heaven be sparing in its recompense?
On the day Jiǎzǐ,
Zhōu Niǔ was implicated in a matter
and granted death.
At that time, Wèi law was severe.
Yuán Hè petitioned:
"Regarding families of rebellion,
males thirteen and under who were not involved in the conspiracy
should be exempted from death and confiscated by the government."
This was adopted.
25Jiāngxià Wáng Yìgōng returned to court.
He returned from Xūyí.
夏,
read Hùyǎ.
朝,
read Zhíyáo.
On the day Xīnwèi,
Yìgōng was appointed Dàjiāngjūn and Nánxúzhōu Cìshǐ,
intending to replace Shǐxīng Wáng Jùn.
26Initially,
when Wèi entered the Central Plains (晉孝武帝太元二十一年, Wèi attacked Yàn,
and by Āndì Lóng'ān two years,
they conquered Zhōngshān,
and first gained the Central Plains).
The Jǐngchū calendar, created by Yáng Wěi,
was implemented in the first year of Cáo Wèi Míngdì Jǐngchū.
See juan 223, year 16.
沮,
read Zǐyú.

"文" (With radicals from "fěi" and "wén").
離而合之於上下 (Separated and combined vertically).
讀如斐字 (Read as "fěi").
In this year,
it was first implemented.
Niè Chóngqí punctuated, Wáng Chóngwǔ re-collated.

compiled by imperial decree.

Tàizǔ Wénhuángdì Xiàzhīxià
Yuánjiā Thirtieth Year (Guǐsì, 453)
1 Spring,
first month,
on the day Wùyín,
Nánqiáo Wáng Yìxuān was appointed Sītú and Yángzhōu Cìshǐ.
The appointment of Yìxuān as Cìshǐ of Yángzhōu was formally decreed only now.
2 Xiāo Dàochéng (蕭道成) and others led Di (氐) and Qiāng (羌) tribesmen to attack Wǔdū (武都) of the Northern Wèi (魏).
Gǒu Mòyú (苟莫于), the garrison commander of Gāopíng (高平) for Wèi (魏), led two thousand light cavalry to rescue it.
Dàochéng (道成) and his forces withdrew to Nánzhèng (南鄭).
Nánzhèng (南鄭) was
the seat of government for the governors of Sòng (宋)'s Liáng (梁) and Nánqín (南秦) prefectures.
As the “Bīng Zhì (兵志)” says,
“knowing when it is difficult and retreating,”
Xiāo Dàochéng (蕭道成) possessed this quality.
3 On the day of Rénwǔ (壬午),
Shǐxīng Wáng Jùn (始興王濬), General Who Conquers the North, was appointed Governor of Jīngzhōu (荊州).
The Emperor’s anger had not yet subsided,
so Jùn (濬) had remained in Jīngkǒu (京口) for a long time;
only after being appointed to Jīngzhōu (荊州)
was he permitted to enter the court.
4 On the day of Wùzǐ (戊子),
an imperial edict ordered Wǔlíng Wáng Jùn (武陵王駿), Governor of Jiāngzhōu (江州), to lead all armies to attack the Xīyáng (西陽) Man (蠻) tribes,
and he encamped at Wǔzhōu (五洲).
The “Shuǐ Jīng Zhù (水經註)” states: “The Jiāng (江) river flows east past the south of the old city of Dàixiàn (軑縣) in Jiāngxià (江夏).”
The county was formerly the state of Xián (弦).
The city is on the sunny side of a mountain,
facing Wǔzhōu (五洲) to the south.
There are five islets connected in the river,
hence the name.
Its location should be between present-day Huángzhōu (黃州) and Jiāngzhōu (江州).
Mèng Kāng (孟康) says: “Dài (軑)
is pronounced tài (汰).”
Shīgǔ (師古) says: “Dài (軑)
is also pronounced as tú xì fān (徒系翻).”
5 When Yán Dàoyù (嚴道育) became a fugitive,
(The matter of Dàoyù (道育) becoming a fugitive began in the previous volume, previous year.)
Dàoyù (道育) changed her clothes to become a nun,
hiding in the Eastern Palace.
She then followed Shǐxīng Wáng Jùn (始興王濬) to Jīngkǒu (京口),
or sometimes stayed at the house of a commoner, Zhāng Ào (張旿).
When Jùn (濬) entered court,
he transported her back to the Eastern Palace again,
intending to take her with him to Jiānglíng (江陵).
On the day of Dīngsì (丁巳),
the Emperor attended the court.
Jùn (濬) entered to receive his appointment.
(He received the appointment as Governor of Jīngzhōu (荊州).)
Someone reported that Dàoyù (道育) was at Zhāng Ào’s (張旿) house.
The Emperor sent men to arrest her,
and they found her two maids,
who said Dàoyù (道育) had returned to the capital with the General Who Conquers the North.
(Jùn (濬) was the General Who Conquers the North,
hence the reference.)
And when it was heard that he was still in contact with her,
the Emperor was filled with sorrow, regret, and alarm.
He then ordered that the two maids be sent from Jīngkǒu (京口),
and after their arrival and verification,
the crimes of Shào (劭) and Jùn (濬) would be dealt with.
(It means to await the arrival of the two maids,
investigate and verify the matter,
and then punish the two sons.)
(Zhì (治) is pronounced zhí zhī fān (直之翻).)
Pān Shú (潘淑) embraced Jùn (濬) and wept, saying:
“The previous matter of your curses has been exposed,
(The matter can be found in the previous volume, previous year.)
(Zhù (祝) is pronounced the same as zhòu (呪),
zhí jiù fān (職救翻).)
Why did you hide Yán Dàoyù (嚴道育) again?
The Emperor is extremely angry.
I begged for mercy by kowtowing but could not appease him.
What good is living now?
You can send the medicine.
I will take my own life first.”
(She meant she wanted to commit suicide first.)
Jùn (濬) stood up, shaking his robes, and said:
“Matters of the world will resolve themselves in due course.
Please be patient and worry less.
I will certainly not bring harm upon you!”
6 On the day of Jǐwèi (己未),
Du Yuánbǎo (杜元寶), Prince of Jīngzhào (京兆) of Wèi (魏), was executed for plotting rebellion;
Chóng (崇), Prince of Jiànníng (建寧), and his son Lì (麗), Prince of Jǐnán (濟南), were both implicated by Yuánbǎo (元寶)
and granted death.
The historians say that the Wèi (魏) troubles had not yet ended.
(Jǐ (濟) is pronounced zǐ lǐ fān (子禮翻).)
7 The Emperor wished to depose Crown Prince Shào (劭)
and grant Shǐxīng Wáng Jùn (始興王濬) death.
He first consulted with Shìzhōng (侍中) Wáng Sēngchuò (王僧綽);
he had Sēngchuò (僧綽) research precedents of deposed crown princes and princes from the Han (漢) and Wèi (魏) dynasties.
(Diǎn (典) refers to standard records.
Gù (故) refers to old affairs.
He sent the precedents to the two men.)
Wǔlíng Wáng Jùn (武陵王駿) was always out of favor,
so he was repeatedly sent to the outer provinces
and was not allowed to stay in Jiànkāng (建康).
After Jùn (駿) returned from Péngchéng (彭城),
he was again sent out to govern Jiāngzhōu (江州).
Shuò (鑠) was the younger sister of Jiāng Zhàn (江湛);
Suí Wáng Dàn (隨王誕) was the daughter of Xú Zhànzhī (徐湛之).
Zhàn (湛) advised the Emperor to establish Shuò (鑠),
while Zhànzhī (湛之) intended to establish Dàn (誕).
The historians say that Jiāng (江) and Xú (徐) each indulged their private interests, thereby bringing chaos to the state and death upon themselves.
“The matter of establishment
depends entirely on Your Majesty’s sacred will.
Your servant believes it is only appropriate to make a swift decision,
and not to delay.
‘If one fails to decide when one should,
one will suffer the consequences of chaos.’
(This refers to the Daoist saying cited by Qi (齊) Prime Minister Shào Píng (召平) in the ‘Hàn Shū (漢書)’.)
(Duàn (斷) is pronounced dìng luàn fān (丁亂翻);
the same below.)
To endure a slight inability
(The ‘Lúnyǔ (論語)’ states: Confucius said, ‘If one is impatient in small matters, it will spoil great plans.’)
it would be best to remain open-minded as before.
(It means to treat them with an open mind,
as in the beginning of the natural father-son relationship.)
Although the secret is well-kept,
it is easily exposed and spread.
One must not let difficulties arise unexpectedly,
becoming a laughingstock for a thousand generations.”
The Emperor said:
“You can be said to be capable of making major decisions.
However, this matter is extremely important,
and one must not fail to consider it thrice with utmost care.
Moreover, Péngchéng (彭城) has just fallen,
(Péngchéng Wáng Yìkāng (彭城王義康)’s death is mentioned in the previous volume, twenty-eighth year.)
(Sān (三) is pronounced xī zàn fān (息暫翻),
also pronounced as written.)
Sēngchuò (僧綽) said:
“Your servant fears that after a thousand generations,
it will be said that Your Majesty could only punish a brother,
but not a son.”
The Emperor was silent.
Jiāng Zhàn (江湛), who was sitting with them,
left the pavilion
and said to Sēngchuò (僧cho):
“Your recent words were perhaps too harsh and direct!”
Sēngchuò (僧綽) said:

"If we take Nánzhōu with 10,000 men,
then Liángshān will be cut off.
Liǔ Yuánjǐng is garrisoned in Nánzhōu as the rear base for Liángshān.
If we take it,
the route at Liángshān will be cut off.
Then Xuánmó will certainly not dare to act.
I, your subordinate, will row in the middle of the river,
heading straight for Shítou.
This is the best strategy."
Shěn Qìngzhī, Xuē Āndū, and others were west of the river.
Liǔ Yuánjǐng, Wáng Xuánmó, and others were in a standoff with Yìxuān.
If Zhì's plan were to be carried out,
Jiànkāng would be in great peril.
*Qù*,
pronounced *qī yù fān*.
Liú Chénzhī secretly said to Yìxuān:
"Zhì seeks to be the vanguard;
his intentions are hard to fathom.
It would be better to commit all our elite forces to attack Liángshān.
Once the task is accomplished, then we can advance rapidly.
This is a strategy for absolute safety."
Yìxuān then stopped.
Zāng Zhì, along with Servant-in-Chief Hú Zifǎn and others, defended the western rampart of Mount Liángshān.
At a time when the southwest wind was strong,
Zhì sent his general Yǐn Zhōu to attack the western rampart.
Leveraging the strong southwest wind to attack the western rampart,
it was difficult for the soldiers of the eastern rampart to come to its aid against the wind.

and 翻.

Wáng Xuánmó heard of it,

Partial general Liú Jìzhī led the naval forces in a desperate battle,
requesting aid from Xuánmó,
but Xuánmó did not send any.
Grand Marshal's Military Advisor Cuī Xūnzhī vehemently argued for it,

By the time they arrived,
the city had already fallen,

Xúnzhī
was Hùzhī's younger brother.
Zifǎn and the others fled back to the eastern bank.
Zhì again sent his general Páng Fǎqǐ with several thousand soldiers to quickly march to Nánpǔ,

Guerrilla General Yuán Hùzhī led the naval forces to engage them in battle,
and defeated them.
The above accounts all concern the battles at Mount Liángshān.
Zhū Xiūzhī cut off the path at Mǎ'ānshān.
The Commentary on the Water Classic states: Tanxi River originates from the foot of Liǔzishān west of Xiāngyáng,
flowing east to form Yāhú Lake.
The lake is northeast of Mǎ'ānshān.

Lǔ Xiù attacked it,

He was repeatedly defeated by Xiūzhī,

Xiūzhī led his troops to pursue him.
Someone advised Xiūzhī to pursue vigorously,
but Xiūzhī said:
"Lǔ Xiù
is a fierce general;
a cornered beast will claw,
and should not be pressed too hard."
The Art of War states: "Know your enemy and know yourself,
and you will not be imperiled in a hundred battles."
Zhū Xiūzhī's conduct in this battle was close to this principle.

Wáng Xuánmó sent Yuán Hùzhī to urgently report to Liǔ Yuánjǐng, saying:
"The western city cannot be held;
only the eastern city with ten thousand men remains.
The bandit army outnumbers us several times,
and the disparity in strength is too great.
I wish to retreat to Gūshú,
join forces with your excellency to withstand them,
and then deliberate further on advancing."
Yuánjǐng did not permit it,
saying:
"The enemy's momentum is currently strong,
and we must not retreat first.
I will don my armor and hasten there."
Hùzhī said:
"The enemy believes Nánzhōu has thirty thousand men,
but your general's command only has one-tenth of that.
If we go to their encampment,
our true strength will be revealed.
Prince of Yù Wáng must not come;
it would be better to divide our forces to reinforce him."
Yuánjǐng said:
"Good!"
Thereupon, he left the weak to defend,
and sent all his elite troops to assist Xuánmó,
displaying many banners and flags.
From Mount Liángshān, it looked as if several tens of thousands of men had arrived,
and everyone believed that all the Jiànkāng troops had arrived,
which then calmed the morale of the multitude.
Zāng Zhì personally requested to attack the eastern city.
Adjutant-Consultant Yán Lèzhī persuaded Yìxuān, saying:
"If Zhì recaptures the eastern city,
then all the great achievements will accrue to him.
It is advisable to send your own subordinates to act."
Yìxuān then dispatched Liú Chénzhī to advance together with Zhì.
On the jiǎyín day,
Yìxuān arrived at Mount Liángshān,
encamping his troops on the western bank.
Yìxuān himself went from Quètóu to the western bank of Mount Liángshān.
Xuánmó commanded all the armies in a great battle.
Xuē Āndū led his elite cavalry to first charge their formation's southeast,
breaching it,
and beheading Chénzhī.
Liú Jìzhī and Zōng Yuè then breached their northwest,
and Zhì's and others' troops suffered a great defeat.
Yuán Hùzhī burned the boats and ships in the river,
and the smoke and flames covered the water,
extending to the western bank's camps, almost destroying them all.
All the armies seized the opportunity to attack them,
and Yìxuān's troops also collapsed.
Yìxuān fled alone in a small skiff,
closing his door and weeping.
Those from Jīngzhōu who followed him still numbered over a hundred skiffs.
Zhì wanted to meet Yìxuān to discuss matters,
but Yìxuān had already left.
Zhì did not know what to do,
and also fled,
his followers all surrendering or dispersing.
On the jǐwèi day,
the alert was lifted.

11. Zāng Zhì arrived at Xúnyáng,
burned the prefectural office buildings,
and fled west with his singing girls and concubines.
He sent his favorite, Hé Wénjìng, to lead the remaining troops in front,

The Administrator of Xīyáng, Lǔ Fāngpíng, deceived Wénjìng, saying:

no one else will be questioned.
It is better to escape."
Wénjìng abandoned his followers and fled.
Zhì had previously made his sister's husband, Yáng Chōng, the Magistrate of Wǔchāng Commandery.
The Jin Records of Daily Life states: In the first year of Tàikāng of Emperor Wǔ, Jiāngxià was renamed Wǔchāng Commandery.
Also according to the Jin Records,
Sun Quán, ruler of Wú, established Wǔchāng Commandery in Dōng'è.
This is the present-day Shòuchāng Army.
Chōng had already been killed by Hú Bìzhī, the Commandery Assistant.
Zhì had nowhere to return,
so he fled to Nánhú.
Nánhú is now eight li east of Wǔchāng County, Shòuchāng Army.
When the pursuing soldiers arrived,
he covered his head with a lotus leaf,
submerged himself in the water,
leaving his nose exposed.
On the wùchén day,
Army Commander Zhèng Jù'ér spotted him,
shot him,
hitting him in the center of his body.
Swords and spears then rained down upon him,
his intestines wrapped around the water plants.
His head was severed and sent to Jiànkāng.
His descendants were all executed in the marketplace,
and his confederates, including Rèn Huìzhī, Administrator of Lè'ān,
Liú Huáizhī, Grand Administrator of Línchuān, and Dù Zhòngrú, Administrator of Póyáng, were also punished.
Zhòngrú
was the son of Jì's elder brother.
Dù Jì
was appointed Inspector of Qīngzhōu during the Yuánjiā era.
Chancellor (丞相) Liú Yìxuān (劉義宣) fled to Jiāngxià (江夏).
He heard there were troops at Bālíng (巴陵).
The troops at Bālíng
were probably Wéi Sōng's (韋崧) soldiers.
Some say they were Liú Zūnkǎo's (劉遵考) soldiers, the Inspector (刺史) of Xiāngzhōu (湘州).
Xià (夏)
is pronounced hùyǎ.
His followers scattered and were almost all gone.
With about ten attendants, he walked on foot.
His feet hurt so much he could not go on.
He hired a civilian's open cart to carry himself,
seeking food along the way.
When he reached the outskirts of Jiānglíng (江陵) city,
he sent someone to inform Zhú Chāomín (竺超民).
Chāomín prepared ceremonial regalia and soldiers to welcome him.
At that time, Jīngzhōu (荊州) still had over ten thousand armed men.
Zhái Língbǎo (翟靈寶), one of his close attendants, cautioned Yìxuān to appease his generals and subordinates,
saying:
"Zāng Zhì (臧質) did not follow appropriate instructions,
thus leading to defeat.
Now, let us reorganize our forces and repair our armor,
and plan for the future.
In ancient times, Emperor Gāo of Hàn (漢高) suffered a hundred defeats,
yet ultimately achieved a great enterprise…"
But Yìxuān forgot Língbǎo's words,
mistakenly saying,
"Xiàng Yǔ (項羽) suffered a thousand defeats."
Everyone covered their mouths.
They covered their mouths and laughed.
Yìxuān was despondent and disheartened,
losing all his presence of mind.
He went inside and did not come out again.
His close confidants gradually deserted him.
Lǔ Xiù (魯秀) fled north.
The *Kǎoyì* (考異) states: The *Sònglüè* (宋略) says:
"Xiù retreated after his defeat at Xiāngyáng (襄陽),
and when he was about to reach Jiānglíng,
he heard of the defeat and fled north."
We follow the *Sòngshū* (宋書) here.
(Yìxuān) wanted to follow Xiù and leave,
so he took his son Tāo (慆),
(息 is) a son.
and dressed him in men's clothing to follow along.
The city was in chaos,
with drawn swords clashing everywhere.
Yìxuān was afraid,
fell from his horse,
and continued on foot.
Zhú Chāomín saw him off outside the city,
gave him another horse,
and then returned to defend the city.
Yìxuān could not find Xiù.
All his attendants abandoned him.
That night,
he returned to the empty office of Nánjùn (南郡);
the Nánjùn Administrator's (太守) office
was probably outside Jiānglíng city.
Xiè (廨)
is pronounced gǔ'ài.
Chāomín arrested and sent an investigator.
Since the Hàn (漢) dynasty,
the ducal administrations had "investigating clerks" (刺姦掾).
Sitting on the ground, Yìxuān sighed and said:
"That old slave Zāng Zhì ruined me!"
His five concubines were soon sent out.
Yìxuān cried,
and said to the prison guard:
"The usual days were not bitter,

Lǔ Xiù's followers dispersed,
and he could not escape.
He returned towards Jiānglíng,

An imperial edict ordered Right Vice Director of the Department of State Affairs (右僕射) Liú Xiào
Sūn (劉孝孫) to go to Jīng (荊) and Jiāng (江) two Prefectures (州),
to distinguish the innocent from the guilty,
and to carry out executions and rewards on the spot.
It also ordered the division of the two prefectures' territories
and discussed establishing new prefectures.
Consequently, parts of Jīng, Xiāng (湘), Jiāng, and Yù (豫) territories were divided to establish Yǐngzhōu (郢州).
Initially,
when the Jìn (晉) clan moved south,
Yángzhōu (揚州) was made the capital region,
from which all grains and silks were sourced.
Jīng and Jiāng were made strategic strongholds,
where all armed forces were gathered.
Important generals were always appointed to govern them.
The households of these three prefectures
constituted half of the area south of the Yangtze River.
The emperor disliked their immense power,
and therefore wished to divide them.
On the day *Guǐwèi* (癸未),
five commanderies (郡) from eastern Zhè (浙) in Yángzhōu were separated to establish Dōngyángzhōu (東揚州),
with its seat in Kuàijī (會稽).
The five commanderies were: Kuàijī (會稽), Dōngyáng (東陽), Yǒngjiā (永嘉), Línhǎi (臨海), and Xīn'ān (新安).
Kuài (會)
is pronounced gōngwài.
Its seat was Jiāngxià.
Eight commanderies were separated: Jiāngxià, Jìnglíng (竟陵), Suí (隨), Wǔlíng (武陵), Tiānmén (天門) from Jīngzhōu, Bālíng from Xiāngzhōu, Wǔchāng (武昌) from Jiāngzhōu, and Xīyáng (西陽) from Yùzhōu.
The *Yǒngchū Jùnguó Zhì* (永初郡國志) and Hé Chéngtiān's (何承天) *Zhì* (志) state that
the Administrator of Jiāngxià originally governed Ānlù (安陸).
After this, it was moved to Xiàkǒu (夏口).
The present Èzhōu (鄂州), governing Jiāngxià county, is this location.
Xià (夏)
is pronounced hùyǎ;
the same for Xiàkǒu below.
Its encampment was moved to Jiànkāng (建康).
Emperor Wǔ of Jìn (晉武帝) established the Protector of the Southern Barbarians (護南蠻校尉) at Xiāngyáng.
It was initially abolished east of the Yangtze River,
but soon re-established at Jiānglíng.
The *Shuǐjīngzhù* (水經註) states: The Southern Barbarian Commandant's (南蠻校尉) residence was in Fāngchéng (方城);
from Yóukǒu (油口) eastward,
the garrisons were continuous,
all being the garrisoned troops of the Southern Barbarian Administration.

Shàngshūlìng (尚書令) Hé Shàngzhī (何尚之) said:

directly opposite Miǎnkǒu (沔口),

From Xiàkǒu entering the Miǎn River,
sailing upstream to Xiāngyáng,
and further upstream to Hànzhōng (漢中),
hence it is said to connect Yǒng and Liáng.
Yǒng (雍)
is pronounced yúyòng.
The foundation is not easily changed.
Xiàkǒu has been a strategic stronghold since the Wú (吳) dynasty.
Its large harbor can accommodate barges,
which is convenient for affairs."
For defending the river,
ships are urgent,
thus a large harbor accommodating barges is convenient.
Fǎng (舫)
is pronounced púwàng.
After this, Jīng and Yáng consequently became depleted.
Shàngzhī requested to reunite the two prefectures,
but the emperor did not permit it.
On the day *Wùzǐ* (戊子),
the office of *Lù Shàngshū Shì* (錄尚書事) was abolished.
The emperor disliked the growing power of the imperial clan
and did not wish for authority to rest with his subordinates.
Grand Tutor (太傅) Yìgōng (義恭), knowing his intent,
therefore requested its abolition.
The emperor sent a letter from the dukes and high officials (王公、八座) to Jīngzhōu Inspector Zhū Xiūzhī (朱脩之).
The *Jìnzhì* (晉志) states: The Five Department Secretaries (五曹尚書), one Vice Director (一僕射), and two Directors (二令) constituted the Eight Seats (八座).
The Sòng (宋) probably had two Vice Directors

Before the letter arrived,

Xiūzhī entered Jiānglíng,
killed Yìxuān,
and also executed his sixteen sons,
along with his partisans Zhú Chāomín, Provisional Secretary (從事中郎) Cài Chāo (蔡超), Advisor (諮議參軍) Yán Lèzhī (顏樂之) and others.
Chāomín's brothers were supposed to be executed.
Hé Shàngzhī memorialized:
"Since the rebel has fled,
a single man can capture him.
If Chāomín had been treacherous and pursued profit,
he would have seized the opportunity,
not only avoiding transgression
but also potentially securing rewards for injustice.
Yet Chāomín had no such intention,
which is sufficient to observe his virtue through his mistakes.
Hé Shàngzhī's words here were to plead for Zhú Chāomín's brothers.
Yāo (要)
is pronounced yīyáo.
He carefully guarded the treasury
and sat calmly awaiting his capture.
Now to execute his brothers as well
would make them no different from the other rebel factions,
which is an excessive measure."
The emperor then pardoned them.
Autumn,
seventh month,
on the day *Bǐngshēn* (丙申), the first day of the month,

in the first month,

Shěn Qìngzhī, the General Who Guards the North and Inspector of Nányānzhōu, requested retirement due to old age;

On the day Xīnsì,

In the summer,
in the fifth month,

Hún, the Prince of Wǔchāng and Inspector of Yōngzhōu,

The Emperor sent Dài Míngbǎo of Dōnghǎi, a Supernumerary Cavalier Attendant-in-Ordinary, to interrogate and reprimand Hún.

An imperial edict commanded sacrifices to the suburban altars and ancestral temples,
and for the first time, ceremonial music was provided,
following the proposal of Xún Wànqiū, the Aide in the Central Bureau of the Front Palace.
When the Jìn clan moved south and were establishing themselves,
there was no music at the two suburban altars;
although there was "ascending song" in the ancestral temples,
there were also no "two dances."
After Fú Jiān was defeated,
and musicians were acquired,
metal and stone music began to be played.
In the 22nd year of Emperor Wén's Yuánjiā reign,
at the southern suburban sacrifice,
"ascending song" was first performed.
This "provision of music"
did not mean providing elegant court music,
but rather the popular music of the Wèi and Jìn eras.
In the 2nd year of Emperor Shùn's Shēngmíng reign,
Wáng Sēngqián said
that "the court's rites and music mostly deviate from old norms,"
likely referring to this kind of situation.
The Emperor wished to weaken the power of princes and marquises.
In the winter,
in the tenth month,
on the day Jǐwèi,
Yìgōng, the Prince of Jiāngxià, and Dàn, the Prince of Jìnglín, submitted a memorial proposing to curtail
the carriages, robes, implements, and music and dance regulations for princes and marquises,
totaling nine items;
the Emperor then subtly influenced the relevant authorities to propose an expansion to twenty-four articles:
In their audience halls,
they were not allowed to sit facing south,
or set up screens.
Officials from tributary states were forbidden from entering the national palace barefoot or serving as attendants to the National Preceptor during the first and last months of the year,
and from transmitting orders or carrying lacquered halberds.
Princesses and order-transmitting officials were not allowed to wear vermilion robes.
Palanquins were not allowed to have multiple bearers.
Screens were not allowed to have pheasant tail feathers.
Spear tassels were not allowed to have peacock feathers or white clam shells.
Flank guards were not allowed to wear crimson jackets.
For flat carriages, the number of horses was not to exceed two.
Barbarian performers were not allowed to wear colorful clothes.
Dancing girls were to wear pleated skirts in the first and last months of the year,
and were not allowed to wear heavy makeup or mask their faces with flowers.
During gatherings in the first and last months, sword dances and cup-and-plate dances were not allowed.
Stilt-walking acts, feats with short swords, Bóshān acts, pole-climbing acts, and five-table acts,
were not allowed unless it was a musical performance at a gathering in the first or last month.
All princes and princesses were not allowed to wear embroidered sashes.
For official banners,
all except those for court officials were to be crimson.
For commandery and county administrators, chancellors, and officials within their enfeoffment,
regarding their enfeoffing lord,
since they were not among the three highest ministers,
after leaving office, they were not to be shown continued reverence;
they were not to address them as "subject,"
but merely show the respect due between superior and subordinate officials.
For the regular carriages of all princes,
the front and rear escorts were not to exceed six teams,
with unadorned palace guards flanking the carriage not included in this limit;
swords were not to have more than silver and copper decorations.
Daughters of princes were enfeoffed as county mistresses,
and descendants of princes who inherited titles,
and the wives of princes and those enfeoffed as marquises,
were not to have a retinue when traveling.
When a prince's son succeeded as prince,
for marriages, funerals, auspicious and inauspicious events,
all were to follow the rites of ducal and marquisates,
and not be the same as those for imperial brothers and sons.
Carriages, unless they were light carts, were not to have lacquered canopies.
Flat boats were all to be flat at both ends,
made in an open, flat shape,
and not allowed to resemble dragon boats.
All were not to have vermilion lacquered awnings.
Chessboards were not to be made in the shape of five flowers or vertical bamboo shoots.
Swords were not to be made in the shape of a deer pulley;
(Jìn Zhuó said: Ancient long swords had jade deer pulley shapes
at their hilts).
They were not allowed to refer to themselves as "subject,"
and after leaving office, they were not to be shown continued reverence.
The edict was approved.
On the day Gēngwǔ,
the Wèi appointed Chángyīng, the Prince of Liáoxī, as Grand Tutor.
On the day Rénwǔ,
Yìgōng, the Grand Tutor, was made Governor of Yángzhōu;
Dàn, the Prince of Jìnglín, was made Minister of Works and Governor of Nánxúzhōu;
and Hóng, the Prince of Jiànpíng, was made Director of the Department of State Affairs.
In this year,
Yuánhé, the son of the deceased Dī king Yáng Bǎozōng, was appointed General Who Subdues the Barbarians,
and Yáng Tóu was appointed General Who Assists the State.
(Tóu was Wéndé's paternal cousin once removed).
Although Yuánhé was the legitimate heir of the Yáng clan,
the imperial court, considering his youth and weakness in talent,
had not yet formally established his title;
his tribes lacked a fixed ruler.
Tóu had previously been garrisoned in Jiālú.
His mother, wife, and children had all been captured by the Wèi.
(In the 20th year of Emperor Wén's Yuánjiā reign,
the Wèi captured Qiúchí,
and Yáng Wéndé was defeated and fled;
Tóu's mother, wife, and children were captured by the Wèi,
which must have happened in that year).
In the 27th year,
Tóu was first sent to garrison Jiālú.
Wáng Xuánmó, the Inspector of Yōngzhōu, submitted a memorial, stating:
"I request that Tóu be appointed Acting Governor of Xīqínzhōu, with the authority to implement the imperial edicts,
to pacify his people.
After a few years,
when Yuánhé is somewhat older,
he can succeed to the former enterprise.
If Yuánhé's talents are insufficient,
then it should revert to Tóu.
If Tóu can defend Hànchuān
and prevent barbarian incursions,
then those four thousand households in a desolate region are hardly worth regretting.
If Jiālú cannot be held,
then Hànchuān will also have no reason to stand."
The Emperor did not comply.
1 In spring,
the first month,
on the *gēngyín* day,
Emperor Xiàowǔ's younger brother Xiūfàn was enfeoffed as the Prince of Shùnyáng,
and Xiūrúo as the Prince of Bālíng.
On the *wùxū* day,
the imperial son Zǐshàng was enfeoffed as the Prince of Xīyáng.
2 On the *rénzǐ* day,
the daughter of Hé Yǔ, General of the Right Guard, was taken as crown princess.
Yǔ
was the great-grandson of Chéng.
On the *jiǎyín* day,
a general amnesty was declared.
3 On the *yǐmǎo* day,
Wèi established Noble Lady Féng as empress.
The empress
was the daughter of Féng Lǎng, Duke of Liáoxī Commandery;
Féng Lǎng's surrender to Wèi is recorded in volume 122, Emperor Wén's Yuánjiā 9th year.
He was executed for an offense,
and the empress was consequently taken into the palace.
This laid the groundwork for Empress Féng to wield exclusive control over Wèi's government.
4 In the second month,
on the *dīngsì* day,
the Wèi ruler established his son Hóng as crown prince.
He first had his mother, Noble Lady Lǐ, itemize her trusted brothers
and then, following custom, granted her death.
5 On the *jiǎzǐ* day,
Zōng Què, the Inspector of Guǎngzhōu, was appointed Inspector of Yùzhōu.
According to custom,
when matters were discussed within a prefecture or province,
they were all recorded clearly on a tally,
and a *diǎnqiān* was appointed to manage them.
During the Sòng dynasty, many imperial princes who were made regional governors were young,
and the rulers at the time often appointed their close attendants and trusted aides as *diǎnqiān*.
The power of the *diǎnqiān* gradually grew.
By this time,
even when an elder prince governed a dependency or a noble family member held an external post,
the *diǎnqiān* handled all official communications,
holding the key to power,
and the inspector could not exercise his duties independently.
When Què became the Inspector of Yùzhōu,
Wú Xǐ of Lín'ān was his *diǎnqiān*.
Wú County was divided from Yúháng to form Línshuǐ County;
in the first year of Tàikāng (280 CE) of Emperor Wǔ of Jìn,
it was renamed Lín'ān
and belonged to Wúxīng Commandery.
Xǐ frequently acted contrary to instructions,
which greatly angered Què,
who said:
"Zōng Què is nearly sixty years old,
and exhausts his life for the country.
I merely hold a province as small as a peck
[Zheng,
one character reads
"zhǐ"].
Xǐ prostrated himself until his forehead bled,
and then stopped.
6 Several thousand Dīnglíng families hid in the Jǐngxíng Mountains to become bandits.
Lù Zhēn, the Wèi Minister of Selection
[Early records state: Emperor Chéng of Hàn established four ministers for the various bureaus.
One of them was called the Minister of Chángshì Bureau;
Emperor Guāngwǔ renamed the Chángshì Bureau the Lìbù (Ministry of Personnel),
responsible for appointments;
Emperor Líng renamed the Lìbù the Xuǎnbù (Ministry of Selection).
In the early Northern Wèi, there were five ministers: Diànzhōng, Yuèbù, Jiàbù, Nánbù, and Běibù.
The Minister of Selection was likely established at this time.]
7 In the intercalary month,
on the *wùwǔ* day,
Liú Zūnkǎo, the Left Minister of the Department of State Affairs, was appointed Administrator of Dānyáng.
8 On the *guǐyǒu* day,
Xiūyè, the Afflicted Prince of Póyáng, died.
9 The Grand Tutor Yìgōng considered Zǐshàng, the Inspector of Nányánzhōu and Prince of Xīyáng, to be favored,
and intended to avoid him,
so he resigned from Yángzhōu.
In autumn,
the seventh month,
Yìgōng was relieved of his post in Yángzhōu;
on the *bǐngzǐ* day,
Zǐshàng was appointed Inspector of Yángzhōu.
At this time, the planet Huǒxīng (Mars) was stationed in Nándǒu.
The emperor abandoned the old western residence
and had Zǐshàng move to the eastern city to suppress the omen.
Shěn Huáiwén, Aide-de-camp of Yángzhōu, said:
"Heaven's way shows change;
it should be responded to with virtue.
Even if the western residence is empty now,
I fear it will be of no benefit."
This was not heeded.
Huáiwén
was the elder brother of Huái Yuǎn.
10 In the eighth month,
Wèi's General Who Pacifies the West, Wèi Juàn, Duke of Yúyáng, attacked Yīwú.
He captured its city,
gained great spoils, and returned.
Lǐ Bǎo had previously surrendered Yīwú and Dūnhuáng to Wèi.
After Bǎo had been received at court,
Yīwú rebelled again,
hence the attack.
Wèi,
read *yūwù* (*wèi*).
Huán,
read *cóngxuān* (*huán*),
also as written.
11 In the ninth month,
on the *rénxū* day,
Liú Zūnkǎo, the Administrator of Dānyáng, was appointed Right Minister of the Department of State Affairs.
12 In winter,
the tenth month,
on the *jiǎshēn* day,
the Wèi ruler returned to Píngchéng.
The place he went to is also not recorded.
13 On the *bǐngwǔ* day,
Grand Tutor Yìgōng was promoted to Grand Preceptor,
concurrently overseeing the Minister of Education.
14 In the eleventh month,
Wèi appointed Yuán Hè, the Minister and Prince of Xīpíng, as Inspector of Jìzhōu,
and further granted him the title of Prince of Lǒngxī.
Hè submitted a memorial, saying:
"Currently, the northern barbarians wander freely,
and the southern bandits rely on difficult terrain.
The border regions
still require defense and garrisoning.
Your humble servant believes
that, unless it is for high treason or murder with bare hands,
those who are condemned to death for bribery, theft, or errors
should all be pardoned
and assigned to guard the frontier;
in this way, bodies that were already severed will receive the grace of rebirth,
and families burdened by forced labor will enjoy the benefit of rest."
Wèi Gāozōng followed his advice.
After a long time,
he said to his close officials:
"I used Hè's words,
and the number of lives saved in a year is considerable,
and the garrison troops also increased significantly.
If all of you were like Hè,
what worries would I have!"
Coincidentally, Shí Huá of Wǔyì accused Hè of plotting rebellion.
Wǔyì County,
in the Former Hàn, belonged to Xìndū;
in the Later Hàn, it belonged to Ānpíng;
Emperor Wǔ of Jìn divided it to establish Wǔyì Commandery;
in the Suí and Táng dynasties, it became the territory of Wǔyì, Wǔqiáng, and Héngshuǐ three counties.
The emperor said:
"Hè serves the country with utmost sincerity.
I vouch for him to you all.
This [accusation] is impossible,
it is clear."
He ordered a thorough investigation;
Huá indeed admitted to the false accusation,
and confessed his guilt of making a false charge.
The emperor then said to his attendants:
"Even with Hè's loyalty,
he still could not avoid false slander.
How can those who are not as good as Hè not be cautious!"
15 In the twelfth month,
Jiāng Lóngjū, the Administrator of Púyáng, and Yáng Zìlún, the Administrator of Xīnpíng, abandoned
their commanderies and fled to Wèi.
According to Shěn Yuē's *Zhì*: Púyáng and Xīnpíng both belonged to Yǎnzhōu, but their administrative seats are not recorded;
they were likely "emigre" commanderies.
Xīnpíng Commandery
was also established in the seventh year of Tàishǐ of Emperor Míng,
this should be investigated.
Also according to the *Wǔdài Zhì*: Juānchéng County originally had Púyáng Commandery.
Pú,
read *bómù* (*pú*).
16 The emperor wished to move the administrative seats of Qīng and Jì two provinces to be co-located in Lìchéng,
but many deliberators disagreed.
Yuán Hùzhī, Inspector of Qīng and Jì two provinces, said:
"To the north of Qīngzhōu are the Yellow River and the Jì River,
and it also has many ponds and marshes,
which the barbarians do not target.
Whenever they raid,
they must pass through Lìchéng.
Co-locating the administrative seats of the two provinces
is a long-term strategic plan.
Furthermore, it is close to the Yellow River to the north,
making it easy for those who submit.
This will relieve the people's suffering in the near term,
extend royal prestige in the long term,
and is the best plan for securing the frontier."
Thus, the plan was decided.
Qīngzhōu was originally administered from Dōngyáng, and Jìzhōu from Lìchéng; now they are combined into one administrative seat.
17 During the Yuánjiā
period, the government minted four-zhū coins.
Their rim and
form were the same as the five-zhū coins.
The cost of their use yielded no profit;
it was said that the cost of minting one coin was exactly equal to the value of one coin,
with no surplus profit.
When the Emperor ascended the throne,
he again minted Xiàojiàn four-zhū coins.
Their form was thin and small,
and the rim was incomplete.
For a coin,
the outer circle is called the lún (rim),
and the inner square is called the guō (frame).
They were mixed with lead and tin;
ancient coins were cut and chiseled,
making the coins progressively thinner and smaller.
Governors and magistrates could not prohibit this,
and those who were executed or dismissed for failing to do so succeeded each other.
Counterfeiting became even more rampant,
commodity prices soared,
and the court was troubled by this.
Last spring,
an edict was issued that all thin, small, and rimless coins were not to circulate,
causing an uproar among the people.
In this year,
Shǐxīng Jùn Gōng Shěn Qìngzhī proposed,
believing
that "the people should be allowed to mint coins.
The commanderies and counties should establish coin bureaus,
and all households willing to mint coins should reside within these bureaus,
where their standards and forms would be equalized,
and their impurities and fakes removed.
The new types prohibited last spring
should be temporarily put into circulation,
and all coins minted now should follow this standard.
A tax of three thousand per ten thousand should be levied,
and counterfeiting strictly inspected."
Jiǎn
means to bind,
and also to investigate.
He believed
that "the weight of the five-zhū coin
was established during the Hàn dynasty;
Emperor Wǔ of Hàn introduced the five-zhū coin in the fifth year of Yuánshòu.
No one has been able to change it;
it is truly because when goods and currency are already balanced,
changing it leads to counterfeiting.
Now it is said that what was prohibited last spring should be temporarily put into circulation;
if both large and small coins circulate without following public minting,
self-interest will become profound,
and deceit will know no bounds.
Private minting and coin cutting will become impossible to prohibit,
wealth and goods will not be sufficient,
large coins will be exhausted,
and within a few years,
all will turn to dust.
The new prohibition has just begun,
and the standards are not yet uniform;
it will stop by itself in a moment,
and is not enough to trouble the Emperor's thoughts.
Only the emptiness of the imperial treasury
is truly a grave concern.
If small coins are now allowed to circulate,
the government will have no reason to increase revenue;
although the common people may be well-off,
it will not alleviate the government's deficiencies.
Only by simplifying expenses and eliminating extravagance,
and focusing on frugality,
is the way to sufficiency.
Nothing is more precious than this."
Other deliberators also believed
that "copper is becoming increasingly difficult to obtain,
and so they wished to mint two-zhū coins."
Jùn said:
"The deliberators believe that the imperial treasury is empty,
and thus coins should be changed and reminted;
that copper is scarce in the world,
and thus the coin's standard should be reduced to remedy the mutual difficulties.
The imperial treasury is empty,
without money for expenses,
and copper is scarce in the world,
so there is no material to mint coins.
This is a mutual difficulty.
The deliberators consequently wish to remint small coins to remedy it.
Shǎo,
pronounced as shǐ zhǎo.
Zhèn
means rich,
and also to help.
Shū
means slow,
and also wide.
Zhèn,
pronounced as jīn rěn.
Now minting two-zhū coins,
allowing new, small coins to circulate freely,
will not alleviate the government's deficiencies,
but great cunning will arise among the people,
and the world's wealth will be completely fragmented and exhausted.
Strict prohibitions will be established in vain,
but the deep profits will be difficult to eliminate;
in less than one or two years,
the harm will become irremediable.
Meaning the harm will become severe without waiting one or two years.
Fù,
pronounced as fú yòu.
Moreover, fearing the recent new prohibition,
there will certainly be disturbances
in the markets.
Distant benefits are not yet heard of,
but urgent problems will broadly arise.
Rich merchants will achieve their ambitions,
while the poor people will be in distress.
All of these are highly undesirable."
Thus, it was stopped.
18 Gāo Yáng Xǔ Zōngzhī, the Inspector of Dìngzhōu in Wèi, was immoderate in his acquisitions.
Mǎ Chāo, a commoner from Shēnzé, slandered and disparaged Zōngzhī.
Shēnzé County
belonged to Zhuójùn during the Former Hàn,
to Ānpíng during the Later Hàn,
and to Bólíngjùn since the Jìn.
During the Later Wèi, Bólíngjùn belonged to Dìngzhōu.
The Táng designated Bólíngjùn as Dìngzhōu,
later Qízhōu was separated from Dìngzhōu,
and Shēnzé County belonged to it.
Fearing that his family members would report him,
Mǎ Chāo was accused of slandering the court.
Emperor Gāozōng of Wèi said:
"This must be false.
The character 'Wèi' is redundant here.
What harm did Mǎ Chāo do to merit such words!
Zōngzhī must have feared punishment and falsely accused Mǎ Chāo."
An investigation
proved it to be true.
Zōngzhī was beheaded south of the capital.
19 Yán Yánzhī, the Jīnzǐ Guānglù Dàfū, passed away.
Yán Yánzhī's son Jùn was honored and wealthy,
but Yán Yánzhī received none of the provisions he offered,
living in plain clothes and a thatched hut,
as detached as before.
He often rode a lean ox in a clumsy cart,
and whenever he encountered Jùn's retinue,
he would immediately stop and move to the side of the road.
The procession's order is called lǔbù.
Píng,
pronounced as bì yǐng.
"I have never liked to see important people in my life;

When Jùn built a residence,
Yán Yánzhī said to him:
"Do it well,
do not let later generations laugh at your clumsiness."
Yán Yánzhī once visited Jùn early in the morning,
seeing guests filling the gate,
while Jùn had not yet risen.
Yán Yánzhī angrily said:
"You emerged from filth
and ascended above the clouds;

Things dread being overly full.
Yán Jùn's misfortune
was known to his father.
Dīng
means to be suitable;

He was appointed Ròujiāngjūn,

Jùn firmly declined,
submitting ten memorials;
shàng,
pronounced as shí zhǎng.
The Emperor did not permit it,

taking him to the commandery office.
Zhī,
means to go.
Jùnshè,
is the Dānyáng Yǐn's yamen.
His robes were lined with colorful silk,

Zhǔyī
managed the imperial clothing,
a position equivalent to the Táng's Shàngyī Fèngyù.
Jiù yī,

The first year of Dàmíng (Dīngyǒu, 457)
1 In spring,
the first month,
on the xīnhài day,
the reign title was changed,
and a general amnesty declared.
2 On the *rénxū* day,

Guōshān is in Guō Xiàn, Yànmén Commandery.
Guō,
pronounced like *gǔ bó*.

3 The Wei appointed Yúyáng Wáng Wèi Juàn as Tàiwèi and Lù Shàngshū Shì.

the Wei people raided Yǎnzhōu,

and defeated Nányáng Liú Hú, the Grand Administrator of Dōngpíng.
Wúyán Xiàn,
since the Hàn dynasty, belonged to Dōngpíng Commandery.
Bèi (敗),
pronounced like *bǔ mài*.
Dōngyáng Tàishǒu Shěn Fǎxì led a naval force,

Shēn Tǎn requested to turn back and suppress them.

When Rènzhēn heard of this,

At that time, there was a drought;
the men and horses were parched and exhausted,

Āndū and Fǎxì were demoted to commoner status while retaining their offices.

I weep for you in the marketplace;
soon I shall join you!"
The officials reported this,

5 In the third month,

on the *jǐsì* day,

6 The Wei emperor enfeoffed his younger brother Xīnchéng as Yángpíng Wáng.
7 Since the emperor's *jí* (吉) day,
the three-year mourning period had ended, and the *jí* day was observed.
He initiated many construction projects.
Dānyáng Yǐn Yán Jùn, as an old official of the princely court,
when the emperor was a prince, Jùn was his subordinate,

When Sòng Wǔdì was Sòng Wáng,

Cháo (朝),
pronounced like *zhí yáo*;
the same applies below.
He did not avoid anything,

Jùn believed his talent was sufficient to manage the affairs of the time,

the seventh month,

The migrant population of the commanderies and counties did not wish to be registered,

At that time, Liǔ Yuánjǐng's clan was powerful;

Liǔ Yuánjǐng,
a native of Xiè in Hédōng,
migrated south,

Cóng (從),
referring to cousins.
Cóng (從),
pronounced like *cái yòng*.
Xuánmó pacified the internal and external situations to resolve the public's confusion,

fully explaining the matter from beginning to end.
The emperor knew it was baseless,

Zhǔshū,

saying: "An old man of seventy,

10 In the eighth month,
on the *jǐhài* day,
the Wei emperor returned to Píngchéng.
11 On the *jiǎchén* day,
Sīkōng and Nánxúzhōu Cìshǐ Jìnglíng Wáng Dàn was transferred to be Nányǎnzhōu Cìshǐ,

Initially,
Gāozǔ's遗诏 (posthumous edict) stated that Jīngkǒu was a strategic location,
being close to Jiànkāng,
and no one outside the imperial clan's close relatives
was allowed to reside there.
Although Yánzūn's ancestors shared the same origin as Gāozǔ,
Gāozǔ belonged to Péngchéng,
and Yánzūn belonged to Jǔxiàn.
The "Nán Shǐ Yánzūn Zhuàn" writes

Lǚxiàn belonged to Péngchéng Commandery,

Upon detailed examination,
Lǚxiàn is correct.
Both Péngchéng and Lǚ counties belonged to Péngchéng Commandery,

Since the emperor had ordered Yánzūn to guard Jīngkǒu,
he then issued an edict to unite his clan with Yánzūn's,

The emperor's conduct within his family was improper;
he made no distinction between relatives,
closeness or distance, status or humility.
Rumors spread among the people,
reaching everywhere.
Dàn was lenient and courteous,
and he had rendered great service in executing Tàizǐ Shào and Chéngxiàng Yìxuān.
Dàn's raising troops to suppress Shào is mentioned in the previous volume, Wéndì Yuánjiā thirtieth year;
his dissuading the emperor from welcoming Yìxuān is mentioned above.
Dàn gathered many talented and strong individuals,
and amassed fine armor and sharp weapons.
The emperor, therefore, feared and resented him,
not wishing Dàn to remain in the central government,

Still finding him too close,
he further transferred him to Guǎnglíng.
Nányǎnzhōu was then governed from Guǎnglíng.
He made him guard Jīngkǒu to prevent trouble.
This set the stage for the emperor to suppress Dàn.

the tenth month,
