where gōng (公), hóu (侯), bó (伯), zǐ (子), and nán (男) are positioned.
Later generations directly referred to "Jiǔ Jí" (九棘) as the "Jiǔ Qīng" (九卿, Nine Ministers).
[They] scorned the households of magistrates;
they successively indulged in arrogance,
vying over trifles,
only considering family background,
not inquiring about talent or ability.
Shè Língyùn (謝靈運) and Wáng Sēngdá (王僧達), with their frivolous talents,
if they had been born into humble families,
would still have been broken;
moreover, relying on their patronage,
it was appropriate that they invited disaster.
11th month, 9th day,
yǐsì (乙巳),
the Wèi (魏) ruler returned to Píngchéng (平城).
He returned from west of the Yellow River.
12th day, bǐngyín (丙寅),
Wèi (魏) declared a general amnesty.
Winter,
10th month,
jiǎxū (甲戌),
the Wèi (魏) ruler went on a northern tour,
intending to attack the Rourán (柔然).
When he reached Yīnshān (陰山),
it snowed.
The Wèi (魏) ruler wanted to return,
but Tàiwèi (太尉) Wèi Juàn (尉眷) said:
"Now, we have mobilized a large army to intimidate the northern barbarians.
If the imperial carriage returns hastily, not far from the capital,
the barbarians will surely suspect we have internal difficulties.
Although the soldiers are cold,
we must not fail to advance."
The Wèi (魏) ruler followed his advice.
Xīnmǎo (辛卯),
the army camped at Chēlún Shān (車崙山).
"Chēlún Shān" (車崙山),
the Běishǐ (北史) writes it as
"Chēlún Shān" (車輪山).
Wèi Shōu's (魏收) Dìxíng Zhì (地形志) says: in Fūchéng (敷城) County, Xiùróng (秀容) Commandery, there is the Chēlún (車輪) Spring God.
Jīshè Jiāngjūn (積射將軍) Yīn Xiàozǔ (殷孝祖) built two forts east of Qīngshuǐ (清水).
In the ninth year of Yuánjiā (元嘉) of Emperor Wén (文), the titles Jīshè Jiāngjūn (積射將軍) and Qiángnǔ Jiāngjūn (強弩將軍) were established.
Shěn Yuē (沈約) said: established in the tenth year of Tàikāng (太康) of Jìn (晉).
Qīngkǒu (清口)戍主, Zhèwēi Jiāngjūn (振威將軍) Fù Gān'ài (傅乾愛) resisted and defeated him.
Xiàozǔ (孝祖) was the great-grandson of Xiànzhī (羨之).
Yīn Xiàn (殷羨)
Yīn (殷),
was Hào (浩) 's father.
Hǔbēn Zhǔ (虎賁主),
commander of Hǔbēn (虎賁) soldiers.
Bēn (賁)
is pronounced "bēn".
Kǎoyì (考異) states: The biography of Sòng (宋) Yán Shībó (顏師伯) says:
"Wèi (魏) sent Qīngshuǐ Gōng (清水公) Shě Bēnchì (捨賁敕) to invade Qīngkǒu (清口),
and Emperor Shìzǔ (世祖) dispatched Mèng Qiú (孟虯) and Yīn Xiàozǔ (殷孝祖) to suppress them."
Wèi Běnjì (魏本紀) says:
"Xiàozǔ (孝祖) built two forts east of Qīngshuǐ (清水),
and an imperial edict ordered Chìwén (敕文) to attack them."
Now we follow this.
Wèi (魏) troops were defeated at Shāgōu (沙溝).
According to this, Qīngkǒu (清口) here is not the mouth where Qīngshuǐ (清水) enters the Huái (淮) River,
but the mouth where Jǐshuǐ (濟水) and Wènshuǐ (汶水) meet.
The Shuǐjīng (水經) says: Jǐshuǐ (濟水) flows northeast past the south of Xī'ānmín Tíng (西安民亭) in Shòuzhāng (壽張) County,
Wènshuǐ (汶水) comes from the northeast and flows into it.
The commentary says: This is what Dài Yánzhī (戴延之) called Qīngkǒu (清口).
Jǐshuǐ (濟水) then flows north past Xūchāng (須昌), Gǔchéng (穀城), Línyì (臨邑), and Lú (盧) counties,
then northeast to merge with Zhōngchuānshuǐ (中川水).
The commentary says: Zhōngchuānshuǐ (中川水) merges with Bīnxīshuǐ (賓溪水) and flows north,
passing east of the old city of Lú (盧) County,
then flows north into Jǐ (濟),
commonly known as Shāgōushuǐ (沙溝水).
Bài (敗),
pronounced "bài".
Jùn (竣)'s paternal cousin.
The emperor dispatched Sīkōng Cānjūn (司空參軍) Bǔ Tiānshēng (卜天生) to lead troops to meet Fù Gān'ài (傅乾愛) and Zhōngbīng Cānjūn (中兵參軍) Jiāng Fāngxīng (江方興) to jointly attack Wèi (魏) troops,
repeatedly defeating them.
Jiāng Fāngxīng (江方興) was probably Sīkōng Zhōngbīng Cānjūn (司空中兵參軍).
Jiàng (將),
pronounced "jiàng".
Same below.
[Wáng Huái] (王褱)
11th month,
Wèi (魏) Zhēngxī Jiāngjūn (征西將軍) Pí Bàozǐ (皮豹子) and others led 30,000 cavalry to assist Fēng Chìwén (封敕文) in raiding Qīngzhōu (青州).
Yán Shībó (顏師伯) resisted them.
Fǔguó Jiāngjūn (輔國將軍) Jiāo Dù (焦度) stabbed Bàozǐ (豹子), who fell off his horse,
and captured his armor, spear, and complete gear,
personally killing dozens of people.
Dù (度)
was originally a Dī (氐) from Nán'ān (南安).
14th day, the Wèi (魏) ruler personally led 100,000 cavalry and 150,000 chariots to attack the Rourán (柔然).
They crossed the great desert,
with banners and flags stretching for a thousand lí (里).
Chǔluó Kèhán (處羅可汗) of the Rourán (柔然) fled far away,
and his separate tribes, such as Wūzhū Jiàtuí (烏朱駕頹), led several thousand encampments to surrender to Wèi (魏).
The Wèi (魏) ruler carved a stone to commemorate his achievements and returned.
15th day, at first,
when the emperor was in Jiāngzhōu (江州),
Dài Fǎxīng (戴法興), Dài Míngbǎo (戴明寶), and Cài Xián (蔡閑) of Shānyīn (山陰) served as Diǎnqiān (典籤).
When he ascended the throne,
they were all made Nántái Shìyùshǐ (南臺侍御史) concurrently with Zhōngshū Tōngshì Shèrén (中書通事舍人).
The Yùshǐ Tái (御史臺) was called Nántái (南臺).
In early Jìn (晉), one Zhōngshū Shèrén (中書舍人) and one Tōngshì (通事) were established respectively.
In the jiāngzuǒ (江左) period, the Shèrén (舍人) and Tōngshì (通事) were combined,
called Tōngshì Shèrén (通事舍人),
responsible for presenting memorials
and also for imperial decrees.
The three Diǎnqiān (典籤) were all granted the title of Xiànnán (縣男) because they had participated in the secret plans at the beginning of the uprising.
Xián (閑) had already died,
so the title was posthumously bestowed upon him.
At that time, the emperor personally oversaw court affairs,
not entrusting them to senior ministers.
However, for close confidants and informants,
he could not but delegate responsibilities.
Fǎxīng (法興) was quite knowledgeable about ancient and modern affairs,
and had long been trusted and favored.
Cháo Shàngzhī (巢尚之) from Lǔ Jùn (魯郡), though of humble origin among scholars,
had a broad knowledge of literature and history,
and was known to the emperor.
He was also made Zhōngshū Tōngshì Shèrén (中書通事舍人).
For all major decisions regarding selections, appointments,
punishments, and rewards,
the emperor consulted with Fǎxīng (法興) and Shàngzhī (尚之);
between the Sòng (宋) and Qí (齊) dynasties,
all who participated in important deliberations
were generally referred to as Cānhuái (參懷).
Much was entrusted to Míngbǎo (明寶).
The three of them wielded great power at the time;
Fǎxīng (法興) and Míngbǎo (明寶), however, accepted many bribes.
All whom they recommended
had their proposals carried out without fail.
People flocked from all over the realm,
making their gates like markets,
and their family wealth accumulated to thousands of gold pieces.
The Minister of Personnel, Gù Jìzhī, alone did not lower his esteem for Fǎxīng and others.
Cài Xīngzōng was good friends with Jìzhī,
and found his moral integrity too severe.
Jìzhī said:
"Xīn Pí had a saying: 'Sūn and Liú will only prevent me from becoming one of the Three Ducal Ministers.'"
During the time of Emperor Míng of Wèi,
Liú Fàng and Sūn Zī controlled the affairs of state.
No high official failed to cultivate their friendship,
but Xīn Pí did not associate with them.
Pí's son Chǎng remonstrated, saying:
"Liú and Sūn are in power,
and everyone attaches themselves to them like shadows.
Your Excellency should lower your esteem somewhat;
otherwise,
there will surely be slanderous remarks."
Pí sternly replied:
"My conduct in life
has its own principles.
Even if I am not on good terms with Sūn and Liú,
it will only mean not becoming one of the Three Ducal Ministers.
Should a man of integrity, wishing for public office, damage his noble principles!"
Jì,
pronounced Jì.
"People's destinies are fixed,
and cannot be altered by wisdom or strength.
One should only respectfully uphold the Way.
But the ignorant do not understand this,
and vainly hope for good fortune,
merely diminishing noble principles
without affecting gains or losses."
He then instructed his disciple Yuán to write the Dìngmìnglùn (Treatise on Fixed Destiny) to explain his ideas.
"Yuán,"
in the Nánshǐ it is written as
"Yuàn."
Punctuation by Niè Chóngqí, reviewed by Wáng Chóngwǔ
Sīmǎ Guāng
Compiled by imperial decree
Hòuxuétiāntái
Emperor Shìzǔ Xiàowǔ, Part II
Dàmíng 3rd year (Jǐhài, 459 CE)
1. Spring,
1st month,
on the day Jǐsì (1st day of the month),
the Yǎnzhōu army battled Wèi's Pí Bàozǐ at Gāopíng;
the Yǎnzhōu army was defeated.
2. On the day Jǐchǒu,
General of Cavalry Piàojì Liǔ Yuánjǐng was appointed Minister of Personnel (Shàngshūlìng),
and Right Assistant Director Liú Zūnkǎo was appointed Commander of the Imperial Guards (Lǐngjūn Jiāngjūn).
3. On the day Jǐyǒu,
Wèi's Duke of Hénán Yī Bó died.
4. 3rd month,
on the day Yǐmǎo,
the six commanderies of Yángzhōu were made the royal domain (wángjī);
the six commanderies were: Dānyáng, Huáinán, Xuānchéng, Wújùn, Wúxīng, and Yìxīng.
The administration was moved to Kuàijī,
and Dōngyángzhōu was established (see Volume V, Xiàojiàn 1st year).
Kuài,
pronounced like "guài" with a rising tone.
Celestial phenomena (see Volume V, Xiàojiàn 3rd year).
5. 3rd month,
on the day Gēngyín,
the Administrator of Yìxīng, Yuán Làng, was appointed Inspector of Yǎnzhōu (Yǎnzhōu Cìshǐ).
Làng
was the son of Zūn.
Yuán Zūn
was Yuán Miáo.
When Emperor Wǔ campaigned west to Cháng'ān,
he ordered Zūn to guard Luòdāngchéng;
the city was situated at the confluence of the Hé and Jǐ rivers,
and later generations called it Yuánmiáochéng.
Shǒu,
pronounced like "shòu" with a rising tone.
6. Summer,
4th month,
on the day Yǐsì,
the Wèi ruler enfeoffed his younger brother Tuī as Prince of Jīngzhào.
7. Prince of Jìnglíng, Dàn, knew that the Emperor was suspicious of him,
and secretly made preparations.
Taking advantage of the Wèi people's incursions,
he repaired city walls, deepened moats,
gathered provisions, and prepared weapons.
Dàn's Staff Officer (Jìshì Cānjūn) Jiāng Zhìyuān knew Dàn had rebellious intentions,
and requested leave to return to Jiànkāng first.
The Emperor appointed him Secretariat Imperial Attendant (Zhōngshū Shìláng).
Zhìyuān
was the nephew of Yí,
Jiāng Yí was the father of Jiāng Zhàn;
Yí's younger brother was Sēng'ān.
Shěn Huáiwén often praised him, saying:
"That which people should have, he has in full;
that which people should not have, he has none of—
could it be none other than Jiāng Zhìyuān!"
At this time,
rumors circulated everywhere that Dàn was rebelling.
A man from Wújùn, Liú Chéng, submitted a memorial stating:
"My son Dàolóng formerly served Dàn,
(xī,
son)
and practiced singing the imperial procession's warning calls."
This refers to the time when Dàn was Inspector of Yángzhōu.
At that time, Dàn was wholeheartedly loyal to the Emperor,
so there would certainly be no such incident;
Liú Chéng was making a false accusation.
Chéng,
pronounced like "shèng" with a rising tone.
"He privately spoke of it with his companions,
and Dàn killed Dàolóng."
A textual variant notes: Sònglüè and Nánshǐ write
"Dàojiù."
Now following Sòngshū.
"My younger brother Yǒngzhī was by Dàn's side,
and saw Dàn write down His Majesty's age, surname, and given name,
and go to the shaman Zhèng Shīlián's house to curse him."
"Yǒngzhī secretly reported this,
and Dàn falsely accused Yǒngzhī of getting drunk and insulting him,
then killed him."
Liú Dàolóng and Chén Yǒngzhī were probably both killed by Dàn earlier,
and their fathers and elder brothers merely seized the opportunity to make false accusations to avenge their sons and younger brothers.
Lì,
pronounced like "lì" with a falling tone.
He requested that Dàn be arrested and handed over to the Grand Judge (Tíngwèi) for punishment.
On the day Yǐmǎo,
an edict demoted Dàn's title to Marquis,
and sent him to his enfeoffed state.
Before the imperial edict was issued,
imperial guards (yǔlín jìnbīng) were first assigned to the Inspector of Yǎnzhōu, Yuán Làng,
so that under the pretext of taking up his post,
he could, with Attendant Censor (Gěishìzhōng) Dài Míngbǎo, attack Dàn by surprise.
Làng arrived at Guǎnglíng,
but Dàn was not yet aware.
Míngbǎo secretly informed Dàn's records officer (diǎnqiān) Jiǎng Chéng that night,
instructing him to open the gate the next morning to act as an inside accomplice.
Chéng reported this to the palace attendant (fǔshèrén) Xǔ Zōngzhī.
Zōngzhī
was an attendant in the Prince of Jìnglíng's palace.
Dàn was startled awake,
called his attendants and the several hundred men he had long kept and trained,
seized Jiǎng Chéng,
and marshaled his troops for self-defense.
As dawn approached,
Míngbǎo and Làng led several hundred elite soldiers and arrived suddenly,
but the gate did not open.
Dàn had already arrayed his troops and ascended the parapets,
and from atop the gate, he beheaded Jiǎng Chéng,
pardoned those sentenced to penal servitude and prisoners,
(zuòtú,
refers to those serving penal servitude;
jìqiú,
refers to those arrested and imprisoned)
and killed him.
A textual variant notes: Sònglüè states that Làng was killed on the day Jǐhài.
According to the basic annals,
Dàn's title was demoted on the day Yǐmǎo,
so we follow this.
An edict ordered preparations internally and externally.
A textual variant notes: Sònglüè states preparations were made on the day Yǐhài.
According to the Long Calendar,
the 1st day of this month was Wùxù,
there was no Yǐhài;
it was probably Jǐhài.
Troops were sent to suppress Dàn.
On the day Jiǎzǐ,
the Emperor personally commanded the imperial guards and encamped at Xuānwǔtáng.
The Inspector of Sīzhōu, Liú Jìzhī,
was a former general of Dàn's.
When Dàn was at Kuàijī,
Jìzhī was his staff officer;
and when Dàn raised troops to attack the Arch-Villain,
he made Jìzhī a general.
Zōng Què was at Yùzhōu,
also overseeing Sīzhōu.
Fearing he would be harmed by Què,
Jìzhī abandoned his post
and secretly returned to the imperial court.
When he reached Xūyí,
the Administrator of Xūyí, Zhèng Yuàn, suspected Jìzhī of conspiring with Dàn,
and intercepted and killed him.
Shěn Qìngzhī arrived at Ōuyáng.
The *Shuǐ Jīng Zhù* states: "The Wú kingdom dug the Hángōu canal
to connect the Jiāng and Huái rivers.
Since the middle of the Yǒnghé reign,
the water in Jiāngdū has been cut off.
Its water rises from Ōuyáng,
drawing the Jiāng River into the weir,
sixty *lǐ* to Guǎnglíng City."
I hold that this place is today's Zhēnzhōu lock.
(Dàn) sent him a jade ring knife as a gift.
Qìngzhī sent Dàomǐn back,
enumerating (Dàn's) crimes.
Dàn burned the outer city and its residences,
driving all residents into the city,
closing the gates and defending himself.
He dispatched letters and proclamations
to invite and gather supporters from far and near.
At that time, Liáng Kuàng, the Internal史 of Shānyáng,
had his family in Guǎnglíng.
Dàn seized his wife and children
and sent an envoy to invite Kuàng.
Kuàng beheaded the envoy and refused (Dàn);
Dàn was enraged
and exterminated his family.
Dàn presented a memorial, throwing it outside the city, saying:
"Your Majesty trusts slanderous words,
thus allowing nameless commoners to come and attack me.
Unable to endure such injustice and cruelty,
(they) immediately inflicted punishment and extermination.
Like sparrows and rats clinging to life,
I respectfully defy the imperial edict.
Now I personally lead my troops
to guard Xú and Yǎn.
What good fortune did (those who came) before them experience
to be born into the imperial family together?
Dàn is of the same blood as the Emperor,
hence this is said.
(Why then) have we become like Hú and Yuè?
Rushing into the sharp points of spears
and halberds,
how could I care about ten thousand deaths?
Ten thousand deaths
is another way of saying 'a myriad deaths'.
I hope (to achieve my goal) in the morning and evening."
He also said:
"The scandals of Your Majesty's palace
cannot be kept secret with three seals!"
The *Jiāyǔ* states: "When Kǒngzǐ observed Zhōu,
he entered Hòujì's temple.
There was a bronze figure
with its mouth sealed thrice, and an inscription on its back read:
'This is a cautious speaker of antiquity.'"
All of Dàn's associates, confidants, kinsmen of the same lineage, and relatives within the mourning period, who were in Jiànkāng, were executed.
"Kinsmen of the same lineage" (tóngjí)
refers to those registered in the same clan as members;
"relatives within the mourning period" (qīqīn)
refers to relatives for whom one wears *qī* mourning clothes.
Some of their family members had already died,
while others fled from within the city.
Qìngzhī arrived below the city walls.
Dàn ascended a tower and said to him:
"Duke Shěn, at your white-haired age,
his white hair hung down,
hence called 'white-haired'.
(Why are you still fighting)?" Qìngzhī replied:
"The court considers you mad and foolish,
and not worth troubling the young and strong, that's all."
The Emperor, fearing Dàn would flee to Wèi,
ordered Qìngzhī to cut off his escape route.
Qìngzhī moved his camp to Báitǔ,
eighteen *lǐ* from the city,
and then advanced his army to Xīntíng.
This Xīntíng was outside Guǎnglíng City,
not the Xīntíng of Jiànkāng.
Shěn Sēngmíng, the Inspector of Yǎnzhōu
and Qìngzhī's nephew,
also sent troops to assist Qìngzhī.
Earlier, Dàn had deceived his followers,
saying:
"Zōng Què is helping me."
When Què arrived,
he rode around the city, leaping and shouting:
"I am
Zōng Què!"
Seeing the large assembly of armies,
Dàn wanted to abandon the city and flee north,
leaving Shēn Língxī, the Staff Officer of the Central Army, to guard Guǎnglíng.
He personally led several hundred infantry and cavalry,
with his trusted followers accompanying him,
announcing he was going out to battle, but secretly heading towards Hǎilíng.
Emperor Ān of Jìn divided Guǎnglíng to establish Hǎilíng Commandery,
which is today's Tàizhōu.
Dàn announced he was going out to battle from Guǎnglíng's north gate,
but secretly turned east,
which was the road to Hǎilíng.
*Qū*
is pronounced *qī yù*.
After Dàn had traveled more than ten *lǐ*,
his followers all did not want to leave
and mutually pleaded with Dàn to return to the city.
Dàn said:
"It is easy for me to return,
but can you all exert your full strength for me?"
They all assented.
Dàn then returned,
built an altar, and swore an oath with his followers by smearing blood on their lips.
All civil and military officials of the *fǔ* and *zhōu* were promoted.
The *fǔ*
refers to the Sīkōng, Jìnglínɡ Wáng's office;
the *zhōu*
refers to Nányǎnzhōu.
Kūnzhī,
Zūnkǎo's son,
Liú Zūnkǎo was then in court as the Right Senior Secretary.
(Dàn ordered Kūnzhī to join him, but Kūnzhī refused, saying:) "Loyalty and filial piety cannot be upheld simultaneously.
My aged father is alive,
so I dare not accept this command."
Dàn imprisoned him for more than ten days,
but he ultimately refused,
so Dàn killed him.
Yuán Hùzhī, the Right General of the Guards, and Yīn Xiàozǔ, the Colonel-Director of the Imperial Guard, etc., returned after attacking Wèi.
When they reached Guǎnglíng,
the Emperor ordered them all to be subject to Qìngzhī's command.
Qìngzhī advanced his camp,
pressing upon Guǎnglíng City.
Dàn sent food to Qìngzhī,
carried by more than a hundred people,
who came out of the North Gate.
Qìngzhī did not open (the gates to) inspect it,
but burned it all.
Dàn delivered a sealed memorial from atop the city wall.
"Delivered" (shòu)
is written as "thrown" (tóu)
in the *Nán Shǐ*,
which should be followed.
Qìngzhī said:
"I received an imperial edict to punish a rebel,
I cannot send a memorial for you.
If you truly wish to surrender and die at court,
you should open the gates and send an envoy yourself;
I will escort him for you."
Dàn did this
because the Emperor was suspicious and cruel,
hoping to create a rift with Qìngzhī.
Qìngzhī decisively rejected him,
which was also a strategy for himself.
*Wéi*
is pronounced *yú wěi*.
Yán Jùn, the Inspector of Dōngyángzhōu, was mourning his mother
and escorting the coffin back to the capital.
The Emperor's favor towards him was still generous,
but Jùn sometimes expressed resentful words to his relatives and old friends,
or spoke about the gains and losses of the court.
It happened that Wáng Sēngdá fell into disfavor.
Sēngdá's death is mentioned in the previous year's chapter.
Before his death,
he fully recounted Jùn's past words of resentment, slander, and criticism.
The Emperor then ordered Yǔ Huīzhī, the Imperial Censor-in-Chief, to impeach and report (Jùn),
dismissing Jùn from office.
Zhèng Qiáo said: "The name 'Imperial Censor' (yùshǐ)
existed in the *Zhōu Guān*,
(but) it was likely a position to assist in writing and issuing laws,
not the current responsibility.
During the Warring States period,
at the Mǐnchí meeting between Qín and Zhào,
each appointed an Imperial Censor to record events.
Also,
Chúnyú Kūn said to King Qí:
'The Imperial Censor is in front,'
so these were all positions for recording events.
It was only in the Qín and Hàn dynasties that it became a position of investigation and supervision."
Jùn submitted a memorial of apology
and also pleaded for his life.
The Emperor became even more enraged
and replied with an edict:
"You have slandered, criticized, and expressed resentment,
already betraying my original hopes;
yet you again excessively worry and overthink,
fearing for your safety.
How can this be the utmost sincerity of a subordinate serving his superior?!"
When Jìnglínɡ Wáng Dàn rebelled,
the Emperor then falsely accused Jùn of conspiring with Dàn.
In the fifth month,
Jùn was arrested and handed over to the Court of Judicial Review.
His feet were first broken,
and then he was granted death.
His wife and children were exiled to Jiāozhōu.
When they reached Gōngtíng Hú,
Gōngtíng Hú
is Pēnglí Hú,
west of Pēngzé County.
In the sixth month,
on the day Wùshēn,
the Wèi ruler went to Yīn Shān.
10 The Emperor ordered Shěn Qìngzhī to establish three signal beacons at Sānglǐ.
Sānglǐ
is southwest of Guǎnglíng city.
One beacon was to be raised upon capturing the inner city,
two beacons upon capturing Liú Dàn,
and three beacons upon seizing his seal.
Imperial rescripts urging action
arrived one after another.
Shěn Qìngzhī burned the east gate,
filled the moats,
constructed assault ramps,
and erected mobile towers and earthworks, along with various siege equipment.
Due to prolonged rain,
they could not attack the city.
The Emperor had Yǔ Huīzhī, the Imperial Censor-in-Chief, submit a memorial to dismiss Shěn Qìngzhī from office,
but issued an edict not to question him, in order to spur him on.
From the fourth month until the seventh month of autumn,
the rain ceased,
but the city was still not taken.
The Emperor was enraged
and ordered the Grand Astrologer to select a day,
intending to cross the Jiāng river himself to attack Dàn.
Tàizǎi Yìgōng strenuously remonstrated,
and so the Emperor desisted.
When Dàn first closed the city gates and refused the envoy,
Shānyīn Hè Bì, the Recorder and Adjutant, strongly remonstrated.
Dàn became angry
and drew his sword at him,
upon which Bì stopped.
Dàn dispatched troops to battle multiple times, but was repeatedly defeated.
Many of his generals and aides climbed over the city walls and surrendered.
Someone advised Bì that he should leave early.
Bì said:
"The Duke has raised troops against the imperial court;
this matter cannot be followed.
Having received great kindness from the Duke,
it would also be unrighteous to betray him.
I can only die to show my sincerity!"
Thereupon, he drank poison and committed suicide.
Cānjūn Hé Kāngzhī plotted to open the gate and admit the imperial army,
but it did not succeed.
He broke through the gate and surrendered.
Dàn built a high tower
and placed Kāngzhī's mother on it,
exposing her to the elements
and denying her food.
The mother called out to Kāngzhī
and died several days later.
Dàn appointed Púyáng Fàn Yì, the Chief Clerk of the Central Army, as Zuǒ Sīmǎ.
Fàn Yì's mother, wife, and children were all in the city.
Someone said to Fàn Yì:
"The situation is bound to fail."
This means Dàn will certainly be defeated and unable to recover.
Fàn Yì said:
"I
am a subordinate official.
A subordinate official
refers to being an assistant official to someone.
An official cannot betray his lord.
If I were to live like Hé Kāngzhī,
I would not do it."
Shěn Qìngzhī led his troops to attack the city,
personally leading his soldiers and exposing himself to arrows and stones.
On the day Yǐsì,
they captured the outer city.
Pressing on with their victory,
they also captured the small city.
When Dàn heard that the troops had entered,
he fled to the rear garden.
Duìzhǔ Shěn Yìnzhī and others pursued and overtook him,
wounded Dàn,
who fell into the water.
He was pulled out
and beheaded.
Dàn's mother and wife both committed suicide.
Dàn's mother was
Wén Dì's Yīn Xiūhuá;
his wife was
from the Xú family.
When the Emperor heard that Guǎnglíng was pacified,
he exited the Xuānyáng Gate
and ordered his attendants to all shout "Long live!"
Shìzhōng Cài Xīngzōng accompanied the imperial carriage.
The Emperor looked back and said:
"Why are you alone not shouting?"
Xīngzōng sternly replied:
"Today, Your Majesty should be shedding tears and executing the punishment.
How can everyone be shouting 'Long live'?"
This refers to siblings killing each other,
which is a distortion of heavenly principles and human ethics.
If one must destroy relatives out of righteousness,
one should weep while carrying out the execution.
An edict was issued to demote Dàn's surname to Liú.
All officials and common people in Guǎnglíng city,
regardless of rank, were ordered to be killed.
Shěn Qìngzhī requested that those under five *chǐ* be spared,
and that the remaining men be killed,
with women given as military rewards.
Still, over three thousand people were killed.
Chángshuǐ Xiàowèi Zōng Yuè, when supervising the executions,
first gouged out intestines and eyes,
or whipped faces and bellies,
poured bitter wine into the wounds,
and then beheaded them.
Bitter wine
is probably a type of vinegar.
*Chuàng* is pronounced *chū liáng fān*.
He seemed delighted, as if he had gained something.
The historian speaks of Zōng Yuè's cruelty.
Shěn Qìngzhī likely presented all their heads,
hence they were piled on the south bank of Shítou.
*Guān* is pronounced *gǔ wán fān*.
This was not heeded.
The historian says that the close attendants at the time were all upright people,
but their remonstrances were not adopted, and their words not listened to.
Initially,
Dàn, knowing he was about to be defeated, sent Huángmén Lǚ Tánjì and his trusted attendants to hide his heir, Jǐngcuì, among the common people.
*Jiāng*
means to carry.
*Tán* is pronounced *tú hán fān*.
"If the matter does not succeed,
I hope you will protect and save him.
If he cannot escape,
bury him deep."
This refers to burying Jǐngcuì's body deep.
After leaving the gate,
they all scattered and fled.
Only Tánjì did not leave;
he carried Jǐngcuì for more than ten days
until they were captured
and beheaded.
Línchuān Nèishǐ Yáng Xuán was imprisoned and died
for his previous good relationship with Dàn.
Liáng Kuàng was promoted to Hòu Jiāngjūn,
and Liú Kūnzhī was posthumously granted the title of Jìshì Huángmén Shìláng.
Cài Xīngzōng was ordered to go to Guǎnglíng to offer condolences.
Xīngzōng had been on good terms with Fàn Yì.
He collected Fàn Yì's body
and sent the funeral procession back to Yùzhāng.
Fàn Yì probably resided in Yùzhāng.
Cài Xīngzōng's ancestors were also from Jìyáng.
*Láo* is pronounced *lì dào fān*.
*Liǎn* is pronounced *lì zhàn fān*.
"How dare you intentionally violate imperial law?"
Xīngzōng replied with firm words:
"Your Majesty kills rebels,
and I bury an old friend.
What is there that is wrong?"
The Emperor showed a look of shame.
Brothers and friends
are both natural human relationships.
Xīngzōng was able to remember an old friend,
while the Emperor cruelly killed his own kin,
hence his shame.
Zōng Yuè managed his army strictly
and was skilled in setting up encampments.
Whenever tens of thousands of men halted and encamped,
Zōng Yuè would ride ahead,
with his soldiers following behind him.
When his horse stopped, the encampment would be formed,
never out of order.
11 On the day Xīnwèi,
a general amnesty was issued.
As Guǎnglíng had been pacified,
a general amnesty was therefore granted.
12 On the day Bǐngzǐ,
Liú Xiùzhī, the Dānyáng Yǐn, was appointed Shàngshū Yòu Púshè.
13 On the day Bǐngxū,
Shěn Qìngzhī, the Nányǎnzhōu Cìshǐ, was appointed Sīkōng;
his position as Cìshǐ remained unchanged.
14 In the eighth month,
on the day Gēngxū,
the Wèi ruler went to Yúnzhōng;
on the day Rénxū,
he returned to Píngchéng.
15 In the ninth month,
on the day Rénchén,
the Shànglínyuàn was built north of Xuánwǔhú.
In the 22nd year of Yuánjiā of Wén Dì,
the northern dyke was built, and Xuánwǔhú was established north of Lèyóuyuàn.
16 In the beginning,
the Jìn people built the Altar of the Southern Suburbs at the sì position.
Xú Ái (徐爰), Right Assistant of the Department of State Affairs, considered this improper.
An imperial edict ordered it moved to the west of Niútóu Shān (牛頭山).
Niútóu Shān is located forty lǐ south of Shàngyuán County in present-day Jiànkāng Fǔ (建康府).
Its two peaks resemble watchtowers.
When the Deposed Emperor (Fèi Dì 廢帝) ascended the throne,
he deemed the old site auspicious
and restored it to its former location.
The Emperor also commanded Xún Wànqiū (荀萬秋), Left Assistant of the Department of State Affairs, to construct five carriages
modeled after the Jīngēn Chē (金根車),
adding feather canopies.
The design of the five carriages differed from the Jīngēn Chē,
and adding feather canopies
made it even more non-ancient.
Shěn Yuē (沈約) said: Qín (秦) reviewed the carriages of the Three Dynasties
and exclusively adopted the Yīn (殷) system.
In ancient times, it was called Sāngēn Chē (桑根車);
Qín called it Jīngēn Chē.
1 Spring,
first month,
on the jiǎzǐ day,
Wèi (魏) granted a general amnesty
and changed the era name to Hépíng (和平).
2 On the yǐhài day,
the Emperor personally plowed the ancestral fields,
and a general amnesty was granted.
3 On the jǐmǎo day,
an imperial edict ordered sacrifices to the suburban altars and ancestral temples,
for which the Yùlù (玉路) was used for the first time.
4 On the gēngyín day,
Imperial Prince Zǐxūn (子勛) was established as Jìn'ān Wáng (晉安王).
Xūn (勛)
is an ancient form of xūn (勳). Zǐxū (子頊) was established as Lìyáng Wáng (歷陽王).
Zǐluán (子鸞) was established as Xiāngyáng Wáng (襄陽王).
5 Féng Chǎn (馮闡), Cavalier Attendant-in-ordinary of Wèi, came as an envoy.
6 Second month,
Yuè'ān Wáng (樂安王) Liáng (良), Wèi General of the Guards, attacked the rebellious Hú (胡) in Hexī (河西).
Observing the text below where rebellious Hú submitted to Cháng'ān (長安) to confess their crimes,
this Hexī likely refers to the west bank of the river from Lóngmén (龍門) east to Huàyīn (華陰).
7 Third month,
Wèi people raided Běiyīnpíng (北陰平).
Yīnpíng (陰平) Dao,
during the Hàn (漢) dynasty, belonged to the Dūwèi (都尉) of Guǎnghàn (廣漢) Commandery.
During the Tàishǐ (泰始) era of Emperor Wǔ of Jìn (晉武帝),
it was divided to establish Yīnpíng Commandery.
Sòng (宋) further divided it to establish the two commanderies of Nányīnpíng (南陰平) and Běiyīnpíng.
The Wǔdài Zhì (五代志) says: Pǔ'ān (普安) Commandery had Yīnpíng County.
Sòng established Běiyīnpíng Commandery.
Sòng Bái (宋白) said: Wénzhōu (文州) Yīnpíng Commandery
was occupied by Dī (氐) and Qiāng (羌) during the Warring States period.
After Yǒngjiā (永嘉),
the Qiāng barbarians frequently rebelled,
so a commandery was established to curb them.
The Yúdì Zhì (輿地志) says: In the late Yǒngjiā era of Jìn,
Governor Wáng Jiàn (王鑒) surrendered the commandery to Lǐ Xióng (李雄).
The Jìn people were then all moved to Shǔ Hàn (蜀漢).
Its Dī and Qiāng all belonged to Yáng Màosōu (楊茂搜).
This commandery no longer received the orthodox calendar,
so the various records in Nánshǐ (南史) do not include it.
Those Jìn people who migrated to Shǔ (蜀)
still established two Yīnpíngs, South and North, in Yìzhōu (益州);
those who migrated to Hànzhōng (漢中)
also established two Yīnpíngs, South and North, in Liángzhōu (梁州).
Kǎoyì (考異) says: The Sòng Dìjì (宋帝紀) states:
"The Suǒ (索) barbarians raided Běiyīnpíng,
and Yáng Guīzǐ (楊歸子), Prefect of Kǒngtí (孔堤), defeated them."
The Sòng Lüè (宋略) says:
"The Suǒ barbarians raided Zhuàngjiàngpíng (壯降平),
and Prefect Yáng Guīzǐ defeated them."
According to county names, there is no
"Zhuàngjiàngpíng"
or
"Kǒngtí"
and
"Běiyīnpíng."
Comparing the two books,
it should be Zhūtí (朱提).
Now, according to Wèi Shōu's (魏收) Dìxíng Zhì (地形志),
Wǔdū (武都) Commandery has Kǒngtí County.
The Wǔdài Zhì says: Wǔdū Jiànwēi (建威) County,
later during the Western Wèi (西魏) and Hòu Zhōu (後周), Kǒngtí Commandery and County were merged into it.
At this time, the Wèi people probably raided Kǒngtí in Běiyīnpíng
and were defeated by Yáng Guīzǐ, Prefect of Běiyīnpíng.
We should follow the Sòng Jì.
Zhūtí Commandery is in Nánzhōng (南中),
at that time belonging to Níngzhōu (寧州),
very far from Yīnpíng.
Kǎoyì probably mistakenly combined the records in Sòng Jì and Sòng Lüè as Zhūtí.
It should be read as Kǒngtí,
belonging to the preceding sentence.
The so-called "Zhuàngjiàngpíng" in Sòng Lüè
is also a mistake for the three characters
"Běiyīnpíng";
the character "Zhū"
has nothing to attach to in the following text
and should be a superfluous character.
8 On the jiǎshēn day,
the Empress personally harvested mulberries in the western suburbs,
and the Empress Dowager observed the ceremony.
9 Summer,
fourth month,
Empress Dowager Cháng (常) of Wèi passed away.
She was originally the Preserving Empress Dowager and was honored as Empress Dowager;
see volume 127, Yuánjiā (元嘉) 30th year of Emperor Wén (文帝).
On the guǐchǒu day,
Wèi buried Empress Zhāo (昭) on Míngjī Shān (鳴雞山).
The Wèi Tǔdì Jì (魏土地記) says: Thirty lǐ northeast of Xiàluò (下洛) City is the Yánhé (延河),
flowing eastward,
with Míngjī Shān to the north.
The Shǐjì (史記) says: Zhào Xiāngzǐ (趙襄子) killed the King of Dài (代) at Xiàwū (夏屋).
His elder sister was the Queen of Dài.
Xiāngzǐ welcomed her.
When she arrived here,
she said:
"Dài has already perished;
where shall I go!"
Thereupon, she rubbed her hairpin on the mountain and committed suicide.
The Dài people pitied her
and established a shrine for her there,
thus naming it Mógēn Shān (磨筓山).
Every night, wild pheasants crowed on the roof of the King's shrine,
so it was also called Míngjī Shān.
Dù Yòu (杜佑) said: Guīzhōu (媯州) governed Huáiróng (懷戎) County,
which had Míngjī Shān,
originally named Mógēn Shān.
10 On the bǐngxū day,
Chǔ Zhànzhī (褚湛之), Left Grand Master of Remonstrance, passed away.
11 Tǔyùhún (吐谷渾) King Shíyín (拾寅) received titles from both Sòng and Wèi.
Tǔ (吐),
from tūn in entering tone.
Gǔ (谷),
pronounced yù.
When he was treated as a king,
the Wèi people were enraged.
Dìngyáng Hóu (定陽侯) Cáo Ān (曹安) reported:
"Shíyín now holds Báilán (白蘭).
If we divide our forces to strike his left and right,
he will surely flee to Nánshān (南山).
Within ten days, both people and livestock will lack food,
and he can be subdued in one swift action."
Sixth month,
on the jiǎwǔ day,
Wèi dispatched Zhēngxī Dàjiāngjūn (征西大將軍) Yángpíng Wáng (陽平王) Xīnchéng (新成) and others to lead the Tǒngwàn (統萬) and Gāopíng (高平) armies out on the southern route.
Nánjùn Gōng (南郡公) Zhōngshān (中山) Lǐ Huì (李惠) and others led the Liángzhōu (涼州) armies out on the northern route
to attack Tǔyùhún.
12 When Cuī Hào (崔浩) of Wèi was executed,
see volume 125, Yuánjiā 27th year of Emperor Wén of Sòng.
By this time, it was restored.
13 The rebellious Hú of Hexī went to Cháng'ān to confess their crimes.
The military might of Yuè'ān Wáng Liáng had pressured them,
hence their confession.
Shǒu (首),
pronounced shìyòu.
14 Autumn, seventh month,
envoys were sent to Wèi.
15 On the jiǎxū day,
Kāifǔ Yítóng Sānsī (開府儀同三司) Hé Shàngzhī (何尚之) passed away.
16 On the rénwǔ day,
the Wèi ruler went to Hexī.
17 The Wèi army reached Xīpíng (西平).
Xīpíng was the land of Hàn Luòdū (漢落都);
Luòdū, the capital of Tūfà (禿髮),
is also Luòdū;
during the Táng (唐) dynasty, it was Shànzhōu (鄯州).
Ninth month,
the Wèi army crossed the river to pursue them,
but encountered an epidemic
and retreated,
capturing over three hundred thousand
assorted livestock.
18 On the gēngwǔ day,
the Wèi ruler returned to Píngchéng (平城).
19 On the dīnghài day,
Imperial Prince Zǐluán of Xiāngyáng was moved to become Xīn'ān Wáng (新安王).
20 Winter,
tenth month,
on the gēngyín day,
an imperial edict ordered Shěn Qìngzhī (沈慶之) to suppress the Mán (蠻) tribes along the river.
Former Administrator of Lúlíng, Zhōu Lǎng,
spoke directly and forcefully about affairs,
as seen in Volume 127, during Emperor Wén’s Yuánjiā 30th year.
The emperor ordered the officials to impeach Lǎng for failing to observe the mourning rites for his mother properly.
He was sent to Níngzhōu
and killed on the way.
When Lǎng was setting off,
Attendant Cài Xīngzōng was on duty
and asked to bid Lǎng farewell.
He was consequently placed under house arrest (lit. made to wear white clothes and hold office).
Cài Xīngzōng, standing in a court full of suspicion and cruelty,
buried Fàn Yì
and bid farewell to Zhōu Lǎng,
defying the anger of the contemporary ruler without suffering punishment.
This was because his usual conduct had earned the trust of others.
In the eleventh month,
Wèi Cavalier Regular Attendant Lú Dùshì and others came to offer tribute.
That year,
the emperor summoned the Governors of Qīngzhōu and Jìzhōu, Yán Shībó, to be Attendant.
Shībó gained favor and trust through flattery and sycophancy;
no other sycophant could compare.
He accepted many bribes,
accumulating thousands of catties of gold in his family.
The emperor once played *chūpú* with him.
The emperor threw and got a *zhì*,
believing he would surely win.
Shībó then threw
and got a *lú*.
The *chūpú* dice throws are named: there are black calves (*hēidú*),
pheasants (*zhì*),
and *lú*.
Getting a *lú* means one wins.
Shībó hastily gathered the pieces and said:
"Almost a *lú*!"
*Zǐ*
refers to the five wooden pieces.
This was also one instance of Shībó's obsequiousness.
"Jī" (幾)
is pronounced *jī*.
Shībo once lost a million.
The Rouran attacked Gāochāng,
killed Jǔqú Ānzhōu,
and annihilated the Jǔqú clan.
In Emperor Wén’s Yuánjiā 16th year,
Wèi conquered Liángzhōu.
Jǔqú Wúhuì and his younger brother Ānzhōu fled west,
taking refuge in Gāochāng.
Now, it was destroyed by the Rouran.
"Jǔ" (沮)
is pronounced *jǔ*.
The kingship of Gāochāng began from this time.
In spring,
the first month,
on the *wùwǔ* day, the first day of the month,
there was the New Year's court assembly.
Snowflakes, six-pointed, fell on Grand Preceptor Yìgōng’s clothes.
Yìgōng reported it as an auspicious omen,
and the emperor was pleased.
Yìgōng, fearing the emperor's suspicious and tyrannical nature and his inability to secure his own position,
always used humble words and submissive expressions,
bending his will to serve respectfully.
Because of this, throughout the emperor's reign,
he was able to avoid misfortune.
In the second month,
on the *xīnmǎo* day,
the Wèi ruler traveled to Zhōngshān.
On the *bǐngwǔ* day,
he arrived in Yè,
and then proceeded to Xìndū.
In the third month,
an envoy was sent to Wèi.
The Wèi ruler conscripted five thousand people from Bīngzhōu and Sìzhōu to repair the Hexi hunting path.
In Wèi Dàowǔ's Tiāncì 2nd year,
the northern part of Bīngzhōu was divided to establish the Jiǔyuán Garrison. In Tàiwǔ's Zhēnjūn 7th year,
Sìzhōu was established.
Sòng Bái said: The *Shísānzhōuzhì* records that at the end of the Hàn dynasty, during the great chaos,
the Xiongnu invaded the border.
From Dìngxiāng westward,
including all of Yúnzhōng and Yànmén,
it became deserted.
Cáo Gōng gathered households from the desolate commanderies
and settled them in the Jiǔyuán area to establish Xīnxīng Commandery,
administering counties like Wǔyuán.
This is the land of Dìngxiāng County in Táng’s Xīnzhōu.
The *Hòuwèishū* states: In Tàipíng 2nd year,
Sìzhōu was established,
its administration provisionally located in Xiùróng City.
Xiùróng County,
where Xīnzhōu's administration was located,
was the Jiǔyuán County established at the end of the Hàn dynasty.
"Zhì" (治)
is pronounced *zhì*.
On the *xīnsì* day,
he returned to Píngchéng.
In summer,
the fourth month,
on the *guǐsì* day,
Zǐshàng, Prince of Xīyáng, was again made Prince of Yùzhāng.
On the *gēngzǐ* day,
an imperial edict ordered the commencement of construction of the Míngtáng,
directly building a grand hall in the *bǐngjǐ* direction.
Its design was like the Grand Ancestral Temple,
with the only difference being its twelve bays.
Yōngzhōu Governor Hǎilíng Prince Xiūmào,
aged seventeen,
had the Commissioner, Yǔ Shēnzhī of Xīnyě, acting as the Administrator of the Prefecture.
Xiūmào was impetuous
and wished to make decisions independently.
Shēnzhī and the chief attendant (*zhǔshuài*) repeatedly restrained him.
*Zhǔshuài*
refers to the *diǎnqiān*.
There was also a *zhǔshuài* within the inner quarters,
called the *zhāishuài*.
"Shuài" (帥)
is pronounced *shuài*.
His retainer Zhāng Bóuchāo was favored
and committed many misdeeds,
for which the chief attendant repeatedly reprimanded him.
Bóuchāo, fearing this,
persuaded Xiūmào, saying:
"The chief attendant is secretly documenting your shortcomings
and intends to report them.
If this happens, I fear it will not end well."
Xiūmào asked:
"What should be done?"
Bóuchāo replied:
"The only option is to kill the acting administrator (*xíngshì*) and the chief attendant.
*Xíngshì*
refers to Yǔ Shēnzhī.
South of the Yangtze, *chángshǐ* and *sīmǎ* who acted as administrators of prefectures were generally called *xíngshì*.
This place is thousands of *lǐ* from the capital.
Yōngzhōu's seat is Xiāngyáng,
over four thousand *lǐ* by water from Jiànkāng.
We could even escape into the barbarian territory and become a king."
Xiūmào agreed.
On the night of the *bǐngwǔ* day,
Xiūmào, with Bóuchāo and others, led the *jiágǔduì* (imperial guards).
Some princes of Sòng had *jiágǔduì*,
which were likely close personal guards who would escort the carriage.
"Shuài" (帥)
is read as *shuài*;
similarly below.
They emerged from Jīnchéng,
killed Shēnzhī and the *diǎnqiān* Dài Shuāng,
summoned and gathered troops,
raised their banners, sent out urgent proclamations,
and made their subordinate officials declare him General of Chariots and Cavalry (*Chēqí Dàjiàngjūn*),
opening a residence with ceremonies equal to the Three Revered Ones (*Kāifǔ Yítóng Sānsī*),
and adding the Yellow Axe (*Huángyuè*).
All prefectural and state officials were called *zuǒlì*.
"Shàng" (上)
is pronounced *shàng*.
"Qí" (騎)
is pronounced *qí*.
Xiūmào killed them.
Bóuchāo monopolized military and political power,
with life and death in his hands.
Xiūmào’s attendant Cáo Wànqī bravely attacked Xiūmào with a sword,
but failed and died.
Xiūmào left the city to establish a camp,
but Advisory Counselor Shěn Chàngzhī and others led the populace to close the gates and resist him.
Xiūmào rushed back
but could not enter.
Yìchéng Administrator Xuē Jìkǎo exerted himself for Xiūmào, attacking the city.
He conquered it,
and beheaded Chàngzhī and dozens of co-conspirators.
On that same day,
Counselor Yǐn Xuánqìng again raised troops to attack Xiūmào.
He was captured alive
and beheaded.
His mother and wife both committed suicide,
and his associates were executed.
The city was in chaos,
with no one to oversee and control.
Middle Army Counselor Liú Gōngzhī,
younger brother of Xiùzhī,
(Liú Xiùzhī, in Xiàojiàn 1st year, did not side with Yìxuān,
and was then Minister of the Right, Executive of the Department of State Affairs.)
Jìkǎo coerced Gōngzhī with soldiers
to write a memorial,
stating that
"Jìkǎo established righteousness,"
and then returned to the capital by express post himself.
The emperor appointed him Advisory Counselor of the Northern Central Army,
and granted him the title Marquis of Guànjūn.
The truth of the matter was soon revealed,
and he was executed.
Xuánqìng was made Commander of the Shooting Sound Guards.
Since the Emperor ascended the throne,
he had suppressed and demoted his younger brothers.
After conquering Guǎnglíng,
he wished to make the regulations even stricter.
Shěn Huáiwén said:
“Emperor Míng of Hàn did not allow his sons to be compared with the sons of Emperor Guāngwǔ,
and former historians regarded this as a beautiful story.
See Volume 45, Emperor Míng of Hàn, Yǒngpíng 15th year.
I wish to uphold the entrustment of Táng and Wèi.”
After King Chéng of Zhōu executed Guǎnshū
and imprisoned Càishū,
he enfeoffed Shūyú in Táng
and Kāngshū in Wèi,
to serve as a protective screen for the Zhōu dynasty.
Tàizǎi Yìgōng, having divined the Emperor's intention,
requested to restrict the various princes,
not allowing them to govern border prefectures,
and to confiscate all their weapons and armor,
and forbid them from receiving guests.
Shěn Huáiwén firmly remonstrated that this was unacceptable,
and so it was stopped.
8 The Emperor indulged in hunting and excursions without restraint.
Once, he went out
and returned at night,
ordering the city gate to be opened.
Shìzhōng Xiè Zhuāng, who was in charge of guarding,
, considering that the authentication token might be false,
refused to obey the order,
insisting that it would only be opened upon receipt of a written imperial edict.
Mòchì (墨敕)
means a handwritten imperial edict.
Calmly, he said:
“Does Your Majesty wish to emulate Zhì Jūnzhāng?”
Zhì Yùn,
whose courtesy name was Jūnzhāng.
The details are in Volume 43, Emperor Guāngwǔ of Hàn, Jiànwǔ 13th year.
Cóng (從),
read as qiān róng.
“I have heard that a ruler's sacrifices, hunting, and excursions,
and his comings and goings, should be regulated.
Now Your Majesty departs in the morning and returns at night,
Xiāo (宵)
means night.
giving rise to arbitrary deceptions.
Therefore, I humbly awaited the imperial handwritten decree
before daring to open the gate.”
9 There was a great drought in Wèi.
An imperial edict stated:
“Within the jurisdiction of all prefectures and commanderies,
all deities, great and small,
shall have their temples swept and prayers offered.
Await abundant harvest,
and then each shall be sacrificed to according to their rank.”
Thereupon, all abandoned common sacrifices were restored to their former state.
The abolition of common sacrifices in Wèi
is recorded in Volume 124, Emperor Wén, Yuánjiā 27th year.
10 In autumn,
in the seventh month,
on the day Wùyín,
the Wèi ruler enfeoffed his younger brother Xiǎo Xīnchéng as Prince of Jìyáng,
In Dàmíng 1st year,
the Wèi ruler enfeoffed his younger brother Xīnchéng as Prince of Yángpíng.
This Xiǎo Xīnchéng
was also the younger brother of the Prince of Yángpíng.
Jì (濟),
read as zǐ lǐ.
and garrisoned Píngyuán.
Píngyuán
was a strategic point on the Yellow River ferry.
At that time, Wèi had not yet acquired Qīng and Qí,
hence a garrison was established here.
He was given the additional title of Grand General of the South-Subduing Army,
and garrisoned Hǔláo.
Hǔláo was the former garrison of Sòng,
and the seat of government for the Cìshǐ of Sīzhōu.
After Wèi acquired it,
they established Sūnzhōu.
He was given the additional title of Grand General of the North-Subduing Army,
and garrisoned Hélóng.
Hélóng was the former capital of Yān,
which Wèi acquired
and established as a garrison.
Later it became Yíngzhōu.
Lèlàng,
pronounced Luò Láng.
11 On the day Rénwǔ,
the Wèi ruler toured the mountains north of the capital.
In the eighth month,
on the day Dīngchǒu,
he returned to Píngchéng.
12 On the day Wùzǐ,
Imperial Prince Zǐrén was enfeoffed as Prince of Yǒngjiā,
and Zǐzhēn as Prince of Shǐ'ān.
13 In the ninth month,
on Jiǎyín shuò,
there was a solar eclipse.
14 Shěn Qìngzhī firmly declined the position of Sīkōng,
and Liǔ Yuánjǐng firmly declined the position of Kāifǔ Yítóng Sānsī.
An imperial edict permitted this.
It was further decreed that Qìngzhī's position in court assemblies would rank next to Sīkōng,
his emolument would be equivalent to that of the Sānsī,
and Yuánjǐng would rank above the Cónggōng.
According to the Jìn system: for civil officials, Guānglù Sāndàfū;
for military officials, Piàojì, Chējì, Wèi Jiāngjūn, and other Grand Generals who held Kāifǔ,
their rank was Cónggōng.
Cóng (從),
read as cóng yòng.
Qìngzhī was illiterate,
but his family was inherently wealthy.
His property amounted to tens of thousands of gold,
and he had thousands of servants and slaves.
He twice presented ten million cash
and ten thousand hú of grain.
He already owned four residences
and also had a garden estate in Lóuhú.
According to the Nánshǐ, Emperor Wǔ of Qí, Yǒngmíng 1st year,
a diviner of qi said: “East of Xīnlín, Lóuhú, and west of Dōngfǔ, there is imperial qi.”
On the day Jiǎzǐ of the first month,
the old Qīngxī Palace was rebuilt,
and the new Lóuhú Garden was constructed to suppress it.
Thus, Lóuhú must have been between Xīnlín and Dōngfǔ.
He moved his children, grandchildren, and maternal and paternal relatives to Lóuhú,
and surrendered his four residences to the government.
Qìngzhī kept many courtesans and concubines,
living a leisurely and carefree life,
indulging fully in pleasure and amusement.
He would not leave his house except for court audiences and greetings.
His carriages and horses were simple,
and his retinue did not exceed three to five people.
Those who met him would not know that he was one of the Sāngōng.
The 15th day of the cyclical designation *jiǎxū* (甲戌).
The seat of the Southern Yùzhōu (南豫州) administration was moved to Hú (湖).
Shěn Yuē's (沈約) *Sòng Zhì* (宋志) states: During the Jìn (晉) dynasty, when the Hu (胡) barbarians on the left bank of the Jiāng (江) became powerful,
the Yù (豫) region was annihilated and overrun.
In the first year of Yǒngchāng (永昌) of Emperor Yuán (元帝),
Zǔ Yuē (祖約), the Inspector of Yùzhōu (豫州 Cìshǐ), retreated from Qiáochéng (譙城) to garrison Shòuchūn (壽春).
In the fourth year of Xiánhé (咸和) of Emperor Chéng (成帝),
a provisional Yùzhōu (豫州) was established,
and Yǔ Liàng (庾亮) was appointed its Inspector,
garrisoning Wúhú (蕪湖).
In the fourth year of Xiánkāng (咸康),
Máo Bǎo (毛寶) was appointed Inspector,
garrisoning Zhūchéng (邾城).
In the eighth year,
Yǔ Yì (庾懌) was appointed Inspector,
again garrisoning Wúhú (蕪湖).
In the first year of Yǒnghé (永和) of Emperor Mù (穆帝),
Inspector Zhào Yìn (趙胤) garrisoned Niúzhǔ (牛渚).
In the second year,
Inspector Xiè Shàng (謝尚) garrisoned Wúhú (蕪湖);
in the fourth year,
he advanced to garrison Shòuchūn (壽春);
in the ninth year,
he returned to garrison Lìyáng (歷陽);
in the eleventh year, he advanced to Mǎtóu (馬頭).
In the first year of Shēngpíng (升平),
Inspector Xiè Yì (謝奕) was stationed at Qiáo (譙).
In the first year of Lónghé (隆和) of Emperor Āi (哀帝),
Inspector Yuán Zhēn (袁真) retreated from Qiáo (譙) to defend Shòuchūn (壽春).
In the first year of Xián'ān (咸安) of Emperor Jiǎnwén (簡文),
Inspector Huán Xī (桓熙) was stationed at Lìyáng (歷陽).
In the first year of Níngkāng (寧康) of Emperor Xiàowǔ (孝武),
Inspector Huán Chōng (桓沖) was stationed at Gūshú (姑孰).
In the tenth year of Tàiyuán (太元),
Inspector Zhū Xù (朱序) was stationed at Mǎtóu (馬頭).
In the twelfth year,
Inspector Huán Shíqián (桓石虔) was stationed at Lìyáng (歷陽).
In the second year of Yìxī (義熙) of Emperor Ān (安帝),
Inspector Liú Yì (劉毅) was stationed at Gūshú (姑孰).
Emperor Wǔ (武帝) of Sòng (宋) wished to expand into Hénán (河南)
and pacify the lands of Yù (豫).
In the ninth year,
the areas west of the Great River and
north of Dàléi (大雷), which belonged to Yángzhōu (揚州), were all
assigned to Yùzhōu (豫州),
thus establishing the foundation of Yù (豫).
In the thirteenth year,
Inspector Liú Yìqìng (劉義慶) garrisoned Shòuyáng (壽陽).
In the second year of Yǒngchū (永初),
the area east of the Huái (淮) was divided to form Southern Yùzhōu (南豫州),
with its seat at Lìyáng (歷陽);
the area west of the Huái (淮) remained Yùzhōu (豫州).
In the seventh year of Yuánjiā (元嘉) of Emperor Wén (文帝),
it was again divided...
In the fifth year,
Huáinán (淮南) of Yángzhōu (揚州) was partitioned,
Xuānchéng (宣城) was also made subordinate to it,
and its administrative seat was moved to Gūshú (姑孰).
Now, according to the records, from the Yuán (元) dynasty of Sòng (宋) onwards,
two Yùzhōu (豫州) administrations were established: Yùzhōu (豫州) governed Huáixī (淮西),
and Southern Yùzhōu (南豫州) governed Shòuyáng (壽陽).
At the beginning of Xiàojiàn (孝建),
Lǔ Shuǎng (魯爽) was the Inspector of Southern Yùzhōu (南豫州), garrisoning Shòuyáng (壽陽),
which clearly indicates this.
The relocation of Southern Yùzhōu (南豫州) to Gūshú (姑孰)
actually occurred in the fifth year of Dàmíng (大明).
From Yǒngchū (永初) to the seventh year of Yuánjiā (元嘉),
the two Yùzhōu (豫zhōu) must have been reunited;
and what is referred to as
"in the fifth year, Huáinán (淮南) of Yángzhōu (揚州) was partitioned,
Xuānchéng (宣城) was also made subordinate to it,
and its administrative seat was moved to Gūshú (姑孰)"
must
refer to the fifth year of Emperor Xiàowǔ's (孝武) Dàmíng (大明) reign.
Later scribes of Shěn (沈) had,
in the context of
"in the seventh year of Yuánjiā (元嘉) of Emperor Wén (文帝), it was again divided,"
omitted parts of the text both above and below.
As for Liú Yìqìng (劉義慶) garrisoning Shòuyáng (壽陽), the *Tōngjiàn* (通鑑) places it in the fourteenth year of Yìxī (義熙);
the abolition of Southern Yùzhōu (南豫州) by incorporating it into Yùzhōu (豫zhōu)
was in the twenty-second year of Yuánjiā (元嘉).
The *dīngchǒu* (丁丑) day:
Zǐfáng (子房), Prince of Xúnyáng (潯陽), was appointed Inspector of Southern Yùzhōu (南豫州).
The 16th day of the intercalary month,
*wùzǐ* (戊子):
Crown Prince Hé Shì (何氏) passed away,
and was posthumously granted the epithet Xiàn (獻).
The 17th day of the cyclical designation *rén'yín* (壬寅):
Zǐxù (子頊), Prince of Lìyáng (歷陽), was again appointed Prince of Línhǎi (臨海).
*Kǎo Yì* (考異) states: *Sòng Lüè* (宋略) writes
"Zǐxiàng" (子項);
here we follow *Sòng Shū* (宋書).
In winter,
the tenth month,
on the *jiǎyín* (甲寅) day:
Liú Yánsūn (劉延孫), Inspector of Southern Xúzhōu (南徐州), was appointed Shàngshū Zuǒpúshè (尚書左僕射).
Liú Xiùzhī (劉秀之), Rìpúshè (右僕射), was appointed Inspector of Yōngzhōu (雍州).
On the *yǐmǎo* (乙卯) day:
Zǐluán (子鸞), Prince of Xīn'ān (新安), was appointed Inspector of Southern Xúzhōu (南徐州).
Zǐluán's (子鸞) mother, Consort Yīn (殷淑儀),
held the emperor's favor more than anyone else in the harem,
and Zǐluán (子鸞) was loved above all other sons.
Whatever was favored by the emperor
would be transferred to Zǐluán's (子鸞) household.
When he became Inspector of Southern Xúzhōu (南徐州),
Wújùn (吳郡) was partitioned and subordinated to him.
Since the Jìn (晉) clan crossed the Jiāng (江), Wújùn (吳郡) had belonged to Yángzhōu (揚zhōu)
and was the most important county near the capital.
Previously,
Xiūruò (休若), Prince of Bālíng (巴陵), was Inspector of Northern Xúzhōu (北徐州).
He appointed Zhāng Dài (張岱) of Shānyīn (山陰) as Cányì Cānjūn (諮議參軍),
acting concurrently as Administrator of the Prefecture, Province, and Principality.
When young princes assumed provincial governorships,
they usually appointed acting administrators for the prefecture and province.
This appointment made Dài (岱) concurrently administer the affairs of Bālíng (巴陵) Principality.
Zǐshàng (子尚), Prince of Yùzhāng (豫章), governed Yángzhōu (揚州);
Zǐxūn (子勛), Prince of Jìn'ān (晉安), governed Southern Yǎnzhōu (南兗州).
Dài (岱) successively served as Cányì (諮議) for these three prefectures and as acting administrator for the three princes,
working with the *diǎnqiān* (典籤) and chief officers.
Tasks were accomplished, and personal relations were not strained.
Someone said to Dài (岱):
"Since the main prince is young,
and ever since the Jìn (晉) crossed the Jiāng (江),
when princes were sent out to govern provinces,
their subordinates addressed them as 'main prince,'
and the various dukes,
their prefectural officials addressed them as 'main duke.'
Yet you are always able to harmonize public and private affairs."
"Jī" (緝)
is also written as
Dài (岱) said:
"The ancients said, 'With one mind, one can serve a hundred rulers.'
My governance is fair and just,
and I treat others with propriety.
Occasions for regret or remorse
have no way to arise;
as for intelligence, dimness, strengths, and weaknesses,
these are merely a matter of one's talent and capacity."
When Zǐluán (子鸞) became Inspector of Southern Xúzhōu (南徐州),
Dài (岱) was again appointed Biéjià (別駕) and acting administrator.
Dài (岱) was the younger brother of Yǒng (永).
Yóu Mínggēn (游明根) and others, members of the Wèi (魏) Yuánwài Sànqí Chángshì (員外散騎常侍), came to offer tribute.
Mínggēn (明根) was a paternal cousin of Yǎ (雅).
Luòhóu (洛侯), Prince of Guǎngpíng (廣平) of Wèi (魏), passed away.
In the twelfth month,
on the *rénshēn* (壬申) day:
Liú Zūnkǎo (劉遵考), Lǐngjūn Jiāngjūn (領軍將軍), was appointed Shàngshū Yòupúshè (尚書右僕射).
On the *jiǎxū* (甲戌) day:
A decree mandated that civilian households annually pay four bolts of cloth.
In this year,
an imperial edict ordered that all gentry who intermarried
with commoners be appointed as generals and officials.
"Intermarriage" (雜婚) refers to marriage with merchants, artisans, and other common households.
"Jiāng" (將) is pronounced *liàng*.
A strict regulation was enacted,
stating that anyone caught would be immediately executed.
Many fled to the lakes and mountains to become bandits.
They would enter lakes by water
and block mountain roads by land,
all relying on treacherous terrain to act as bandits.
It was not heeded.
In spring,
the first month,
on the *guǐwèi* (癸未) day:
Wànshòu (萬壽), Prince of Lèlang (樂浪) of Wèi (魏), passed away.
On the *xīnmǎo* (辛卯) day:
The emperor for the first time offered sacrifices to the Five Emperors in the Míngtáng (明堂),
and a general amnesty was declared.
On the *dīngwèi* (丁未) day:
Talents (xiùcái, 秀才) and Filial and Incorrupt (xiàolián, 孝廉) were examined in the Central Hall.
"Xiù" (秀) and "xiào" (孝) refer to *xiùcái* (秀才) and *xiàolián* (孝廉).
"If the source is clear, the stream will be pure;
if the gods are holy, punishments will be complete.
Transforming oneself is easier than influencing the wind from above;
moral instruction spreads faster than grass bending."
The meaning of Gù Fǎ's (顧法) reply in the examination
was to wish the emperor to be circumspect in his personal conduct within the palace and among his concubines,
so that he could transform the world.
"Yì" (易) is pronounced *shì*.
He disliked its "liàng" (諒).
Xǔ Shèn's (許慎) *Shuōwén* (說文) states: "Liàng" (諒)
means trustworthiness.
No scholar explaining the Classics could change this meaning.
Here, it should be understood as "honest and straightforward."
Consulting the Classics,
"straight" (直) is indeed "straight,"
and "trustworthy" (諒) is indeed "trustworthy."
"Wù" (惡)
is pronounced *wūlù*.
4 In the second month,
on the *yǐmǎo* day,
the salaries of all officials were restored.
In the twenty-seventh year of Emperor Wén's Yuánjiā era,
due to military expenses, the salaries of all officials, both central and local, were reduced by one-third;
subsequently, the state faced internal troubles,
leaving no time to attend to this matter.
Now, the salaries of all officials were finally restored.
5 In the third month,
on the *gēngyín* day,
Imperial Prince Zǐyuán was established as the Prince of Shàolíng.
6 Initially,
Grandee Secretary Shěn Huáiwén
frequently offended the emperor with his direct remonstrances.
Shěn Huáiwén had always been on good terms with Yán Jùn and Zhōu Lǎng.
The emperor said to Shěn Huáiwén:
"If Yán Jùn knew I would kill him,
he still wouldn't dare act like this."
Shěn Huáiwén remained silent.
Grandee Secretary Wáng Yù,
during a conversation, praised the talents of Yán Jùn and Zhōu Lǎng.
Shěn Huáiwén echoed his sentiments.
Yán Shībó reported this to the emperor,
which made the emperor even more displeased.
The emperor once went out hunting pheasants.
Since the Cao Wèi dynasty,
rulers typically enjoyed hunting pheasants themselves.
(*shè*,
also pronounced *fān*.)
Shěn Huáiwén, Wáng Yù, and Jiāng Zhìyuān agreed to remonstrate together.
When summoned into the pheasant field,
Shěn Huáiwén said:
"With such wind and rain,
it is not suitable for Your Sacred Person to be exposed."
Wáng Yù said:
"What Shěn Huáiwén has suggested
should be followed."
Before Jiāng Zhìyuān could speak,
the emperor aimed his crossbow and said with a stern expression:
"Do you wish to emulate Yán Jùn?
Why do you always know everything about others' affairs!"
He also said:
"That young scoundrel Yán Jùn,
I regret not having whipped his face sooner!"
Whenever the emperor held a banquet,
all those present were made to get thoroughly drunk,
and their jesting and mockery knew no bounds.
Shěn Huáiwén never drank alcohol
and did not enjoy playful teasing.
The emperor believed he deliberately sought to be different.
Xiè Zhuāng once warned Shěn Huáiwén:
"You are always different from others;
how can this last long!"
Shěn Huáiwén replied:
"I have been like this since I was young;
how can I change overnight!
It is not that I wish to be different;
it is my nature."
The emperor then exiled Shěn Huáiwén, making him the Chief Clerk to Zǐxūn, Prince of Jìn'ān, who held the title of General Who Subdues the Barbarians.
Zǐxūn held the title of General Who Subdues the Barbarians,
so Shěn Huáiwén was his Chief Clerk.
Zǐxūn was stationed in Nányǎnzhōu,
thus Shěn Huáiwén, as Chief Clerk, also held the position of Administrator of Guǎnglíng.
When Shěn Huáiwén went to Jiànkāng for the New Year's court assembly,
("going to court,"
means attending the New Year's court assembly.)
(*cháo*,
pronounced *zhíyáo*.)
he requested an extension due to his daughter's illness.
(*shēn*,
means "repeat";
*shēnqī*,
means to set a new date.)
He was dismissed from
office
and forbidden from holding official posts for ten years.
Shěn Huáiwén sold his residence,
intending to return east.
(Shěn Huáiwén
was from Wúxìng;
Wúxìng is east of Jiànkāng.)
The emperor was greatly enraged
and had him arrested and handed over to the Grand Judge.
On the *dīngwèi* day,
Shěn Huáiwén was granted death.
Shěn Huáiwén's three sons,
Dàn, Yuān, and Chōng,
cried and pleaded for their father's life as they walked,
moving those who saw them.
Liǔ Yuánjǐng wanted to save Shěn Huáiwén
and said to the emperor:
"Shěn Huáiwén's three sons
are in a state of utter misery, unbearable to behold;
(*jiàn*,
means "to see";
it means they are in such a state of utter misery
that one cannot bear to look at them.)
Those who speak of swiftly punishing his crime
are subtly guiding you,
suggesting that if his crime is duly punished,
it should not lead to death."
7 In the summer,
the fourth month,
Shúyí Yīn passed away.
(*Kǎoyì* says: *Nánshǐ* states: Shúyí Yīn
was the daughter of Yìxuān, Prince of Nánjùn;
after Yìxuān's defeat,
the emperor secretly took her,
assigning her the surname Yīn;
many who revealed this secret were put to death.
Some say
she was a servant of Yīn Yǎn's family,
entered Yìxuān's household,
and after Yìxuān's defeat,
entered the palace.
Now following *Sòngshū*.)
She was posthumously named Xuān.
The emperor grieved uncontrollably,
his mind becoming bewildered,
(*wǎngwǎng*,
means to be disoriented,
as if existing and not existing.)
(*wéi*,
pronounced *yúwěi*.)
8 In the fifth month,
on the *rén yín* day,
Grand Tutor Yìgōng was relieved of his concurrent post as Minister of Works.
9 In the sixth month,
on the *xīnyǒu* day,

They ran from Chānghémén (閶闔門) to Zhūquèmén (朱雀門),
and also from Chéngmíngmén (承明門) to Xuánwǔhú (玄武湖).
They were restored to the Yuanjiā (元嘉) system.
Cài Xīngzōng (蔡興宗), a Grand Minister (Shàngshū), lamented at the Metropolitan Office (Dūzuò) and said to Yán Shībó (顏師伯):
This "Dūzuò"
refers to the place where the Eight Grand Ministers (Shàngshū Bāzuò) would meet,
similar to today's metropolitan hall (dūtáng).
"Although the late Emperor was not a ruler of great virtue,
he did adhere to the Way from beginning to end.
'Three years without change'
is what is valued in classical texts.
The *Lúnyǔ* (論語) says: 'If for three years he does not alter the ways of his father, he may be called filial.'
The imperial mausoleum is not yet distant,
yet all institutions and constructions,
regardless of their merits,
have been entirely abolished.
Even during a dynastic change,
it would not reach such an extent.
The discerning people of the realm
will judge others by this."
Shībó did not agree.
Tàizǎi Yìgōng (太宰義恭) had always feared Dài Fǎxīng (戴法興), Cháo Shàngzhī (巢尚之), and others.
Although he received the dying Emperor's charge to assist in government,
he withdrew himself and avoided involvement,
thus power devolved to the Emperor's close attendants.
Fǎxīng and others monopolized court authority,
wielding influence far and wide,
and all imperial decrees (zhàochì) originated from them.
All matters, great and small, concerning the Grand Ministers (Shàngshū)
were decided by them.
Yìgōng and Yán Shībó merely held empty titles.
Yìgōng was recorded as overseeing the Grand Ministers' affairs (Lù Shàngshūshì),
and Shībó served as Imperial Secretary (Púyè),
but the Grand Ministers' affairs were decided by Fǎxīng and others,
which is why they held empty titles.
Cài Xīngzōng (蔡興宗) considered his own position to be in charge of selection and evaluation.
Xīngzōng was the Minister of Personnel (Lìbù Shàngshū).
He frequently presented Yìgōng with proposals for promoting worthy scholars,
and also offered admonitions on successes and failures,
discussing court policies broadly.
Yìgōng was by nature timid and weak.
*Kuāng* (恇)
means timid.
*Náo* (撓)
means yielding.
*Kuāng* (恇),
pronounced *qùwáng fān*.
*Náo* (撓),
pronounced *nújiāo fān*.
He constantly worried about displeasing the Emperor.
When he heard Xīngzōng's words,
he would tremble with fear and offer no reply.
Whenever Xīngzōng presented selection matters,
Fǎxīng, Shàngzhī, and others would immediately mark them for alteration or replacement,
with only a few remaining as originally proposed.
Xīngzōng said to Yìgōng and Shībó in the court hall:
"The Emperor is in mourning (liàng'àn)
and does not personally attend to all affairs of state;
yet secret matters of selection
are largely deleted or altered,
and they are not even written by you, sir.
We do not know whose imperial will (tiānzǐ yì) this is!"
He frequently argued with Yìgōng and others over selection matters,
engaging in repeated debates.
Yìgōng and Fǎxīng both disliked him.
Xīngzōng was demoted to Administrator of Xīnchāng (Xīnchāng Tàishǒu).
In the third year of Jiànhéng (建衡) of Sūn Hào (孫晧) of Wú,
Xīnxīng Commandery (Xīnxīng Jùn) was established by dividing Jiāozhǐ (交趾).
In the third year of Tàikāng (太康) of Jìn Wǔdì,
it was renamed Xīnchāng Commandery (Xīnchāng Jùn),
belonging to Jiāozhōu (交州).
The *Wǔdài Zhì* (五代志) states: Jiāoníng County (Jiāoníng Xiàn) in Jiāozhōu
previously had Xīnchāng Commandery established there.
He was then retained in Jiànkāng (建康).
On the 12th day, *bǐngchén*,
Lady Hé (Hé) was posthumously honored as Empress Xiàn (Xiàn Huánghòu).
Lady Hé
had died in the fifth year of Dàmíng (大明).
On the 13th day, *yǐchǒu*,
Wáng Zǐluán (王子鸞), Prince of Xīn'ān (Xīn'ān), was relieved of his post as Grand Minister of War (Sītú).
Dài Fǎxīng (戴法興) and others disliked Wáng Xuánmó (王玄謨) for his sternness and integrity.
In the eighth month,
on the day *dīngmǎo*,
Xuánmó was made Inspector of Nánxúzhōu (Nánxúzhōu Cìshǐ).
The Empress Dowager Wáng (Wáng Tàihòu) was gravely ill
and sent for the deposed Emperor.
The Emperor said:
"Sick people's rooms are full of ghosts,
how can I go!"
The Empress Dowager was enraged
and said to her attendants:
"Bring me a knife,
I will cut open my belly,
how could I have given birth to such a child!"
On the day *jǐchǒu*,
the Empress Dowager passed away.
In the ninth month,
on the day *xīnchǒu*,
the Wei ruler (Wèi Zhǔ) returned to Píngchéng (平城).
He returned from west of the Yellow River.
On the 16th day, *guǐmǎo*,
Liú Zūnkǎo (劉遵考), the Left Imperial Secretary (Shàngshū Zuǒ Púyè), was appointed Grand Master of Splendid Happiness (Tèjìn) and Right Grand Minister of the Household (Yòu Guānglù Dàfū).
On the 17th day, *yǐmǎo*,
Empress Wénmù (Wénmù Huánghòu) was buried in Jǐngníng Líng (景寧陵).
Since Empress Wáng (Wáng Hòu) followed the posthumous title of Emperor Xiaowǔ (Xiàowǔ Dì),
it should be "Wǔmù" (武穆).
In winter,
in the twelfth month,
on the day *rénchén*,
the commanderies within the royal domain (wángjī) were made Yángzhōu (揚州).
In the third year of Dàmíng (大明),
six commanderies, including Dānyáng (丹楊), were designated as the royal domain.
Kuàijī (會稽) was made Yángzhōu (揚zhou),
also seen in the third year.
On the day *guǐsì*,
Wáng Zǐshàng (王子尚), Prince of Yùzhāng (Yùzhāng), was appointed Grand Minister of War (Sītú) and Inspector of Yángzhōu (Yángzhōu Cìshǐ).
In this year,
Qīngzhōu (青州) moved its seat of government to Dōngyáng (東陽).
Qīngzhōu (青州) moved its seat of government to Lìchéng (歷城),
as seen in the previous scroll, the third year of Xiàojiàn.
Within Sòng's borders,
there were twenty-two zhōu,
two hundred seventy-four jùn,
one thousand two hundred ninety-nine xiàn,
and nine hundred forty thousand households with an excess.
This is roughly based on Shěn Yuè's Sòng Zhì.
When Shěn Yuè compiled the Zhì,
it was roughly based on this year as accurate.
However, in this year there were only twenty-one zhōu.
The twenty-two zhōu mentioned in Shěn Zhì
were achieved by dividing Jiāo and Guǎng to establish Yuè Zhōu in the seventh year of Míng Dì's Tàishǐ era;
but at this time, Sī Zhōu had already been abolished.
Thus, there were indeed only twenty-one zhōu.
Yáng Zhōu governed Dānyáng, Wúxīng, Huáinán, Xuānchéng, and Yìxīng, five jùn.
Dōngyáng Zhōu governed Kuàijī, Dōngyáng, Línhǎi, Yǒngjiā, and Xīn'ān, five jùn.

Nánxú Zhōu governed Nándōnghǎi, Nánlángyé, Jìnlíng, Wú, Nánlánlíng, Nándōngguǎn, Huáilíng, Línhuái, Nánpéngchéng, Nánqīnghé, Nángāopíng, Nánpíngchāng, Nánjìyīn, Nánpúyáng, Nántàishān, Jìyáng, and Nánlǔjùn, seventeen jùn.
Xú Zhōu governed Péngchéng, Pèi, Xiàpī, Lánlíng, Dōnghǎi, Dōngguǎn, Dōng'ān, Lángyé, Yángpíng, Jìyīn, and Běijìyīn, twelve jùn.
Nányǎn Zhōu governed Guǎnglíng, Hǎilíng, Shānyáng, Xūyí, Qín Jùn, Nánpèi, Zhōnglí, Běipèi, and Línjiāng, nine jùn.
Yǎn Zhōu governed Tàishān, Gāopíng, Lǔ, Dōngpíng, Yángpíng, and Jìběi, six jùn.

Nányù Zhōu governed Lìyáng, Nánqiáo, Lújiāng, Nánruyīn, Nánliáng, Jìnxī, Yìyáng, Ānfēng, Nánrunán, Nánxīncài, Dōng Jùn, Nányǐng, Nányǐngchuān, Xīruyīn, Nánruyáng, Nánchénliú, Nánchén Zuǒjùn, Biānchéng Zuǒjùn, and Guāngchéng Zuǒjùn, nineteen jùn.
Yù Zhōu governed Runán, Xīncài, Qiáo, Liáng, Chén, Nándùn,
Yǐngchuān, Ruyīn, Ruyáng, Chénliú, and Mǎtóu, eleven jùn.
Jiāng Zhōu governed Xúnyáng, Yùzhāng, Póyáng, Línchuān, Lúlíng, Ānchéng, Nánkāng, Nánxīncài, Jiàn'ān, and Jìn'ān, ten jùn.
Qīng Zhōu governed Qí, Jìnán, Lè'ān, Gāomì, Píngchāng, Běihǎi, Dōnglái, Tàiyuán, and Chángguǎng, nine jùn.
Jì Zhōu governed Guǎngchuān, Píngyuán, Qīnghé, Lèlíng, Wèi, Héjiān, Dùnqiū, Gāoyáng, and Bóhǎi, nine jùn.
Sī Zhōu governed Yìyáng, Suíyáng, Ānlù, and Nánrunán, four jùn.
Jīng Zhōu governed Nán Jùn, Nánpíng, Yídū,
Bādōng, Wènyáng, Nányìyáng, Xīnxīng, Nánhédōng, Jiànpíng, Chángníng, and Wǔníng, eleven jùn.
Yǐng Zhōu governed Jiāngxià, Jìnglíng, Suí, Wǔlíng, Tiānmén, Bālíng, Wǔchāng, and Xīyáng, eight jùn.
Xiāng Zhōu governed Chángshā, Héngyáng, Guìyáng, Línglíng, Yíngyáng, Xiāngdōng,
Shàolíng, Shǐxīng, Línqìng, and Shǐ'ān, ten jùn.
Yōng Zhōu governed Xiāngyáng, Nányáng, Xīnyě, Shùnyáng, Jīngzhào, Shǐpíng, Fúfēng, Nánshàngluò, Hénán, Guǎngpíng, Yìchéng, Féngyì, Tiānshuǐ, Jiànchāng, Huàshān, Běihénán, and Hóngnóng, seventeen jùn.

Liáng Zhōu governed Hànzhōng, Wèixīng, Xīnxīng, Xīnchéng, Shàngyōng, Jìnshòu, Huáyáng, Xīnbā, Běibāxī, Běiyīnpíng, Nányīnpíng, Bāqú, Huái'ān, Sòngxī, Báishuǐ, Nánshàngluò, Běishàngluò, Ānkāng, Nándàngqú, and Huái'ān, twenty jùn.
Qín Zhōu governed Wǔdū, Lüèyáng, Āngù, Xījīngzhào, Nántàiyuán, Nán'ān, Féngyì, Lǒngxī, Shǐpíng, Jīnchéng, Āndìng, Tiānshuǐ, Xīfúfēng, and Běifúfēng, fourteen jùn.

Yì Zhōu governed Shǔ Jùn, Guǎnghàn, Bāxī, Zǐtóng, Bā Jùn, Suìníng, Jiāngyáng, Huáiníng, Níngshǔ, Yuèsuí, Wènshān, Nányīnpíng, Qiánwéi, Shǐkāng, Jìnxī, Jìnyuán, Yǒngníng, Āngù, Nánhànzhōng, Běiyīnpíng, Wǔdū, Xīnchéng, Nánxīnbā, Nánjìnshòu, Sòngxīng, Nándàngqú, Tiānshuǐ, Dōngjiāngyáng, and Shěnlí, twenty-nine jùn.
Níng Zhōu governed Jiànníng, Jìnníng, Zāngkē, Píngmán, Yèláng, Zhūtí,
Nánguǎng, Jiàndū, Xīpíng, Xīhéyáng, Dōnghéyáng, Xīngníng, Xīnggǔ, and Liángshuǐ, fifteen jùn.

Guǎng Zhōu governed Nánhǎi, Cāngwú, Jìnkāng, Xīnníng, Yǒngpíng, Yùlín, Guìlín, Gāoliáng, Xīnhuì, Dōngguān, Yì'ān, Sòngkāng, Suíkāng, Hǎichāng, Sòngxī, Níngpǔ, Jìnxīng, Lèchāng, and Línzhāng, nineteen jùn.
Jiāo Zhōu governed Jiāozhǐ, Wǔpíng, Xīnchāng, Jiǔzhēn, Jiǔdé, Rìnán, Hépǔ, Yìchāng, and Sòngpíng, nine jùn.
This totals two hundred sixty-eight.
By newly establishing Bǎiliáng, Sū, Yǒngníng, Ānchāng, Fùchāng, and Nánliú, six jùn,
it completes the two hundred seventy-four.
Among these, there were jùn in remote, desolate areas without xiàn,
xiàn without households or population,
and household counts without population counts.
These cannot be detailed.
Qí,
pronounced like "yí."
The eastern jùn
refer to the Three Wú and the five jùn east of Zhèjiāng.
Jiànkāng also reached over a hundred qián,
with six or seven tenths dying of starvation.
