On the day Jǐ-mǎo,
Wáng Yàn entered the city,
killed Suī,
and captured Zǐ-fáng (子房), the son of Xún-yáng, in a separate residence.
Zhāng Suī had probably moved Zǐ-fáng to a separate residence,
hence Wáng Yàn went there to capture him.
The treasury was all empty;
Kǒng Zǎo was captured
and killed.
On the day Gēng-chén,
the people of Jí-shān bound Kǒng Jì and sent him to Yàn.
Yàn said to him:
"This matter was done by Kǒng Zǎo,
and has nothing to do with you, sir.
You can write a statement of your surrender,
and I will present it on your behalf."
Jì said:
"The arrangements in Jiāng-dōng
were all made by me;
to shift the blame and seek survival is simply the way you gentlemen operate."
Yàn then beheaded him.
The histories say that Kǒng Jì did not change his principles even unto death.
He surrendered and pleaded guilty.
There were seventy-six principal commanders of the eastern army.
The commander of an army
is called a jūn-zhǔ.
All others were pardoned.
This set the stage for Wú Xǐ's downfall.
陳,
read as zhèn.
16 Xuē Suǒ-ér (薛索兒) attacked Shēn Chǎn (申闡)
but could not take him for a long time;
he sent Shēn Lìng-sūn (申令孫) to Suī-líng to persuade Chǎn.
Chǎn came out and surrendered.
Suǒ-ér then killed both him and Lìng-sūn.
Ancient people have said:
"No disaster is greater than killing those who have surrendered."
This set the stage for Shēn Lìng-sūn's son to kill Xuē Suǒ-ér.
說,
pronounced as shuì.
降,
pronounced as xiáng;
same below.
17 Shān-yáng 王 Xiū-yòu (休祐) was in Lì-yáng.
Fǔ-guó Jiāng-jūn Liú Miǎn (劉勔) advanced his army to Xiǎo-xiàn.
Péi Jì-zhī (裴季之), the Nán-Rǔ-yīn Tài-shǒu appointed by Yīn Yǎn (殷琰), surrendered with Hé-féi.
Shěn Yuē (沈約) said: In Jiāng-zuǒ, Nán-Rǔ-yīn Commandery was established,
its seat being Hé-féi County.
降,
pronounced as xiáng.
18 Dèng Wǎn (鄧琬) was vulgar, ignorant, greedy, and stingy by nature.
After seizing great power,
he and his son sold official posts and noble titles,
and even had his maids and servants sell goods in the market;
he indulged in singing, drinking, and gambling
day and night without cease.
He was extremely arrogant and self-important;
guests who came to his gate
could not be admitted for weeks.
He entrusted all internal affairs to Chǔ Líng-sì (褚靈嗣) and two others,
who, being minor figures, acted recklessly and domineeringly,
vying with each other to wield power.
Consequently, the gentry and common people were indignant and resentful,
and morale was lost both internally and externally.
The histories explain the reason for Xún-yáng's downfall.
橫,
pronounced as hèng.
Wǎn sent Sūn Chōngzhī to command Longxiáng General Xuē Chángbǎo, Chén Shàozōng, Jiāo Dù, and others with an army of ten thousand as the vanguard,
to occupy Zhěqí.
Liú Xù said: Chízhōu’s Nánlíng County,
was the land of Hàn’s Chūngǔ County,
Qín established Nánlíng County,
governing Zhěqí City,
Táng in the fourth year of Cháng’ān moved its governance to Qīngyáng City.
帥 [shuài],
read as 率 [shuài].
赭 [zhě],
pronounced zhě.
圻 [qí],
pronounced jí.
"Our boats are ready,
provisions and weapons are also in order,
檝 [jí],
same as 楫 [jí].
Men are vying to offer their lives;
We desire to follow the current with hoisted sails,
and directly take Báixià.
Báixià
is at the Jiāngníng County border, at the Línjiāng ford.
By dividing and holding Xīntíng and Nánzhōu,
the matter will be settled with a single wave of the banner."
Zǐxún promoted Chōngzhī to Zuǒwèi General;
appointed Táo Liàng as Yòuwèi General,
commanding the armies of Yǐng, Jīng, Xiāng, Liáng, and Yōng five prefectures,
a total of twenty thousand men,
all descending at the same time.
Táo Liàng originally lacked strategy,
hearing that Jiàn'ān Prince Xiūrén had arrived from upstream,
and Yīn Xiàozǔ also arrived,
he dared not advance,
and encamped his army at Quèzhōu.
Quèzhōu
is in Xuānchéng Commandery, Nánlíng County,
the Què'àn of the Zuǒzhuàn.
Dù Yù said: Què'àn
refers to Quèwěizhǔ in Lújiāng’s Shū County.
If this is correct,
then Quètóu is in Xuānchéng’s territory,
Quèwěi in Lújiāng’s territory,
and Quèzhōu is an island in the river.
Yīn Xiàozǔ, relying on his sincerity and integrity,
Sincerity and integrity
refers to being entrusted with a command to serve the king,
regardless of wife and children.
陵 [líng],
means to invade,
and to insult.
轢 [lì],
means to be crushed by a cart,
pronounced láng dí fān.
Xiàozǔ wished to manage everything himself.
南 [nán],
refers to the southern army.
南 [nán],
refers to Xúnyáng being in the south,
the capital army goes upstream along the Yangtze River to attack it.
治 [zhì],
zhí zhī fān.
No one was willing to be used.
Níngshuò General Shěn Yōuzhī,
internally appeased his officers and soldiers,
externally harmonized with the generals,
and everyone relied on him.
Whenever Xiàozǔ fought,
he always carried a drum and a canopy with him,
and the soldiers in the army said to each other:
"General Yīn can truly be called a dead general!
Now he engages the enemy,
and marks himself conspicuously with feathered regalia,
if ten good archers were to shoot at him together,
could he avoid death?
Impossible!"
In the third month,
on the day Gēngyín,
the combined forces advanced by water and land,
attacking Zhěqí;
Táo Liàng and others led their troops to rescue it.
Xiàozǔ was struck by a stray arrow in battle,
and died.
Army Commander Fàn Qián led five hundred men and surrendered to Liàng.
Public sentiment was shocked and terrified,
and everyone said that Shěn Yōuzhī should replace Xiàozǔ as commander.
At this time, Jiàn'ān Prince Xiūrén was stationed at Hǔlán,
and sent Níngshuò General Jiāng Fāngxīng and Longxiáng General Liú Língyí of Xiāngyáng, each leading three thousand men, to Zhěqí.
Yōuzhī believed that since Xiàozǔ was dead,
Liàng and others would have the desire to capitalize on their victory.
If they did not attack again tomorrow,
it would show weakness.
Fāngxīng's rank and position were similar,
he would definitely not be subordinate to him;
Yōuzhī and Fāngxīng were both Níngshuò Generals,
hence the remark that their rank and position were similar.
亞 [yà],
means second.
This was a cause for defeat.
So he led the army commanders to Fāngxīng and said:
"Now all four directions have rebelled,
and the country we protect
no longer has a hundred li of land.
Only Yīn Xiàozǔ was entrusted by the imperial court,
but as soon as weapons clashed,
his corpse was carried back,
causing both civil and military officials to lose heart,
and the court and people to be anxious.
Whether the matter succeeds or fails
depends solely on one battle tomorrow morning;
if the battle is not victorious,
the great cause will be lost.
For tomorrow morning's task,
some people say I should command it,
but I consider myself timid and weak,
and my strategy is not as good as yours.
I now recommend you as the commander,
we simply need to work together with all our might."
Fāngxīng was very pleased
and agreed.
After Yōuzhī left,
the army commanders all criticized him,
Yōuzhī said:
"I originally aimed to save the country and protect our families,
why should I consider such promotions or demotions!
Moreover, I can submit to him,
but he cannot necessarily submit to me,
how can we create discord ourselves!"
Shěn Yōuzhī achieved success at Xúnyáng,
that was humility;
the defeat at Yǐngchéng,
that was arrogance.
下 [xià],
hù jià fān.
Sūn Chōngzhī said to Táo Liàng:
"Xiàozǔ was a fierce general,
he died in one battle,
the affairs of the world are settled,
there is no need to fight again,
we should go straight for the capital."
Liàng did not follow.
Sūn Chōngzhī, emboldened by Yīn Xiàozǔ’s death,
wished to advance rapidly with the current.
His underestimation of the enemy was like this,
if Táo Liàng had followed his plan,
he would certainly have met Shěn Yōuzhī and others,
and would also have been defeated by underestimating the enemy.
梟 [xiāo],
jiān yáo fān.
將 [jiàng],
jí liàng fān.
復 [fù],
fú yòu fān.
On the day Xīnmǎo,
Fāngxīng led the generals to advance and fight.
Jiàn'ān Prince Xiūrén also sent Army Commander Guō Jìzhī, Infantry Commandant Dù Yǒuwén, Tunqí Commandant Yuán Gōngzǔ, Longxiáng General Jìdì Dùnshēng of Jīngzhào, Duàn Fóróng,
The four characters "濟地頓生" [Jìdì Dùnshēng]
must be an error.
From the hour of Yín to the hour of Wǔ,
they inflicted a great defeat,
pursuing the fleeing enemy to Mǔshān before returning.
Today, forty-five li northwest of Dāngtú County in Tàipíngzhōu, there is Címǔshān;
also, there is Mǔshān in Cháohú Lake.
This was Jì’s son.
During the Yuánjiā era,
Dù Jì held a frontier post.
Sūn Chōngzhī was at Húbáikǒu,
the mouth of Cháohú and the mouth of Báishui.
Army Commander Zhāng Xīngshì of Jìnglíng attacked and captured it.
On the day Rénchén,
an imperial edict appointed Shěn Yōuzhī as Fǔguó General, acting as Jiǎjié,
to replace Yīn Xiàozǔ as supervisor of the vanguard armies.
Táo Liàng heard that Hú and Bái two cities could not be held,
was greatly frightened,
and urgently recalled Sūn Chōngzhī to Quèwěi,
leaving Xuē Chángbǎo and others to defend Zhěqí;
he had previously established camps at Mǔshān and various ridges,
but they also dispersed and returned,
jointly holding Nónghú.
Nónghú is below Quèwěi.
先 [xiān],
xī jiàn fān.
At that time, a large army was raised,
and national resources were insufficient.
People who donated money and grain were rewarded
with desolate counties and desolate commanderies,
or various ranks of honorary titles from fifth grade to third grade.
Desolate commanderies and desolate counties
were remote commanderies and counties devastated by war;
to reward them
meant to bestow upon them the titles of commandery prefect, county magistrate, and their subordinates.
上 [shàng],
shí zhǎng fān.
散 [sǎn],
xī dǎn fān.
The army had little food.
Jiàn'ān Wáng Xiūrén (建安王休仁) comforted and looked after the officers and soldiers,
distributing provisions equally between the abundant and scarce,
mourning the dead and inquiring about the wounded,
personally giving relief and compassion.
"Yǐn" (隱)
means to measure,
and also to feel pain.
"Xù" (恤)
means to worry,
and also to pity.
No one harbored disloyal thoughts.
Dèng Wǎn (鄧琬) dispatched his Yùzhōu Cìshǐ (豫州刺史) Liú Hú (劉胡) to lead a force of thirty thousand men,
two thousand cavalry,
to set up camp east of Quèwěi (鵲尾),
making a total of over one hundred thousand including the old troops.
"Old troops"
refers to the troops previously dispatched by Xúnyáng (尋陽), such as Táo Liàng (陶亮) and Sūn Chōngzhī (孫沖之).
reads as 'qí' and 'jì' (奇寄翻);
same below. Liú Hú (劉胡) was a veteran general,
brave, strong, resourceful, and cunning,
having won many battles,
and was feared by the officers and soldiers.
The Sītú Zhōngbīng Cānjūn Guànjūn (司徒中兵參軍冠軍) Cài Nà (蔡那),
Cài Nà (蔡那)
was a native of Guànjūn (冠軍) in Nányáng (南陽).
"Guàn" (冠),
reads as 'guàn' (古玩翻).
Whenever Hú (胡) went into battle,
he would hang Cài Nà's (蔡那) children and younger relatives outside the city walls;
Liú Hú (劉胡) had seized Cài Nà's (蔡那) children and younger relatives from Xiāngyáng (襄陽) as he descended eastwards
and kept them with his army.
This established a precedent for Cài Dàoyuān (蔡道淵) capturing Zǐxūn (子勛).
After Wú Xǐ (吳喜) had pacified the three Wú (吳) commanderies,
he led his five thousand men,
and also transported supplies,
to Zhèqí (赭圻).
The historian states that the military strength of Jiànkāng (建康) was growing.
Xuē Suǒ'ér (薛索兒) led over ten thousand infantry and cavalry from Suīlíng (睢陵) across the Huái (淮) River,
advancing to threaten the camp of the Qīng (青) and Jì (冀) Èrzhōu Cìshǐ (二州刺史) Zhāng Yǒng (張永).
On the day of Bǐngshēn (丙申)
(30th day of the 11th lunar month), an imperial edict appointed Nánxúzhōu Cìshǐ (南徐州刺史) Guìyáng Wáng Xiūfàn (桂陽王休範) as commander-in-chief of all armies for the northern expedition,
to advance and occupy Guǎnglíng (廣陵);
another edict ordered Xiāo Dàochéng (蕭道成) to lead troops to relieve Zhāng Yǒng (張永).
On the day of Wùxū (戊戌)
(2nd day of the 12th lunar month), Zǐfáng (子房), Prince of Xúnyáng (尋陽), arrived in Jiànkāng (建康).
The Emperor pardoned him,
but demoted his peerage to Sōngzī Hóu (松滋侯).
On the day of Gēngzǐ (庚子)
(4th day of the 12th lunar month), Wèi (魏) appointed Lǒngxī Wáng Yuán Hè (隴西王源賀) as Tàiwèi (太尉).
The Emperor dispatched Níngshuò Jiāngjūn (寧朔將軍) Liú Huáizhēn (劉懷珍) to lead Lóngxiáng Jiāngjūn (龍驤將軍) Wáng Jìngzé (王敬則) and others with five thousand infantry and cavalry,
to assist Liú Miǎn (劉勔) in attacking Shòuyáng (壽陽),
and they beheaded Lújiāng Tàishǒu (廬江太守) Liú Dàowèi (劉道蔚).
Huáizhēn (懷珍) was the cousin of Shànmíng (善明).
Liú Shànmíng (劉善明) was the cousin of Mí (彌).
"Wèi" (蔚),
reads as 'yūwù' (紆勿翻).
"Cóng" (從),
reads as 'cái yòng' (才用翻).
Zhōngshū Shèrén (中書舍人) Dài Míngbǎo (戴明寶) submitted a memorial to the Emperor,
requesting to dispatch military commander Jìnglíng (竟陵) Huáng Huí (黃回) to recruit soldiers to attack and behead Wáng Guǎngyuán (王廣元), who had been appointed Mǎtóu Tàishǒu (馬頭太守) by Xúnyáng (尋陽).
Dù Yòu (杜佑) said: Mǎtóu (馬頭) City is north of Shèngtáng (盛唐) County in Shòuzhōu (壽州).
The former Fèngcháoqǐng (奉朝請) Zhèng Hēi (鄭黑) of Shòuyáng (壽陽)
raised an army on the Huái (淮) River to respond to Jiànkāng (建康),
defending against Yīn Yǎn (殷琰) to the east,
and resisting Cháng Zhēnqí (常珍奇) to the west;
on the day of Yǐsì (乙巳)
(9th day of the 12th lunar month), Zhèng Hēi (鄭黑) was appointed Sīzhōu Cìshǐ (司州刺史).
Observing Zhèng Hēi's (鄭黑) defense to the east and resistance to the west,
it is likely that his uprising on the Huái (淮) River
was between Dōngzhèng (東正) and Xīzhèng (西正).
"Cháo" (朝),
reads as 'zhí yáo' (直遙翻).
The "Kǎoyì" (考異) states: the biography of Sòng Yīn Yǎn (宋殷琰) records
"Zhèng Mò" (鄭墨);
here we follow the Sòng Běnjì (宋本紀) and Sòng Lüè (宋略).
Yīn Yǎn's (殷琰) generals Liú Shùn (劉順), Liǔ Lún (柳倫), Huángfǔ Dàoliè (皇甫道烈), Páng Tiānshēng (龐天生), and others, with eight thousand infantry and cavalry, fortified Wǎntáng (宛唐) to the east.
"Wǎntáng" (宛唐),
according to the Shuǐjīngzhù (水經註), is recorded as
"Sǐyú" (死雩).
It says: the Féishuǐ (肥水) flows past the northwest of Chéngdé (成德) County in Jiǔjiāng (九江),
entering Sháopí (芍陂);
then further north,
it merges with the Yánrùn Shuǐ (閻潤水) on the right,
the water accumulating to form Yánghú (陽湖).
The Yánghú (陽湖) water flows from the northwest of Táng (塘),
passing through Sǐyútíng (死雩亭).
In the early Tàishǐ (泰始) era of Sòng (宋),
Liú Shùn (劉順) occupied it to resist Liú Miǎn (劉勔).
Dù Yòu's (杜佑) Tōngdiǎn (通典) records it as
"Sǐhǔ" (死虎),
saying: Sǐhǔ (死虎) is a place name,
about forty *li* east of Shòuchūn (壽春) County in Shòuzhōu (壽州).
"Páng" (龐),
reads as 'pí jiāng' (皮江翻).
They set up camp a few *li* from Liú Shùn (劉順).
At that time, all the armies dispatched by Yīn Yǎn (殷琰)
were under Liú Shùn's (劉順) command;
however, because Huángfǔ Dàoliè (皇甫道烈) was a local magnate,
and Liǔ Lún (柳倫) was dispatched by the imperial court,
while Liú Shùn (劉順) was originally of humble origin,
he was not allowed to command these two armies.
If local magnates could not be commanded,
and those dispatched by the court could also not be commanded,
then what was the purpose of appointing a commander?
Their defeat was inevitable.
Their trenches and ramparts were not yet established;
Liú Shùn (劉順) wanted to attack,
but Huángfǔ Dàoliè (皇甫道烈) and Liǔ Lún (柳倫) disagreed,
so Liú Shùn (劉順) could not advance alone
and stopped.
After Liú Miǎn's (劉勔) camp was established,
it could no longer be attacked,
so they entered a stalemate.
On the day of Rénzǐ (壬子)
(16th day of the 12th lunar month), the new coins were abolished,
and the Yuánjiā (元嘉) four-zhu coins and
Xiàojiàn (孝建) four-zhu coins
were all abolished and ceased to be used.
"Duàn" (斷),
reads as 'duǎn' (短).
Shěn Yōuzhī (沈攸之) led all armies to besiege Zhèqí (赭圻).
Xuē Chángbǎo (薛常寶) and others ran out of provisions
and requested aid from Liú Hú (劉胡);
Liú Hú (劉胡) filled bags with rice,
tied them to drifting rafts and the bottoms of boats,
deliberately capsized the boats,
and let them drift downstream with the wind to supply the city.
Shěn Yōuzhī (沈攸之), suspecting something unusual,
sent men to retrieve the boats and rafts,
and found many bags of rice.
On the day of Bǐngchén (丙辰)
(20th day of the 12th lunar month), Liú Hú (劉胡) led ten thousand infantry,
and at night
cut a path through the mountains,
using cloth bags to transport rice to supply Zhèqí (赭圻).
At dawn,
they reached the base of the city wall,
but were still separated by a small trench
and could not enter.
Shěn Yōuzhī (沈攸之) led his armies to intercept them,
fighting a desperate battle.
Liú Hú's (劉胡) forces were greatly defeated,
abandoning their provisions and armor,
fleeing along the mountains.
Many were killed or captured.
Liú Hú (劉胡) was wounded
and barely managed to return to his camp.
Xuē Chángbǎo (薛常ǎo) and others were terrified,
and in summer,
the fourth month,
on the day of Xīnyǒu (辛酉)
(5th day of the 4th lunar month), they opened the city gates, broke through the siege,
and fled back to Liú Hú's (劉胡) army.
Shěn Yōuzhī (沈攸之) captured Zhèqí (赭圻) City,
beheaded its Níngshuò Jiāngjūn (寧朔將軍) Shěn Huáibǎo (沈懷寶) and others,
and accepted the surrender of several thousand people.
Chén Shàozōng (陳紹宗) fled to Quèwěi (鵲尾) in a single boat.
Jiàn'ān Wáng Xiūrén (建安王休仁) advanced from Hǔlán (虎檻) to station at Zhèqí (赭圻).
Liú Hú (劉胡) and other forces were still strong.
The Emperor wished to appease the people,
and dispatched Lìbù Shàngshū (吏部尚書) Chǔ Yuān (褚淵) to Hǔlán (虎檻)
to select and appoint officers and soldiers.
At that time, many were appointed officials for military merit,
so many that the wooden tablets were insufficient.
Chéng Dàchāng (程大昌) said: from Wèi (魏) and Jìn (晉) to Liáng (梁) and Chén (陳) dynasties,
official appointments were made on tablets,
which were one foot two inches long,
one inch thick,
and seven inches wide.
The text of the official appointment
was written on the tablet,
in the form of "què tóu shū" (鵲頭書).
Dèng Wǎn (鄧琬), acting under the command of Jìn'ān Wáng Zǐxūn (晉安王子勛),
summoned Yuán Yǐ (袁顗) to Xúnyáng (尋陽).
Yuán Yǐ (袁顗) swiftly led all the forces of Yōngzhōu (雍州) to descend.
Dèng Wǎn (鄧琬) appointed Huángmén Shìláng (黃門侍郎) Liú Dàoxiàn (劉道憲) to act as Jīngzhōu (荊州) affairs,
and Shìzhōng (侍中) Kǒng Dàocún (孔道存) to act as Yōngzhōu (雍州) affairs.
Shàngyōng Tàishǒu (上庸太守) Liǔ Shìlóng (柳世隆) took advantage of the emptiness to attack Xiāngyáng (襄陽),
but failed.
Shìlóng (世隆) was the nephew of Yuánjǐng (元景).
28 Sànqí Shìláng Míng Sēnggǎo (明僧暠) raised an army,
attacking Shěn Wénxiù (沈文秀) in response to Jiànkāng (建康).
The Míng (明) clan claimed to be descendants of Wú Tàibó (吳太伯).
Bǎilǐ Xī's (百里奚) son, Mèngmíng Shì (孟明視), took Míng as his surname.
散,
is pronounced as Sàn, xī dǎn fān.
騎,
is pronounced as Qí, qí jì fān.
暠,
is pronounced as Gǎo, gōng lǎo fān.
On the Rénwǔ (壬午) day,
Sēnggǎo (僧暠) was appointed Governor of Qīngzhōu (青州).
Wáng Xuánmò (王玄默), the Administrator of Píngyuán (平原) and Lè'ān (樂安) commanderies, occupied Lángxié (琅邪).
When Emperor Wǔ (武帝) pacified Qí (齊),
he established Píngyuán Commandery at Liángzōu (梁鄒)
and Lè'ān Commandery at Qiānchéng (千乘).
Xuánmò (玄默) raised an army at Lángxié (琅邪),
not within his commandery.
Liú Xù (劉昫) said: Píngyuán (平原)
was renamed Gōngqiū (龔丘) during the Suí (隋) dynasty,
belonging to Yǎnxzhōu (兗州).
Emperor Wǔ (武帝) established Qīnghé Commandery (清河郡) at Pányáng (盤陽)
and Guǎngchuān Commandery (廣川郡) at Wǔqiáng (武強).
The Wǔdài Zhì (五代志) states: Chángshān (長山) County in Qí Commandery (齊郡),
formerly called Wǔqiáng (武強),
established Guǎngchuān (廣川),
and later merged the two commanderies of Dōng Qīnghé (東清河) and Píngyuán (平原) into it,
renaming it Dōng Píngyuán Commandery (東平原郡);
the Suí (隋) dynasty abolished the commandery,
and renamed Wǔqiáng (武強) to Chángshān (長山).
Thus, Píngyuán (平原), Qīnghé (清河), and Guǎngchuān (廣川) three commanderies were all established within the boundaries of Suí's Chángshān County.
Pányáng (盤陽)
was the Hàn (漢) Bānyáng (般陽) County,
belonging to Jǐnán Commandery (濟南郡).
Yìng Shào (應劭) said: It is located on the sunny side of the Bān (般) River.
According to the Shuǐjīng Zhù (水經註): Bānyáng (般陽) County's southwest is Liángzōu (梁鄒) County.
Liú Xù (劉昫) said: Táng (唐) Zīzhōu (淄州) Zīchuān (淄川) County
is the area of Hàn (漢) Bānyáng (般陽) County.
Emperor Wén (文帝) established Gāoyáng Commandery (高陽郡) in the Lè'ān (樂安) area.
Emperor Xiàowǔ (孝武) established Bóhǎi Commandery (勃海郡) in the Línzī (臨淄) area;
Línjì (臨濟) County belonged to Lè'ān Commandery.
According to the Shuǐjīng Zhù (水經註): Línjì (臨濟) County is northeast of Liángzōu (梁鄒).
臨濟,
is pronounced as Línjì, zǐ lǐ fān.
Xuánmiǎo (玄邈)
was Xuánmó's (玄謨) paternal cousin;
Chéngmín (乘民)
was Mízhī's (彌之) paternal nephew.
Shěn Wénxiù (沈文秀) sent his army commander Xiè Yànshì (解彥士) to attack Běihǎi (北海),
capturing it
and killing Liú Mízhī (劉彌之).
Chéngmín's (乘民) paternal cousin, Bózhōng (伯宗),
gathered the local gentry
and recaptured Běihǎi (北海),
then led his troops towards Dōngyáng Chéng (東陽城), where Qīngzhōu (青州) was administered.
Dù Yòu (杜佑) said: Dōngyáng Chéng (東陽城)
is the east city of Yìdū (益都) County, where Qīngzhōu (青州) was administered.
治,
is pronounced as Zhì, zhí zhī fān.
Bózhōng (伯宗) died in battle.
Sēnggǎo (僧暠), Xuánmò (玄默), Xuánmiǎo (玄邈), and Chéngmín (乘民) combined their forces to attack Dōngyáng Chéng (東陽城).
Each battle saw them defeated by Wénxiù (文秀).
They dispersed and reunited more than ten times,
but ultimately could not conquer it.
This means they could not conquer Dōngyáng Chéng (東陽城).
卒,
is pronounced as Zú, zǐ xù fān.
29 Dù Shūbǎo (杜叔寶) said that the imperial army was stationed at Lìyáng (歷陽)
and could not advance quickly.
When Liú Miǎn (劉勔) and others arrived,
everyone, high and low, was terrified.
Liú Shùn (劉順) and his troops had only brought a month's provisions when they set out.
Now that they were locked in a standoff with Miǎn (勔),
their provisions were exhausted.
Shūbǎo (叔寶) dispatched fifteen hundred carts
loaded with rice to supply Shùn (順),
personally leading five thousand elite soldiers to escort them.
Lǚ Ānguó (呂安國) heard of this
and said to Liú Miǎn (劉勔):
"Liú Shùn (劉順) has eight thousand elite armored troops.
Our forces are not even half that.
After a prolonged standoff,
the strength and weakness are clearly disparate.
If we delay any further,
we will not be able to hold our ground.
What we rely on
is that their provisions are about to run out,
while we have surplus food.
If Shūbǎo's (叔寶) rice arrives,
not only will it be difficult to achieve our objective,
but we also won't be able to hold out for long.
Now, we can only take a secret path to ambush their rice carts,
catching them off guard.
If we can seize them,
they will flee without a fight."
Miǎn (勔) thought this was sound,
leaving the exhausted and weak to guard the camp,
and selecting a thousand elite soldiers to accompany Ānguó (安國) and Lóngxiáng Jiāngjūn Huáng Huí (龍驤將軍黃回),
instructing them to take a secret path behind Shùn's (順) forces
and intercept them at Héngtáng (橫塘).
The Shuǐjīng Zhù (水經註) states: The Yánrùn (閻潤) River originates from the Shī (施) River north of Héféi (合肥) County,
then flows west of the county,
forming Yánghú (陽湖).
The Yánghú (陽湖) water flows from northwest of the dike,
passing south of Sǐyútíng (死雩亭), and flows west of Héngtáng (橫塘).
In the early Tàishǐ (泰始) era of the Sòng (宋) dynasty,
Liú Shùn (劉順) occupied it to resist Liú Miǎn (劉勔).
Dù Shūbǎo (杜叔寶) delivered provisions to Sǐyú (死雩),
and Liú Miǎn (劉勔) defeated him at this dike.
驤,
is pronounced as Xiáng, sī jiāng fān.
抄,
is pronounced as Chāo, chǔ jiāo fān.
When Ānguó (安國) first set out,
he brought two days' cooked rations.
When the food ran out
and Shūbǎo (叔寶) had not arrived,
the officers and soldiers wanted to return.
Ānguó (安國) said:
"You all have eaten once this morning.
The rice carts must surely arrive this evening.
If they don't,
it won't be too late to leave tonight."
Shūbǎo (叔寶) indeed arrived.
He arranged the rice carts in a box formation,
with Shūbǎo (叔寶) acting as a mobile force outside.
The banner commander Yáng Zhònghuái (楊仲懷) led five hundred men at the front.
Ānguó (安國) and Huí (回) attacked and decapitated him,
and all his soldiers were wiped out.
When Shūbǎo (叔寶) arrived,
Huí (回) wanted to press the attack while victorious.
Ānguó (安國) said:
"They will flee on their own;
there's no need to attack again."
They retreated thirty lǐ,
halted for the night,
and sent scouts during the night.
Shūbǎo (叔寶) indeed abandoned the rice carts and fled.
Ānguó (安國) then went back at night to burn the rice carts
and drove back over two thousand cattle.
In the fifth month,
on the Dīnghài (丁亥) day, the first day of the month,
that night,
Liú Shùn's (劉順) forces disintegrated,
fleeing west to Huáinán (淮西) to join Cháng Zhēnqí (常珍奇).
Cháng Zhēnqí (常珍奇) occupied Xuánhù (懸瓠) west of the Huái (淮) River.
走,
is pronounced as Zǒu, yīn zòu.
They then advanced towards Shòuyáng (壽陽).
Shūbǎo (叔寶) gathered the residents and scattered soldiers,
barricading themselves within the city walls,
while Miǎn (勔) and the various armies set up separate camps outside the city.
Shānyáng Wáng Xiūyòu (山陽王休祐) wrote a letter to Yīn Yǎn (殷琰),
explaining the advantages and disadvantages, and the Emperor (上) also sent the Imperial Censor Wáng Dàolóng (王道隆) with an edict to pardon Yǎn's (琰) crimes.
Miǎn (勔) wrote to Yǎn (琰),
and also sent him a letter from Yǎn's (琰) brother Yuàn's (瑗) son Miǎo (邈).
Yǎn (琰) and Shūbǎo (叔寶) both intended to surrender,
but the general sentiment was not unified,
so they again fortified themselves within the city walls and held fast.
The Yìyáng (弋陽) western mountain barbarians' Tián Yìzhī (田益之) raised an army in response to Jiànkāng (建康).
An edict appointed Yìzhī (益之) as Fǔguó Jiāngjūn (輔國將軍),
overseeing the affairs of the Yìyáng (弋陽) western barbarians.
On the Rénchén (壬辰) day,
Fǔguó Jiāngjūn Shěn Yōuzhī (輔國將軍沈攸之) was appointed Governor of Yōngzhōu (雍州).
On the Dīngwèi (丁未) day,
Shàngshū Zuǒpúyè Wáng Jǐngwén (尚書左僕射王景文) was appointed Zhōngjūn Jiāngjūn (中軍將軍).
On the Gēngxū (庚戌) day,
Níngshuò Jiāngjūn Liú Chéngmín (寧朔將軍劉乘民) was appointed Governor of Jìzhōu (冀州).
Shěn Yōuzhī (沈攸之) was at the front of the southern expeditionary army,
intended to replace Yuán Yǐ (袁顗).
Liú Chéngmín (劉乘民) was at Línjì (臨濟),
and was thus granted Jìzhōu (冀州).
30 On the Jiǎyín (甲寅) day,
Empress Dowager Zhāo (昭太后) was buried at Xiūníng Líng (脩寧陵).
Empress Dowager Lù (路太后) was posthumously honored as Zhāo (昭);
Xiūníng Líng (脩寧陵) is southeast of Emperor Xiàowǔ's (孝武) mausoleum.
Zhāng Yǒng (張永), Xiāo Dàochéng (蕭道成) and others fought with Xuē Suǒ'ér (薛索兒).
They decisively defeated him.
Suǒ'ér (索兒) retreated to defend Shíliáng (石梁).
Today, Líu Hé Xiàn (六合縣) in Yángzhōu (揚州) has Shíliáng Hé (石梁河).
On the east bank of the Jiāng (江), Shíliáng Jùn (石梁郡) was established.
Between the Suí (隋) and Táng (唐) dynasties, Shíliáng Xiàn (石梁縣) was established.
[They] went to Lèpíng (樂平).
Lèpíng Xiàn (樂平縣) [was in]
the Former Hàn (漢) called Qīng (清),
belonging to Dōng Jùn (東郡).
In the Later Hàn (漢), Emperor Zhāng (章帝) renamed it Lèpíng (樂平).
Civilians from Lèpíng Xiàn (樂平縣) on the east bank of the Jiāng (江) who had become displaced,
temporarily established Lèpíng Xiàn (樂平縣) within Zhōnglí Jùn's (鍾離郡) borders.
Shēn Xiàoshú (申孝叔) avenged his father.
[He] went to Péi Jìzhī (裴季之) to surrender.
Fù Língyuè (傅靈越) fled to Huáixī (淮西).
Wǔwèi Jiāngjūn (武衞將軍) Wáng Guǎngzhī (王廣之) of Pèijùn (沛郡) captured him alive,
and sent him to Liú Miǎn (劉勔).
Miǎn (勔) interrogated him about his rebellion.
Língyuè (靈越) said:
"The nine provinces raise the banner of righteousness,
why should it be only up to me!
Duke Xuē (薛公) could not solely rely on his wisdom and bravery,
entrusting [affairs] to his nephews and sons.
This is why he failed.
A man's life ends in death.
I truly have no face to beg for life."
Miǎn (勔) sent him to Jiànkāng (建康).
The emperor wanted to pardon him,
but Língyuè (靈越)'s refusal did not change to the end,
so he was killed.
Dèng Wǎn (鄧琬), seeing that Liú Hú (劉胡) and Shěn Yōuzhī (沈攸之) and others had been stalemated for a long time,
then added Yuán Yǐ (袁顗) as Dū Zhēngtǎo Zhū Jūnjì (督征討諸軍事) (Supervisor of All Military Affairs for Campaigning).
In the sixth month,
on the jiǎxū (甲戌) day,
Yǐ (顗) led a thousand樓船 (lóuchuán) (tower ships)
and twenty thousand soldiers,
and entered Quèwěi (鵲尾).
Yǐ (顗) originally lacked military strategy,
and his nature was timid and weak.
In the army, he never wore military attire,
and his conversations never touched upon battle formations.
He only composed poetry and discussed philosophy,
no longer showing care or concern for the various generals.
Whenever Liú Hú (劉胡) discussed matters,
Yǐ (顗)'s responses were very brief.
Because of this, he greatly lost popular support,
and Hú (胡) constantly gnashed his teeth in resentment.
Hú (胡), as the rice from the south had not yet arrived,
and the soldiers were in want,
asked Yǐ (顗) to borrow funds from Xiāngyáng (襄陽).
Yǐ (顗) refused,
saying:
"My two residences in the capital are not yet completed,
and require management."
With two enemies facing each other,
the decision of victory or defeat,
and survival or destruction, depended on it.
Yet Yuán Yǐ (袁顗) wanted to keep the funds from Xiāngyáng (襄陽) to manage his private residences!
Zǐxūn (子勛) having already been defeated,
how could the two residences in the capital belong to Yǐ (顗)?
It was said,
"Rice in Jiànkāng (建康) is expensive,
a dou (斗) reaching several hundred,"
believing that [the enemy] would collapse without attack,
and thus he held his forces to await them.
Yǒng jiǎ (擁甲)
is similar to saying yǒng bīng (擁兵) (holding troops).
Sòng Bái (宋白) said: Yìyáng (義陽) was originally the land of Yìyáng Xiāng (義陽鄉) in Píngshì Xiàn (平氏縣) of the Hàn (漢).
During the Huángchū (黃初) era of the Wèi (魏),
Píngshì (平氏) was divided and belonged to Yìyáng Jùn (義陽郡) and Yìyáng Xiàn (義陽縣).
Yìzhī (益之) fled without a fight.
Wáng Shízhī (王識之), the Administrator of Shǐ'ān (始安).
The Kǎoyì (考異) says the Sòng Shū (宋書) writes
"Wáng Zhízhī (王職之)".
We follow Sòng Lüè (宋略) here.
Both came with their entire commanderies to surrender.
Xí (襲)
was the grandson of Dàolián (道憐).
Dàolián (道憐)
was the younger brother of Emperor Wǔ (武帝).
Dèng Wǎn (鄧琬) sent an envoy to arrest and imprison him.
His household retainer, Huán Kāng (桓康) of Lánlíng (蘭陵), carried Zé (賾)'s wife Péi Shì (裴氏) and their sons Chángmào (長懋) and Zǐliáng (子良) and escaped into the mountains.
With Zé (賾)'s clansman Xiāo Xīnzǔ (蕭欣祖) and others, they gathered over a hundred men
to attack the commandery,
broke into the prison, and released Zé (賾).
Shěn Sùzhī (沈肅之), the Administrator of Nánkāng (南康), led his officers and clerks to pursue Zé (賾).
Zé (賾) fought with them
and captured him.
Zé (賾) proclaimed himself Níngshuò Jiāngjūn (寧朔將軍),
occupied the commandery and raised an army,
responding to Liú Xí (劉襲) and others.
Wǎn (琬) appointed Yīn Fú (殷孚) as Yùzhāng Tàishǒu (豫章太守),
supervising the five upstream commanderies:
Yùzhāng (豫章), Lúlíng (廬陵), Línchuān (臨川), Ānchéng (安成), and Nánkāng (南康), these five commanderies
were all in the upper reaches of the southern Jiāng (江).
and attacked Hé Huìwén (何慧文), the Acting Administrator of Xiāngzhōu (湘州), in Chángshā (長沙).
Yìngzhī (應之) and Huìwén (慧文) left their armies and fought in person.
Yìngzhī (應之) hacked Huìwén (慧wén) eight times.
Huìwén (慧wén) hacked Yìngzhī (應zhī), severing his foot,
and killed him.
Yuán Tányuǎn (袁曇遠), the Inspector of Guǎngzhōu (廣州), sent his general Lǐ Wànzhōu (李萬周) and others to suppress them.
Sìzǔ (嗣祖) deceived Wànzhōu (萬周), saying,
"Xúnyáng (尋陽) has already been pacified."
Wànzhōu (萬周) returned and attacked Pānyú (番禺),
captured Tányuǎn (曇遠),
and beheaded him.
The emperor appointed Wànzhōu (萬周) to act as the Inspector of Guǎngzhōu (廣州).
Yáng Yuánhé (楊元和), King of Wǔdū (武都), governed Báishuǐ (白水).
According to the Běi Shǐ (北史),
this is the Báishuǐ (白水) of Wǔdū (武都).
According to the Wǔdài Zhì (五代志): Jiànwēi Xiàn (建威縣) in Wǔchāng (武昌) previously established Báishuǐ Jùn (白水郡).
Jiànwēi (建威) was merged into Jiēzhōu (階州) Jiānglì Xiàn (將利縣) during the Táng (唐).
He abandoned his kingdom and fled to Wèi (魏).
Yuánhé (元和)'s cousin Sēngsì (僧嗣) then re-established himself [as king],
stationing at Jiālú (葭蘆).
Fèi Xīnshòu (費欣壽) arrived at Bādōng (巴東).
Rèn Shú'ér (任叔兒) of Bādōng (巴東) occupied Báidì (白帝),
proclaimed himself Fǔguó Jiāngjūn (輔國將軍),
attacked Xīnshòu (欣壽),
and beheaded him.
Xiāo Huìkāi (蕭惠開) had sent Xīnshòu (欣壽) downstream,
as seen in the first month.
The Jiāng (江) river from Bādōng (巴東) to Yílíng (夷陵),
within that stretch are Guǎngxī Xiá (廣溪峽), Wū Xiá (巫峽), and Xīlíng Xiá (西陵峽),
which are called the Three Gorges.
Another saying is that
the Three Gorges are
Xī Xiá (西峽), Guī Xiá (歸峽), and Wū Xiá (巫峽).
For seven hundred lǐ (里),
the mountains on both banks are continuous,
almost without gaps,
hiding the sky and obscuring the sun,
so that unless it is noon or midnight,
the sun and moon are not seen.
Yáng Sēngsì (楊僧嗣) led his Qíang (㣥) and Dī (氐) to block the road.
A secret envoy reported this.
Autumn,
seventh month,
on the dīngyǒu (丁酉) day,
Sēngsì (僧嗣) was appointed Inspector of Běiqínzhōu (北秦州) and King of Wǔdū (武都).
and no decision had been reached for a long time.
Lóngxiáng Jiāngjūn (龍驤將軍) Zhāng Xìngshì (張興世) proposed:
"The enemy occupies the upper reaches,
with strong forces and a favorable position.
Although we have more than enough to hold them, we lack the means to control them.
If we send several thousand elite troops to stealthily go upstream of them,
establish a fortified position based on the terrain,
and act when an opportunity arises,
making them confused at both ends,
and hesitant to advance or retreat,
and if the middle course is blocked,
their food supply will naturally become difficult.
This is a brilliant strategy to control the enemy.
The bank of Qiánxī (錢溪) Jiāng (江) is the narrowest.
The Xīn Táng Shū Dìlǐ Zhì (新唐書地理志) says: Xuānzhōu (宣州) Nánlíng Xiàn (南陵縣) has the Méigēn Jiān Qiánguān (梅根監錢官) (Méigēn Mint Office).
It further says: Chén Qìng (陳慶) reached Qiánxī (錢溪)
and camped at Méigēn (梅根),
which is probably today's Méigēn Gǎng (梅根港).
Because there was a mint office,
it was called Qiánxī (錢溪).
Below it lies Huífú (洄洑).
A swirling current is huí (洄),
a hidden current is fú (洑).
There is also Hēngpǔ (橫浦) where ships can be hidden.
A thousand men defending the pass
cannot be overcome by ten thousand men.
No strategic location
is more crucial than this."
Shěn Yōuzhī (沈攸之) and Wú Xǐ (吳喜) both praised his plan.
Coincidentally, Páng Mèngqiú (龐孟虯) led his troops to assist Yīn Yǎn (殷琰).
Páng Mèngqiú (龐孟虯) came from Yìyáng (義陽) to reinforce Shòuyáng (壽陽).
Jiàn'ān Wáng (建安王) Xiūwéi (休仁) wanted to send Xìngshì (興世) to relieve them.
Shěn Yōuzhī (沈攸之) said:
"Mèngqiú (孟虯)'s gathering is like ants,
he will surely be ineffective.
Sending a few thousand infantry and cavalry under another general
will be enough to control them.
Xìngshì (興世)'s mission [to Qiánxī]
is a critical strategic move for our safety and danger,
and absolutely cannot be stopped."
So, Duàn Fórong (段佛榮) was sent to lead troops to assist Miǎn (勔),
and seven thousand elite soldiers and two hundred light boats were assigned to Xìngshì (興世).
Zhāng Xìngshì (張興世) led his troops upstream a little,
then retreated again.
This happened for several days.
Liú Hú (劉胡) heard of it
and laughed, saying:
"I still don't dare cross below them to take Yángzhōu (揚州),
Yángzhōu (揚州)
refers to Jiànkāng (建康).
They want to lightly seize above me!"
He made no preparations for it.
One night,
at the fourth watch,
a favorable wind arose, and
Xìngshì (興世) hoisted sails and advanced directly,
crossing Húbái (湖白)
and passing Quèwěi (鵲尾).
When Hú (胡) realized it,
he sent his general Hú Língxiù (胡靈秀) with troops to the east bank,
advancing alongside them.
On the evening of *wùxū* (戊戌),
Xìngshì (興世) camped at Jǐnghóng Pǔ (景洪浦),
and Língxiù (靈秀) also remained there.
Xìngshì (興世) secretly dispatched his general Huáng Dàobiāo (黃道標) leading seventy *gě* (舸) directly to Qiánxī (錢溪),
where they established a camp;
on *jǐhài* (己亥),
Xìngshì (興世) led his troops to occupy it,
and Língxiù (靈秀) could not stop him.
On *gēngzǐ* (庚子),
Liú Hú (劉胡) personally led twenty-six divisions of infantry and naval forces to attack Qiánxī (錢溪).
*Kǎoyì* (考異) says: *Sònglüè* (宋略) says:
"Hú (胡) advanced to Quètóu (鵲頭),
and sent his general Chén Qìng (陳慶) with three hundred *gě* (舸) to press Qiánxī (錢溪)."
We now follow the *Sòng Shū* (宋書).
Xìngshì (興世) restrained them, saying:
"The enemy is still far away,
their morale is high, and their arrows are numerous;
but numerous arrows are easily exhausted,
meaning arrows are easily exhausted.
*Yì* (易)
is pronounced like *shì* (豉);
same below.
It's better to wait for them."
He ordered his generals and soldiers to fortify the city as before.
Soon, Hú (胡) came closer,
and his boats entered the whirlpools;
Xìngshì (興世) ordered Shòu Jìzhī (壽寂之) and Rèn Nóngfū (任農夫) to lead several hundred brave warriors to attack them,
and the various armies followed in succession, advancing together.
Hú (胡) was defeated and fled,
several hundred heads were severed.
Hú (胡) gathered his troops and withdrew.
At this time, Xìngshì's (興世) camp was not yet secure,
and the Prince of Jiàn'ān (建安), Xiūrén (休仁), feared that Yuán Yǐ (袁顗) would combine forces and attack Qiánxī (錢溪) again,
so he wanted to divide their strength.
On *xīnchǒu* (辛丑),
he ordered Shěn Yōuzhī (沈攸之) and Wú Xǐ (吳喜) to advance and attack Nónghú (濃湖) with leather ships,
covering the ships with cowhide to ward off arrows and stones,
hence they were called leather ships.
*Jiàn* (艦)
is pronounced like *hù àn* (戶黯);
same pronunciation.
On this day,
Liú Hú (劉胡) led twenty thousand infantry and one thousand iron cavalry, intending to attack Xìngshì (興世) again.
Before reaching Qiánxī (錢溪) by several tens of *lǐ* (里),
Yuán Yǐ (袁顗), due to the urgency at Nónghú (濃湖),
hastily recalled him,
and the city of Qiánxī (錢溪) was thus able to be established.
Hú (胡) sent men to spread the word,
"Qiánxī (錢溪) has been pacified,"
and all the troops were alarmed.
Shěn Yōuzhī (沈攸之) said:
"Not so.
If Qiánxī (錢溪) had truly fallen,
at least one person out of ten thousand should have escaped and returned.
This must be their loss in battle,
and they are spreading empty rumors to confuse the multitude."
He ordered the army not to move recklessly;
*lè* (勒)
means to restrain.
Yōuzhī (攸之) showed the ears and noses of Hú's (胡) soldiers sent from Qiánxī (錢溪) to Nónghú (濃湖),
and Yuán Yǐ (袁顗) was terrified.
Yōuzhī (攸之) led his troops back at dusk.
40 The General of Soaring Dragon, Liú Dàofú (劉道符), attacked Shānyáng (山陽),
and Chéng Tiānzuò (程天祚) requested to surrender.
Chéng Tiānzuò (程天祚) was allied with Zǐxūn (子勛),
seen in the first month above.
41 Páng Mèngqiú (龐孟虯) advanced to Yìyáng (弋陽),
and Liú Miǎn (劉勔) sent Lǚ Ānguó (呂安國) and others to meet and attack him at Liáotán (蓼潭).
The *Hàn Zhì* (漢志) states that
Liù'ān Guó (六安國) had Liáo Xiàn (蓼縣),
which belonged to Ānfēng Jùn (安豐郡) in the Jìn (晉) dynasty.
The *Shuǐjīng Zhù* (水經註) says: The Juéshuǐ (決水) flows east of the old city of Liáo Xiàn (蓼縣),
where the Guànshuǐ (灌水) joins it.
The so-called Liáotán (蓼潭)
should be in this place.
Mèngqiú (孟虯) fled towards Yìyáng (義陽).
Wáng Xuánmó's (王玄謨) son, Tánshàn (曇善), raised troops and occupied Yìyáng (義陽) in response to Jiànkāng (建康),
and Mèngqiú (孟虯) fled and died among the barbarians.
42 Liú Hú (劉胡) sent his General Pacifying the State, Xuē Dàobiāo (薛道標), to raid Héféi (合肥),
killing the Administrator of Rǔyīn (汝陰), Péi Jìzhī (裴季之).
Péi Jìzhī (裴季之) surrendered Héféi (合肥) to Liú Miǎn (劉勔),
seen in the second month above.
Hóng (閎)
was Láng's (閬) younger brother;
Yuán Láng (垣閬) is seen in Volume 129, Emperor Xiàowǔ's (孝武帝) Dàmíng (大明) third year.
He was Āndū's (安都) son.
43 Zhèng Shújǔ (鄭叔舉) of Huáixī (淮西) raised troops and attacked Cháng Zhēnqí (常珍奇) in response to Zhèng Hēi (鄭黑);
on *xīnhài* (辛亥),
Shújǔ (叔舉) was appointed Governor of Běi Yùzhōu (北豫州).
44 Cuī Dàogù (崔道固) was attacked by local people
and defended himself by closing the gates.
Cuī Dàogù (崔道固) made Lìchéng (歷城) respond to Xúnyáng (尋陽),
seen in the first month above.
Dàogù (道固) requested to surrender.
On *jiǎyín* (甲寅),
Dàogù (道固) was again appointed Governor of Xúzhōu (徐州).
Dàogù (道固) was originally Governor of Jìzhōu (冀州).
*Fù* (復)
is pronounced *fú yòu* (扶又);
the same applies to *bù fù* (不復) and *zú fù* (足復) below.
45 In the eighth month,
Huángfǔ Dàoliè (皇甫道烈) and others, hearing of Páng Mèngqiú's (龐孟虯) defeat,
all opened their gates and surrendered.
The Dead Tiger army collapsed,
and Huángfǔ Dàoliè (皇甫道烈) probably fled back to Shòuyáng (壽陽).
46 Since Zhāng Xìngshì (張興世) had occupied Qiánxī (錢溪),
the Nónghú (濃湖) army lacked food.
Dèng Wǎn (鄧琬) sent a large quantity of provisions,
but feared Xìngshì (興世)
and dared not advance.
Liú Hú (劉胡) led four hundred light *gě* (舸) along the inner route from Quètóu (鵲頭) to attack Qiánxī (錢溪).
Quèzhōu (鵲洲) is in the middle of the river;
the river splits into branches,
hence there is an inner route and an outer route.
*Gě* (舸)
is pronounced *gǔ wǒ* (古我).
"I have been accustomed to land warfare since childhood,
and am not skilled in naval combat.
If it were land warfare,
I would always be among tens of thousands of men;
but in naval combat, on a single *gě* (舸),
each *gě* (舸) advances independently,
without mutual support,
only among thirty men.
This is not a foolproof plan,
and I will not do it."
So he feigned malaria,
stayed at Quètóu (鵲頭) and did not advance.
He sent the General of Soaring Dragon, Chén Qìng (陳慶), with three hundred *gě* (舸) towards Qiánxī (錢溪),
instructing Qìng (慶) not to fight:
"I know Zhāng Xìngshì (張興世) very well,
he will naturally flee."
Chén Qìng (陳慶) reached Qiánxī (錢溪)
and encamped at Méigēn (梅根).
Hú (胡) sent another general, Wáng Qǐ (王起), with one hundred *gě* (舸) to attack Xìngshì (興世).
Xìngshì (興世) attacked Qǐ (起),
and routed him.
Hú (胡) led the remaining *gě* (舸) back quickly,
and said to Yǐ (顗):
"Xìngshì's (興世) camp is already established,
it cannot be attacked suddenly;
the small battle yesterday
was not enough to cause damage.
Chén Qìng (陳慶) has already joined the Nánlíng (南陵) and Dàléi (大雷) armies to block them upstream,
our main army is here,
and the generals at Quètóu (鵲頭) have cut off their downstream route;
they have fallen into an encirclement,
there is no need to worry further."
Yǐ (顗) was angry that Hú (胡) did not fight,
and said:
"The food supply is blocked,
what should be done?"
*Gěngsè* (鯁塞)
means like a fishbone stuck in the throat.
*Sè* (塞)
is pronounced *xī zé* (悉則).
"They can still go upstream and pass us,
why can't this transport go downstream and pass them?!"
So he sent the Sīmǎ (司馬) of the Ānběi (安北) commandery, Shěn Zhòngyù (沈仲玉), with a thousand men on foot to Nánlíng (南陵) to receive provisions.
Zhòngyù (仲玉) arrived at Nánlíng (南陵),
loaded three hundred thousand *hú* (斛) of rice and several dozen barges of money and cloth,
and erected planks to form a wall,
intending to break through.
He reached Guìkǒu (貴口),
but dared not advance.
The *Shuǐjīng Zhù* (水經註) says: The Jiāngshuǐ (江水) flows east from Shíchéng (石城) to form Guìkǒu (貴口).
The present-day Chíkǒu (池口) in Guìchí Xiàn (貴池縣), Chízhōu (池州) is Guìkǒu (貴口).
Zhāng Shùnmín (張舜民) says: From Tónglíng (銅陵), one sails about sixty *lǐ* (里) to Méigēn Gǎng (梅根港),
and another fifty *lǐ* (里) to Guìchíkǒu (貴池口).
He ordered a heavy army to come to his aid.
Zhāng Xìngshì (張興世) sent Shòu Jìzhī (壽寂之) and Rèn Nóngfū (任農夫) with three thousand men to Guìkǒu (貴口) to attack them.
Zhòngyù (仲玉) fled back to Yǐ's (顗) camp,
and all his supplies were captured;
Hú's (胡) troops were terrified,
and Hú's (胡) general Zhāng Xǐ (張喜) surrendered.
The Army Counselor of the Pacifying East, Liú Liàng, advanced his troops and pressed on Hú's camp.
Hú could not defend it.
Yuán Yǐ said in fear:
“The rebels have entered our vital organs;
how can we survive!”
Hú secretly planned to escape.
On the day Jǐmǎo,
he tricked Yǐ, saying:
“I want to lead another 20,000 infantry and cavalry
to take Qiánxī upstream
and also secure the remaining supplies at Dàléi downstream.”
He ordered Yǐ to select all the horses and provide them to him.
On that very day,
Hú abandoned Yǐ and left,
heading directly for Méigēn.
He had previously ordered Xuē Chángbǎo to prepare boats,
and he mobilized all the troops from Nánlíng,
burned the various cities at Dàléi, and fled.
By night,
Yǐ finally realized it.
He was furious
and cursed, saying:
“This year I have been misled by that brat!”
He called for his favorite horse,
“Fēiyàn,”
and told his followers:
“I will pursue him myself!”
Then he also fled.
On the day Gēngchén,
Jiàn'ān Wáng Xiūrén led his troops into Yǐ’s camp,
accepted the surrender of 100,000 soldiers,
and dispatched Shěn Yōuzhī and others to pursue Yǐ.
Yǐ fled to Quètóu,
and went with the garrison commander Xuē Bózhēn and several thousand of his men,
intending to go to Xúnyáng.
At night,
they stopped in a mountainous area.
Yǐ slaughtered horses to reward his officers and soldiers.
He looked at Bózhēn and said:
“It's not that I cannot die;
I just want to go to Xúnyáng first
to apologize to the Emperor,
and then I will slit my own throat.”
Then he indignantly shouted at his attendants for a "jié" (a symbol of authority),
but no one responded.
At dawn,
Bózhēn requested to speak privately.
He then beheaded Yǐ.
(The Nán Shǐ says: Yǐ fled to Qīnglín Shān and was killed.)
His head was given to Yú Zhànzhī of Xiāngyáng.
Zhànzhī then beheaded Bózhēn
and sent both heads as his own merit.
Liú Hú led 20,000 men towards Xúnyáng,
deceiving Jìn'ān Wáng Zǐxūn, saying:
“Yuán Yǐ has already surrendered,
and his army has dispersed.
Only I am returning with my own troops;
you should make arrangements quickly
to provide funds for a battle.
I will hold Pénchéng
and swear to die rather than be disloyal.”
Then, outside the river, he secretly headed for Miǎnkǒu at night.
There were numerous islands and sandbanks in the river.
Boats traveling close to the south bank were said to be on the "inner route,"
and those close to the north bank were on the "outer route."
Dèng Wǎn heard that Hú had left,
and was worried and at a loss for what to do.
He called the Central Secretariat Palace Assistant Chǔ Língsì and others to deliberate,
but no one knew what to do.
Zhāng Yuè pretended to be ill
and called Wǎn to discuss matters,
ordering his attendants to hide behind the tent
and instructing them:
“If you hear me ask for wine,
then come out.”
When Wǎn arrived,
Yuè said:
“You initiated this plan.
Now that the situation is critical,
what is your next move?”
Wǎn replied:
“We should simply execute the Prince of Jìn'ān,
seal the imperial treasury,
and apologize to the Emperor.”
Yuè said:
“Today, how can we betray His Highness to save our own lives!”
Then he called for wine.
Zǐxún (Yuè's son) came out with a knife and killed Wǎn.
Xún
was Yuè's son.
He then led his troops.
Yuè sent someone to tell him:
“Dèng Wǎn plotted rebellion and has now been executed.”
Xún was delighted and returned.
He took Wǎn's sons
and killed them all.
Yuè then, in a single small boat,
carried Wǎn's head and rushed downstream,
presenting it to Jiàn'ān Wáng Xiūrén to surrender.
Xúnyáng was in chaos.
There was no ruler,
hence the chaos.
The Department of Works,
responsible for manufacturing weapons,
was located outside Xúnyáng city.
They seized Zǐxūn
and imprisoned him.
Shěn Yōuzhī's armies arrived at Xúnyáng,
executed Jìn'ān Wáng Zǐxūn,
and sent his head to Jiànkāng.
He was eleven years old at the time.
Jìn'ān's raising of an army
was indeed a righteous act.
Dèng Wǎn is not worth mentioning,
but how can one say that Yuán Yǐ and Kǒng Jì did not meet their proper end?
The world should not judge based on success or failure.
Earlier,
Dèng Wǎn sent the Administrator of Línchuān, Zhāng Yān, from Póyáng via the mountain pass into Sān Wú.
He garrisoned at Shàngráo.
(The Jìn Tàikāng Dì Zhì states: Póyáng Commandery had Shàngráo County,
but the Jìn Shū does not mention it.
It was probably established by Wú.
Today it is Xìnzhōu,
and there is a road connecting to Póyáng.)
(Sòng Bái said: Shàngráo County in Xìnzhōu
was originally part of Qín's Fān County territory.
During the Hàn, it was Fányáng County.
The ruins of the old city of the present prefecture
are the old Shàngráo that was abolished during the Kāihuáng period.)
(The so-called Shàngráo
was named because of the Xiàráo Prefecture beside it.)
(The Jiǔ Yù Zhì states: Fányáng is five hundred forty li southeast of Shàngráo.)
His deputy, the Administrator of Póyáng, Fèi Yè, beheaded Yān and surrendered.
Yān
was Chàngzhī's son.
(Zhāng Chàng,
at the end of Yuánjiā,
followed Shìzǔ as the Chief Clerk of Xúzhōu.)
(Fèi,
his father's name is Fèi, pronounced fù.)
During the reign of Fèi Dì,
the gentry feared disaster
and all wished to leave far away.
By this time, they were scattered and suffering from external calamities,
with scarcely one in a hundred surviving.
The people then acknowledged Cài Xīngzōng's foresight.
(Foresight,
the matter is found in the first year of the previous volume.)
In the ninth month, on the day Rénchén,
Shānyáng Wáng Xiūyòu was appointed Governor of Jīngzhōu.
On the day Guǐsì,
the emergency measures were lifted,
and a general amnesty was issued.
On the day Gēngzǐ,
the Grand Commandant Xiūrén arrived at Xúnyáng.
He dispatched Wú Xǐ and Zhāng Xīngshì towards Jīngzhōu,
Shěn Huáimíng towards Yǐngzhōu,
Liú Liàng and the General Who Pacifies the North, Zhāng Jìng'ér of Nányáng, towards Yōngzhōu,
Sūn Chāozhī towards Xiāngzhōu,
Shěn Sīrén and Rèn Nóngfū towards Yùzhāng,
to pacify the remaining rebels.
Liú Hú fled to Shíchéng.
(This is Shíchéng of Jìnglíng,
which is now Chángshòu County in Yǐngzhōu.)
He was beheaded.
The acting Governor of Yǐngzhōu, Zhāng Shěn, disguised himself as a Buddhist monk
and secretly fled,
but was pursued, captured,
and killed.
The acting Governor of Jīngzhōu, Liú Dàoxiàn, heard that Nónghú was pacified,
dispersed his troops,
and sent an envoy to confess his crimes.
The Vice Administrator of Jīngzhōu, Zōng Jǐng, and others led troops into the city,
killed Dàoxiàn,
and seized Línhǎi Wáng Zǐxū and surrendered.
Kǒng Dàocún knew that Xúnyáng had been pacified
and sent an envoy to request surrender.
Soon after, he heard that Liǔ Shìlóng and Liú Liàng were about to arrive.
Dàocún and his three sons all committed suicide.
(Kǒng Dàocún was then the acting Governor of Yōngzhōu.)
(He possessed both military talent
and administrative talent.)
(Jiàng,
meaning liàng.)
(Huìwén said:
“Having already fallen into rebellion
and personally harmed loyal and righteous individuals,”
meaning he killed Wáng Yīngzhī.)
(He then committed suicide.)
(The history states that Hé Huìwén refused to live in disgrace.)
Liú Shùn and the remaining partisans in Jīngzhōu were all executed.
(Liú Shùn fled from Zǐhǔ to Huáixī,
and then from Huáixī to Jīngzhōu.)
The meritorious individuals were awarded and promoted accordingly.
47 Jǐyǒu,
Wèi established commandery schools for the first time,
setting up Bóshì, Zhùjiào, and students.
This was at the request of Zhōngshūlìng Gāo Yǔn and Xiāngzhōu Cìshǐ Lǐ Xīn.
In ancient times,
each family had a shú,
each xiǎng had a xiáng,
Wèi had an xù,
and the state had schools.
Although Qín burned books and buried scholars alive,
scholars in Qí and Lǔ never abandoned their studies.
When Hàn Wén Wēng was governor of Shǔ,
he established official schools,
and the number of scholars rivaled those of Qí and Lǔ.
Emperor Wǔ ordered all commanderies and states under heaven to establish official schools.
Thus, the establishment of official schools is an ancient practice.
The statement in this book that Wèi first established commandery schools, set up officials and students,
probably expresses sorrow that due to the wars among the Wǔ Hú,
there was no time to establish schools,
and Wèi, having risen in the northern wilderness,
only reached this stage after several generations.
While regretting this,
it is still fortunate that this culture, which had fallen to the ground, was revived.
Xiāng,
pronounced xì liàng fān.
Xīn,
pronounced xǔ jīn fān.
He was the son of Chóng.
This is a different Lǐ Chóng,
not Lǐ Chóng of Dùnqiū.
48 After the Emperor executed Prince Zǐxūn of Jìn'ān and others,
he treated all the sons of Shìzǔ as he did on normal days.
Sītú Xiū Rén returned from Xúnyáng
and said to the Emperor:
"The brothers of Sōngzīhóu are still alive.
This is not a good plan for the future of the state.
They should be dealt with early."
In winter,
the tenth month,
Yǐmǎo,
Sōngzīhóu Zǐfáng, Yǒngjiā Wáng Zǐrén, Shǐ'ān Wáng Zǐzhēn, Huáinán Wáng Zǐmèng, Nánpíng Wáng Zǐchǎn, Lúlíng Wáng Zǐyú, Zǐqū, Zǐqī, and Dōngpíng Wáng Zǐsì, Zǐyuè were all granted death,
as well as Zhènběi Zīyì Cānjūn Lù Xiūzhī and Sītú Cóngshì Zhōngláng Lù Màozhī.
These two Lùs
were all nephews of Zhāo Tàihòu.
All twenty-eight sons of Shìzǔ ended here.
The calamity of Xiū Rén's degradation from Shàngshū
was brought upon himself.
He guided the Emperor to eliminate his nephews;
the Emperor's hand was unsteady,
what would become of his own brothers?
Xiāo Qí changed the dynasty,
and the Líu clan was exterminated.
Kinsfolk slaughtered each other,
and calamity reached its extreme.
May those who possess states and families
learn from this!
He was the son of Yìxīn.
49 Líu Miǎn besieged Shòuyáng,
and Yuán Hóng attacked Héféi;
neither had yet fallen.
Miǎn was troubled by this and
convened his generals for a meeting.
The cavalry commander Wáng Guǎngzhī said:
"If I can have the general's mount,
I am certain I can pacify Héféi."
Pàn
means "to decide"
or "to determine."
"Guǎngzhī dares to take the commander's horse;
he can be executed!"
Miǎn laughed and said:
"Judging from his intention,
he will certainly achieve merit."
He immediately pushed the saddle and dismounted, giving the horse to him.
Guǎngzhī went to attack Héféi and
in three days
captured it.
Xuē Dàobiāo broke through the encirclement and fled to Huáinán, returning to Cháng Zhēnqí.
Miǎn promoted Guǎngzhī to Jūnzhǔ.
Guǎngzhī said to Sù:
"If the commander had followed your words,
how would we have pacified the rebels?
You do not appreciate talent,
and it comes to this!"
Sù had scholarly achievements,
and after Miǎn died,
he relied on Guǎngzhī,
who recommended him to Qí Shìzǔ as Dōnghǎi Tàishǒu.
The historian completed this matter
to show that Wáng Guǎngzhī was able to turn resentment into gratitude through kindness.
50 Shěn Língbǎo led troops from Lújiāng to attack Jìnxī.
Emperor Ān of Jìn divided Lújiāng to establish Jìnxī Commandery;
modern Shūzhōu is that place.
Jìnxī had previously sided with Xúnyáng,
hence the attack.
51 Xúzhōu Cìshǐ Xuē Āndū, Yìzhōu Cìshǐ Xiāo Huìkāi, and Liángzhōu Cìshǐ Liǔ Yuángù
(Kǎoyì says: Sònglüè has
"Yuánzhé."
We now follow the Sòngshū.) (Kǎoyì says: Sònglüè has
"Bì Zhēn,"
and the Hòuwèishū says
"his nickname was Nà."
We now follow his biography.)
all sent envoys to surrender.
Xúnyáng having been pacified,
they all requested to surrender.
Shǐ
is pronounced shū lì fān.
Jiàng
is pronounced hù jiāng fān.
Wishing to demonstrate power north of the Huái River,
on Yǐhài,
the Emperor ordered Zhèn Jūn Jiāngjūn Zhāng Yǒng and Zhōng Lǐngjūn Shěn Yōuzhī to lead fifty thousand armored soldiers to welcome Xuē Āndū.
Cài Xīngzōng said:
"Āndū's submission
is truly not false,
and only requires a single envoy with a letter.
Now, by sending heavy troops to meet him,
he will inevitably become suspicious and fearful;
he might even attract the northern barbarians,
leading to even deeper trouble.
If you consider the crime of a rebellious subject to be too severe
to not be executed,
then those who were pardoned previously were already many.
Moreover, Āndū holds a large stronghold externally,
close to the frontier.
His terrain is treacherous and his troops strong,
making attack and encirclement difficult to overcome.
Considering the national interest,
it is especially advisable to pacify him.
If he defects externally,
it will become a worry for the court that will keep it from eating until dusk."
The Emperor did not heed him.
This laid the groundwork for the Emperor to later be ashamed of Cài Xīngzōng.
Gàn
is pronounced kǔ hàn fān.
"I am now embarking on a northern expedition.
What do you think of this?"
He replied:
"Āndū has cunning to spare.
Now, pressing him with troops,
I fear it is not beneficial for the state."
The Emperor said:
"All my armies are fierce and sharp;
where can they not conquer?
You need not say more!"
Cài Xīngzōng
and Xiāo Dàochéng,
though their positions were different,
their insights were not.
Indeed, recognizing the times and adapting to change
is something only the wise can do;
there is no difference in the way of civil and military matters.
The topography
is high in the northwest and
low in the southeast.
The waters of Jì, Sì, and Yí all flow south,
passing through Péngchéng and emptying into the Huái.
Therefore, the southern army moving northward is called Běishàng.
Shàng
is pronounced shí zhǎng fān.
(He) sent envoys to surrender to Wèi.
Cháng Zhēnqí also surrendered Xuánhù to Wèi.
(Kǎoyì says: Sònglüè:
"In the twelfth month,
Jiǎyín,
Zhēnqí rebelled again with the commandery."
This was probably when the Sòng court first heard of it.)
52 Wùyín,
the Emperor's son Yù was established as Crown Prince.
53 Xuē Āndū sent his son as a hostage to Wèi.
Wèi sent Zhèndōng Dàjiāngjūn Dàirén Wèi Yuán and Zhèndōng Jiāngjūn Wèijùn Kǒng Bógōng and others to lead ten thousand cavalry out of the eastern route
to relieve Péngchéng.
Zhènxī Dàjiāngjūn Xīhé Gōng Shí and Dūdū Jīng Yù Nányōngzhōu Zhū Jūnfāng Zhāng Qióngqí went out of the western route
to relieve Xuánhù.
Āndū was appointed Dūdū Xú Yōng
and other five prefectures' military affairs, Zhènnán Dàjiāngjūn, Xúzhōu Cìshǐ, and Hédōng Gōng.
Cháng Zhēnqí was appointed Píngnán Jiāngjūn, Yùzhōu Cìshǐ, and Hénèi Gōng.
Yǎnzhōu Cìshǐ Shēn Zuǎn feigned surrender to Wèi.
Wèi Yuán accepted it but secretly prepared for it.
When the Wèi army reached Wúyán,
Zuǎn closed the gates and resisted.
This laid the groundwork for Wèi to attack and kill Shēn Zuǎn.
When Xuē Āndū summoned the Wèi troops,
Bì Zhòngjìng did not go along with him,
and sent an envoy to request surrender.
In the spring of that year,
Bì Zhòngjìng rebelled against Jiànkāng and followed Xuē Āndū;
when Āndū surrendered to Wèi,
Zhòngjìng then did not go along with him.
Zhòngjìng's son, Yuánbīn, was in Jiànkāng,
and had earlier been executed for another crime.
Kǎoyì says: The biography of Zhòngjìng in Hòu Wèi Shū states:
“Yuánbīn had committed another crime,
and Yù alone did not spare him.”
Sòng Lüè says
“his son in the capital had already been executed,”
and we follow this.
He was enraged,
drew his sword and chopped at a pillar, saying:
“I am white-headed with only one son,
and cannot preserve him;
what use is it for me to live alone!”
In the eleventh month,
on the day Rénzǐ,
the Wèi army arrived at Xiáqiū,
and Zhòngjìng requested to surrender to Wèi.
Wèi Yuán sent his subordinate general to first occupy the city.
Zhòngjìng felt regret and remorse,
and did not eat for several days.
Yuán marched straight ahead,
and in the twelfth month,
on the day Jǐwèi,
camped at Gē.
Gē County,
during the Hàn dynasty, belonged to the Jìyīn Commandery;
it was abolished during the Later Hàn.
Its territory should be in the current Cáo Zhōu area of the Táng dynasty.
Mèng Kāng says: Gē,
is pronounced like 'dù'.
When Xīhé Gōng Shí arrived at Shàngcài,
Cháng Zhēnqí, leading civil and military officials, came out to greet him.
Shí wanted to station his army north of the Rǔ river,
and not enter the city immediately.
Xuánhù city was south of the Rǔ river.
“Although Zhēnqí has come today,
his intentions cannot be measured.
It is better to enter his city directly,
seize his keys and locks,
Guǎn (管)
means 'key'.
Yuè (籥)
means 'bolt'.
control his vital organs,
that is the safest strategy.”
Shí then spurred his horse into the city,
and thereupon held a feast and amusement.
Xī said:
“Zhēnqí's expression seems very displeased;
we must be prepared.”
So he readied his troops and set up defenses.
That evening,
Zhēnqí sent people to burn the government buildings,
intending to cause trouble,
but stopped because Shí was prepared.
Xī was
Huò's great-grandson.
Many people in the seven commanderies of Huáinán did not wish to belong to Wèi,
and they formed continuous camps and fled south.
The seven commanderies of Huáinán were: Rǔnán, Xīncài, Rǔyáng, Rǔyīn, Chénjùn, Nándùn, and Yǐngchuān.
When there were people who had been captured by the army and made into slaves,
Bó freed them all,
and the new populace was delighted.
54On the day Yǐchǒu,
an edict was issued, stating that those who had been removed from office, stripped of rank, and imprisoned for siding with Xúnyáng,
were all to be pardoned and reinstated,
and appointed according to their talents.
55Liú Miǎn besieged Shòuyáng.
From early spring to late winter,
he attacked from within and defended from without,
winning every battle,
and gained the hearts of his officers and soldiers through his magnanimity.
After Xúnyáng was pacified,
the Emperor ordered the Zhongshū to draft an edict to persuade Yīn Yǎn.
Cài Xīngzōng said:
“Now that the empire is settled,
this is the day for Yǎn to reflect on his mistakes.
Your Majesty should personally write a few lines in an imperial edict to comfort and guide him.
'Comfort' (wèi) means
to reassure his heart;
'guide' (yǐn) means
to lead him to submit.
Háng (行)
is pronounced 'hù gāng'.
He will certainly suspect it is not genuine,
which is not the way to quickly resolve the current difficulties.”
The Emperor did not follow this advice.
When Yǎn received the edict,
he believed Liú Miǎn had falsely fabricated it,
and dared not surrender.
Dù Shúbǎo blocked all news of the defeat at Xúnyáng,
and killed anyone who spread it,
making the defenses even stronger.
Whenever there were those who surrendered,
the Emperor would send them to the foot of Shòuyáng city
to speak with the people inside the city,
whereby the morale of the populace disintegrated.
Yǎn wanted to request surrender to Wèi.
His chief clerk, Xiàhóu Xiáng of Qiáojùn, advised Yǎn, saying:
“Today's actions
were originally to demonstrate loyalty and integrity.
If the altars of soil and grain have a master,
then you should return to the imperial court;
how can you face north and wear the barbarian costume!
Moreover, the Wèi army is now close to the Huái river,
referring to the army of Xīhé Gōng Shí in Rǔnán.
If we establish an envoy to show sincerity,
‘Jiàn shǐ’ (建使)
should be
‘qiǎn shǐ’ (遣使).
Kuǎn (款)
means 'sincerity'.
Shǐ (使)
is pronounced 'shū lì'.
it will not only be a matter of escaping punishment.”
Yǎn then sent Xiáng out to see Liú Miǎn.
Xiáng advised Miǎn, saying:
“The officers and people in the city now know they are in trouble but still hold firm
because they fear the general's execution;
they all want to surrender to Wèi.
I hope the general will be lenient and pardon them,
then everyone will lead each other to come.”
Miǎn agreed,
and sent Xiáng to the foot of the city,
to call out to the people in the city,
and convey Miǎn's intentions.
On the day Bǐngyín,
Yǎn, leading his generals and aides, came out tied hand and foot to surrender.
Miǎn comforted and appeased them all,
not executing a single person.
Upon entering the city,
he disciplined his officers and soldiers,
and the property and wealth of the officers and people
were not lost in the slightest.
The people of Shòuyáng were greatly pleased.
The Wèi army reached the Shī River.
Shuǐ Jīng Zhù says: The Shī River originates from Mount Dàkuì,
then flows north past the west of Mount Xiánshǒu,
then east past the north of the old city of Yìyáng.
The Nánběi Duìjìng Tú indicates: The Shī River is in the northwestern boundary of present-day Luóshān County, Xìnyángjūn.
Hearing that Yǎn had already surrendered,
they then plundered several thousand people from Yìyáng and departed.
After a long time,
Yǎn again served as Shàofǔ and then died.
56Xiāo Huìkāi was in Yìzhōu,
where he frequently resorted to severe punishments,
causing suspicion and resentment among the people of Shǔ.
Hearing of Fèi Xīnshòu's defeat and death,
and Chéng Fǎdù's inability to advance,
these events are all mentioned in the sixth month above.
Shěn Yuē says: Lǐ Xióng divided Jiāngyuán and Línqióng of Shǔjùn into Hàn Yuánjùn,
and Emperor Mù of Jìn renamed it Jìnyuán.
During the Táng dynasty, it was Shǔzhōu.
He assembled his forces and besieged Chéngdū.
There were less than two thousand eastern troops in the city.
Huìkāi sent all the Shǔ people out,
and defended only with the eastern troops.
Eastern troops refers to
Huìkāi's personal retinue.
They vied to butcher the city,
with the crowd reaching over ten myriad people.
Whenever Huìkāi sent troops out to battle,
they never failed to be victorious.
The Emperor sent his younger brother, Huìjī, by land to Chéngdū,
pardoning Huìkāi's crimes.
When Huìjī reached Fú,
the Shǔ people blocked and detained Huìjī,
not allowing him to proceed.
Huìjī led his retinue to attack them,
beheading their leader,
and only then was he able to advance.
Huìkāi received the imperial decree and surrendered,
and the city's siege was lifted.
The Emperor dispatched Bǎoshǒu (寶首), a clansman of Huìkāi (惠開), from the waterway to console Yìzhōu (益州).
Bǎoshǒu wished to take credit for pacifying Shǔ (蜀),
so he further incited and persuaded the people of Shǔ
to attack Huìkāi.
Thereupon, uprisings erupted everywhere,
and all those who had scattered reunited at once,
advancing with Bǎoshǒu to threaten Chéngdū (成都).
Their forces numbered 200,000.
Huìkāi wanted to attack them,
but his generals and subordinates all said:
"Now that the envoy of consolation has arrived, how can we justify ourselves
by resisting him?"
Huìkāi said:
"The path for submitting memorials and reports is now cut off.
If we do not fight, how can we communicate with the capital?"
He then dispatched Xiāo Huìxùn (蕭惠訓), the Grand Administrator of Sòngníng (宋寧), and others to lead 10,000 troops to battle them,
greatly defeating them.
Bǎoshǒu was captured alive
and imprisoned in Chéngdū.
Shěn Yuè (沈約) said: In the tenth year of Yuánjiā (元嘉) of Emperor Wén (文),
Wúyíng (吳營) was abolished,
and Sòngníng Commandery was established as a provisional entity,
with its provisional seat of government in Chéngdū.
Jiàng (將)
is pronounced like liàng (亮);
the same below.
The Emperor ordered Bǎoshǒu to be arrested and sent away,
and summoned Huìkāi back to Jiànkāng (建康).
The Emperor questioned him about the circumstances of raising an army.
Huìkāi said:
"Your subject only knows what is rebellious and what is loyal,
but does not understand Heaven's mandate;
moreover, without your subject, there would be chaos;
without your subject, there would be no peace."
The Emperor released him.
In this year,
Yǎnzhōu (兗州) was provisionally established,
with its seat of government in Huái'yīn (淮陰);
Xúzhōu (徐州) had its seat in Zhōnglí (鍾離);
Qīng (青) and Jì (冀) provinces shared one inspector,
whose seat was in Yùzhōu (鬱洲).
Since Yǎn, Xú, Qīng, and Jì had all surrendered to Wèi (魏),
these provisional provinces were established.
They spanned several hundred *lǐ*,
with cities built of piled stones,
eight or nine *chǐ* high,
and commanderies and counties were set up in name,
with few desolate common people.
Zhāng Yǒng (張永) and Shěn Yōuzhī (沈攸之) advanced their troops, pressing towards Péngchéng (彭城),
encamping at Xiàkuí (下礚). They
detached Yǔlín Supervisor Wáng Mùzhī (王穆之) to lead 5,000 soldiers to guard the baggage train at Wǔyuán (武原).
The Shuǐjīngzhù (水經註) states: Wǔyuán County is northwest of Xiàpī (下邳) County.
According to research,
Wǔyuán County,
since the Hàn (漢) dynasty, belonged to Péngchéng Commandery.
The Sòng Zhì (宋志) states that
Nánpéngchéng (南彭城) Commandery had Wǔyuán County,
but Xúzhōu's Péngchéng did not.
This is probably because, since the Yongjiā (永嘉) disturbance of the Jìn (晉) dynasty,
its people migrated south,
and the former county became ruins.
Dù Yòu (杜佑) said: North of Sìzhōu (泗州)'s Xiàpī County is the old city of Hàn's Wǔyuán County.
Chóng (重)
is pronounced like zhíyòng (直用).
Wèi's Wèi Yuán (尉元) arrived at Péngchéng,
and Xuē Āndū (薛安都) went out to welcome him.
Wèi Yuán sent Lǐ Càn (李璨) with Āndū to enter the city first
to collect its keys;
he then separately dispatched Kǒng Bógōng (孔伯恭) with 2,000 elite armored soldiers to pacify the interior and exterior,
before entering himself.
He received the surrender as if facing an enemy;
Wèi Yuán managed it well.
Zhāng Yǒng attacked the south gate,
but failed and retreated.
Wèi Yuán treated Xuē Āndū disrespectfully,
and Āndū regretted surrendering,
plotting again to rebel against Wèi.
Wèi Yuán
became aware of it,
but the plot did not materialize.
"Hé zhī" (和之) means
to reconcile.
Some say that
"hé zhī" (和之)
should be
"zhī zhī" (知之) (knew of it).
He blamed his son-in-law Péi Zǔlóng (裴祖隆) and killed him.
Wèi Yuán sent Lǐ Zhū (李珠)
to guard Péngchéng with Āndū,
and personally led troops to attack Zhāng Yǒng,
cutting off his supply route,
and also defeating Wáng Mùzhī at Wǔyuán.
Mùzhī led the remnants of his forces to join Yǒng,
and Wèi Yuán advanced to attack them.
Niè Chóngqí (聶崇岐) punctuated, Wáng Chóngwǔ (王崇武) re-collated.
Sīmǎ Guāng (司馬光)
compiled by imperial command.
Hòuxuétiāntái (後學天台)
Tàizōng Mínghuángdì (太宗明皇帝) Middle
Tàishǐ (泰始) 3rd Year (Dīngwèi, 467)
1. Spring,
1st month.
Zhāng Yǒng and others abandoned the city and fled by night.
The Kǎoyì (考異) says: The Sòng Běnjì (宋本紀) states that
in the winter of the previous year,
"Yǒng and Yōuzhī suffered a great defeat,
and consequently lost the four provinces north of the Huái (淮) and the land west of the Huái in Yùzhōu (豫州)."
The Sònglǜe (宋略) states that
in the 1st month of this year,
"Yǒng and Yōuzhī's army was near Péngchéng when
the barbarians ambushed their baggage train,
defeating Wáng Mùzhī at Wǔyuán.
Xuē Āndū opened Péngchéng to admit the barbarians,
and Yǒng and others withdrew;
the barbarians pursued them,
and the imperial army was routed;
Bì Nà (畢捺) also surrendered Yǎnzhōu to the barbarians,
thus losing the land north of the Huái."
The Wèi Dìjì (魏帝紀) states that
in the 9th month of the previous year,
"Cháng Zhēnqí (常珍奇) and Xuē Āndū submitted internally,
Zhāng Yǒng and Shěn Yōuzhī attacked Āndū.
An edict ordered Wèi Yuán to save Péngchéng,
and Xīhé Gōng (西河公) Shí (石) to save Xuánhù (懸瓠).
In the 11th month,
Bì Zhòngjìng (畢衆敬) submitted internally.
On the *jǐwèi* (己未) day of the 12th month,
they arrived at Dí (秺).
Zhōu Kǎi (周凱), Zhāng Yǒng, and Shěn Yōuzhī retreated one after another."
On the *guǐsì* (癸巳) day of the 1st month of this year,
"Wèi Yuán defeated Yǒng and Yōuzhī east of Lǚliáng (呂梁).
In the intercalary month,
Shěn Wénxiù (沈文秀) and Cuī Dàogù (崔道固) surrendered their provinces internally."
According to this, Qīng and Jì began to rebel against Sòng this year;
how could they have already lost the land north of the Huái last year?
Āndū was pressed by Yǒng and Yōuzhī,
hence he surrendered to Wèi;
how could Yǒng and Yōuzhī only now be nearing Péngchéng this year,
and Āndū only now be admitting Wèi troops?
It is probable that Mùzhī and others were already defeated and retreated last winter,
and Yǒng suffered a great defeat this spring.
We now follow the Hòuwèi Dìjì (後魏帝紀).
The Sìshuǐ (泗水) froze over,
and Yǒng and others abandoned their boats and fled on foot.
More than half of the soldiers froze to death,
and seven or eight tenths had their hands and feet severed.
Wèi Yuán blocked them in front,
and Xuē Āndū attacked from the rear,
greatly defeating Yǒng and others east of Lǚliáng.
The Shuǐjīngzhù states: The Sìshuǐ flows southeast from Péngchéng past the south of Lǚ County.
There is a stone bridge over the Sìshuǐ,
hence it is called Lǚliáng.
Wèi (尉)
is pronounced like yūwù (紆勿).
Corpses lay for over sixty *lǐ*,
and the abandoned military supplies and equipment were beyond counting;
Yǒng also lost toes,
and he and Shěn Yōuzhī barely escaped with their lives.
Yuán Gōngzǔ (垣恭祖), the Inspector of Liáng (梁) and Nánqín (南秦) provinces, and others were captured by Wèi.
When the Emperor heard of it,
he summoned Cài Xīngzōng (蔡興宗),
showed him the defeat report, and said:
"I am deeply ashamed before you!"
Yǒng was demoted to General of the Left;
Yōuzhī was dismissed from office,
but held his post as Duke of Zhēnyáng (貞陽),
and returned to garrison Huái'yīn.
The Hàn Zhì (漢志) states: Guìyáng (桂陽) Commandery had Zhēnyáng (湞陽) County.
The Shěn Yuè Zhì states: In Tàishǐ 3rd year of Sòng, Zhēn (湞) was changed to Zhēn (貞),
belonging to Guǎngxīng Gōng Xiāng (廣興公相).
The four provinces north of the Huái were Qīng, Jì, Xú, and Yǎn.
Yùzhōu west of the Huái refers to the commanderies of Rǔnán (汝南), Xīncài (新蔡), Qiáo (譙), Liáng, Chén (陳), Nándùn (南頓), Yǐngchuān (潁川), Rǔnán, and Rǔyīn (汝陰).
The Kǎoyì says: The Hòuwèi Dìjì states: In the intercalary month,
"Shěn Wénxiù and Cuī Dàogù surrendered their provinces internally."
The Sòng Suǒlǔ Zhuàn (宋索虜傳) says:
"After Yǒng and Yōuzhī were defeated and retreated,
the barbarians attacked Qīng and Jì provinces,
capturing Wénxiù and Dàogù.
An imperial decree was also issued saying:
'All crimes committed by the people of the three provinces north of the Huái
before dawn on the *rén'yín* (壬寅) day of the 1st month of Tiān'ān (天安) 2nd year
are entirely pardoned.'"
According to this, Qīngzhōu (青州) was captured in the 5th year,
so the "three provinces north of the Huái" probably refers to Xú, Sī (司), and Yù.
*Rén'yín* is the 20th day, *rénzǐ* (壬子) is the 30th day.
Péi Zǐyě (裴子野) discussed, saying: "In ancient times, Qí Huán (齊桓) was arrogant at Kuíqiū (葵丘), and nine states rebelled.
The *Gōuyáng Zhuàn* (公羊傳) states: At the Guànzé (貫澤) covenant,
Dūke Qí Huán (齊桓公) had a concern for the Central States.
Those who came without being summoned
were the Rén (人) from Jiāng (江) and Huáng (黃).
At the Kuíqiū (葵丘) covenant,
Dūke Huán (桓公) was awe-inspiring and arrogant,
and nine states rebelled.
See Volume 65, Jiàn'ān (建安) Thirteenth Year of Emperor Xiàn (獻帝) of Hàn (漢).
The difference is immense.
In Tàizōng's (太宗) early days,
the reach of his authority
was less than a hundred *lǐ* (里).
If there were sudden signs of disloyalty,
his officers would not show firm resolve.
Yet he was able to open his sincere heart
and show genuine sincerity,
and none failed to feel grateful for his virtue
and dedicate themselves to him, risking their lives.
Thus, he crushed the west and swept away the north,
opening up the entire realm.
Soon, after the six armies presented their victories
and all regions submitted,
the Son of Heaven wished to exploit his remaining might.
He launched campaigns without justification,
and north of the Chánghuái (長淮)
suddenly became a frontier region.
What a pity!
If he had maintained the same open-mindedness as before,
neither arrogant nor boastful,
then why would the three rebellions have arisen?
The three rebellions were those of
Xuē Āndū (薛安都), Bì Zhòngjìng (畢衆敬), and Cháng Zhēnjī (常珍奇).
The territory that was opened up,
later generations of his descendants
daily saw a hundred *lǐ* (里) shrink away.
The *Dàyǎ* (大雅) poem 'Zhào Mín' (召旻) says: 'In ancient times, the former kings received the Mandate,
like Dūke Zhào (召公),
daily expanding the state by a hundred *lǐ* (里);
now, daily the state shrinks by a hundred *lǐ* (里).'
How can one say it is easy?"
Wèi Wèiyuán (魏尉元), seeing that Péngchéng (彭城) had been ravaged by war,
with public and private resources exhausted,
requested to dispatch grain from the four *zhōu* (州) of Jì (冀), Xiàng (相), Jǐ (濟), and Yǎn (兗),
and to take nine hundred boats abandoned by Zhāng Yǒng (張永),
to transport goods along the Qīngshǔi (清水)
to relieve the new populace.
"New populace"
refers to the people of Xúzhōu (徐州) newly acquired;
"transport along the Qīngshǔi (清水)" means transport along the Qīngshǔi (清水) river.
艘 (sōu),
read *sū zāo*.
賑 (zhèn),
read *jīn rěn*.
Wèi Dōngpíng Wáng Dàofú (魏東平王道符) rebelled in Cháng'ān (長安),
killing the deputy general and *fùmǎ dūwèi* (駙馬都尉) Wàn Gǔzhēn (萬古真) and others.
"Deputy general"
refers to the deputy garrison commander.
將 (jiàng),
read *jí liàng*;
the same below.
On the *bǐngwǔ* (丙午) day,
*Sīkōng* (司空) Hé Qínú (和其奴) and others led palace troops to suppress him.
On the *dīngwèi* (丁未) day,
Dàofú's (道符) *sīmǎ* (司馬) Duàn Tàiyáng (段太陽) attacked Dàofú (道符)
and beheaded him.
Lù Zhēn (陸真), the *Ānxī Jiāngjūn* (安西將軍), was made the garrison commander of Cháng'ān (長安) to pacify the region.
Dàofú (道符)
was the son of Hàn (翰).
Qín Wáng Hàn (秦王翰) died in the upheaval involving Zōng Ài (宗愛) in Zhèngpíng (正平).
In the intercalary month,
Wèi (魏) appointed Dùnqiū Wáng Lǐ Jùn (頓丘王李峻) as *Tàizǎi* (太宰).
Shěn Wénxiù (沈文秀) and Cuī Dàogù (崔道固) were attacked by local people.
"Local people"
refers to the people of Qīng (青) and Jì (冀) two *zhōu* (州).
They also requested troops to save themselves.
In the second month,
Wèi Xīhé Gōng Shí (魏西河公石) led troops from Xuánhù (懸瓠) to attack Zhāng Chāo (張超), the Administrator of Rǔyīn (汝陰),
but did not succeed.

According to records, Yuán (元) received the imperial decree to rescue Xuē Āndū (薛安都) in the ninth month of Tàishǐ (泰始) second year (466 CE).
This memorial says,
"I received the command to go beyond the border,

This suggests that the memorial was submitted in late spring or early summer of the fourth year.
Furthermore, Shěn Yōuzhī (沈攸之) deployed his army in the eighth month of the third year,
and soon after was defeated and retreated.
Thus, the memorial must have been submitted after Yōuzhī's (攸之) defeat.
However, this memorial only mentions Chén Xiǎndá (陳顯達) following Sùyù (宿豫),
and does not mention Yōuzhī (攸之) rescuing Xiàpī (下邳).

In the fifth month,
on the day Rénxū (壬戌),
Yuán Càn (袁粲), the太子詹事 (Tàizǐ Zhānshì), was appointed Shàngshū Yòupúyè (尚書右僕射).
Shěn Yōuzhī (沈攸之) personally escorted rice shipments to Xiàpī (下邳).
Shěn Yōuzhī (沈攸之) traveled from Huái'yīn (淮陰) to Xiàpī (下邳).
"Xuē Āndū (薛安都) wishes to surrender and requests an army to receive him."

there is no need for you to make a fruitless journey back and forth."
From then on, they left and never returned.
This was because Yōuzhī (攸之) knew their true intentions.
Xuē Āndū's (薛安都) son, Lìngbó (令伯), fled between Liáng (梁) and Yōng (雍) provinces,

In the autumn, seventh month,
Bālíngwáng Xiūrǔo (巴陵王休若), the governor of Yōngzhōu (雍州), sent Nányáng (南陽) Administrator Zhāng Jìng'ér (張敬兒) and others to attack and kill him.
The emperor again sent Zhōnglǐngjūn (中領軍) Shěn Yōuzhī (沈攸之) and others to attack Péngchéng (彭城).
Yōuzhī (攸之) believed that the Qīng (清) and Sì (泗) rivers were currently dry,

Wèi's Wèi Yuán sent Kǒng Bógōng to command ten thousand infantry and cavalry to resist Shěn Yōuzhī.

1 In spring,

In ancient times, the Duke of Zhōu sacrificed to Hòujì to match Heaven,
and offered ancestral sacrifices to King Wén in the Bright Hall to match the Supreme Emperor.
Sacrifices to the suburbs every three years
began with Emperor Wǔ of Hàn.
During the Yuánshǐ era of Emperor Píng,
the rite of combined ancestral sacrifices in the Bright Hall began to be performed.
In the early Yǒngpíng era of Emperor Míng,
its ceremonies became grand;
it was also called ancestral sacrifice.
The Gōngyáng Zhuàn says: In ancient times, major ancestral sacrifices were performed twice in five years,
referring to combined ancestral sacrifices.
However, what was called combined ancestral sacrifice in ancient times
was a joint sacrifice in the temple of the great ancestor;
while the ancestral sacrifice in the Bright Hall
involved matching the revered father with the Emperor.
This is why the explanations of earlier Confucian scholars differ.
Cài Yōng believed that the Bright Hall was the Grand Ancestral Temple,
perhaps he saw something in this!
However, the Bright Hall had nine chambers while the Grand Ancestral Temple had seven chambers,
so they cannot be combined.
Sacrifices every other year
were not ancient,
hence it is called "initially decreed."
