Xún Bóyù of Guǎnglíng, a Cānjūn of the Guānjūn, advised Dàochéng to send several tens of cavalry into Wèi territory,
to set up markers and banners.
Dàochéng was at the time provisionally General of Guānjūn,
and had Bóyù as his Cānjūn.
冠 (guān),
pronounced gǔ wán.
Dàochéng reported this,
and the emperor ordered Dàochéng to resume his original post.
Autumn,
the ninth month.
Dàochéng was ordered to move his garrison to Huái'yīn.
According to records, in the eighth month of the third year,
Xiāo Dàochéng, acting as Governor of Xúzhōu, was garrisoned at Huái'yīn,
because of Shěn Yōuzhī’s northern expedition,
and was made the rear garrison.
When Yōuzhī returned from the north,
Dàochéng replaced him as Inspector of Nányánzhōu,
garrisoned at Guǎnglíng,
and now he was again ordered to move his garrison to Huái'yīn.
He was garrisoned at Guǎnglíng.
12On Wùyín,
the Zǒngmíngguān was established,
with one Jìjiǔ,
and ten scholars each for Confucianism, Metaphysics, Literature, and History.
In the 15th year of Yuánjiā of Emperor Wén,
the four academies of Confucianism, Metaphysics, Literature, and History were established.
Now, a Jìjiǔ of the Zǒngmíngguān was appointed to oversee them.
觀 (guān),
pronounced gǔ wán.
13Zhēn Kèhán of the Ròurán tribe invaded Wèi.
可 (kè),
pronounced with the entering tone from kān.
汗 (hán),
pronounced hán.
Shàngshū Yòuyíshè Nánpíng Gōng Mùchén said:
“If the imperial carriage personally campaigns,
the capital will be in danger and fear.
It is better to act with caution and hold fast to our defenses.
The barbarians have advanced deep with a detached force;
their supply lines will be cut off,
and they will soon retreat on their own.
If we then send generals to pursue and attack them,
we are sure to defeat them.”
Jǐshìzhōng Zhāng Báizé said:
“These foolish savages
lightly transgress the royal boundaries.
Dù Yù said: ‘Luè
means boundary.’
Máo Huǎng said: ‘Luè
means border.’
They will surely scatter at the sight of our banners;
how can we sit idly and let the enemy escape?
For a sovereign of myriad chariots
to defend himself by merely holding a city
is not how one inspires awe and submission in the Four Barbarians.”
The Wèi ruler followed his advice.
Báizé
was Gǔn’s grandson.
When Wèi Dàowǔ established the state,
Zhāng Gǔn had rendered meritorious service.
The Wèi ruler ordered Jīngzhào Wáng Zǐtuī and others to lead the armies out the western route,
Rènchéng Wáng Yún and others to lead the armies out the eastern route,
Rǔyīn Wáng Tiāncì and others to lead the armies as the vanguard,
Lǒngxī Wáng Yuánhè and others to lead the armies as the rear support,
and Zhènxī Jiāngjūn Lǚ Luóhàn and others to manage the affairs of the capital's defense.
All the generals met the Wèi ruler on the banks of the Nǚshuǐ,
and engaged the Ròurán in battle.
The Ròurán were utterly defeated.
Taking advantage of the victory, they pursued the fleeing enemy,
beheading 50,000,
capturing over 10,000,
and acquiring countless warhorses and equipment.
In nineteen days,
they traveled over 6,000 *lǐ* round trip.
The Nǚshuǐ was renamed Wǔchuān.
According to Wèi annals, Nǚshuǐ should be west of Chángchuān,
northwest of Chìchéng.
The Later Wèi established Wǔchuān Zhèn there.
Suíshū states: Yǔwén Shù
was a native of Wǔchuān, Dàijùn.
Dàijùn
refers to the capital Píngchéng.
The Wèi capital Píngchéng
was called Dàidū.
North of Dàidū,
a series of garrisons were established.
Later, the garrisons were abolished and prefectures were set up,
so Wǔchuān belonged to Dàijùn.
Because the army formation was not orderly,
they were dismissed from office.
On Rénshēn,
they returned to Píngchéng.
At this time,
Wèi officials were not given salaries,
and few could maintain their integrity.
It was previously stated that the Wèi ruler promoted upright officials
and dismissed corrupt ones,
and only then did Wèi's governors and prefects begin to be known for their integrity.
This states that few of Wèi's officials
could maintain their integrity.
This implies that the law was applied in the provinces and prefectures,
but not yet in the imperial court.
少 (shào),
pronounced shī zhǎo.
“If an official receives one sheep or one *hú* of wine from those under his supervision,
he shall die;
those who give shall be judged as accomplices;
if anyone can expose the crimes of officials from Shàngshū downwards,
they shall be given the office of the exposed official, according to its rank.”
Zhāng Báizé advised:
“In ancient Zhōu, even lower-ranking scholars
still had salaries sufficient to substitute for farming.
Mèngzǐ said: ‘The Zhōu dynasty granted ranks and salaries.
Lower-ranking scholars and commoners holding office received the same salary,
a salary sufficient to substitute for their farming.’
To work diligently without reward;
if those who receive gifts are punished physically,
‘receive gifts’ refers to receiving gifts of sheep and wine;
‘punished physically’ refers to having physical punishment inflicted upon them.
朝 (cháo),
pronounced zhí yáo.
I fear that wicked people will spy,
and loyal ministers will become negligent.
If this is the case, to seek ease in administration and peace for the people,
will it not be difficult?”
“I request that we revert to the old laws and regulations,
and continue to issue salaries to reward honest officials.”
The Wèi ruler then abolished the new law.
14Winter,
the tenth month.
On Xīnmǎo,
an imperial edict stated that Shìzǔ had inherited the throne,
and was utterly flawless in upholding the constitution.
This event is recorded in volume 1, year 2.
He was established as Wǔlíng Wáng.
Emperor Xiàowǔ's temple name was Shìzǔ.
The *Kǎoyì* states: The Sòng edition records
“Zhìzàn,”
the *Sònglüè* records
“Zàn,”
and the biographies record
“Zhìsuí.”
According to records, Tàizōng performed divination for all his sons,
and used the resulting hexagram as their courtesy name.
Here, we follow the biographies.
15Previously,
Wèi Yǐhún monopolized power.
This event is recorded in volume 1, years 1 and 2.
The Wèi ruler later regretted this,
and so accused Bái Yào of rebellion,
executing him
and his brother Rúyì.
16 In the beginning,
Wèi (魏) Southern Bộ Shàngshū (南部尚書) Lǐ Fū (李敷),
Yícáo Shàngshū (儀曹尚書) Lǐ Xīn (李訢),
Xiāo Zǐxiǎn (蕭子顯) said: The Wèi (魏) Southern Bộ Shàngshū (南部尚書) was in charge of the southern provinces and commanderies.
The Yícáo Shàngshū (儀曹尚書) presumably managed rites and ceremonies.
According to records, in the early Wèi (魏), there were five Shàngshū (尚書): Diànzhōng (殿中), Yuèbù (樂部), Jiàbù (駕部), Nánbù (南部), and Běibù (北部).
Yícáo (儀曹), Xuǎncáo (選曹) and other Shàngshū (尚書) positions
were established in the middle period.
Xīn (訢),
pronounced Xǔ Jīn (許斤).
Along with Zhōngshū Shìláng (中書侍郎) Lú Dùshì (盧度世), both were favored and trusted by Shìzǔ (世祖) and Xiǎnzǔ (顯祖) for their talent,
participating in confidential matters
and issuing imperial edicts.
Afterwards, Xīn (訢) was appointed as Cìshǐ (刺史) of Xiāngzhōu (相州).
He accepted bribes,
and was accused by someone.
Fū (敷) covered for him.
When Xiǎnzǔ (顯祖) heard of it,
he had Xīn (訢) brought back in a cage cart.
The investigation proved him guilty,
and he was sentenced to death.
At this time, Fū (敷)'s younger brother Yì (奕) was favored by Empress Dowager Féng (馮),
and the Emperor's affection for Fū (敷) had already cooled.
The authorities, following an imperial hint, prompted Xīn (訢) to expose the secret misdeeds of Fū (敷)'s brothers,
promising him a pardon.
Xīn (訢) said to his son-in-law Péi Yōu (裴攸):
"Although my clan and Fū (敷)'s are distantly related,
our bond is like that of brothers by birth.
Now, the officials are urging me to do this.
'Officials'
refers to the authorities,
meaning those in charge of Fū (敷)'s case.
I have repeatedly tried to stab myself with my hairpin,
and strangle myself with my belt,
but I still cannot die.
Moreover, how could I know their secret misdeeds!
What should I do?"
Yōu (攸) said:
"Why die for someone else!
There is a Féng Chǎn (馮闡)
who was previously ruined by Fū (敷),
and his family deeply resents him.
If we question his younger brother,
Fū (敷)'s secret misdeeds can be uncovered."
Xīn (訢) followed this advice.
Also, Fàn Biāo (范檦) of Zhàojùn (趙郡) itemized over thirty charges against Fū (敷)'s brothers.
The authorities reported this to the Emperor.
The Emperor was furious
and executed Fū (敷)'s brothers.
Fàn Biāo (范檦) was the one who accused Lǐ Fū (李敷)'s brothers,
after Empress Dowager Féng (馮) poisoned Zhāng Běn (張本) of Wèi (魏).
Afterwards, it was also Fàn Biāo (范檦) who accused Lǐ Xīn (李訢).
He was whipped, had his hair shaved, and was assigned to penal labor.
Not long after,
he was reinstated as Tàicāng Shàngshū (太倉尚書),
concurrently managing the affairs of the Southern Bộ (南部).
In the middle period of Wèi (魏), the warehouses managed by the Diànzhōng Shàngshū (殿中尚書) were divided,
and a Tàicāng Shàngshū (太倉尚書) was established,
in charge of grain storage.
Jǐ (幾),
pronounced Jū Qǐ (居豈).
Fù (復),
pronounced Fú Yòu (扶又).
He was the son of Shùn (順).
Lǐ Shùn (李順) served Wèi (魏) Tàiwǔ (太武) with his talent but was accused by Cuī Hào (崔浩) and executed.
17 Xīnchéng (新成), Prince Yángpíng (陽平) of Wèi (魏), passed away.
18 In this year,
Lóngxiáng Jiāngjūn (龍驤將軍) Zhōu Shāntú (周山圖) of Yìxīng (義興) was ordered to lead troops to garrison Jiákoǔ (浹口) and suppress Tián Liú (田流),
which he accomplished.
19 The Rouran (柔然) attacked Yútián (于闐).
Yútián (于闐) sent an envoy, Sùmùjiā (素目伽), with a memorial to Wèi (魏) seeking aid.
The Wèi (魏) ruler ordered his high-ranking officials to deliberate on the matter.
They all said:
"Yútián (于闐) is tens of thousands of lì (里) from the capital.
Běishǐ (北史) says: The kingdom of Yútián (于闐) is nine thousand eight hundred lì (里) from Dài (代).
Tián (闐),
pronounced Tú Xián (徒賢),
also Táng Jiàn (堂見).
Shǐ (使),
pronounced Shū Lì (疏吏).
Jiā (伽),
pronounced Qiú Jiā (求迦).
Jǐ (幾),
pronounced Jū Yī (居依).
They cannot besiege cities;
if it were possible to attack,
it would have already fallen.
Even if we wished to send an army,
the situation would make it impossible to reach them in time."
The Wèi (魏) ruler showed the deliberation to the envoy,
who also agreed.
Thereupon, he issued an edict saying:
"Zhen (朕) ought to urgently command all armies to save you from your distress.
However, the vast distance between us
makes it impossible to provide immediate relief.
You should understand this!
Zhen (朕) is now training soldiers and raising troops.
Within one or two years,
I will personally lead mighty generals
to remove your affliction.
You should carefully maintain your defenses and await the grand expedition!"
Punctuation by Niè Chóngqí (聶崇岐), collated by Wáng Chóngwǔ (王崇武)
Edited by Sīmǎ Guāng (司馬光)
by imperial decree
Hòu (後) Xué (學) Tiān (天) Tái (台)
Tàizōng Míng Huángdì (太宗明皇帝) (Part II)
Tàishǐ (泰始) 7th year (Xīnhài (辛亥), 471 CE)
1 In spring,
in the second month,
on the day Wùxū (戊戌),
Jiāozhōu (交州) and Guǎngzhōu (廣州) were divided to establish Yuèzhōu (越州),
with its seat of government at Línzhāng (臨漳).
Liú Xù (劉昫) said: Liánzhōu (廉州) was governed from Hépǔ Xiàn (合浦縣),
which was the territory of Qín (秦)'s Xiàngjùn (象郡).
Wú (吳) renamed it Zhūguān Jùn (珠官郡).
Sòng (宋) divided it to establish Línzhāng Jùn (臨漳郡) and Yuèzhōu (越州),
administering three commanderies,
with its seat here.

Moreover, according to Shěn Yuē (沈約)'s record: Yuèzhōu (越州) administered nine commanderies: Bǎiliáng (百梁), Lóngsū (龍蘇), Yǒngníng (永寧), Yǒngchāng (永昌), Fùchāng (富昌), Nánliú (南流), Línzhāng (臨漳), Hépǔ (合浦), and Sòngshòu (宋壽).
Xiāo Zǐxiǎn (蕭子顯) said: Línzhāng Jùn (臨漳郡) was originally the northern boundary of Hépǔ Jùn (合浦郡).
According to Shěn Yuē (沈約)'s Sòng (宋) Records, it is written as
"Línzhàng" (臨障).
Sòng Bái (宋白)'s Xù Tōngdiǎn (續通典) writes it as
"Línzhàng" (臨瘴),
named for bordering the unhealthy Jiāng (江) river within the region.
Zhàng Jiāng (瘴江)
is also called Hépǔ Jiāng (合浦江).
2 In the beginning,
when the Emperor was a prince,
he was lenient and harmonious, with a good reputation,
and was especially close to Shìzǔ (世祖).
At the beginning of his reign,
many of the faction of Yìjiā (義嘉) were fully pardoned,
Prince Zǐxūn (子勛) of Jìn'ān (晉安) had adopted the reign title Yìjiā (義嘉).
They were treated like old retainers.
But in his later years,
he became increasingly suspicious, cruel, and tyrannical.
He was fond of spirits and gods,
and had many taboos.
In speech and writing,
there were hundreds or thousands of categories of words related to disaster, ruin, misfortune, or mourning, as well as ambiguous terms that were to be avoided.
Anyone who violated these taboos was punished or executed.
He changed
the character "guā" (騧)
to "fú" ([AS-98CA])
because it resembled the character for "huò" (禍) (disaster).
If his attendants displeased him,
they were often disemboweled or chopped up.
At that time, military campaigns were ongoing in Huái (淮) and Sì (泗),
and the imperial treasury was depleted.
All officials, both inside and outside the court,
had their salaries suspended.
Yet, his extravagant spending was excessive.
Every item he ordered to be made
had to have thirty pieces each for the principal, deputy, and second deputy versions.
Favored cronies held power,
and bribery was rampant.
The Emperor had no sons by birth.
He secretly took pregnant concubines of other princes into his palace.
If they gave birth to a boy, he would kill the mother
and have a favored concubine adopt the child as her own.
At this point, he fell ill,
and as the Crown Prince was young and weak,
he deeply feared his younger brothers.
The Governor of Nánxúzhōu, Jìnpínglì Wáng Xiūyòu,
had previously been stationed at Jiānglíng.
He was avaricious and tyrannical without limit.
*Xiūyòu’s posting to Jiānglíng first appears in volume 131, second year.*
剌 [lì],
*pronounced like gē in gēlì, or lì.*
He was kept in Jiànkāng,
and his senior subordinate was sent to manage the affairs of the prefecture.
*Senior subordinate [shàngzuǒ],*
*refers to a chief clerk [chángshǐ] or a military administrator [sīmǎ].*
He had displeased the Emperor on more than one occasion,
and the Emperor had harbored resentment that he could not quell.
Moreover, fearing that he would be difficult to control in the future,
he wished to eliminate him through opportune means.
*To employ strategies and kill him by taking advantage of convenience.*
On *jiǎyín*
Xiūyòu accompanied the Emperor on a pheasant hunt at Yánshān.
*According to Xiūyòu’s biography,*
*Yánshān is south of the city of Jiànkāng.*
*Also according to the Sòng Jì,*
*Yánshān is within the borders of Mòlíng Xiàn, where Shìzǔ Jǐngníng Líng is located.*
射 [shè],
*pronounced like ér in éryì.*
As dusk approached,
the Emperor sent several of his attendants, including Shòu Jìzhī,
to force Xiūyòu to fall from his horse,
then they jointly beat him
and pulled him apart, killing him.
They shouted,
“The Grand General [Piàojì] has fallen from his horse!”
The Emperor feigned surprise
and sent imperial physicians one after another to attend to him.
*Luòyì [絡驛],*
*is the same as luòyì [絡繹].*
Xiūyòu had already died.
His chariot wheels were removed,
and he was carried back to his residence.
He was posthumously granted the title of Sīkōng,
and buried with due ceremony.
In Jiànkāng, a rumor circulated among the people
that the Governor of Jīngzhōu, Bālíng Wáng Xiūròu, possessed the physiognomy of extreme nobility.
The Emperor reported this rumor to him,
and Xiūròu became anxious and fearful.
On *wùwǔ,*
Xiūròu was appointed Governor of Nánxúzhōu, replacing Xiūyòu.
Xiūròu’s trusted generals and subordinates
all believed that if Xiūròu returned to court,
he would certainly not escape misfortune.
Zhōngbīng Cānjūn, Jīngzhào Wáng Jìngxiān, persuaded Xiūròu, saying:
“The present Emperor is critically ill,
and his dying decree states: ‘The illness is very advanced,
it is close to the end.’
*‘The disease progresses daily, and he lingers.’*
*Lǚ Zǔqiān said: ‘A serious illness that greatly advances and is on the verge of death; a disease that worsens daily and then lingers.’*
*Xià Zhuàn said: ‘A serious illness is called bìng. It means a serious illness arrives daily and also lingers in the body, without ever lessening, indicating inevitable death.’*
The scoundrels are agitated,
wishing to eliminate all imperial relatives for their own selfish ends.
Your Highness’s reputation is known throughout the realm,
and if you accept the summons to court,
you will surely go and not return.
Jīngzhōu has over one hundred thousand armed men,
and its territory spans several thousand *lǐ*.
Upward, you can assist the Son of Heaven [tiānzǐ] and eliminate corrupt officials;
downward, you can protect your territory [jìngtǔ] and preserve yourself.
What would that be like, compared to being granted a sword at your residence,
making your servants and concubines weep silently without daring to bury you?”
*Lǚ Xiàng said: Qì [泣] means tears; when tears enter the mouth, it is called yǐn [飲].*
He feigned agreement.
When Jìngxiān left,
Xiūròu had him seized
and reported him to the Emperor, who then executed him.
3 In the third month,
on *xīnyǒu,*
Wèi dispatched Xíng Yòu, acting as Supernumerary Palace Gentleman-in-Waiting [Yuánwài Sànqí Chángshì], to present credentials.
4 The Wèi Emperor ordered Diànzhōng Shàngshū Hú Mòhán to select Western Chìlè tribesmen to be imperial guardsmen [Diànzhōng Wǔshì].
*Wèi Shū, Guānshì Zhì: Tuòbá Lín changed his elder brother’s surname to Gǔgǔ Shì, later changed to Hú Shì.*
*After Wèi Shìzǔ defeated the Rouran, Gāochē and Chìlè all surrendered.*
*Their tribes settled along the frontier. West of Wǔzhōu’s frontier was called the Western part; east was called the Eastern part; those dwelling south of the desert were called the Northern part.*
The masses were angered
and killed Mòhán and Xī Líng, the acting Garrison Commander [Jiǎ Zhènjiàng] of Gāopíng.
*Acting Garrison Commander [jiǎ zhènjiàng] means not yet a true one.*
將 [jiàng],
*pronounced like jì liàng; the same below.*
In the fourth month,
all the Chìlè tribes rebelled.
The Wèi Emperor ordered Rǔyīn Wáng Tiāncì to lead troops to suppress them,
with Gěishì Zhōng Luó Yún as the vanguard.
The Chìlè feigned surrender,
attacked Yún,
and killed him.
Tiāncì barely escaped with his life.
5 After Jìnpínglì Wáng’s death,
Jiàn’ān Wáng Xiūrén became increasingly uneasy.
The Emperor and his favored ministers, such as Yáng Yùncháng, made plans for after his death.
Yùncháng and others also worried that if the Emperor died,
Xiūrén would take power,
and they themselves would not be able to wield exclusive authority,
so they further supported the plan.
The Emperor’s illness had once become extremely severe,
and everyone inside and outside the court looked to Xiūrén,
from the chief scribes downward, all went to the Eastern Prefecture [Dōngfǔ] to visit Xiūrén’s trusted confidants,
making connections in advance.
Those who were on duty and could not leave
were all fearful.
The Emperor heard of this,
and disliked him even more.
In the fifth month,
on *wùwǔ,*
Xiūrén was summoned to an audience.
Afterwards, the Emperor said to him:
“Stay overnight in the lower sub-department of the Secretariat [Shàngshū Xiàshěng] tonight,
and come early tomorrow.”
That night,
he sent someone to deliver medicine and bestow death upon him.
Xiūrén cursed, saying:
“When Your Majesty gained the empire,
whose strength was it?
*This event is recorded in volume 131, first and second years.*
His descendants will be exterminated.

*Emperor Xiàowǔ exterminated his brothers, referring to the killing of Nánpíng Wáng Shuò, Jìnglíng Wáng Dàn, and Hǎilíng Wáng Xiūmào; their descendants were exterminated during the Tàishǐ era, all previously recorded.*
How long can the Sòng dynasty last?!”
The Emperor feared a disturbance,
and despite his illness, rode in his imperial carriage out through the Duānmén gate.
Only after Xiūrén’s death
did he re-enter.
An imperial edict was issued, stating:
“Xiūrén conspired to gather imperial guards [jìnbīng]
and plotted rebellion.
I could not bear to apply the law immediately,
so I issued an edict to admonish him severely.
Xiūrén, ashamed of my grace and fearing punishment,
hastily took his own life.
His two sons may be pardoned,
demoted to Prince of Shǐ’ān Xiàn,
and his son Bóróng is permitted to inherit the enfeoffment.”
The Emperor feared that people would be displeased,
so he issued an edict to all his ministers and regional governors,
stating:
“Xiūrén and Xiūyòu were deeply intimate and closely connected.
Xiūrén said to Xiūyòu: ‘You just act as a sycophant,
this method is enough to keep yourself safe;
I have gained considerable power from this in the past.’
Xiūyòu’s demise
was originally intended to remove a scourge for the people,
but Xiūrén from then on became daily more agitated and fearful.
Whenever I called him to the imperial office,
he would immediately enter and resign to Yáng Tài.
*Yáng Tài was Xiūrén’s birth mother.*
Sometimes he would not come out in cloudy or rainy weather,
and Xiūrén would often say to his attendants:
‘I have gained another day today.’
Xiūrén had already campaigned in the south,
*referring to his southward resistance against the army of Xúnyáng.*
I had been unwell for many days previously,
*‘unwell’ refers to feeling unwell in the body.*
yet he always appeared with a pleasant expression,
treating me with great solicitude and comfort.
His true intentions,
no one could fathom.
The situation was unavoidable,
I deliberated repeatedly,
and had no choice but to make the recent arrangements.
I fear that this may not be immediately understood,
hence I inform you.”
The Emperor and Xiū-Rén had always been close.
Though he killed him,
the Emperor often said to people:
"I was neighbors with Jiàn'ān for many years;
meaning our ages were not far apart.
Between Jǐng-Hé and Tài-Shǐ,
his achievements and sincerity were truly profound.
Due to the urgency of circumstances,
I had no choice but to eliminate him.
The pain and sorrow are so deep,
I cannot control myself."
Then he shed tears uncontrollably.
"Shǎo"
is read "zhào" (翻).
"Shèng"
is read "shēng."
The historians say the Emperor cruelly harmed his relatives,
unable to conceal the wounds to his own nature.
In the beginning,
while the Emperor was still a prince, he was on good terms with Chǔ Yuān due to their refined and simple temperaments.
"Fēng-sù xiāng shàn" means
they were on good terms because of their elegant and unadorned dispositions.
Xiāo Zǐ-Xiǎn's Qí Shū
has "sù"
for
"fēng."
They deeply trusted and relied on each other.
When the Emperor was seriously ill,

In the 20th year, gengyin,

This refers to the old commanderies of Lángyé and Lánlíng,

In the 22nd year, the emperor converted his former residence into Xiānggōng Sì.

1st month,

In the fifth year of Wèi Shìzǔ's Tàipíng Zhēnjūn reign,
Lǐ Bǎo came to court,
and his son Chōng subsequently became noble and prominent in Wèi.
The Grand Empress Dowager, believing herself to have lost her good conduct,
feared people's discussions about her.
When speeches by her subordinates slightly involved suspicion or taboo,
she would immediately have them killed.
However, for her favored attendants,
if they had even a minor fault,
she would surely have them flogged,
sometimes up to a hundred or more strokes;
but she held no grudges,
and soon treated them as before,
or they might even become wealthier and more honored because of it.
Thus, even though her attendants were punished,
they never became disloyal.
6. On the *Yǐhài* day,
Xiāo Dàochéng was promoted to *Shàngshū Zuǒpúshè*,
Liú Bǐng to *Zhōngshūlìng*.
7. Yáng Yùncháng, Ruǎn Tiánfū, and others became increasingly jealous of Jiànwáng Jǐngsù.
(The *Tōngjiàn* states that the calamity began in the previous year of the upper volume.)
(Tián,
pronounced like *tián*.)
*Zhōngbīng Cānjūn* Yuán Qìngyán of Lüèyáng, *Cānjūn* Shěn Yǒng, Zuǒ Xuān, and others plotted a strategy for their own survival.
They sent people back and forth to Jiànkāng,
recruiting men of talent and strength.
*Guānjūn Jiāngjūn* Huáng Huí, *Yóujī Jiāngjūn* Gāo Dàoqìng, *Fǔguó Jiāngjūn* Cáo Xīnzhī, *Qiánjūn Jiāngjūn* Hán Dàoqīng, *Chángshuǐ Xiàowèi* Guō Lánzhī, *Yǔlín Jiān* Yuán Zhīzǔ,
(Under the Hàn dynasty, the system of the Eastern capital had
*Yǔlín Zuǒjiān* and *Yǔlín Yòujiān* commanding the *Yǔlín* cavalry,
subordinate to the *Guānglùxūn*;
by the Jìn dynasty,
the *Yǔlín* belonged to the two guards,
and the *jiān* was not seen in records.
It must have been re-established south of the Yangtze.)
(Guān,
pronounced *gǔwán fān*.)
(Jiào,
pronounced *hùjiào fān*.)
Martial men who were discontented
all rallied to him.
At that time, the Emperor liked to go out alone to roam the countryside.
Xīnzhī plotted to seize Shítóuchéng
and wait for the Emperor to go out to start a rebellion.
Dàoqīng and Lánzhī wanted to persuade Xiāo Dàochéng to seize the Emperor when he went out at night
and welcome Jǐngsù.
If Dàochéng refused,
they would kill him;
Jǐngsù repeatedly ordered them to slow down.
Yáng and Ruǎn vaguely heard about the plot,
and sent the barbarian Zhōu Tiāncì to pretend to join Jǐngsù,
urging him to raise an army.
Jǐngsù knew of this,
beheaded Tiāncì, and sent his head to the court.
In autumn,
in the seventh month,
Zhīzǔ led several hundred men from Jiànkāng to Bēnjīngkǒu,
claiming that the capital had collapsed into chaos
and urging Jǐngsù to enter quickly.
Jǐngsù believed him.
On the *Wùzǐ* day,
he occupied Jīngkǒu and raised an army;
thousands of soldiers and civilians flocked to him.
Yáng and Ruǎn, hearing that Zhīzǔ had rebelled and fled,
immediately ordered preparations.
On the *Jǐchǒu* day,
they dispatched *Xiāoqí Jiāngjūn* Rèn Nóngfū, *Lǐngjūn Jiāngjūn* Huáng Huí, and *Zuǒjūn Jiāngjūn* Lánlíng Lǐ Ānmín to lead the infantry,
and *Yòujūn Jiāngjūn* Zhāng Bǎo to lead the naval forces,
to suppress the rebellion;
on the *Xīnmǎo* day,
they also appointed *Nányùzhōu Cìshǐ* Duàn Fórong as commander-in-chief (*Dūtǒng*).
(The title of *Dūtǒng* began here.)
Thus, Ānmín and Fórong were sent to accompany him.
Dàochéng knew that Huáng Huí was not loyal to him.
He used him to suppress Jǐngsù,
and then to suppress Shěn Yōuzhī.
Once these two difficulties were resolved,
he would then kill him.
This shows that Huí had strategic talent at the time,
and Dàochéng's wisdom and cunning were unmatched at that time.
"If you encounter Jīngkǒu's army on the road,
do not fight."
Dàochéng stationed troops at Xuánwǔhú,
and *Guānjūn Jiāngjūn* Xiāo Zé garrisoned Dōngfǔ.
Shǐ'ānwáng Bóróng
and Dūxiānghóu Bóyóu
were both sons of Jiàn'ānwáng Xiūrén.
Yáng and Ruǎn feared their age
and proclaimed an imperial edict to force them all to commit suicide.
Jǐngsù wanted to block Zhúlǐ to resist the imperial army.
Yuán Qìngyán, Yuán Zhīzǔ, and Shěn Yǒng all said:
"The weather is hot and dry today.
The imperial army has traveled a long distance and is exhausted.
Lure them here,
and wait for them in a state of rest to fight the fatigued.
We can win in one battle."
Yīn Ní and others strongly disagreed,
but could not prevail.
Nóngfū and others arrived
and set fire to the city.
Qìngyán and the others looked at each other,
none having the will to fight;
Jǐngsù originally lacked authority and strategy,
and was flustered, not knowing what to do.
Huáng Huí, pressured by Duàn Fórong,
and seeing the Jīngkǒu army was weak,
did not act.
Zhāng Bǎo anchored at Xīzhǔ.
(Xīzhǔ is west of Jīngkǒu city,
now the Xīzǐn Dùkǒu.)
They united among themselves
and advanced to attack the naval forces.
On the *Jiǎwǔ* day,
Zhāng Bǎo was defeated and died,
but the various generals did not respond to assist him,
and were again defeated by the imperial army.
As the imperial army approached the city walls,
Yǒng first led his troops to flee,
followed by Zhīzǔ,
and the rest of the armies successively retreated.
Only Zuǒ Xuān fought fiercely with the imperial army under Wànsuìlóu;
but his assigned forces were very weak,
and he could not resist and dispersed.
On the *Yǐwèi* day,
Jīngkǒu was captured.
Huáng Huí's army entered first.
Believing he had sworn not to kill any princes,
he yielded Jǐngsù to *Diànzhōng Jiāngjūn* Zhāng Nínú.
Nínú captured Jǐngsù,
beheaded him,
along with his three sons.
His accomplices, Yuán Zhīzǔ and dozens of others, were all executed.
Xiāo Dàochéng released Huáng Huí and Gāo Dàoqìng without punishment,
treating them as before.
(To pacify those who were wavering,
but after the matter was settled, he certainly could not tolerate them.)
The martial law was lifted.
On the *Bǐngshēn* day,
a general amnesty was declared.
Originally,
the barbarians of Bādōng and Jiànpíng rebelled,
and Shěn Yōuzhī sent troops to suppress them.
When Jǐngsù rebelled,
Yōuzhī urgently recalled the troops in the gorges to rush to Jiànkāng.
*Bādōng Tàishǒu* Liú Rǎngbīng and *Jiànpíng Tàishǒu* Liú Dàoxīn suspected Yōuzhī of having ulterior motives,
and ordered their troops to block the gorges,
preventing the army from passing.
Rǎngbīng's son, Tiāncì, was *Jīngzhōu Xīcáo*.
(*Xīcáo* was the *Xīcáo Yuán* in the public offices of Hàn and Jìn.)
Rǎngbīng knew that Jǐngsù had indeed rebelled,
so he laid down his armor and apologized for his error.
Yōuzhī treated him as before.
Liú Dàoxīn stubbornly held Jiànpíng.
Rǎngbīng tried to persuade him, but he would not turn back,
so he and the barbarian-suppressing army attacked and beheaded him.
Shěn Yōuzhī employed Liú Rǎngbīng,
and was ultimately harmed by Rǎngbīng;
Xiāo Dàochéng employed Huáng Huí,
and skillfully used the situation to accomplish his goals.
It is not that employing people is difficult,
but employing power is difficult.
(Shuō,
pronounced *shūruì fān*.)
8. On the *Jiǎchén* day,
the Wèi Emperor posthumously honored his mother, Consort Lǐ, as Empress Sī.
(Consort Lǐ was Lǐ Huì's daughter,
and the mother of Gāozǔ.)
(This was to lay the groundwork for later honoring Lǐ Huì.)
9. In the eighth month,
on the *Dīngmǎo* day,
the Emperor's younger brothers, Huì, was made Prince of Nányáng,
Sōng, Prince of Xīnxīng,
and Xǐ, Prince of Shǐjiàn.
10. On the *Gēngwǔ* day,
*Gěishì Huángmén Shìláng* Ruǎn Tiánfū was appointed *Nányùzhōu Cìshǐ*,
but remained stationed in the capital.
11. In the ninth month,
on the *Wùzǐ* day,
*Xiāoqí Jiāngjūn* Gāo Dàoqìng was given death.
12. In winter,
in the tenth month,
on the *Xīnyǒu* day,
*Lìbù Shàngshū* Wáng Sēngqián was appointed *Shàngshū Zuǒpúshè*.
13. In the eleventh month,
on the *Wùzǐ* day,
Wèi appointed *Tàiwèi* and *Ānlèwáng* Chánglè as *Dìngzhōu Cìshǐ*,
and *Sīkōng* Lǐ Xīn as *Xúzhōu Cìshǐ*.
Emperor Shùn
personal name was Zhǔn,
courtesy name was Zhòngmó.
He was the third son of Emperor Míng,
and his childhood name was Zhīguān;
he was actually the son of Guìyángwáng Xiūfàn.
(According to the rules for posthumous names: "One who is benevolent, harmonious, and universally obeyed is called Shùn.")
The Xiāo family named him Shùn because
he complied with the will of Heaven and the hearts of the people in abdicating the throne.
In the first year of Shēngmíng (Dīngsì, 477 CE):
In the seventh month of this year,
the Emperor ascended the throne,
and first changed the reign title to Shēngmíng.
1 In spring,
the first month,
on the day Yǐyǒu,
Wèi changed its reign title to Tàihé.
2 On the day Jǐyǒu,
Wáng Yuánshòu, a commoner from Luèyáng, gathered over five thousand households
and proclaimed himself Chōngtiān Wáng;
in the second month,
on the day Xīnwèi,
Wèi's Inspector of Qín and Yì two prefectures, Wèi Luòhóu, attacked and defeated them.
Qín and Yì two prefectures
are what Wèi called Nánqín and Dōngyì.
尉 (Wèi)
is pronounced "yū wù fān."
3 In the third month,
on the day Gēngzǐ,
Wèi appointed Dōngyáng Wáng Pī as Sītú.
4 In summer,
the fourth month,
on the day Dīngmǎo,
the Wèi ruler went to Báidēng;
on the day Réngshēn,
he went to Guōshān.
Initially,
Cāngwú Wáng, while in the Eastern Palace,
liked to climb up the lacquered tent poles,
more than a丈 (zhàng) above the ground;
his temper was erratic,
and the principal supervisors could not restrain him.
Principal supervisors
refers to the principal supervisors within the Eastern Palace's fasting chambers.
帥 (shuài)
is pronounced "suǒ lèi fān."
Lady Chén
was Cāngwú Wáng's mother.
Upon his ascension,
she was honored as Tàihòu.
捶 (chuí)
is pronounced "zhǐ ruǐ fān."
Internally fearing the Tàihòu and Tàihòu,
and externally apprehensive of the various high officials,
he did not dare to indulge himself.
After he came of age (literally, put on the cap of adulthood),
the internal and external authorities gradually lost their ability to control him,
and he frequently went out to roam.
When he first left the palace,
he still maintained a formal imperial procession.
Soon, riding in a light carriage,
accompanied by a few close attendants,
he would sometimes go out to the countryside,
or sometimes enter the markets.
The Tàihòu often rode in a blue ox cart;
a blue ox cart
is a blue-canopied ox cart.
According to Jìn regulations,
all princes used blue-canopied carriages.
At that time, an official memorialized
that the Imperial Tàihòu's carriage and attire should follow the precedent of Jìn Xiàowǔ's Empress Lǐ.
Later, he would ride light cavalry far away for ten to twenty lǐ,
and the Tàihòu could no longer chase him;
the imperial procession, also fearing disaster, dared not pursue him,
but merely kept their formation in a separate place,
watching and waiting.
Initially,
Tàizōng had once bestowed Lady Chén upon his favorite, Lǐ Dào'ér,
but later had her brought back,
and she gave birth to the Emperor.
已 (yǐ)
means "already" or "subsequently";
it means she was subsequently brought back.
嬖 (bì)
is pronounced "bēi yì fān,"
and also "bó jì fān."
He called himself
"Liú Tǒng" —
"Liú Tǒng"
means he claimed to rule all under Heaven,
just as Fú Jiān called himself
"Fú Zhào,"
and Huán Xuán called himself
"Huán Zhào" —
and "General Lǐ."
He often wore short trousers and a jacket,
penetrating every camp, office, alley, and street;
sometimes he would spend the night in an inn,
sometimes lie by the roadside during the day,
shoving and pushing servants,
and trading with them;
sometimes he would suffer rudeness and insults,
and receive them with pleasure.
For all base crafts,
such as tailoring clothes or making hats,
he could master them by just observing;
he had never played a chǔ,
but could play a tune once he held the instrument.
韻 (yùn)
means "harmonious" or "concordant."
His arrogance and indulgence were extreme;
there was not a day he did not go out,
leaving in the evening and returning in the morning,
or leaving in the morning and returning in the evening.
His followers all carried spears;
no pedestrians, men or women, or dogs, horses, oxen, or donkeys
who encountered them escaped harm.
The common people were terrified and disturbed;
merchants and vendors all ceased their business,
doors were closed during the day,
and pedestrians almost disappeared.
Needles, awls, chisels, and saws
were never far from his side;
if there was the slightest disagreement,
he would immediately dismember them.
If he did not kill for a day,
he would be dejected and unhappy;
the palace halls and offices were filled with anxiety and dread,
and people could not be assured of their lives.
Ruan Diánfū, along with Zhíhé Jiāngjūn Shēn Bózōng and others,
planned to take advantage of the Emperor's trip to Jiāngchéng to shoot pheasants,
claiming it was a decree from the Tàihòu,
to call the imperial procession back,
close the city gates,
send people to seize and depose the Emperor,
and enthrone Ānchéng Wáng Zhǔn.
When the plot was discovered,
on the day Jiǎxū,
the Emperor arrested and killed Diánfū and the others.
The Tàihòu repeatedly admonished the Emperor,
but the Emperor was displeased.
It happened to be the Duānwǔ Festival,
and the Tàihòu gifted the Emperor a feather fan.
Feather fan
refers to a fan made of feathers.
The "Kǎo Yì" states:
The "Sòng Lüè" simply says "Tàihòu bestowed" (太賜),
now we follow the "Sòng Shū."
He ordered the imperial physician to boil medicine,
intending to poison the Tàihòu.
His attendants stopped him, saying:
"If Your Majesty carries out this deed,
Your Majesty will then have to act as a filial son;
how could Your Majesty still go out and play mischievously?"
The Emperor said:
"Your words make great sense!"
And so, he stopped.
In the sixth month,
on the *jiǎxū* day,
there was an accusation that Sànqí Chángshì Dù Yòuwén (杜幼文), Sītú Zuǒ Chángshǐ Shěn Bó (沈勃), and Yóují Jiāngjūn Sūn Chāozhī (孫超之) were conspiring with Ruǎn Diànfū (阮佃夫).
Dì (帝) personally led his guards,
surrounded the three families,
and executed them all.
Dēng (登),
means *dēngshí* (登時);
*dēngshí* (登時)
is equivalent to saying “immediately.”
Sàn (散),
*xī dàn fān* (悉亶翻).
Qí (騎),
*qí jì fān* (奇寄翻).
Shuài (帥),
read as *lǜ* (率).
The *Kǎoyì* (考異) states: The *Nán Shǐ* (南史) says:
“Xiàowǔ (孝武) had twenty-eight sons.
Tàizōng (太宗) killed sixteen of them,
and the rest were all killed by Dì (帝).”
According to the *Sòng Shū* (宋書),
of Xiàowǔ’s (孝武) sons,
ten died young,
two were killed by Jǐnghé (景和),
and the rest were all killed by Tàizōng (太宗).
None survived until Cāngwú’s (蒼梧) time.
The *Nán Shǐ* (南史) is mistaken.
Even infants were not spared.
Shěn Bó (沈勃) was then observing mourning in a *lú* (廬).
Lú (廬),
refers to an *yǐlú* (倚廬).
According to ritual: one observing mourning
resides in an *yǐlú* (倚廬),
sleeping on straw and pillowing on a clod.
Mèng Kāng (孟康) annotated: *Yǐlú* (倚廬)
is constructed by leaning against a wall to the ground,
without a lintel or pillars.
Kǒng Yǐngdá (孔穎達) said: Residing in an *yǐlú* (倚廬)
means building a hut by leaning wood against the east wall,
outside the central gate.
Another explanation states: Generally, if not the legitimate son,
one resides in a hut in a secluded place from the time before burial.
Zhèng (鄭) annotated: Not wishing to attract attention,
it is usually in the southeast corner.
Dì (帝) brandished his saber and advanced alone.
Bó (勃) knew he could not escape,
and wrestled with Dì’s (帝) ear,
spitting and cursing him, saying:
“Your crimes surpass those of Jié (桀) and Zhòu (紂)!
Your slaughtering will not last long!”
He then died.
On this day,
a great amnesty was declared.
Dì (帝) once directly entered the Lǐngjūn Fǔ (領軍府).
It was very hot at the time,
and Xiāo Dàochéng (蕭道成) was sleeping naked.
Dì (帝) made Dàochéng (道成) stand inside the room,
drew a target on his belly,
drew his bow to full,
intending to shoot him.
Dàochéng (道成) bowed and said:
“Your old servant is innocent.”
His attendant Wáng Tiān'ēn (王天恩) said:
“Lǐngjūn (領軍) has a large belly,
which makes a good shooting target;
Péng (堋),
*bǔ dèng fān* (補隥翻).
Shèpéng (射堋),
is what is now called *shèduǒ* (射垜).
There will be no more shooting later;
why not shoot him with a blunt arrow?”
Dì (帝) then changed to a blunt arrow and shot,
hitting him squarely in the navel.
He threw down his bow and laughed loudly, saying:
“How is this shot!”
Dì (帝) was wary of Dàochéng’s (道成) prestige,
and once personally sharpened a spear,
saying:
“Tomorrow I will kill Xiāo Dàochéng (蕭道成).”
Chén Tài (陳太) scolded him, saying:
“Xiāo Dàochéng (蕭道成) has rendered service to the state.
If you harm him,
who will then exert themselves for you?”
Dì (帝) then stopped.
Dàochéng (道成) was anxious and fearful,
and secretly conspired with Yuán Càn (袁粲) and Chǔ Yuān (褚淵) to depose the emperor and establish a new one.
Càn (粲) said:
“The present emperor is young,
and minor transgressions are easy to correct.
The affairs of Yī (伊) and Huò (霍) are not actions for a degenerate age;
even if successful,
there will ultimately be no safe place.”
Yuān (淵) remained silent.
At this time, Yuān (淵) had already secretly pledged allegiance to Dàochéng (道成).
“Now the imperial court is in chaos,
and people cannot protect themselves;
the hopes of the empire
are not with Yuán (袁) and Chǔ (褚).
How can Mínggōng (明公) sit idly by and be exterminated?
The critical moment of survival or destruction
awaits your careful consideration.”
Dàochéng (道成) agreed with this.
Dàochéng (道成) was then Zhōng Lǐngjūn (中領軍),
and appointed Sēngzhēn (僧真) as Gōngcáo (功曹).
Xī (希),
means *wàng* (望) (hope).
Someone advised Dàochéng (道成) to flee to Guǎnglíng (廣陵) and raise an army.
Dàochéng’s (道成) eldest son, Zé (賾),
was then Jìnxī Wáng Chángshǐ (晉熙王長史),
acting in charge of Yǐngzhōu (郢州) affairs.
Dàochéng (道成) wished to have Zé (賾) lead the Yǐngzhōu (郢州) troops eastward to meet at Jīngkǒu (京口).
Dàochéng (道成) secretly sent his confidant Liú Sēngfù (劉僧副) to inform his cousin Liú Shànmíng (劉善明), who was acting Cǐshǐ (刺史) of Qīng (青) and Jì (冀) provinces,
saying:
“Many people advise me to hold Běigù (北固) and Guǎnglíng (廣陵),
but I fear this is not the best strategy.
Now that autumn winds are about to rise,
if you and Yuán Dōnghǎi (垣東海) can slightly stir up the barbarians,
then all my plans can be established.”
He also informed the Tàishǒu (太守) of Dōnghǎi (東海), Yuán Róngzǔ (垣榮祖).
Shànmíng (善明) said:
“The Sòng (宋) dynasty is about to perish,
which both the foolish and the wise know.
If the northern barbarians move,
it will instead become a problem for you.
Your divine martial prowess is exceptional;
you should simply wait quietly,
and act when the opportunity arises.
Your achievements will naturally be established.
You must not go far from your base
and bring disaster upon yourself.”
Róngzǔ (榮祖) also said:
“The Lǐngfǔ (領府) is a hundred paces from the Tái (臺).
Lǐngfǔ (領府)
refers to the Lǐngjūn Fǔ (領軍府).
Who doesn't know this?
If you travel lightly on a single horse,
and the people of Guǎnglíng (廣陵) close their gates and refuse you,
where will you go?
If you so much as move your foot off the bed now,
I fear someone will immediately knock on the Tái (臺) gate,”
meaning someone will report you.
Jì Sēngzhēn (紀僧真) said:
“Although the emperor is tyrannical,
the state’s foundation, accumulated over generations, is still secure.
You have a hundred family members;
you certainly cannot all cross to the north.
Even if you secure Guǎnglíng (廣陵) city,
the Son of Heaven resides in the deep palace,
issues decrees,
and labels you a rebel.
How will you avoid that?
This is not a foolproof plan.”
Dàochéng’s (道成) cousin, Zhènjūn Chángshǐ Shùnzhī (鎮軍長史順之)
Shùnzhī (順之)
was the father of Xiāo Yǎn (蕭衍).
The *Kǎoyì* (考異) states: In the *Qí Gāodì Jì* (齊高帝紀) and Yáo Sīlián’s (姚思廉) *Liáng Shū Wǔdì Jì* (梁書武帝紀),
from Xiāngguó (相國) Hé (何) to the imperial father, over ten generations,
all have names and official positions.
This is likely the embellishment of the historians,
and is not adopted here.
All agreed:
“The emperor likes to travel alone on the roads;
devising a plan at this point
makes success easy.
Raising an army in an outer province
rarely leads to victory,
and merely causes one’s predecessors to suffer calamity.”
Dàochéng (道成) then stopped.
Lǐ Ānmín (李安民), Sīmǎ (司馬) of Dōng Zhōngláng (東中郎) and acting Jùnshì (郡事) of Kuàijī (會稽) Commandery, wished to support Jiāngxià Wáng Jī (江夏王躋) and raise an army in the east.
In the seventh year of Míng Dì Tàishǐ (明帝泰始), Prince Jī (躋) was made heir to Jiāngxià Wáng Yìgōng (江夏王義恭).
At that time, Jī (躋) was probably Dōng Zhōnglángjiāng (東中郎將),
and Ānmín (安民) was made his Sīmǎ (司馬) and acting Jùnshì (郡事).
Huì (會),
*gōng wài fān* (工外翻).
Xià (夏),
*hù yǎ fān* (戶雅翻).
Jī (躋),

When Dàochéng quelled the Guiyang rebellion,
he was promoted to county duke,
and Zé was made his heir apparent.
Zé,
read Shì Gè fān.
Zhì,
read Zhí Zhī fān.
He appointed Zé as General of the Left Guard,
and they both went down.
Liú Huáizhēn said to Dàochéng:
"Xiàkǒu is a strategic choke point;
it should be entrusted to the right person."
Dàochéng wrote to Zé, saying:
"Since you are entering the court,
you must find someone who possesses both civil and military talents and is agreeable to you,
to whom you can entrust the future affairs."
Zé then recommended Xiè's Sīmǎ, Liǔ Shìlóng, to take his place.
Dàochéng appointed Shìlóng as Grand Administrator to Wǔlíng Wáng Zàn,
acting as Governor of Yǐngzhōu.
As Zé was about to depart,
he said to Shìlóng:
"If Yōuzhī suddenly creates trouble,
burns the boats at Xiàkǒu,
and sails downstream eastward,
he will be unstoppable.
But if Yōuzhī is held back by attacking Yǐngchéng,
he will certainly not be able to conquer it quickly.
You will be within,
and I will be without,
and we are sure to defeat him."
When Yōuzhī raised his army,
Zé traveled to Xúnyáng,
but had not yet received instructions from the court.
The troops wanted to rush to Jiànkāng,
but Zé said:
"Xúnyáng is situated in the middle reaches of the river,
close to the imperial domain.
If we encamp at Pénkǒu,
we can protect the court from within,
support Xiàshǒu from without—
Xiàshǒu
is Xiàkǒu—
and control the southwest.
Our gathering here today
is by Heaven's will."
Some thought Pénkǒu's city was too small to be easily defended,
but Zuǒ Zhōngláng Jiàng Zhōu Shāntú said:
"Now that we occupy the middle reaches,
serving as a strategic support for all directions,
we cannot be deterred by a minor difficulty;
if the hearts of the people are united,
the mountains and rivers themselves are our city walls."
On the day Gēngwǔ,
Zé, accompanying Xiè, garrisoned Pénkǒu;
Zé fully entrusted all affairs to Shāntú.
Shāntú commandeered planks from passing boats to build watchtowers,
and erected a water barricade,
completing everything within ten days.
When Dàochéng heard this,
he joyfully exclaimed:
"Zé is truly my son!"
He appointed Zé as the Western Punitive Commander-in-Chief,
and Zé recommended Shāntú as his deputy.
At that time, the Governor of Jiāngzhōu, Shàolíng Wáng Yǒu, was stationed in Xúnyáng.
Zé believed Xúnyáng city was not secure enough,
and memorialized to move Yǒu to garrison Pénkǒu with him.
Xúnyáng was then governed from Cháisāng;
today, ninety lí southwest of Déhuà in Jiāngzhōu, there is Cháisāngshān.
Pénkǒu is one lí west of Déhuà Xiàn.
Jiāngzhōu was governed from Déhuà,
which was probably near the ancient city of Pénkǒu.
The Governor of Xiāngzhōu, Wáng Yùn, retired from office due to his mother's mourning.
Upon reaching Bālíng,
he formed a deep alliance with Shěn Yōuzhī.
Bālíng is over four hundred lí from Jiānglíng,
so it was likely through messengers that they formed a deep bond.
Yùn passed through Yǐngzhōu,
intending to take advantage of Xiāo Zé's visit to offer condolences to create trouble
and seize Yǐngchéng.
Zé, knowing this,
did not go out.
Upon his return,
when he reached Dōngfǔ,
he again intended to take advantage of Xiāo Dàochéng's visit to offer condolences to create trouble,
but Dàochéng also did not go out.
"To create trouble"
means to kill them.
Nán,
read Nǎi Dàn fān.
The generals Huáng Huí, Rèn Hòubó, Sūn Tánguàn, Wáng Yíxìng, Bǔ Bóxìng, and others were all involved in the conspiracy.
Bóxìng
was the son of Bǔ Tiānyǔ.
Bǔ Tiānyǔ died during the rebellion of the primary culprit, Liú Shào.
When Dàochéng first heard that Yōuzhī had started his rebellion,
he went in person to see Yuán Càn,
but Càn refused to see him.
Tōngzhí Láng Yuán Dá told Càn,
"It is not advisable to show dissent."
Tōngzhí Láng
is Tōngzhí Sànqí Shìláng.
Jìn Wǔdì established Yuánwài Sànqí Shìláng;
in Yuándì's Tàixīng Èrnián,
he made two individuals share the same duties as Sànqí Shìláng,
hence they were called Tōngzhí Sànqí Shìláng.
"If he [Dàochéng] thinks that the lord is young and the times are difficult,
no different from the Guiyang period—
referring to the time when Guìyáng Wáng Xiūfàn rebelled—
what reason do I have to refuse him?
If we were to live together one day,
how could we differ?"
Dàochéng then summoned Chǔ Yuān,
sat with him,
and involved Yuān in every matter.
It turned out just as Yuán Càn had predicted.
He entered and stood guard in the Ménxià Shěng;
a textual critique states: In the Nán Qí Shū,
"Yùn"
is
written as "Tāo";
we now follow the Sòng Shū and Nán Shǐ.
Huáng Huí and the other generals all moved to garrison Xīntíng.
Initially,
Chǔ Yuān was a Guard General.
When he mourned his mother, he resigned from office,
and though the court pressed him,
he did not return.
Càn had always had a great reputation,
and he personally went to persuade him.
Pìshuō
means to advise.
Shuō,
read Shū Ruì fān.
When Càn became Shàngshū Lìng
and mourned his mother,
Yuān's persuasion was earnest and sincere,
but Càn still did not return,
which made Yuān resent him.
Yuān resented Càn
because Càn had thwarted his will and made him fail in his duty as a son.
Yet, by killing Càn to overthrow the Sòng,
he also failed in his duty as a minister.
He lost both loyalty and filial piety.
Dàochéng discussed this with Yuān.
Yuān said:
"The crisis in the west will certainly come to nothing;
you should first prepare internally."
This refers to preparing against Yuán Càn and others.
He intended to inform Yuān;
the crowd said that Yuān and Dàochéng had always been on good terms,
so he should not be informed.
Càn said:
"Although Yuān and he are good friends,
how can there be great differences between them?
If we don't inform him now,
we should remove him once the matter is settled."
He then informed Yuān of the plan.
Yuán Càn still treated Chǔ Yuān with his old intentions.
Dàochéng had also previously heard of their plot
and sent his army commanders Sū Liè, Xuē Yuān, and Tàiyuán Wáng Tiānshēng to lead troops to help Càn defend Shítou.
Xuē Yuān firmly declined,
but Dàochéng insisted,
and Yuān, having no choice,
tearfully bowed and took his leave.
Dàochéng said:
"You are so close to Shítou,
coming and going daily,
why are you so sad,
and why do you refuse?"
Yuān replied:
"I am not sure if you can ensure that Yuán Gōng and I will be one family.
If I go now,
if I side with him, I will betray you;
if I don't, I will immediately suffer disaster.
How can I not be sad?"
Dàochéng said:
"The reason I sent you
is precisely because you can handle matters appropriately on the spot
and spare me worries from the west."
Shítou was west of Táichéng,
hence the saying.
Wèi,
read Yú Wěi fān.
"No need for further words."
Yuān
was the cousin of Āndū.
Dàochéng also appointed Xiāoqí Jiāngjūn Wáng Jìngzé as Zhíhé,
to jointly command the imperial guards with Bóxìng.
Yuán Càn (袁粲) plotted to forge an edict from the Empress Dowager,
ordering Yùn (韞) and Bóxīng (伯興) to lead the palace guards to attack Dào Chéng (道成) in the imperial court,
while Huí (回) and others would lead their subordinates to respond.
Liú Bǐng (劉秉) and Rèn Hòubó (任候伯) all rushed to Shítou (石頭).
They had originally planned to launch on the night of *rénshēn* (壬申),
but Bǐng (秉), flustered and not knowing what to do,
began to pack his bags after the late afternoon (bū) hour;
as he was about to leave,
he drank some soup,
spilled it on his chest,
and his hands trembled uncontrollably.
Before dark,
he loaded his women,
and with his entire household fled to Shítou (石頭),
with several hundred of his retainers,
majestically filling the road.
When he arrived,
he saw Càn (粲).
Càn (粲) exclaimed in surprise,
"Why have you come so suddenly?
We are ruined now!"
Bǐng (秉)'s flight to Shítou (石頭)
meant that the affair was completely exposed,
hence Càn (粲) said they were surely ruined.
Bǐng (秉) said, "To be able to see Your Grace,
what regret could there be in dying ten thousand times!"
Sūn Tánguàn (孫曇瓘) heard of this
and also fled to Shítou (石頭).
Wáng Xùn (王遜), the Assistant of Dānyáng (丹陽), and others ran to inform Dào Chéng (道成),
and the matter was then completely revealed.
Xùn (遜)
was the son of Sēngchuò (僧綽).
Wáng Sēngchuò (王僧綽) wielded power at the end of Yuánjiā (元嘉).
Dào Chéng (道成) secretly sent someone to inform Wáng Jìngzé (王敬則).
At that time, the palace gates had already closed.
Jìngzé (敬則) wanted to open the gates and go out,
but Bǔ Bóxīng (卜伯興) had soldiers standing by in readiness.
Jìngzé (敬則) then sawed through the wall of the house where he was staying to get out,
and went to the Zhōngshū Shěng (中書省) to arrest Yùn (韞).
Yùn (韞) had already *chéngyán* (成嚴).
*Yán* (嚴)
means "to dress up";
*chéngyán* (成嚴)
means that his preparations were complete,
awaiting the appointed time to depart.
Seeing Jìngzé (敬則) arrive suddenly,
he rose in surprise to greet him,
saying,
"How is it that my brother is able to visit tonight?"
Jìngzé (敬則) sternly rebuked him, saying,
"How dare you, young man, act like a rebel!"
Yùn (韞) embraced Jìngzé (敬則),
and Jìngzé (敬則) punched him in the cheek, knocking him to the ground and killing him.
He also killed Bóxīng (伯興).
Bǔ Bóxīng (卜伯興) and his son both died in the rebellion of the Liú (劉) clan.
Jìngzé (敬則) occupied Cāngchéng (倉城) to resist Càn (粲).
Cāngchéng (倉城)
was the Cāngchéng (倉城) of Shítou (石頭).
Càn (粲) sighed, saying,
"The plan has failed!"
He frantically led several hundred of his retainers towards Shítou (石頭).
They had originally planned to open the south gate,
but it was a dark night,
and Xuē Yuān (薛淵) held the gate and shot at them.
Yùn (蘊) thought Càn (粲) had already been defeated,
so he scattered and fled.
Dào Chéng (道成) dispatched the army commander Dài Sēngjìng (戴僧靜) of Kuàijī (會稽) to lead several hundred men towards Shítou (石頭) to assist Liè (烈) and others.
They entered through the Cāngmén (倉門)
and joined forces to attack Càn (粲).
Sūn Tánguàn (孫曇瓘) was fierce and skilled in battle,
and over a hundred of the imperial troops died.
Wáng Tiānshēng (王天生) fought to the death,
thus enabling the standoff to continue.
From the *hài* (亥) hour to the *chǒu* (丑) hour, Dài Sēngjìng (戴僧靜) divided his troops to attack the west gate of the府 (fǔ),
and burned it.
Càn (粲) and Bǐng (秉) were at the east gate of the city.
Seeing the fire,
they wanted to return to the府 (fǔ).
Bǐng (秉) and his two sons, Yǔ (俁) and Gāi (陔), scaled the wall and fled.
Càn (粲) descended from the wall,
lit candles to illuminate himself,
and said to his son Zuì (最),
"I knew from the beginning that a single timber could not stop the collapse of a great mansion,
but I came to this point for the sake of integrity."
Sēngjìng (僧靜) took advantage of the darkness, scaled the wall, and advanced alone.
Zuì (最) sensed an unusual person,
and used his body to shield Càn (粲).
Sēngjìng (僧靜) went straight forward and struck him.
Càn (粲) said to Zuì (最),
"I do not lose a loyal minister,
and you do not lose a filial son!"
Thereupon, father and son both died.
The *Kǎo Yì* (考異) states: The *Nán Shǐ* (南史) says:
"Sēngjìng (僧靜) bravely drew his sword and went straight forward,
intending to cut him down.
His son Zuì (最) cried out,
embraced his father, begging to die first,
and every soldier could not help but shed tears.
Càn (粲) said, 'I do not lose a loyal minister,
and you do not lose a filial son.'
He then asked for a brush to write a memorial, saying, 'Your subject has righteously served the Great Sòng (宋),
and has fulfilled both roles.
Now I shall return my spirit to the tomb,
and forever rest in the mountains.'
Sēngjìng (僧靜) then cut them both down."
This implies that at the time, Sēngjìng (僧靜) caught Càn (粲) unprepared,
and rushed straight forward by himself;
how could he allow Càn (粲) to write a memorial
with such composure!
The *Sòng Shū* (宋書) has no such accounts.
Therefore, it is not adopted here.
A folk rhyme says:
"Alas for Shítouchéng (石頭城)!
Better to die for Yuán Càn (袁粲)
than to live as Chǔ Yuān (褚淵)!"
Liú Bǐng (劉秉) and his sons fled to Éyán Hú (額檐湖).
Xiāo Zǐxiǎn's (蕭子顯) *Qí Shū* (齊書) writes
"Luòyán Hú" (雒檐湖).
*Yán* (檐)
is pronounced *yú lián fān* (余廉翻).
They were killed there.
Rèn Hòubó (任候伯) and others all took boats to Shítou (石頭).
When they arrived,
the imperial army had already gathered,
and they could not enter,
so they galloped back.
Huáng Huí (黃回) had prepared his troops according to the schedule.
At dawn,
he led his subordinates from the imperial road directly to the palace gate to attack Dào Chéng (道成).
Hearing that the plot was exposed,
he dared not act.
Dào Chéng (道成) treated him as before.
Wáng Yùn (王蘊) and Sūn Tánguàn (孫曇瓘) both went into hiding.
Yùn (蘊) was captured first,
and executed.
The rest of Càn (粲)'s faction were not questioned.
Càn (粲)'s clerk Mò Sìzǔ (莫嗣祖) had facilitated the secret plotting between Càn (粲) and Bǐng (秉).
Dào Chéng (道成) summoned and questioned him,
saying,
"Yuán Càn (袁粲) conspired to rebel,
why did you not report it?"
Sìzǔ (嗣祖) replied,
"This humble man is ignorant;
I only know to repay kindness.
How would I dare reveal his great plan!
Now that Duke Yuán (袁公) is dead,
it would be disloyal to seek survival."
Yùn (蘊)'s favorite, Zhāng Chéngbó (張承伯), concealed Yùn (蘊).
Dào Chéng (道成) pardoned and employed them both.
Historians say that Xiāo Dào Chéng (蕭道成) was able to "cherish resentment and record talent."
*Bì* (嬖)
is pronounced *bēi yì fān* (卑義翻)
and also *bó jì fān* (博計翻).
Càn (粲) was simple and plain,
but lacked the talent for governing the world;
he was fond of drinking wine
and enjoyed reciting poetry.
Though holding an important office,
he was unwilling to handle affairs.
When his subordinates frequently came to him for consultation and decision,
*zhǔshì* (主事)
refers to the *zhǔshì* (主事) of the Shàngshū Shěng (尚書省);
each bureau of the Shàngshū (尚書) had its *zhǔshì* (主事).
He would sit idly and recline,
with no miscellaneous guests at his gate,
detached from worldly affairs,
which led to his defeat.
Péi Zǐyě (裴子野) commented: "Yuán Jǐngqiàn (袁景倩)
was the hope of the people and the glory of the nation."
Yuán Càn (袁粲)'s courtesy name was Jǐngqiàn (景倩).
"His wisdom was insufficient to eliminate wickedness,
and his power was insufficient to handle change.
He was desolate and scattered,
in danger but unable to provide support.
When the Nine Tripods (九鼎) had become light
and the Three Powers (三才) were about to change,
within a mere 'bucket-city' (斗城),
*dòuchéng* (斗城)
means the city was as small as a bucket.
He merely clung to the principles of a common man
and lacked the qualities of a pillar."
Péi Zǐyě's (裴子野) commentary
contains the *Chūnqiū* (春秋) spirit of faulting the worthy,
which is why the *Tōngjiàn* (通鑑) adopted it.
a general amnesty was declared.
Wáng Sēngqián (王僧虔), the Shàngshū Púyè (尚書僕射), was appointed Zuǒ Púyè (左僕射).
Wáng Yánzhī (王延之), newly appointed Zhōngshū Lìng (中書令), was appointed Yòu Púyè (右僕射).
Zhāng Dài (張岱), the Dùzhī Shàngshū (度支尚書), was appointed Lìbù Shàngshū (吏部尚書).
Wáng Huàn (王奐), the Lìbù Shàngshū (吏部尚書), was appointed Dānyáng Yǐn (丹楊尹).
Yánzhī (延之)
was the grandson of Yù (裕).
Liú Bǐng’s younger brother, Liú Xiá, served as the Grand Administrator of Wúqùn.
Zhāng Huái (with the radical 王), the Right Chief Clerk of the Minister over the Masses,
was the son of Zhāng Yǒng.
Zhāng Yǒng served the three emperors Wén, Wǔ, and Míng in succession.
Huái (with the radical 王),
pronounced like ‘guī’ in ancient times.
His family was originally prominent and prosperous.
Xiāo Dàochéng ordered Zhāng Huái to seize an opportunity to capture Liú Xiá.
It so happened that Liú Xiá summoned Zhāng Huái to his office.
Zhāng Huái led more than ten of his personal troops directly into the antechamber,
apprehended Liú Xiá,
and beheaded him.
No one in the commandery dared to move.
When Dàochéng heard of it,
he informed Zhāng Huái’s paternal cousin, the Commander of the Army, Zhāng Chōng.
Zhāng Chōng said:
“Zhāng Huái gambled with a hundred lives and
threw the dice, landing a ‘lú’ (the highest throw in a dice game).”
Dàochéng immediately appointed Zhāng Huái as the Grand Administrator of Wúqùn.
Dàochéng moved his encampment to Yuèwǔtáng.
He still entrusted heavy troops to Huáng Huí and sent him westward,
but he assigned his trusted confidants to him.
Assigning confidants
was to guard against Huáng Huí.
Shàng,
pronounced like ‘zhǎng’ at the time.
Fearing that Yíxīng would betray his plans,
in the intercalary month,
on the day Xīnsì,
he arrested Yíxīng on some pretext
and executed him.
All the generals said that Huáng Huí, commanding strong troops, would certainly rebel.
Huán Kāng, the General Who Pacifies the North, requested to go alone to assassinate him.
Dàochéng said:
“Why do you hesitate, gentlemen!
He can do nothing.”
Historians say that Dàochéng’s talent and discernment surpassed all others of his time.
Shěn Yōuzhī dispatched Sūn Tóng and four other generals, staff officers of the central army, with thirty thousand men as the vanguard;
Liú Rǎngbīng and four other generals, staff officers, followed with twenty thousand men.
He also sent Wáng Língxiù and three other generals, staff officers of the central army, to divide their forces and move out from Xiàkǒu
to occupy Lǔshān.
On the day Guǐsì,
Yōuzhī arrived at Xiàkǒu.
The “Kǎo Yì” states:
“Shěn Yuē’s ‘Qí Jì’ says:
‘In the eleventh month,
Yōuzhī finally plotted rebellion.
Zhāng Jìng'ér sent an envoy to Yōuzhī to celebrate the winter solstice.
Yōuzhī called the envoy into a secret chamber and said to him: “By order of the Empress Dowager,
I have received letters from Minister over the Masses Yuán, Liú Dānyáng, and others,
urging me to come down quickly;
you can let Yōngzhōu know this intention.”
He replied to Zhāng Jìng'ér’s letter saying: “A few words,”
and sealed some chicken feathers and peach leaves in the box.
Jìng'ér’s envoy for the winter solstice immediately rode a post-horse to inform the Duke.
On the twelfth day, Rénchén,
Yōuzhī sent Sūn Tóng and others to set off first.
On the seventeenth day, Dīngyǒu,
Zhāng Jìng'ér’s envoy arrived.
On the eighteenth day, Wùxū,
the Duke led his troops into the imperial court for garrison duty.
On the fourteenth day of the intercalary month, Guǐsì,
Yōuzhī arrived at Xiàkǒu.”
Based on this, the Sòng calendar of that year had an intercalary twelfth month beginning on Gēngchén,
and the Wèi calendar had an intercalary eleventh month beginning on Gēngxū.
Thus, the winter solstice must have been on the last day of the eleventh month.
Yōuzhī still kept secrets when facing Zhāng Jìng'ér’s envoy for the winter solstice;
how could he have dispatched troops eastward on the twelfth day?
Moreover,
if Yōuzhī had raised troops in Jiānglíng on the twelfth day,
how could it take him more than sixty days to reach Xiàkǒu?
Furthermore, the “Sòng Shùndì Jì” states:
“In the twelfth month,
Yōuzhī rebelled.
On Dīngmǎo,
the King of Qí entered and guarded the imperial court.”
Dīngmǎo was the eighteenth day of the twelfth month.
“On Guǐsì of the intercalary month,
Yōuzhī besieged Yǐngchéng.”
Yōuzhī’s biography states:
“He rebelled in the eleventh month.
On the twelfth day of the twelfth month,
he sent Sūn Tóng and others eastward. He arrived at Xiàkǒu on the fourteenth day of the intercalary month.”
The “Sòng Lüè” states:
“In the twelfth month,
Shěn Yōuzhī started a rebellion.
On Dīngmǎo,
Xiāo Dàochéng entered and garrisoned the imperial court.
On Guǐsì of the intercalary month,
Yōuzhī’s army reached Yǐngzhōu.”
The “Nán Qí Gāodì Jì” states:
“In the twelfth month,
Yōuzhī raised an army.
On Yǐmǎo,
Grand Ancestor (Gāozǔ) entered and resided in the imperial court.”
Most of these records generally concur,
only the “Qí Jì” is different;
probably the “Qí Jì” is erroneous,
so we do not adopt it.
He showed signs of arrogance.
Considering Yǐngchéng to be weak and small,
not worth attacking,
he said,
“I wish to inquire after the General of the West (Ānxī Jiāngjūn),”
and temporarily anchored at Huángjīnpǔ.
At that time, Wǔlíng Wáng Zàn was probably garrisoning Yǐng as the General of the West.
Huángjīnpǔ is on Yīngwǔzhōu (Parrot Island),
traditionally believed to be named after the Wú general Huáng Gài who once stationed troops there.
“I have received an order from the Empress Dowager
to return to the capital temporarily.
Since you and I are both serving the state,
I presume you understand this intention.”
Liǔ Shìlóng said:
“The eastward expeditionary force
has long been rumored.
Yǐngchéng is a small town,
only capable of defending itself.”
Zōng Yǎnzhi advised Yōuzhī to attack Yǐngchéng;
Zāng Yín believed:
“Although Yǐngchéng has few soldiers, its terrain is treacherous.
The circumstances of attack and defense are different;
it cannot be taken in a matter of days.
If it is not taken promptly,
Mencius said: ‘To attack a state of ten thousand chariots with a state of ten thousand chariots, and conquer it in fifty days.’
The ‘Zhànguó Cè’ says: ‘Bái Qǐ conquered Yān and Yǐng in one battle.’
Jǔ means
to conquer.
Now, by driving straight downstream,
victory can be achieved in a matter of days.
Once the foundation is overturned,
how can Yǐngchéng stand firm by itself!”
Yōuzhī adopted his plan,
intending to leave a detachment to guard Yǐngchéng
and lead the main force eastward himself.

During the Xiàojiàn and Tàishǐ reigns,
the imperial authority operated independently.
But because punishments and governance were tangled and numerous,
it was difficult to understand everything thoroughly.
Thus, those entrusted with the emperor's ears and eyes
were the close attendants.
They would observe the emperor’s joy and displeasure,
and gauge his sorrow and cheerfulness.
Their actions consistently resonated with the emperor’s feelings,
and their every suggestion was without error.
The ruler believed that because they were of humble status and low position,

They did not realize that a rat relies on the altar's prestige,
and a fox borrows a tiger's might.
Shèng, King Jìng of Zhōngshān during the Hàn dynasty, said: "The altar rat is not smoked out

The Empress Dowager praised him for his loyalty
and trusted him even more.
Historians say Empress Fēng used public justice to further her private interests.
10 Sixth month,
on the Dīngyǒu day,
Fǔguó Jiāngjūn Yáng Wénhóng was appointed Běiqínzhōu Cìshǐ and Wǔdū Wáng.
11 On the Gēngzǐ day,
Wèi Huángshū Ruò died.
12 Xiāo Dàochéng noted that since Dàmíng,
both public and private sectors had become extravagant.
Autumn,
eighth month,
he memorialized to abolish the Imperial Treasury (Yùfǔ).
The office of Yùfǔ Lìng
has existed since the Hàn dynasty.
In Hàn, it belonged to the Shǎofǔ;
in Jìn, it belonged to the Guānglùxūn.
According to the Sòng Jì,
in the fourth year of Shìzǔ Dàmíng,
the office of Xìzuò Shǔ Lìng was changed to Zuǒyòu Yùfǔ Lìng.
On the Xīnmǎo day,
he again memorialized to prohibit ostentatious and fraudulent miscellaneous items among the populace,
a total of seventeen articles.
According to Xiāo Zǐxiǎn's Qí Shū,
the memorial prohibited: not to use gold or silver as foil;
horse harnesses not to be plated with gold or silver;
not to weave embroidered skirts;
not to wear brocade shoes on roads;
not to use red for banners, canopies, or clothing;
not to cut colored silk into various flowers;
not to use figured silk for various clothes and decorations;
not to beat deerhide into brocade or use "jújiǎo chēngbǎi chuángyá" (a type of decorated bed frame),
boxes, baskets, or miscellaneous items;
colored silk for screens;
brocade-edged mats;
not to privately make weapons;
not to adorn musical instruments with "qǐbǎo" (seven treasures);
also, various decorative items not to use gold or silver for flowers or beasts;
not to cast gold or bronze into images without authorization: all were promulgated by imperial decree,
a total of seventeen articles.
13 On the Yǐwèi day,
Xiāo Zé was appointed Lǐngjūn Jiāngjūn,
and Xiāo Ní was appointed Jiāngzhōu Cìshǐ.
14 Ninth month,
on the Yǐsì first day of the month,
there was a solar eclipse.
15 Xiāo Dàochéng wished to invite virtuous men of the time to assist in his great endeavor.
At night,
he summoned Piàojì Chángshǐ Xiè Fēi.
Dismissing his attendants, he spoke with him.
For a long time,
Fēi said nothing.
Only two young boys held candles.
Dàochéng feared Fēi found it difficult,
so he took the candles and sent the boys away,
but Fēi still said nothing.
Dàochéng then called for his attendants.
Fēi
was the son of Zhuāng.
Tàiwèi Yòuchángshǐ Wáng Jiǎn understood his intention.
Another day,
he requested a private audience with Dàochéng and said:
"Those whose achievements are too great to be rewarded
are not few throughout history.
With your current position,
do you intend to remain a subject till the end?
Is that possible?"
Dàochéng sternly rebuked him,
yet his demeanor inwardly showed harmony.
Jiǎn then said:
"I have received your special favor,
which is why I utter what is difficult to utter.
Why do you reject it so vehemently?
The Sòng house has lost its virtue;
without you, how could there be peace again?
But human nature is fickle
and cannot last long.
If you hesitate and postpone even a little,
the people's hopes will be lost.
Not only will the great enterprise forever fall,
but even your seven-foot body cannot be preserved."
七尺 (qīchǐ)
refers to one's seven-foot tall body.
"What you say is not without reason."
Jiǎn said:
"Your current title and position
are already those of a regular prime minister.
You should cease paying respects to the Empress Dowager
and subtly hint at a change.
You should first inform Chǔ Gōng of this,
and I request to convey your message."
Dàochéng said:
"I will go myself."
After a few days,
Dàochéng went to Chǔ Yuān's residence himself
and spoke intimately for a long time.
He then said:
"I dreamt I should obtain an official position."
Yuān replied:
"You have just been appointed;
this refers to being promoted to Grand Preceptor (Tàiwèi) or Commander-in-Chief (Dūdū).
Moreover, a propitious dream may not necessarily manifest in the immediate future."
Dàochéng returned
and told Jiǎn.
Jiǎn said:
"Chǔ has not yet grasped the situation."
Jiǎn then initiated the proposal to promote Dàochéng to Grand Preceptor (Tàifù),
granting him the Yellow Axe (Jiǎ Huángyuè),
and ordered Zhōngshū Shèrén Yú Zhěng to draft the imperial edict.
**Dào Chéng**’s trusted aide, **Xiá**, said:
“This is a major matter;
we should report it to Lord **Chǔ**.”
**Dào Chéng** said:
“What if Lord **Chǔ** does not comply?”
“What then?”
**Xiá** said:
“**Yànhuí** cherishes his life and protects his wife and children;
he possesses no extraordinary talent or unique integrity.
I, **Xiá**, can control him.”
**Yuān** indeed offered no objection.
**Chǔ Yuān**’s
courtesy name was **Yànhuí**.
Historians say that as a person, **Chǔ Yuān**
could be easily insulted and belittled by anyone.
On the day of Bǐngwǔ,

an imperial edict promoted **Dào Chéng** to Acting Bearer of the Yellow Axe, Grand Commander of All Military Affairs Inside and Outside the Capital, Grand Tutor, and concurrently Governor of **Yángzhōu**,
with the privileges of wearing swords and shoes into the palace hall,
not needing to hurry when entering court,
and not having his name announced during ceremonies.
His previous titles of Bearer of the Imperial Insignia, Grand Commandant, General of Agile Cavalry, Director of the Imperial Secretariat, and Inspector of **Nán Xúzhōu** remained as before.
**Dào Chéng** firmly declined these special honors.
Wearing swords and shoes into the palace hall, not hurrying when entering court, and not having one's name announced during ceremonies
were all special honors.
16 The Inspector of **Yángzhōu**, Prince **Xiè** of **Jìnxī**, was appointed Minister of Education.
17 On the day of Wùshēn,
Grand Tutor **Dào Chéng** appointed **Xiāo Yìng** as Inspector of **Nán Yǎnzhōu**.
In winter,
the tenth month,
on the day of Dīngchǒu,
**Xiāo Huǎng** was appointed Inspector of **Yùzhōu**.
18 On the day of Jǐmǎo,
**Sūn Tánguàn** was captured
and executed.
During the disaster at **Shítou**,
**Tánguàn** had escaped.
The character "曇" (**tán**)
is pronounced *tán*.
19 **Zhèng Xī**, an Auxiliary Palace Attendant from **Wèi**, came as an envoy.
20 On the day of Rén Yín,
Empress **Xiè Shì** was established.
The Empress
was the granddaughter of **Zhuāng**.
21 In the eleventh month,
on the day of Guǐhài,
**Liú Huǎng**, the Marquis of **Línlǐ**, was executed for conspiracy to rebel,
along with all his confederates.
**Huǎng**
was a cousin's son of **Bǐng**.
The **Shěn Yuē Zhì** states: **Línlǐ** County
was established in the fourth year of **Tàikāng** of Emperor **Jìn Wǔdì**'s reign,
and belonged to **Tiānmén** Commandery.
The character "澧" (**lǐ**)
is pronounced *lǐ*.
22 On the day of Jiǎzǐ,
Prince **Huì** of **Nányáng** was transferred to become Prince of **Suí** Commandery.
23 The **Wèi** Empress Dowager **Féng** resented **Lǐ Huì**, the Prince of **Nánjùn** and Inspector of **Qīngzhōu**.
The mother of Emperor **Gāozǔ**
was **Huì**’s daughter,
hence the resentment.
In the twelfth month,
on the day of Guǐsì,
**Huì**, his wife, and his children and younger brothers were all executed.
The Empress Dowager, due to suspicion and animosity, eradicated over ten families,
but **Huì** had implemented good governance wherever he served,
so the people of **Wèi** particularly mourned and pitied him.
24 **Wáng Sēngqián**, the Director of the Imperial Secretariat, submitted a memorial stating:
“The court’s ritual music
often deviates from proper standards.
During the **Dàmíng** era, the *Gōngxuán* (palace-suspended bells and chimes) were combined with *Pífú* (drum and whisk dance).
The **Jìn Zhì** states: the origin of the *Píwǔ* (drum dance) is not precisely known,
but it was already used in feasts and entertainments during the **Hàn** dynasty.
The *fù* (rhapsodies) composed by **Fù Yì** and **Zhāng Héng**
all describe this.
There were five old songs: one,
‘Virtuous Woman in **Guāndōng**’;
two,
‘In the Second Year of **Zhānghé**’;
three,
‘May Joy Last Long’;
four,
‘Emperor of the Four Directions’;
and five,
‘Sweet Osmanthus Grows Before the Hall’: their lyrics are all lost.
**Wèi** created five new songs.
During the **Tàishǐ** era, new songs were separately composed,
and all their titles were changed.
The *Fúwǔ* (whisk dance) originated in the region east of the **Jiāng** River (**Jiāngzuǒ**),
and was formerly called the **Wúwǔ** (Wú dance).
Upon examining its lyrics,
they are not **Wú** lyrics.
It was also performed in the imperial court.
**Yáng Hóng**’s preface says: ‘Since arriving in **Jiāngnán**, I have seen the *Bái Fúwǔ* (white talisman dance),
or some say *Bái Fújiūwǔ* (white wild duck dance),
and it is said to have existed for several decades.
Examining its meaning,
it is actually about the people of **Wú** suffering from **Sūn Hào**’s tyrannical rule
and longing to belong to **Jìn**.’
Its songs include: ‘White Dove’, ‘Numerous’, ‘Solitary Deer’, ‘Jiéshí’, and ‘Prince of **Huáinán**’, five pieces.
I consider their lyrics to be far superior to those composed by the various lords of **Wèi** and **Jìn**,
but they are excessively sorrowful,
and not the sounds of a well-governed era.
The character ‘縣’ (**xuán**)
is pronounced *xuán*.
The character ‘鞞’ (**pí**)
is the same as ‘鼙’ (**pí**).
I fear it may contradict elegant form.
Furthermore,
the *Qīngshāng* (pure commercial music) of today
actually originated from the **Tóngjué** (Bronze Sparrow Terrace).
The elegant style of the Three Founders (**Sān Zǔ**),
with their lingering melodies filling the ears,
was highly regarded in **Jīng** (the capital) and **Luò** (Luòyáng),
and became even more prized in **Jiāngzuǒ** (the region east of the **Jiāng** River).
Emperor **Wèi Tàizǔ** built the **Tóngjuétái** (Bronze Sparrow Terrace) in **Yè**,
composed *yuèfǔ* (music bureau songs) himself,
and set them to pipes and strings.
Later, the Office of *Qīngshāng* Director was established to manage it,
under the Grand Master of Ceremonies.
The Three Founders
refer to Emperors **Wèi Tàizǔ**, **Gāozǔ**, and **Lièzǔ**.
The **Táng Huìyào** states: ‘Since the **Jìn** dynasty’s migration,
ancient music became dispersed and did not survive.
When **Fú Jiān** destroyed **Liáng**,
he first obtained the *Qīngshāng* music of **Hàn** and **Wèi**,
which was transmitted to the Former and Later **Qín** states.
When Emperor **Sòng Wǔ** pacified **Guānzhōng**,
he collected it and brought it into **Jiāngnán**.
When **Suí** conquered **Chén** and acquired it,
Emperor **Suí Wén** said:
“This is the true sound of **Huáxià**.”’
Then the *Qīngshāng Shǔ* (Office of Pure Commercial Music) was established,
and all of it was collectively called *Qīngyuè* (pure music).
Nothing is closer to this.
However, as sentiments changed and tastes shifted,
it gradually declined.
In just over a decade,
nearly half of it was lost.
The common people competed to create new tunes and miscellaneous songs,
which were excessively complicated and licentious.
It is advisable to command the relevant officials to thoroughly rectify them.”
The court complied.
25 In this year,
**Gāo Yǔn**, Inspector of **Huáizhōu** in **Wèi**, retired to his hometown due to old age and illness.
Soon after, he was again summoned to **Píngchéng** in an "Anché" (comfortable carriage),
and appointed General Who Guards the Army and Supervisor of the Central Secretariat.
He firmly declined,
but was not permitted.
He was allowed to ride his carriage into the palace hall,
and not bow during court audiences.
Punctuated by **Niè Chóngqí**, proofread by **Wáng Chóngwǔ**
